Lourdes: Everything you need to know about Pope Leo XIV's visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
08:02:51 UTC
17:02:51 KST

After spending two days in Paris, Leo XIV is set to land at Tarbes Lourdes Pyrénées airport on Saturday evening. He will then begin his visit to Lourdes with Mass at the Massabielle grotto.
Pope Leo XIV is set to travel to the shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes on Saturday as part of his official visit to France this week.
Nestled in the Pyrenees near the Spanish border, the small town of Lourdes draws millions of pilgrims every year. Here is everything you need to know about the pope's visit, the town, and the shrine.
Leo XIV will be the first pontiff to set foot in Lourdes since Benedict XVI, who visited in September 2008 to mark the 150th anniversary of the Virgin's apparitions to Bernadette Soubirous.
Now one of the world's foremost Catholic pilgrimage sites, Lourdes owes its fame to Soubirous.
A young girl from a modest background, she said she witnessed 18 apparitions of a lady dressed in white in the Massabielle grotto, near Lourdes, between February and July 1858.
Believers say that during the ninth apparition, Bernadette heard the words: "Go and drink at the spring and wash yourself there."
In 1862, the Catholic Church officially recognised that the apparitions were those of the Virgin Mary and later built a shrine on the site. Millions of pilgrims from around the world have since flocked to the Massabielle grotto.
These days, Lourdes welcomes around three million pilgrims a year. According to the town hall, it is the fourth most visited Catholic pilgrimage site in the world, after the Vatican, the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City and the Basilica of Our Lady of Aparecida in Brazil.
Although Lourdes has a population of just 13,000 residents, it has almost 10,000 hotel rooms and around 21,200 beds to accommodate the many visitors.
Finding affordable accommodation during Pope Leo's visit, however, has proved challenging, with huge crowds expected to gather for the event and some hotels charging more than €2,000 euros per night.
According to the latest figures released by the authorities, close to 200,000 people are expected to converge on Lourdes over two days, including around 150,000 who have registered to take part in the celebrations at the shrine.
Leo XIV's visit comes at a time when the number of baptisms in France is rising sharply.
Over the past five years, the number of adults being baptised has risen by 28%, while the number of teenagers baptised has increased by 10%. A total of 21,386 baptisms were recorded in 2026 - more than three times the figure from a decade ago.
After spending two days in Paris, Leo XIV is set to land at Tarbes Lourdes Pyrénées airport on Saturday evening. He will then begin his visit to Lourdes with Mass at the Massabielle grotto.
The pope is also due to hold private talks with seven victims of sexual abuse.
The visit comes at a particularly sensitive time for the Catholic Church in France. In 2021, the Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church estimated that 216,000 minors had been sexually abused by priests or members of religious orders between 1950 and 2020. That figure rose to around 330,000 when laypeople working in Church-related institutions were included.

Purple reins: Philippine export ban casts shadow over UK’s love of ube
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
08:00:30 UTC
17:00:30 KST

In a corner of north London on a weekday morning, Filipino cuisine is thriving: diners at Mama & Sons in Kentish Town are making their choices, and one of the most popular items on the menu is the ube ice-cream sandwich. It’s easy to see the appeal of the light, fluffy bun encasing a purple scoop of ice-cream.
The owner of the cafe, Omar Shah, says ube – a vibrantly purple root vegetable long-beloved in the Philippines – has exploded in popularity in the UK. Just when he thinks it has reached its peak, it becomes “even more popular”. And this year, he says, has been no exception.
The purple yam has found its way into lattes, pastries and desserts, earning comparisons with the global matcha craze. Pret A Manger introduced the Ube Brûlée Iced Latte in May 2025 as a limited-edition summer drink featuring ube’s sweet, nutty flavour. Starbucks and Costa Coffee, two of the world’s largest coffee chains, introduced ube-flavoured drinks this year, marking the yam’s mainstream adoption.
Which is why the Philippines’ ban on fresh ube exports is causing such a stir. A shortage of planting material, coupled with concerns over maintaining control of the crop, has prompted the government to halt the exports.
“We severely lack planting material ourselves, and we don’t want to export it to countries that could use Philippine ube varieties to compete with us,” said the agriculture secretary, Francisco P Tiu Laurel Jr, in a statement.
The export ban will not restrict sales of processed or frozen products, which are the primary ingredients used in the US and Europe.
However, Shah, who also owns London’s oldest Filipino restaurant and five other eateries, says that he cannot get hold of any ube at the moment, although he has enough stock to last a year. “Has the price [of ube] gone up? Yeah, I mean, but it was always up anyway … if it goes up any more it’s going to be considered a luxury product,” he says.
Jonas Salvador, 25, is at the cafe on Thursday and says he likes how experimental ube has become, with lots of “creative takes” on how it can be used. His friend, José James, 22, agrees that “ube is having a moment”. He is from the Philippines “so it’s a taste from home”.
Ube production in the Philippines rose 17% in the first half of this year to 5,660 tonnes, according to the national statistics authority. But Tiu Laurel said the industry was “growing faster than its ability to produce”. The government wanted to expand domestic production before developing ube into a larger export earner, he added.
Guillermo “Ige” Ramos, a food scholar and founder of the Ugnayan Center for Filipino Gastronomy, argues in a position paper that “when global market demand surged, local farmers exhausted their stockpiles of raw tubers to fulfil lucrative international export orders”. He adds that this effectively depleted “the planting stock required for the subsequent agricultural cycle”.
Ramos says: “Ube is not a manufactured colorant or a fleeting aesthetic trend; it is an ancestral root crop whose genetic continuity is under threat.”
Shah says part of ube’s rise in popularity could be attributed to social media and the yam’s striking colour. Jennifer Creevy, content director at the analysis firm WGSN Food & Drink, agrees. She says that, “coupled with its visual appeal”, demand is “very much coming on the back of the matcha effect”.
Shah has been working with ube for a decade, and says supply shortages have occasionally made it difficult to get hold of. He has therefore put controls in place to maintain enough stock to last a year in case supplies become difficult to secure. “If all else fails and we cannot get hold of it, there are so many other ingredients from the Philippines that are versatile and just as delicious,” he says.
One of those is “calamansi”, an ingredient indigenous to the Philippines that he describes as “incredible”, saying that it works particularly well in sorbets and pastries.
Creevy says: “South-east Asian ingredients and flavours will continue to rise, so if brands needed to look for alternatives, there are plenty. Two also from the Philippines [that] we’ve already called out are pandan and calamansi. Both have beautiful colour, and also fall into that gentle experimentation category.”
Omar says his parents, who run London’s oldest Filipino restaurant, have always loved ube.
“It’s always been there. It’s never been a trend for them; it’s just something they’ve had all their life. So to see it outside, it’s nice. To see the flag being flown.”

British firms to train drone AI on Ukrainian combat footage
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:00:22 BST
17:00:22 KST

British defence companies will be allowed to train artificial intelligence models on more than five million annotated frames of Ukrainian battlefield footage under a new UK-Ukraine programme, with the United Kingdom becoming the first international partner to gain access to Ukraine’s Avengers Labs platform, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
Up to 12 British companies will be selected through a Ministry of Defence competition, with their AI models tested and trained inside the secure Avengers Labs environment rather than being given access to download the underlying dataset. The first competition is focused on models for uncrewed systems operating in difficult battlefield conditions, particularly where communications with human operators are unreliable or access to global navigation satellite systems is limited.
The platform is built around more than five million annotated battlefield images, most collected through uncrewed systems and Ukraine’s DELTA combat system. The material is anonymised and delayed before use, and includes imagery of tanks, artillery, air defence systems, infantry and aerial targets such as Shahed-type attack drones and reconnaissance UAVs. Ukraine says the dataset is continually updated as new battlefield material is collected.
A major focus of the UK-Ukraine work will be AI for groups and swarms of uncrewed systems, allowing individual platforms to share information, identify threats and enemy targets and operate with less direct human control. Ukraine said such technology could support missions ranging from logistics to precision targeting, while the first British competition is specifically intended to test how well systems continue functioning when communications or navigation are degraded.
The selection is being led by the UK’s Rapid AI Delivery Task Force, with up to 12 companies whose proposals meet requirements set by the British and Ukrainian defence ministries expected to be chosen within weeks. Access to Avengers Labs will follow once Ukrainian export-control procedures have been completed.
The programme follows an artificial intelligence partnership agreement between the two countries, signed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Ukraine said the arrangement forms part of the wider 100-year partnership between Britain and Ukraine.
More than 30 Ukrainian defence companies are already using Avengers Labs to train their own models, with three products developed through the platform now being used on the battlefield. The Ukrainian Ministry of Defence says AI tools are already reducing the time analysts spend searching photographs and video for enemy targets by as much as 90%.
For British companies, the attraction is access to battlefield data that would be extremely difficult to reproduce through normal exercises or synthetic datasets, while the secure model means the underlying combat material remains inside the Ukrainian system. The result is a way for British developers to test AI against the same communications failures, navigation problems and target-recognition conditions being encountered in the war in Ukraine without taking possession of the raw dataset itself.

EnerVenue, a start-up co-founded by Full Vision Capital, the family office of Hong Kong tycoon Peter Lee Ka-kit, has begun manufacturing a new battery it expects to challenge existing energy-storage technologies dominated by mainland Chinese players, amid surging global demand for green energy.

Ohio steelmaker gets $995M deal for artillery shell steel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:56:29 UTC
16:56:29 KST

- The Defense Logistics Agency awarded Metallus a sole-source contract worth up to $995 million for HF-1 steel used in 155 mm artillery shells.
- The five-year contract runs through Sept. 24, 2031, and covers the U.S. Army, U.S. Marine Corps, U.S. Navy, U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force.
The Defense Logistics Agency has awarded Ohio steelmaker Metallus a contract worth up to $995 million for High Fragmentation 1 steel, the special alloy used to make the bodies of U.S. 155 mm artillery shells, the U.S. Department of War announced.
The five-year, firm-fixed-price contract runs through Sept. 24, 2031, and has no option periods. The U.S. Army, U.S. Marine Corps, U.S. Navy, U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force are listed as the using services. The $995 million figure is a ceiling; the announcement did not say how much steel will be bought or how much will be spent in the first year. Funding will come from fiscal 2025 through 2029 accounts. The Defense Logistics Agency’s contracting office in Columbus, Ohio, is managing the contract.
The agency awarded it without competition under a federal rule that allows sole-source deals to keep a producer available for industrial mobilization or a national emergency.
The steel, known as HF-1, is formulated to break into lethal fragments when a shell explodes. It forms the body of the 155 mm M795 high-explosive round and the M1128 extended-range round, the main artillery shells fired by U.S. howitzers. An M795 weighs about 47 kg (103 pounds) and carries 10.8 kg (23.8 pounds) of TNT or IMX-101 explosive inside its HF-1 casing.
Metallus, formerly TimkenSteel, is based in Canton and has produced HF-1 steel for the U.S. military continuously since 1993. It normally sells the steel as a subcontractor, supplying billets to companies such as General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems, which forge them into shell bodies.
The U.S. Army has spent the past two years expanding Metallus’ output as part of its push to build 100,000 155 mm shells a month. In February 2024, the Army signed an agreement worth up to $99 million with Metallus, funded by Ukraine supplemental appropriations, to raise HF-1 capacity from 1,500 to 6,720 tons a month. It was the first time Metallus had held a prime contract with the U.S. military.
On Aug. 26, the Army and Metallus commissioned a new bloom reheat furnace, a roller furnace and supporting equipment at the company’s Canton facilities. The Army said that at full capacity the plant will make enough HF-1 steel for more than 120,000 155 mm shell bodies a month.
The Army says its ammunition enterprise has opened 16 new facilities over the last two years as part of nearly $6 billion in investments in the defense industrial base.

U.S. Marine Corps buys more anti-ship missile launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:51:19 UTC
16:51:19 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps awarded Kongsberg a contract worth up to $404.4 million for full-rate production of Naval Strike Missile launchers and fire control systems.
- Work will take place in Norway and Pennsylvania through September 2034, with funds obligated only as individual orders are placed.
The U.S. Marine Corps has awarded Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace a contract worth up to $404.4 million for full-rate production and support of Naval Strike Missile launchers and the fire control system that aims them, the U.S. Department of War announced Sept. 25.
The firm-fixed-price contract covers the Naval Strike Missile Launcher Unit, its Weapon Control System and related support equipment. Kongsberg will do 85% of the work in Kongsberg, Norway, and 15% in Johnstown, Pennsylvania, through Sept. 24, 2034. No money was obligated at award. The Marine Corps will fund the work through individual orders as it places them, so the final amount spent depends on how much it buys.
The Marine Corps did not compete the award, citing a federal rule that allows sole-source contracts when only one company can meet the requirement. The Marine Corps’ Portfolio Acquisition Executive at Quantico, Virginia, is managing the contract. The announcement did not say how many launchers or control systems the Marine Corps plans to order.
The Marine Corps fires the Naval Strike Missile from the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, or NMESIS. Each NMESIS launcher carries two missiles on an unmanned, remotely driven version of the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle built by Oshkosh Defense, called ROGUE-Fires. With no crew cab, the vehicle can hide among coastal terrain and move between firing positions while its operators stay out of the target area.
The Naval Strike Missile is a stealthy, sea-skimming anti-ship missile that flies at high subsonic speed and weighs 407 kg (897 pounds). It finds its target with an imaging infrared seeker and an onboard database that lets it pick out the right ship on its own. Kongsberg lists its range as more than 300 km (186 miles). The Marine Corps has described NMESIS as having a striking range of about 185 km (115 miles). Raytheon is Kongsberg’s U.S. production partner, and the U.S. Navy also carries the missile on its warships.
The 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment received the first NMESIS launchers in November 2024. Marines took the system to the Philippines for Balikatan 2025, flying launchers across northern Luzon and the Batanes Islands, and to Okinawa, Japan, that summer for its first training there. During Balikatan 2026, they moved NMESIS by C-130J to the island of Itbayat and landed it by ship on Calayan, both in the Luzon Strait north of the Philippine main islands.
The Marine Corps has made NMESIS its main long-range anti-ship weapon and dropped plans for a ground-launched Tomahawk. Its fiscal 2027 budget request includes 32 NMESIS launchers and 103 Naval Strike Missiles. In May, Oshkosh received a delivery order for more ROGUE-Fires vehicles, due through September 2028. In July, Kongsberg received a $50.3 million modification for launcher missile modules for the program.

Can Israel continue to define its future primarily through security and territorial control? Russian Oligarchs Eye Usmanov and Fridman Precedents to Reclaim Frozen Assets

- Category
- World
Russian Oligarchs Eye Usmanov and Fridman Precedents to Reclaim Frozen Assets
Russian billionaires have begun studying the pathways used by Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman to escape European Union sanctions, Bloomberg reports on September 25.
The lifting of EU restrictions on the two businessmen offered a glimmer of hope to other Russian oligarchs whose assets have been frozen in the West for years, forcing them to limit their travel primarily to Asia and the Middle East.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
However, many of the country's wealthiest individuals see few prospects for a swift end to their isolated status, believing the decisions regarding Usmanov and Fridman stemmed from unique circumstances.
At least two figures interviewed indicated plans to closely examine Fridman’s legal approach as a potential precedent for their own claims.
Emulating Usmanov’s path would require building close relationships with political leaders across Central Asia, the Caucasus, and beyond, noting that leaders from Turkey, Slovakia, and the former Hungarian government actively lobbied on his behalf.
Fridman’s case could serve as a broader practical guide, according to Sergei Glandin, as reported by Bloomberg, a sanction law specialist and partner at the Moscow law firm BGP Litigation.
Glandin noted that investment arbitration offers an effective tool to pressure Western authorities into opening negotiations or lifting restrictions, adding that "the larger the amount of the claim, the faster the process can move."
According to Bloomberg, Fridman previously filed a $16 billion lawsuit against Luxembourg, arguing that freezing his assets breached an investment protection treaty and demanding compensation for damages.
Following France’s intervention for Usmanov, Luxembourg stated its legal position in court had weakened and requested Fridman’s exclusion as well.
Some Russian billionaires reacted to Usmanov and Fridman’s success with dark humor, remarking that they could not find enough European prisoners in sympathetic countries.
Others expressed concern that conditions could worsen for Russian companies still operating in Europe, fearing retaliatory measures from the EU over the damage caused to the bloc's sanction policies by the decisions regarding the two businessmen, Bloomberg reports.
Previously, European Union envoys agreed to exclude billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list while extending restrictions for the remaining 3,000 individuals and entities for three years.
The decision came after Latvia lifted its veto and abstained during a tense negotiation process, avoiding a situation where member states would fail to extend the broader sanctions regime. France and Luxembourg pushed for the removal of the two tycoons, facing resistance until the final stages of the talks, while Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha sharply criticized the move as unjustified.

Storms wreak havoc in Thailand and US, force Ed Sheeran concert cancellations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Severe weather is battering the U.S. East Coast and Thailand. In the United States, a powerful storm reached the East Coast, threatening about 40 million people. On Friday, it struck coastal communities with winds of about 50 mph, causing widespread power outages and flooding. The severe weather also forced the cancellation of an Ed Sheeran concert in Massachusetts.
In Thailand's capital, Bangkok, several areas were flooded after continuous rain that began Thursday. Floodwaters spread across the city, especially in central and eastern districts, causing traffic disruptions and forcing residents to evacuate flooded areas.
Videos circulating online showed inundated roads and cars abandoned by drivers unable to continue. Major canals in Bangkok filled after accumulated rainfall exceeded 20 centimeters, or nearly 8 inches.
Bangkok Gov. Chadchart Sittipunt said city officials were working to drain the water as quickly as possible and that water levels in flooded areas were expected to fall after the rain stopped.
Several shelters were opened for residents forced to evacuate. Parking areas were also set up for vehicles that had been abandoned and removed from flooded roads.
Thailand's Meteorological Department said rain across the country was expected to continue through Sunday. Officials said about 84,000 people had been affected by flooding since Thursday.

One dead, 5 missing after explosion destroys building in Athens
ATHENS, Sept 26 - A woman has died and five people are missing after a residential building collapsed following an explosion in a tourist area of central Athens, a Greek fire brigade official said on Saturday.
The blast on Friday destroyed a two-storey building in Plaka, near some of Athens' most visited sites including the Acropolis and the Temple of Zeus, injuring three people and damaging houses, shops and cars.
Emergency crews assisted by rescue dogs were looking for an elderly couple who lived in one apartment and four tourists who were staying in another. They found the body of a young woman early on Saturday as they removed rubble from the building which was reduced to a mess of twisted metal, broken balconies and hanging concrete slabs, the fire brigade official said.
The tourists - whose nationalities are not confirmed - were expected to check out to catch a flight from Athens airport at 3 p.m. on Friday but they didn't show up, a police official said.
It was not immediately clear what caused the blast in an area which is home to many hotels and short-term rentals. Athens mayor Haris Doukas said on Friday it was likely linked to gas infrastructure. "Something went terribly wrong." REUTERS

Asian Games | China finishes canoe sprint with eight golds, Uzbekistan, South Korea and Japan also medal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:46:45 CST
16:46:45 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- China swept all three canoe sprint events it entered on the final day of competition at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Saturday, capping its campaign with eight gold medals and two silvers.
Racing in rainy conditions, Wang Nan won the women's K1 500 meters in one minute, 55.999 seconds, finishing 1.770 seconds ahead of the Uzbek runner-up.
"I executed the tactics set by my coach very well today, and the whole race was under my control," Wang said.
She added that she had wished for a smooth race while celebrating her birthday a day earlier.
"Now that wish has come true, so I am very happy," she said.
China added two more titles in the mixed doubles events. Wu Shengyue and Ma Yanan won the mixed C2 500m in 1:48.377, ahead of Uzbekistan's Vladlen Denisov and Nilufar Zokirova, who took silver in 1:49.674. Kazakhstan's Sergey Yemelyanov and Rufina Iskakova finished third in 1:51.124.
Denisov was among Uzbekistan's leading performers in the sprint competition, having also taken silver in the men's C1 500m earlier in the Games.
In the mixed K2 500m, Li Chenhao and Zhang Luxi gave China its third gold of the day in 1:39.444. South Korea's Choi Minkyu and Seon Minju took silver in 1:40.349, while Japan's Rin Fukuda and Akihiro Inoue claimed bronze in 1:40.720.
Ma said she had trained with her mixed doubles partner immediately after completing the women's doubles event on Friday because of the differences between the two races.
"I am very satisfied to win my second gold medal at these Asian Games, and it has also given me a lot of confidence," she said.
"We finished with an excellent result of eight golds and two silvers. The eight gold medals have further strengthened the athletes' confidence as they prepare for the Los Angeles Olympics," said Li Xin, deputy team leader of China's canoe sprint squad.
Li said the two silver-medal events showed no clear gap in strength between China and its rivals, adding that the team still needed to
improve their attention to detail in pre-race preparation, mental adjustment and tactical planning through winter training and next season.
Canoe slalom events will begin on Sept. 29. ■

Russian attacks kill 6, injure 45 across Ukraine as Kyiv faces second day of nonstop strikes
Russian attacks killed six people and injured 45 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Sept. 26.
Kyiv has faced a second consecutive day of Russian attacks involving jet-powered drones. By 10 a.m. local time on Sept. 26, air raid alerts had been issued six times in the capital. Five people were injured in Russian attacks across four districts of the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitshchko said.
In Kyiv Oblast, two people were also injured in the Boryspil district, southwest of the capital, Ukraine's Emergency Service said.
read also
Alongside attacks on Kyiv and neighboring regions, Russian forces launched 173 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on Sept. 26, 50 of which were jet-powered, the Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defense intercepted 134 drones. Drone strikes were recorded at 19 locations, while falling debris from downed targets was reported at eight locations, the report read.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed two people in the town of Druzhkivka and injured eight others across the region, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two women were killed and seven others injured in Russian attacks in the city of Zaporizhzhia and Zaporizhzhia district, local authorities said.
In Sumy Oblast, a Russian drone attack killed a 69-year-old man, while Russian guided-bomb strikes injured 10 people, including a 1.5-month-old infant and a 15-year-old boy, local authorities said.
Other Russian drone attacks in the region also injured a 75-year-old man and a 14-year-old girl.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks targeted 35 settlements, killing one person and injuring three others, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks injured four people in the regional center of Kharkiv, as well as a 27-year-old man in the village of Zolochiv, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, four people were injured in Russian attacks in Nikopol district. Two of the injured were hospitalized, one of them in serious condition, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.

"I'm not particularly excited yet. I made some mistakes in my fifth dive, and I need to improve them in the following training," Lu said.

The Chinese pair won by 110.31 points, but Wang said they could still improve their execution, particularly in the final two dives.

The 20-year-old Zheng also has a longer-term goal in mind, hoping to continue developing alongside Wang and eventually compete with him at the Los Angeles Olympics.

the runway tells you where to look: 10 fashion shows that rewrote the catwalk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:45:56 UTC
16:45:56 KST

the path of the runway rewritten
Fashion shows typically begin with a straightforward diagram. Models move along a prescribed path, its edges lined with spectators, and everyone knows where to look. In general this basic layout has remained consistent across time. Yet some of the strongest runway sets begin by disturbing that diagram.
Across four decades, designers and scenographers have buried the catwalk beneath the floor, broken it into a grid, or removed the act of walking all together. In these shows, set design shapes much more than just a decorative backdrop. It determines when a model appears and how long they stay visible. It can even determine whether two viewers sitting a few feet apart experience the same sequence. During this season of fashion weeks, we return to ten examples where the runway itself became part of the choreography.
thierry mugler turns the catwalk into an arena
For Thierry Mugler’s fall 1984 show at Le Zénith in Paris, the runway unfolded through the concert venue like a pair of wings. It was one of the first examples of a runway show dreaming beyond the quiet, standard setup. More than 6,000 people filled the room, including paying members of the public, pushing the fashion show beyond the scale of the usual industry presentation. Models could appear at different points across the extended stage, and the audience watched from a wide field instead of a narrow strip beside the garments.
The plan suited Mugler’s theatrical language, but its effect was spatial first. Distance became part of the show. A figure could register as a silhouette from across the arena before moving closer into view, while the runway reached outward toward spectators instead of holding them along one straight edge. The traditional catwalk had been stretched into something closer to a diagram for a crowd.
Thierry Mugler Fall/Winter 1984, Paris | image © Paul van Riel / HH
maison martin margiela shares the runway with its audience
Maison Martin Margiela’s spring/summer 1990 show, presented in fall 1989, moved fashion onto a playground in Paris’s 20th arrondissement. Local children sat along the dirt paths, then began moving among the models as the show continued. The route never hardened into a polished runway. It remained part of the ground everyone was already occupying.
The photographs are completely changed because of that looseness. Models pass close to seated guests, children enter the frame, and the edge between watcher and participant keeps shifting. The runway becomes shared territory. Instead of a protected corridor cut through an audience, Margiela works with a path that can be crossed, crowded, and briefly taken over.
Martin Margiela Spring/Summer 1990, Paris | image © Jean-Claude Coutausse
viktor & rolf stop the runway entirely
Viktor & Rolf pushed the idea in another direction for their fall 1999 couture collection, Russian Doll. Maggie Rizer stood on a rotating platform while Viktor Horsting and Rolf Snoeren dressed her layer by layer, building the collection onto a single body. There was no procession of models moving past the audience. The audience kept returning its gaze to the same point.
The rotating platform turns the usual relationship between clothing and movement inside out. Rizer stays almost fixed while the silhouette expands around her, and the show advances through accumulation instead of distance. The catwalk has effectively collapsed into a circle a few feet wide.
Viktor & Rolf, Russian Doll, Fall/Winter 1999–2000 | video still
alexander mcqueen turns the gaze back on the room
Alexander McQueen’s spring/summer 2001 show, Voss, begins before a model appears. Guests sit around a huge two-way mirrored box and see their own reflections staring back at them. Once the lights shift, the interior becomes visible from outside, while the models inside remain unable to see the audience.
McQueen takes the separation already built into a runway and makes it physical. The model route is contained inside the box, the spectators stay outside it, and the glass controls who gets to see whom. The audience moves from watching itself to observing bodies that cannot return the gaze. Few runway designs make the mechanics of spectatorship so visible.
Alexander McQueen, Voss, Spring/Summer 2001 | image courtesy Alexander McQueen
prada breaks the front row into a field
For Prada men’s spring/summer 2012, AMO treated seating and catwalk as a single plan. Six hundred guests sat on individual blue foam blocks spaced across a 1.5-by-1.5-meter grid, while models followed several choreographed routes through the gaps. Artificial grass covered the floor, turning the hall into a strangely ordered field.
There is no single runway edge to claim. A model might pass directly beside one spectator, then turn through the grid and move toward another. From above, the set reads almost like graph paper filled with people. At eye level, it creates a sequence of brief encounters. The audience is no longer arranged around the route. It helps form the route.
Prada, Field, Men’s Spring/Summer 2012, set design by OMA / AMO, Prada Fondazione, Milan © OMA | image by Agostino Osio
anya hindmarch hides a spiral beneath the floor
At first glance, Anya Hindmarch’s spring/summer 2017 set looked almost empty. A white circular platform sat in the Royal Horticultural Halls in London. When the show began, the platform lifted to reveal a sunken amphitheater and a spiral path beneath it, with a model ascending through the newly opened center. Above, a circular canopy rotated and tilted as the show progressed.
The surprise works because the runway begins as concealed architecture. Its route appears only once the floor moves, turning an apparently flat stage into a section of ramps and levels. Models circle upward through the space, and spectators read their movement across depth as well as distance. The runway is discovered during the show.
Anya Hindmarch, Circulus, Spring/Summer 2017 | image © Neil Mason
dior puts the runway itself in motion
For Dior Men’s fall 2019 show, Kim Jones replaced the conventional catwalk with a 76-meter moving walkway inside a dark box. The models stood still as the belt carried them past the audience, posed almost like figures in a long moving frieze. Jones linked the format to couture salon presentations, where clothing could be observed on relatively stationary bodies.
It is a small reversal with a strange effect. Walking, usually the basic action of a runway, disappears. The floor controls speed and direction instead, sending each look past the same line of viewers at an even pace. The model becomes stationary and the architecture takes over the choreography.
Dior Men’s, Fall/Winter 2019-2020 | video still
balenciaga winds the audience into a double spiral
Balenciaga’s spring/summer 2020 show filled a 2,000-square-meter room with around 500 seats arranged as an elliptical double spiral. Guests sat in a single row that climbed across five levels, all inside a field of saturated blue conceived in reference to a parliamentary chamber. The corridors created by that seating system became the catwalk.
The spiral removes the easy distinction between runway center and audience edge. Spectators face across the room toward one another, while models wind through the same geometry at changing distances. A person several turns away can enter your sightline long before reaching your section. The show becomes something seen across layers of other spectators.
Balenciaga Spring/Summer 2020, set design by SUB | image © Boris Camaca
dior opens the floor beneath the entire cast
Dior Men’s summer 2024 presentation initially offered a broad field of polished metal tiles. Then 51 panels slid open in a three-by-seventeen grid and the full cast rose from beneath the runway on individual lifts. For a few seconds, the collection appeared all at once across the floor before the models began moving through the show.
The entrance usually sits at the end of a runway, somewhere backstage and outside the audience’s view. Here, every point on the floor becomes an entrance. The first image is spatial as much as sartorial: 51 bodies distributed across a precise grid, each occupying a position that had appeared empty seconds earlier.
Dior Men’s summer 2024, set design by Villa Eugénie | image © Adrien Dirand
willo perron sends chanel across two crossing ramps
For Chanel’s spring/summer 2025 haute couture show, Willo Perron laid two broad curving ramps through the Grand Palais. Together they traced Chanel’s double C into a figure-eight path, with the walkways rising and crossing over one another like bridges. The runway became a continuous loop with models moving through changing heights and directions.
Seen from above, the structure reads immediately as geometry. From a seat beside it, that geometry becomes circulation. One model climbs while another passes through a different section of the curve, and the crossing ramps create views above and across the audience’s usual eye line. Perron turns the catwalk from a strip of floor into a route with elevation and overlap.
Chanel Spring/Summer 2025, set design by Willo Perron | image courtesy Chanel
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

AI generated
GENEVA – The United Nations rights chief warned on Sept 25 of the threat the escalating fighting in Ethiopia poses to civilians, adding that “deeply troubling” internet and telecommunications interruptions were increasing the risks.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) seized local airports and launched attacks into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara this week with the support of local armed groups, saying they were once again in a “full-blown war” with the federal government.
“I am deeply alarmed by the recent escalation in hostilities... and the harmful impacts it is already having on civilians,” said a statement from UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk.
“All parties must urgently de-escalate tensions and avoid a return to full-scale war.”
The UN rights office highlighted reports that airstrikes by the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF), some carried out using drones, had hit five Tigray schools on Sept 22, resulting in deaths and injuries.
“A mortar strike on Sept 23 in Kobo town in Amhara reportedly by the ENDF also resulted in civilian deaths,” it said.
Turk called on the parties to ensure civilians were protected and to allow “safe and unimpeded humanitarian access to all who need it”.
He also criticised the near total disruption of phone networks and the internet, which has raised fears in Tigray of a return to the devastating blockade the northern region experienced during the last civil war.
The 2020-22 conflict was one of the deadliest of recent times, with an estimated death toll of more than 600,000 – when electricity, banking, and almost all aid were cut off.
Turk also deplored an ongoing campaign of “forced mass recruitment of civilians, including children, by TPLF across Tigray”, that included reprisal against anyone resisting recruit – and their families.
Turk also mentioned “disturbing reports of arbitrary conscription by government forces”. AFP

Europe is home to more than 200 languages. The European Union alone has 24 official languages and more than 60 regional or minority languages. On 26 September we celebrate the richness of our many languages and cultures on the European Day of Languages. Language and cultural institutes, associations, universities and schools will take part in a wide range of events across the EU.
Linguistic diversity is part of our identity and our shared European heritage and learning languages helps build bridges between people and cultures. Moreover, multilingualism boosts personal fulfilment, improves job opportunities and encourages active citizenship.
The European Day of Languages is therefore not only about celebrating the linguistic diversity that exists in the EU, but also about highlighting the benefits of learning languages.
This year’s theme ‘languages unite’, focuses on the importance of learning languages in the interests of inclusion, democracy and social cohesion. You can join the celebrations and learn more about how languages shape inclusion by registering and attending our virtual conference on 30 September. You can also join one of the events around EU countries.
The European Day of Languages was launched in 2001 and is celebrated in the EU and beyond. Last year, to mark the 25th anniversary, the Motivation Manifesto was launched, which explains why motivation is so important in the process of learning languages.

The secret behind the Sagrada Familia's final towers: Stone, steel and 21st-century glue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:40:22 UTC
16:40:22 KST

An innovative modular construction system and 24 tonnes of structural adhesive have dramatically accelerated work on Gaudí's Sagrada Familia. More than 140 years after construction began, the Barcelona basilica is reaching one of the defining milestones in its extraordinary history.
Some projects defy the passage of time. And then there is the Sagrada Família. In the heart of Barcelona, Antoni Gaudí's masterpiece has been under construction for more than 140 years. That prospect did not seem to trouble the architect, who was fond of saying, "My client is not in a hurry" — a reference to God.
This year, however, after accidents, delays, a pandemic and countless other setbacks, the basilica could finally emerge from its now-familiar scaffolding.
The moment coincides with two remarkable milestones: the centenary of Gaudí's death, after he was struck by a tram in 1926, and the completion of the Tower of Jesus Christ, which has taken the basilica to a height of 172.5 metres, surpassing Germany's Ulm Minster as the world's tallest church.
Behind that achievement lies one of the most fascinating aspects of the Sagrada Família's construction: the convergence of Gaudí's 19th-century geometric vision with 21st-century engineering and materials science. It is a combination that would surely have fascinated an architect who always knew that future generations would have to complete his greatest work.
Mysticism carved in stone
The Sagrada Familia is not simply something to be seen; it is a building to be experienced and deciphered. Gaudí, a devout Catholic who is in the process of beatification, did not merely design a church; he conceived a Bible in stone, one that speaks through organic forms and layers of symbolism. The building has 12 towers representing the 12 apostles, while its floor plan evokes the body of Christ and each façade depicts different episodes in the life of Jesus, from the Nativity to the Passion.
Look closely at the Passion Façade and you can find a tribute to the Catalan architect himself: his face is immortalised in one of its figures.
Higher up, the depiction of the crucified Christ departs from traditional iconography. Christ appears naked, while his head is replaced by the geometric form of an open book - a striking symbol in a building Gaudí conceived as a "stone catechism", a book through which the faithful could read the Christian story.
Gaudí, who devoted 43 years of his life to the project, used real people as models for his sculptures. During the final 12 years of his life, he devoted himself entirely to the Sagrada Familia, turning down other commissions and seeking private funding. The temple received no public money; its construction was financed by donations from the faithful.
'Star Wars' and the legend of Saint George and the dragon
The temple's blend of Gothic and naturalistic elements - its interior evokes a forest, with coloured light filtering through the stained-glass windows and bathing the columns - has proved so captivating that its influence has even reached popular culture.
The basilica's guides point to a curious connection between Gaudí, Barcelona and 'Star Wars'. According to a story they tell visitors, George Lucas found inspiration for the helmets of his iconic Stormtroopers in the figure of a Roman soldier depicted on the façade.
Another curiosity within the basilica evokes the legend of Saint George and the dragon. Inside, a figure of the saint stands beneath a white structure whose twisting form suggests the body of the dragon.
The basilica's latest milestone, however, is one that has transformed Barcelona's skyline. Last week, Pope Leo XIV visited the city to bless the imposing Tower of Jesus Christ, the central and tallest tower of the Sagrada Familia.
Inside the tower is a striking sight: a glass lamb created by Italian artist Andrea Mastrovito, through which the warm Mediterranean light filters into the space. From 2027, the tower is expected to open to the public, offering a walkable viewing platform at the highest vantage point in the Catalan capital.
A titanic puzzle: stone, steel and invisible chemistry
Gaudí knew that he would not live to complete the monumental work he had envisioned for Barcelona. He therefore left behind models and instructions, trusting future generations to carry on the construction of the Sagrada Familia.
In 1926, at the age of 73, Gaudí was struck by a tram. Contemporary accounts describe how, as he attempted to cross the Gran Via, he avoided one tram only to be hit by another. He died from his injuries a few days later, leaving the project in the hands of his closest collaborators.
Since his death, generations of architects have taken up the challenge of continuing Gaudí's vision while inevitably leaving their own mark on one of the world's most iconic buildings. Among the greatest structural challenges has been the construction of the six central towers: complex, hyperbolic structures designed to withstand wind, seismic forces and immense loads. The most ambitious of them is the Tower of Jesus Christ, crowned by a monumental 17-metre cross.
How has a seemingly endless process been sped up?
The answer lies partly in modern engineering: a structural adhesive developed by Henkel after a decade of research and testing.
Step 1: Modular construction
Instead of placing individual stones hundreds of metres above the ground, the towers were divided into a giant puzzle of 826 modular panels incorporating more than 2,100 stone pieces, which are pre-assembled at the quarry.
Step 2: Bonding stone and steel
To make the stone and steel work together as a single structural unit, engineers apply Loctite EA 9497, a two-component epoxy adhesive developed by German manufacturer Henkel and produced at its factory in Montornès del Vallès. Around 30 kilograms of epoxy resin are used for each panel.
Step 3: Controlled curing
The panels undergo a 24-hour curing process under controlled temperature conditions. As the adhesive cures, it fills the microscopic gaps between the materials, creating a durable bond between the steel and stone.
Step 4: Final lifting
The completed panels were transported to the basilica, lifted into position and assembled level by level with millimetre precision, like building blocks on a monumental scale.
This modular approach has allowed construction to progress up to ten times faster than with traditional methods. According to project manager Begoña Cantera, work completed in barely eight years would have taken between 50 and 60 years using conventional construction techniques. That leap in efficiency has helped bring the central towers to completion in time for the centenary of Gaudí's death.
Designed to withstand time and the city
The structure stands out not only for its architectural complexity, but also for the engineering designed to protect it from the stresses of its urban and coastal environment. In total, 24 tonnes of adhesive have been used in a structure exposed to a demanding combination of environmental conditions:
- Marine environment: located just 2.5 kilometres from the Mediterranean Sea, the basilica is exposed to salt-laden air, which can accelerate the corrosion of steel.
- High humidity: relative humidity levels of between 65% and 75% place additional demands on the materials over time.
- Thermal cycles: temperatures ranging from around 5°C in winter to more than 30°C in summer cause repeated expansion and contraction of the materials.
- Urban vibrations: two metro lines pass beneath the basilica, generating vibrations that must also be taken into account in the structural design.
The resin used in the project is designed to accommodate small movements between the steel and stone without cracking. According to the project team, the bonded structure can withstand loads equivalent to the weight of around 100,000 people per square metre - roughly the combined weight of a capacity crowd at FC Barcelona's stadium. That strength is particularly important for supporting the monumental cross that crowns the Tower of Jesus Christ.
Antoni Gaudí did not live to see his masterpiece completed, but today he rests in the crypt of the basilica to which he devoted the final years of his life.
Gaudí designed the Sagrada Familia with the height of Montjuïc in mind, believing that the work of man should not surpass the work of nature.
Today, at 172.5 metres, the basilica has become the tallest church in the world. It has reached that height not through the construction methods of Gaudí's time alone, but through a combination of his original vision and technologies developed generations after his death.
More than a century later, stone, glass, steel and modern engineering are bringing a project once thought almost impossible closer to completion.

The president thanked Guterres for his positions and sympathy with the Iranian people, saying that during his presidency, the United States had betrayed diplomacy three times, severely damaging Iran’s trust in Washington.
On Iran’s nuclear program, Pezeshkian rejected allegations that Tehran seeks nuclear weapons as an illusion and slander, saying Iran seeks peaceful nuclear knowledge and technology and rejects nuclear weapons.
He also described US and Israeli acts of aggression against Iran as contrary to the UN Charter and international law, calling them war crimes.
Pezeshkian stressed that Iran had not left the negotiating table but said past experiences had left Tehran without trust in Washington. He added that Iran seeks peace and security in the region and would not allow external pressure to force it into submission.
He said Iran does not seek confrontation with regional countries, emphasizing the deep historical and cultural ties among the peoples of the region.
The president said Iran was seeking to localize security in the Persian Gulf and the Middle East and resolve regional issues through cooperation among regional countries, without intervention by extra-regional forces. He added that many problems could be resolved if the United States left the region.

The UN chief said he planned to visit the region the following week and would urge countries to support the diplomatic process and play a constructive role.
He stressed that despite difficult conditions in parts of the region, including Lebanon and Yemen, efforts to find political and diplomatic solutions must continue.

South African women runners arm themselves after string of killings

- The killings sparked national protests, vigils, and demands for government action against gender-based violence, which is declared a national disaster in South Africa.
- Police made three arrests, but public anxiety remains high; President Ramaphosa called the violence a national shame and affirmed women's right to safety.
AI generated
Johannesburg - Before lacing up her running shoes, Nancy Masha checked the knife and pepper spray she carried to protect herself on her daily jog, a ritual born of fear after the murder of a fellow runner sent shock waves across South Africa.
Masha is among those taking extra precautions after nine women, including avid runner Elizabeth Moselakgomo, were found murdered in Johannesburg’s East Rand in two months – some of them partially naked and battered.
“Our runner was brutally killed. I needed a way to protect myself because I am a woman and also a runner,” Masha, 39, who usually runs alone, told AFP.
Moselakgomo, 38, left home on Sept 9 for a run and never returned, leaving behind her eight-year-old daughter.
Her body was found three days later in the same area around Kempton Park where eight others were discovered since mid-July, prompting police to investigate whether a serial killer or killers were responsible, and fuelling anxiety and anger across the country.
Two days after Moselakgomo’s body was found, Masha started carrying pepper spray and a knife on her daily runs.
“Her murder really traumatised me,” the mother-of-two said. “We run in awkward spaces and at awkward times. But I won’t stop running.”
Masha said she had once taken part in a marathon with Moselakgomo, whom she described as “bubbly”.
National disaster
The discovery of the bodies has triggered vigils, protests and solidarity runs across South Africa, drawing hundreds of people from Kempton Park to Cape Town to honour the victims and demand action to protect women.
Gender-based violence remains endemic in South Africa, despite years of government pledges to tackle the problem and its declaration in 2025 as a national disaster.
The government said its 24-hour Gender-Based Violence Command Centre received 6,782 distress calls between Sept 1 and 16, averaging 424 a day, a 21-per cent increase from the same period in August.
The killings have heightened concerns among women already accustomed to taking precautions in their daily lives.
Chulumanco Mahamba, 31, said since Moselakgomo’s death, she has cut back her daily walks to twice a week.
The discovery on Sept 20 in Johannesburg’s Soweto area of another woman – whose body was wrapped in a duvet – made her question her routine.
Mahamba already carried pepper spray as a precaution. Now she avoids secluded routes and shares her live location with loved ones before leaving home.
She also sends photographs of what she is wearing.
“It feels unfair that we have to change our routines, but I do feel safer when I’m carrying pepper spray,” she said.
But not all women feel comfortable carrying a weapon.
“We are not trained to use those things,” said Hlompho Matji, 47, a data analyst and runner.
“It’s also a risk to carry pepper spray because someone could overpower you and use it against you. The same goes for a knife. We don’t know how to use them.”
Babalwa Melitafa, 46, said she did not consider carrying weapons but preferred running only within a gated community’s sports oval.
“I would not run outside the oval alone because of what has happened. I am scared,” she told AFP.
‘We want to live’
Even in Cape Town, some 1,400km away, women said the killings had altered their routines.
Film-maker Andiswa Siwela, 43, a runner and mountain hiker, said the killings had left her more suspicious of strangers.
Siwela said she had always carried her car keys to use as a weapon, but now also takes pepper spray, which she previously left in her car.
“We want to be free. We want to do things without fear; we want to live,” she said.
Nkululeko Molosi, 47, captain of the Sunrise Athletics Club, said runners should not have to “choose between our passion for the sport and our personal safety”.
South African police have so far arrested three people in connection with the Kempton Park killings, which they have not said are linked.
A man is in custody for one of the murders and two women have been charged over another.
But the arrests have done little to ease concerns.
Speaking at a public holiday gathering on Sept 24, President Cyril Ramaphosa said the “pain and suffering that the women of South Africa have been put through stands out as a national shame”.
“The women of South Africa have the right to walk the streets of their country at any hour without fear.” AFP

Powerful new British nuclear attack submarine starts trials
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
08:28:35 BST
16:28:35 KST

HMS Agamemnon, the Royal Navy’s sixth Astute-class attack submarine, has left BAE Systems’ yard at Barrow-in-Furness and entered open water for the first time as it begins sea trials ahead of joining the fleet, according to BAE Systems.
The 7,400-tonne, 97-metre submarine moved through the shipyard’s dock system into the Walney Channel before continuing into the Irish Sea. Agamemnon will now undergo a programme of sea trials before joining HMS Astute, HMS Ambush, HMS Artful, HMS Audacious and HMS Anson in Royal Navy service.
Steve Timms, Managing Director of BAE Systems’ Submarines business, said: “The Astute class submarines are equipped with the latest technologies to silently circumnavigate the globe without surfacing, whilst fulfilling a range of tactical roles for the Royal Navy.
“The departure of HMS Agamemnon, the sixth of seven such submarines that we are building here in Barrow, demonstrates the growing momentum underpinning our submarines business and is a proud moment for everyone involved across the UK’s submarine enterprise.”
First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said Agamemnon would move to HMNB Clyde after sea trials and join the Royal Navy’s operational submarine force. He said: “In an increasingly dangerous world, sea power remains fundamental to keeping our country and people safe. Our submarine fleet is essential to that effort, which is why I am delighted that HMS Agamemnon, the sixth of our Astute-class submarines, has now begun sea trials and will soon arrive at HMNB Clyde to join the fleet.
“She embodies the best of British engineering and the professionalism of our submariners and will be one of the most advanced submarines ever operated by the Royal Navy.
“As we continue to strengthen our warfighting readiness, HMS Agamemnon will play a central role in keeping the United Kingdom safe, contributing to NATO’s collective defence and ensuring we are ready to lead, fight and win.”
Work is meanwhile continuing on Achilles, the seventh and final Astute-class submarine, which BAE Systems said is at an advanced stage of construction. The Barrow yard is also building all four Dreadnought-class ballistic missile submarines which will replace the Royal Navy’s Vanguard-class boats carrying the UK’s nuclear deterrent.
BAE Systems is also carrying out early design and concept work on SSN-AUKUS, the next generation of nuclear-powered attack submarines intended eventually to replace the Astute class. The company and the wider Defence Nuclear Enterprise are expanding infrastructure, technology and workforce capacity at Barrow to support the overlapping Astute, Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS programmes.

Are you in pain?  In some cases, exercising may be as good as painkillers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:22:13 UTC
16:22:13 KST

From pilates to tai chi, even modest amounts of exercise can relieve pain as effectively as common pain medicines, opening the door to holistic therapeutic approaches, according to a new study.
Whether you often suffer from migraines, period cramps or chronic pain, exercise could help ease the symptoms in a similar way to common painkillers.
Across a wide range of conditions, exercise can significantly reduce acute and chronic pain, a new study by Adelaide University has found after analysing 157 systematic reviews encompassing 2,736 randomised controlled trials and over 220,000 participants.
“At a time when we’re looking for safe and effective ways to manage pain beyond medication, these findings provide strong evidence for making exercise a more routine part of pain care,” said Carol Maher, senior researcher at Adelaide University.
The researchers examined how the type, intensity and duration of exercise influenced pain relief.
Overall, exercise reduced pain by around 1.1 points on a zero-to-10 scale – a reduction roughly 60% larger than the average relief reported for common medications in separate chronic pain trials.
Low-intensity exercise produced greater pain relief than moderate-to-vigorous activity and shorter programs, of around 12 weeks, showed larger effects than longer ones.
“Importantly, we found that more exercise wasn’t necessarily better. In fact, shorter-duration and lower-intensity programs showed greater reductions in pain, suggesting people may not need to exercise harder or for longer to experience meaningful benefits,” said lead researcher Ben Singh.
Programmes under 120 minutes per week were more effective than higher weekly-duration ones that can feel unattainable for people living with chronic pain, the researchers wrote.
“When we exercise, our body releases chemicals including endorphins and serotonin that can help reduce how strongly we feel pain and increase our pain tolerance,” said Singh, adding that exercising helps calm inflammation and change the way the brain responds to pain, while also improving mood.
Despite these findings, the study noted that exercise remains underused as a treatment for pain: it is not yet routine practice and is rarely prescribed with the same precision as medication.
“Instead, people experiencing pain may be told to ‘stay active’, rather than being given a specific, evidence-based exercise program that considers what type of exercise to do, how hard to work and for how long,” added Singh.
Healthcare providers need definitive guidance, not just whether exercise helps, but which exercises work for which patients, and how to prescribe them effectively, the authors added.
Yet, they warn that exercise should not be considered a universal solution or expected to eliminate pain, as its effects depend on individual factors such as the condition causing the pain, a person's level of fitness, and adherence to the programme.

NATO deputy supreme commander: If we must attack to defend, that's what we'll do
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:20:00 UTC
16:20:00 KST

NATO deputy supreme commander: If we must attack to defend, that's what we'll do
NATO would strike targets on another country's territory if needed to defend its members, NATO's top commander in Europe, Air Chief Marshal Sir Johnny Stringer told Postimees.
In an interview with the paper during the ongoing Estonian Defense Week, Stringer, Deputy Supreme Allied Command Europe (DSACEUR), said although NATO is a defensive alliance, "sometimes to defend, you have to attack."
The commander declined to put any timeline on a possible Russian attack, saying he would not "get drawn into discussions about whether we are talking about months or years."
He did say large-scale attacks would give NATO "indicators and warnings," though smaller operations can be organized more quickly and require constant readiness.
Stringer said NATO has spent several years developing deterrence and defense plans for the Euro-Atlantic area, with close attention paid to defending the three Baltic states.
Asked whether deep strikes against Russia would be needed, he said that if NATO found itself in a military conflict, attacking targets to ensure the security of European countries "is what we would do."
He said the course of what Russia called a three-day special operation, now in its fourth and a half year, "has not gone very well for Mr Putin."
On hybrid threats below the Article 5 collective defense threshold, the commander said NATO's military response is only one part of a wider collective response, with member states able to impose sanctions and expel diplomats.
Stringer said he was NATO's air and missile defense commander when the alliance shot down its first drones over Poland last September, and that rules of engagement and authorization are clearly defined.
Stringer noted NATO has since developed its approach further in response to a changed threat, adding: "You will see a new approach, although I cannot go into the details of it."

Tracked storks from northern Türkiye reach Egypt, Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:17:28 UTC
16:17:28 KST

Migratory white storks stand resting inside their large, stick-built nest positioned securely on top of a tall wooden pole against a partly cloudy sky. (AA photo)
Two storks tracked with satellite transmitters from Türkiye’s northern province of Sinop reached Egypt and a third arrived in Syria as part of a multi-agency conservation project mapping migration routes.
The birds began their journeys in August. A stork departing on Aug. 27 traveled 650 kilometers to reach the Syrian city of Aleppo. The other two, leaving on Aug. 11 and Aug. 17, flew 1,500 and 1,200 kilometers respectively to Egypt, where they are currently resting to feed and regain strength.
The Agriculture and Forestry Ministry’s Nature Conservation and National Parks General Directorate attached the devices to three chicks hatched this year in the Cuma Plain. The effort falls under a population monitoring project launched in 2022 led by Sinop University. The project features contributions from Ondokuz Mayıs University, Ankara University and Saraydüzü Mehmet Akif Ersoy Anatolian High School.
Nature Conservation and National Parks 10th Regional Director Ali Bozkurt said his directorate has made significant contributions to the 5-year project, tracking the birds daily to gather vital information on their movements.
“We will be able to instantly see what routes our storks take, how long they stay and where they stop,” he said. “We will have obtained important data on this subject.”
Türkiye serves as a primary transit corridor for migratory birds traveling between Europe and Africa each year, with millions of birds passing over the Anatolian peninsula. Storks typically migrate south in late summer to escape plunging temperatures and find abundant food sources before returning in the spring to breed. Tracking helps officials protect habitats across international borders.

Egyptian intelligence chief visited Israel days before Oct. 7 to issue security warning - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:17:18 UTC
16:17:18 KST

Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel secretly visited Israel just 11 days before the October 7 attack and delivered a warning that Hamas was preparing for a significant attack and that time to prevent further escalation was running out, an investigation by The Atlantic revealed on Saturday.
The investigation found that on September 26, 2023, as senior Israeli officials gathered in Jerusalem to mark the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War, a chartered Cessna aircraft linked to Egyptian intelligence services landed at Ben-Gurion Airport. The aircraft stopped in an isolated area of the airport used, the report said, for sensitive diplomatic and security missions.
On board was Kamel, who at the time served as head of Egypt’s General Intelligence Service and was one of the closest figures to Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. The aircraft reportedly remained in Israel for only 67 minutes before returning to Cairo, with The Atlantic saying that the timing appears in Israel Airports Authority flight logs and is also documented by independent flight-tracking services.
Israeli, Arab, American and European officials briefed after October 7 on the visit said Kamel warned that Hamas appeared to be preparing for a major attack, the report mentioned, adding that he urged Israel to take economic steps to reduce tensions in the Gaza Strip. A former Israeli official briefed on the meeting described the Egyptian message this way: “If you don’t change course, Gaza is going to explode in your face.”
The warning did not include a specific attack plan
The investigation noted that Kamel did not provide a date for a possible attack, identify targets, or share concrete details about the nature of the threat. It remains unclear who exactly he met with during his hour-long visit to Israel.
At the time, most warnings focused on the possibility of escalation, rocket fire, or renewed violence in Gaza, rather than the coordinated, multi-front assault Hamas carried out on October 7.
Despite this, officials from seven countries who spoke with The Atlantic argued that the fact that the head of Egyptian intelligence personally traveled to Israel for such a short and urgent visit should have drawn the attention of Israel’s political and security leadership.
“The messenger was the message,” a former Israeli official said, adding that no scenario existed in which senior Israeli officials met with the head of Egyptian intelligence without Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu being aware of it.
An Egyptian official told The Atlantic that Kamel’s brief visit to Israel indicated that Sisi believed he needed to travel personally to deliver the message.
Egyptian warnings continued until days before the attack
Several days after the October 7 attack, the Prime Minister’s Office rejected reports that Egypt had issued a warning before the attack. It said at the time that Netanyahu “has not spoken or met with the head of Egyptian intelligence since the establishment of the government, neither directly nor indirectly.”
The Atlantic said Netanyahu’s and Sisi’s offices did not respond to inquiries regarding the newly revealed details about Kamel’s visit. Tzachi Hanegbi, who served at the time as head of the National Security Council, told the magazine this week that Kamel did not visit Israel and that no Egyptian warning was delivered.
Israeli, Egyptian and American officials said Egyptian warnings continued until two days before the attack. On October 5, Egypt sent another message to Israel warning that the situation could not continue and expressing urgency over the possibility of an attack. That message also did not include a date or method of operation.
The investigation noted that on the same day Kamel landed in Israel, Netanyahu attended a ceremony marking the anniversary of the Yom Kippur War. In his speech, he referred to the intelligence failure of 1973 and said Israel does not take any threat lightly. His public schedule showed that he later attended a classified briefing that day.

Six takeaways from a turbulent week of United Nations diplomacy - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:17:18 UTC
16:17:18 KST

Limousines whisked world leaders away from the United Nations on Friday after a week of speeches, meetings, and hallway diplomacy.
While they reached no breakthroughs on the world's most intractable conflicts, talks on the Iran and Ukraine wars inched forward, and global powers used the venue to debate AI risks with industry leaders.
Here are the big takeaways from scores of panels, hundreds of meetings, hours spent in lines and listening to speeches – and countless cups of coffee:
Reboot of US-Iran diplomacy
The UN was probably most useful for facilitating the first shuttle talks between American and Iranian officials since the collapse of a ceasefire in July. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators.
The efforts must continue, a senior Iranian official told Reuters, even as Iranian and American leaders exchanged sharp words at the General Assembly hall, with the US threatening to "annihilate" Iran and Iran accusing the US of a "bullying mentality."
The senior Iranian official said Tehran was reviewing Washington's response to its proposals, which include lifting a US naval blockade on Iranian ports and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
But no agreement appeared imminent. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio cautioned that a deal would involve hard work over time.
Ukraine, grain, and energy
Rubio also held talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, after which he said Ukraine and Russia had both voiced an interest in a limited ceasefire involving grain and energy-related targets.
Ukraine and its allies are racing to secure limited agreements on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping before winter, fearing renewed Russian strikes on power and heating facilities.
But hours after Rubio spoke on Wednesday, Lavrov addressed the Security Council meeting on Ukraine, showing no indication Russia was prepared to engage on any subject. "Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause, and it wants to use it to pump the Kyiv regime with weapons," Lavrov said.
AI steals climate change's spotlight
Climate change - a focus of UN discussions in recent years - was largely pushed aside by debate over artificial intelligence.
The festival of diplomacy coincided with an unprecedented outpouring of concern around AI after several safety breaches, and as top researchers warned it could destroy humanity.
The UN convened a Security Council meeting featuring OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who made an appearance in person, as well as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. The industry leaders appealed for governments to work together to manage AI.
Underscoring the concerns, just as they spoke, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that an AI agent developed by OpenAI infiltrated an Australian government website in June, accessing public and non-public files.
US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed AI risks as a "hoax" and "sick conspiracy," told the UN he "rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control" AI, describing it as amazing while promising the US would be careful.
Surprise arrival of Venezuela's interim president
The biggest surprise arrival at the UN was Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who used her trip to hold first in-person talks with Trump since coming to power after US forces grabbed then-President Nicolas Maduro in a dramatic nighttime raid.
The Venezuelan delegation's focus was on restructuring its billions of dollars in sovereign debt as it met US officials, multilateral lenders and companies.
Trump used his speech to the body dedicated to global peace to declare that in Venezuela: "to the victor belong the spoils," and called an oil deal the US signed with Caracas last month "perhaps the biggest deal ever made."
As Rodriguez and Trump met in New York, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado made three unsuccessful bids to return to her country.
Surprise absence of Sudanese army chief
The biggest surprise absence was the Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. The US withheld his visa in a move that Sudanese and other sources said was linked to a US-backed ceasefire proposal that Khartoum has resisted.
The dispute, first reported by Reuters, threatened to deepen tensions between Washington and Sudan's army at a critical moment in the civil war, which the UN calls the world's largest humanitarian crisis.
Burhan had represented Sudan at the General Assembly since the coup. Another notable absentee was Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, who addressed delegates by video and condemned US curbs on the Palestinian mission's access to the UN.
UN's future uncertain as funding crisis continues
The cash-strapped United Nations may no longer be in "freefall," but it remains stuck in an "open-ended crisis," International Crisis Group analyst Richard Gowan said. The organization is grappling with shrinking budgets, waning influence and mounting geopolitical conflicts.
Wars in Ukraine and Iran rage on, while Trump has denounced the 193-member body as bloated and globalist, slashed US funding and withdrawn from dozens of UN agencies.
As UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres received a standing ovation after his final General Assembly speech, a small group of politicians and former UN officials lobbied publicly and behind closed doors to succeed him. His second five-year term ends on December 31, leaving little time for the world's major powers to agree on a replacement.
The race, conducted according to an arcane multi-step process involving "straw polls," has no clear frontrunner, but former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan and Guyana's UN Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett are leading the pack.
Whoever gets the world's most difficult job will inherit an organization buffeted by crises, low morale, and declining political relevance. That person, too, will welcome the leaders to New York for next year's summit.

Aspendos excavations reveal 6,000-year-old settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:17:15 UTC
16:17:15 KST

The ancient city is best known for its nearly 2,000-year-old Roman theater, considered among the best-preserved ancient theaters in Anatolia.
Recent excavations at Aspendos have revealed that the site was inhabited as early as 6,000 years ago.
Located in the Serik district of the southern province of Antalya, Aspendos, an ancient city known for its exceptionally well-preserved theater and aqueducts, was one of the important cities of ancient Pamphylia. Excavations are being conducted under the direction of Mustafa Bilgin, an associate professor at Afyon Kocatepe University, as part of the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s Heritage for the Future Project.
The ancient city is best known for its nearly 2,000-year-old Roman theater, considered among the best-preserved ancient theaters in Anatolia. It also features aqueducts, an agora, a monumental fountain, a temple, a stadium, a council building and an ancient theater street. Recent excavations have also uncovered a depiction of the river god Eurymedon dating to the third century, adding to the site’s archaeological significance.
The discoveries have pushed the known history of settlement at Aspendos back well before the Iron Age.
Bilgin told state-run Anadolu that the ancient theater was a rare example in Anatolian and Mediterranean archaeology because it has retained nearly all of its architectural elements.
He said most of the structures are standing almost to roof level, while monumental structures reflecting the landscape of the period can still be seen on the acropolis.
“Through our recent excavations, we understood that the history of the ancient city dates back 6,000 years from today,” Bilgin said.
“This fertile geography was not an area that had only been settled from the Iron Age onward. We realized this, and it was an important archaeological finding for us,” he said.
Archaeologists found evidence dating to the Late Chalcolithic Period in soundings beneath the floors of two-story shops, Bilgin said.
“Plates, bowls and various tools from that period revealed that the historical past of Aspendos’ acropolis dates back to 3500-4000 B.C.,” he said.
Bilgin described Aspendos as a “multilayered archaeological site,” noting that most of its structures have survived in a form consistent with their identity in antiquity.
“This makes Aspendos an important destination in terms of tourism and archaeology,” he said.
The site has also drawn increased visitor interest since the Culture and Tourism Ministry introduced night museum visits.
“Visiting the ancient theater and monumental structures at night, in that atmosphere, is very enjoyable for visitors,” he said.
