Behind the scenes: How the C8 summit and an oil deal exposed fragile Hungary-Ukraine ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
06:42:04 UTC
15:42:04 KST

A dispute over Hungary’s role in Ukraine’s Carpathian Eight summit and the disclosure of an oil-storage deal between MOL and Naftogaz have further strained ties between Budapest and Kyiv, as a separate row over minority rights continues to hold up Ukraine’s EU accession talks.
A diplomatic dispute over Hungary’s participation in a Ukrainian-led regional summit, followed by the disclosure of an oil-storage agreement between Hungarian energy group MOL and Ukraine’s Naftogaz, has driven relations between Budapest and Kyiv to a new low.
The Carpathian Eight (C8) summit, a new regional cooperation framework bringing together eight neighbouring countries, was held last week with the aim of strengthening investment and regional ties.
Instead, it reignited long-standing tensions between Hungary and Ukraine just as the two countries were working to repair relations and pave the way for Ukraine to open more negotiating chapters in its EU accession talks.
Both governments had hoped to ease tensions after years of hostility under Magyar's predecessor, Viktor Orbán, who built his election campaign on portraying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as a threat.
Instead, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha clashed publicly on X on Monday night. The Ukrainian foreign minister accused Magyar of following in Orbán’s footsteps after the Hungarian prime minister told parliament that Hungary had been added to the C8 initiative against its will.
"What we've been hearing from Budapest lately leaves us confused," Sybiha wrote. "It seems that while Viktor Orbán is gone, his policies of obstructionism and isolationism continue to thrive."
Magyar rejected the accusation.
"To claim that a sovereign country is a member of an international cooperation (Carpathian Integration) without prior consultation or consent of the country concerned is completely unacceptable," he replied.
The exchange made headlines in both countries. It marked a serious setback after months of work to repair ties and to allow Ukraine to open more negotiating chapters with the EU.
Carpathian Eight or Carpathian Seven?
Zelenskyy opened the summit last Thursday in Bukovel, Western Ukraine, with regional leaders including Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić. He listed eight participating countries: Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary. But the family photo he posted showed only six foreign leaders, without Magyar.
Hungary was represented by its chargé d'affaires in Ukraine, a low-level diplomat, who did not sign the summit's closing statement. Kyiv nevertheless regarded the attendance as formal participation.
Ukraine had lobbied intensively for Magyar to attend and had invited him repeatedly.
"Very active consultations took place at the level of Foreign Ministers Andrii Sybiha and Anita Orbán, as well as at the level of our representatives in Brussels and between the capitals” a Ukrainian diplomat said, speaking on the condition of anonymity, because of the sensitivity of the matter.
The diplomat told Euronews that Kyiv considered Hungary a participating member because it was officially represented by a diplomat.
"They informed us in Budapest that they would be represented at this summit by the Chargé d'Affaires of the Hungarian Embassy in Ukraine. It is not a high-level representation – let's be frank, it is a low-level one – but they will be taking part" the source added.
A Hungarian diplomat involved in the preparations gave a different account, saying Budapest had made clear before the summit that Magyar would not attend and that Hungary did not consider itself a member of the initiative without the presence and signature of its leader.
"The story is about Ukrainians being unashamed. They were lobbying very hard in Budapest for weeks for Magyar's presence," the source said. "Magyar made it clear beforehand that he is not going. The membership is only approved by the presence of leaders and their signature. The Chargé d'Affaires was just an observer."
In Hungarian government circles, portraying the country as a C8 member was seen as a mistake, but Sybiha's comparison of Magyar with Orbán inflamed the situation. The Hungarian Foreign Ministry said in a statement to Euronews:
"Since taking office, the new Hungarian Government has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to rebuild pragmatic, constructive and mutually respectful relations with Ukraine. Against that background, we do not believe that comparisons with the obstructionist policies of the previous Hungarian government are accurate or helpful."
The Hungarian diplomatic source said Magyar's government had no intention of harming Ukraine, and that the recent tensions had damaged bilateral ties.
"Now there is bad blood. Hungary does not want to harm Ukraine in any way; we understand that they are at war, and the situation today is much better compared to the Orbán era. What we have now, after the C8 mashup, is cold peace between the two countries. Under Orbán, we had a cold war."
Minority rights at the heart of the dispute
The row also revived a long-running dispute over the language and cultural rights of Ukraine’s Hungarian minority, which numbers around 100,000 people in the Transcarpathia region. Magyar, according to our sources, made it clear that he is only interested in the Carpathian summit if there is real progress on the minority file, which he could present as a success at home.
In June, Kyiv and Budapest agreed on an action plan to broaden minority rights. In response, Hungary approved the opening of two negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks.
Since then, Budapest has blocked the opening of further clusters and is demanding that Ukraine's parliament, the Rada, adopt the relevant legislation. Under the joint action plan, the Rada must adopt the laws by the end of the year.
"The ball is in Ukraine's court. They need to solve the minority issue. If this law had been adopted earlier, Magyar could have been at the Carpathian summit," the Hungarian diplomatic source said.
Magyar and Zelenskyy had earlier planned a bilateral meeting, but Magyar made any meeting with the Ukrainian President conditional on the settlement of the minority legislation. After years of anti-Ukrainian campaigning in Hungary, conservative voters are still largely sceptical about fostering ties with Kyiv, but the promotion of the rights of Hungarians living abroad is very popular in the same segment.
Ukraine says it has already delivered on the minority issue by signing the joint declaration with Hungary.
"Ukraine considers that it has fulfilled its part of the agreement. And we expect that Hungary, as it promised, will fulfil its part of the agreement, which consists of unblocking all negotiation clusters with the European Union, rather than coming up with additional conditions on the go and inventing further obstacles as to why it cannot do so," the Ukrainian source told Euronews.
Oil storage row inflamed tensions
In addition, the disclosure of talks between MOL and Naftogaz on the sidelines of the summit quickly caused a political stir and prompted Magyar to respond.
On Saturday, the two companies signed a memorandum of understanding to explore storing Ukrainian crude oil at facilities in Hungary. The arrangement could benefit both sides: MOL has spare storage capacity, while Ukraine could protect its supplies from potential Russian strikes by storing them in a NATO member state.
Such memorandums are typically confidential, but Naftogaz disclosed the plans on its Telegram channel. Magyar, who had not been informed of the agreement, was caught off guard and reacted angrily, mostly because of political risks.
Orbán’s Fidesz opposition party quickly seized on the issue, accusing Magyar of putting Ukraine’s interests ahead of Hungary’s and jeopardising the country’s security.
"Under my government, no such storage will be built at the Hungarian-Ukrainian border, or anywhere else," the prime minister said on Monday.
He also warned MOL to consult the government before pursuing similar deals, noting that the Hungarian state holds a 25% stake in the company. "MOL's practice is completely unacceptable; from now on, I expect the company to treat the Hungarian state as a 25% owner. We'll see what the consequences of this will be," Magyar said.
MOL Group said in a statement to Euronews that the memorandum was part of normal business practice to explore potential opportunities.
"MOL Group, like many other industry players, has several non-binding memoranda of understanding in the energy sector. Such agreements typically represent the first step in exploring potential areas of cooperation and launching a preparatory process that may or may not lead to a concrete project," the group said.
MOL's spokesperson, Ambrus Halász, said it would consult the Hungarian government on any future steps.
"No decision has been made, and MOL fully understands the standpoint of the Hungarian Government. Should the preliminary assessments and feasibility studies move forward, and should the project receive the necessary support from relevant decision-makers, any subsequent steps would be taken in close consultation with all relevant stakeholders and Governments and in full compliance with the applicable regulatory framework," Halász told Euronews.
A Ukrainian source, speaking on condition of anonymity, argued that such deals would benefit Hungary as well.
"If Hungarian businesses see this value for themselves, then why is the Hungarian government stating so categorically and bluntly that they do not need it, that it is, in fact, incomprehensible, and that they do not wish to participate in it?"
Russian threats in the background
The risk of provoking Moscow and disrupting Hungary’s energy supplies may also be a factor behind Magyar’s firm opposition to storing Ukrainian oil in Hungary, according to sources with an overview of Hungary's energy policy.
Hungary and Slovakia still consume large volumes of Russian oil and gas through the Soviet-era pipeline network. Any cut in Russian supplies would push up prices in Hungary and could damage the government's support.
Responding to the MOL–Naftogaz memorandum, Igor Yushkov, a leading analyst at Russia's National Energy Security Fund, warned that it could trigger a cut-off.
"Theoretically, we could halt supplies, especially now that Hungary has seen a significant leadership change and maintaining diplomatic contact with the local government is becoming increasingly difficult," Yushkov said in an interview with Russia's Absatz Media. "A memorandum from the Hungarians in this context could serve as a trigger to halt domestic supplies to them."
Earlier this summer, Andrei Kolesnik, a member of Russia's State Duma, threatened Hungary with an energy blockade in response to a new Hungarian foreign policy doctrine that describes Russia as a security threat.
"I think oil and energy supplies to Hungary from Russia are now in doubt following such statements," Kolesnik told Gazeta.ru.
Ties between Budapest and Moscow, which were close under Orbán, have deteriorated quickly under the new government. Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats from the Russian embassy in Budapest for "unacceptable activities", which analysts largely regard as spying. Moscow promised strong countermeasures.
Last week, Hungarian Economy Minister István Kapitány said the country would be ready to decouple from Russian supplies within a year.
Dialogue to continue
Despite the latest tensions, both governments stressed their willingness to keep channels of dialogue open.
"Despite these statements, we still reiterate Ukraine's willingness and openness to developing mutually beneficial, pragmatic, and respectful bilateral cooperation with Hungary," Sybiha said.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán told Index.hu that she had resolved the misunderstandings surrounding the C8 summit with her Ukrainian counterpart in New York, and did not rule out Hungary joining the initiative at a later stage.

Addressing a high-level meeting of the Global Development Initiative on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Friday, Araghchi said the need to put development at the heart of international cooperation has never been more urgent.
“Developing countries continue to face persistent poverty and hunger, widening inequalities, rising debt burdens, gaps in financing and technology, and growing environmental challenges,” he said.

“From our perspective, the devastating impact of these measures on ordinary people constitutes economic terrorism,” Araghchi said. “The United Nations must stand against such coercive measures and call for their complete and unconditional lifting.”
Araghchi also condemned the ongoing US-Israeli aggression against Iran as “a clear violation of international law and the UN Charter.”

Three adults and 14 minors were charged with training for terrorist activities, incitement to commit hate crimes, and propaganda after an Italian General Investigations and Special Operations Division (DIGOS) investigation into online neo-Nazi and white supremacist groups, the Italian state police announced on Friday.
DIGOS officers in multiple areas of Italy executed search warrants on the suspects' computers and belongings. They uncovered bladed weapons, paraphernalia with Nazi symbolism, and electronic devices used to spread propaganda.
Italian authorities launched the investigation after monitoring online channels linked to accelerationist, white supremacist, and neo-Nazi ideologies.
According to the police, the suspects actively participated in two groups on a private social network.
Suspects engaged in Holocaust denial, discussed white supremacist attacks
One group was active chatrooms tied to the “New European Order,” a movement based on Nazi propaganda, white supremacy, and antisemitism. The chatrooms focused on Holocaust denial, Nazi ideology, and the dissemination of instructions for making explosive devices.
The other suspects engaged in online communities for the Italian Fascist Front, a group that promotes hatred and violence towards Jewish people, people of color, and the LGBTQ+ community, according to the DIGOS investigation.
In the online groups and chatrooms, the suspects praised Adolf Hitler and discussed details of attacks carried out by white supremacist extremists, including weapons and tactics used.
The suspects also shared instructions for handling guns and knives, as well as manuals for making and detonating homemade explosives designed to maximize lethal impact.
The suspects also played online games together in which they recreated simulations of violence and attacks against minority groups.

====================================================================================================

Saudi Arabia’s security needs expose limits of diplomacy, give Israel an opportunity - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
06:24:47 UTC
15:24:47 KST

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has weapons and enough money to buy more, but the crisis with the Houthis is showing him how difficult it is to buy something else: a country willing to use force to defend him from Iran and its proxies.
Twice on the same day at the beginning of the month, bin Salman called US President Donald Trump and asked him to attack the Houthis. The American president refused, agreeing instead to provide intelligence assistance and targeting information. Ten days later, he came much closer to intervention: targets had been selected, bombs had been loaded onto American aircraft, and a strike in Yemen was about to begin. At the last moment, Trump halted it.
The Saudis returned to bombing Yemen. It did not solve the problem. Britain sent a refueling aircraft to temporarily support the defensive operations of the Saudi Air Force; Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s Turkey and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s Pakistan expressed support for Riyadh, and Ankara announced that it was prepared to assist with technical military needs under the defense agreement signed between the countries.
Riyadh has no shortage of friends willing to stand beside it. Far fewer are willing to enter a war themselves.
The limits of Saudi Arabia’s security strategy
Three and a half years ago, it appeared that bin Salman had found a formula. After years of confrontation with Iran, Saudi Arabia reached a reconciliation agreement with Tehran mediated by China. The logic was simple: since there was no certainty that the US would aid it in every crisis, Riyadh sought to reduce the number of crises it might face in the first place.
At the same time, it expanded ties with China, Russia, Turkey and Pakistan. On August 7, it signed a joint defense agreement in Mecca with Ankara and Islamabad, stating that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be considered an attack against all three.
America remained the main security pillar. Saudi Arabia continued buying weapons from Washington and relying on it, while simultaneously acquiring several additional insurance policies of its own.
Now comes the moment of reckoning. The question is what each of these policies is worth when missiles begin falling: weapons and intelligence, air defense, soldiers, or a statement of support. During peacetime, it is easier to blur the differences. During war, they are exposed quickly.
The Houthis are targeting Saudi Arabia’s economic foundations
The reconciliation with Tehran did not stop the Houthis, and the Mecca defense agreement has so far not brought Turkey and Pakistan into the war. Riyadh is not necessarily expecting a Turkish division to race toward Sanaa. The more immediate problem is air defense: Saudi Arabia is seeking interceptors and assistance against Houthi missiles and drones from its allies, after prolonged fighting in the region has also depleted American stocks.
It also needs intelligence, early warning capabilities and protection for energy infrastructure. The practical value of its new alliances will be measured by this assistance.
For bin Salman, the insult is the less important part. The bill presented by the crisis to the kingdom is far more concerning. The Houthis threaten two of the foundations on which bin Salman has built his new Saudi Arabia: security and business.
The war brings back the old security risk precisely as the crown prince tries to convince the world that the new Saudi Arabia is a place where it is possible to invest for the long term. Ultimately, he needs investors, tourists and international company executives to continue viewing the kingdom as stable enough to invest in.
Vision 2030, the future cities, tourism, foreign investment, business centers and ports, the entire Saudi project of the past decade, is based on the assumption that the kingdom can transform itself from a country living from crisis to crisis into a place that is boring in the best sense of the word: stable, predictable and open to capital.
Missiles over Riyadh and war in Bab al-Mandab are a poor advertisement for that product.
Oil also returned to remind everyone who still pays the bills. For decades, Saudi Arabia invested in the East-West Pipeline, a roughly 1,200-km route built to let the kingdom bypass the Strait of Hormuz during a crisis and transport oil from the Gulf to Yanbu on the Red Sea.
The more Riyadh used it, the more important the western route became, and the more exposure it brought. In June, 92% of Saudi crude oil exports by sea passed through the Yanbu terminal. The East-West Pipeline, which became a central artery after disruptions in Hormuz, carried four million to five million barrels per day. Until September 11, when drones arriving from Iraq struck three of its pumping stations, temporarily halting oil flows through the pipeline.
At the same time, the Houthis are pressuring the western export route. In July, they announced a naval boycott against Saudi shipping, and the multinational maritime task force warned that they had moved from threats to active attacks against vessels identified with Saudi Arabia and its interests.
Riyadh was forced to reroute oil exports destined for Asia through the Suez Canal, significantly lengthening the journey compared with passage through Bab al-Mandab.
Shipowners, insurers and trading companies do not need a sinking vessel to change course. The possibility that the Houthis will choose them as targets is enough. The risk immediately enters the price: insurance becomes more expensive, voyages become longer, and the advantage of the shorter route through the Red Sea is eroded.
Sometimes the missile can remain on the launcher. The Houthis only need to create a credible and sustained risk to cause economic damage far greater than the force they invest.
Riyadh has found itself inside an almost perfect geographical trap: Hormuz is disrupted in the east, three pumping stations on the pipeline designed to bypass it have been hit, and in the west the Houthis are threatening the export route through the Red Sea.
The alternatives Saudi Arabia built over years to spread its risk are now exposed themselves.
Saudi Arabia does not lack oil. It is harder to guarantee the route that carries it to the market. Geography does not give bin Salman any favors. Saudi Arabia can buy more aircraft and interceptors, but it cannot move Hormuz or Bab al-Mandab.
Freedom of navigation largely determines how much of its economic power it can truly realize.
The Houthis' continued dependence on Tehran for weapons and funding still them. Control of the coast, ports and energy resources, alongside revenues and the millions of residents under their rule, would give them far greater freedom of action.
Their goals have long extended beyond another hill in Yemen. After taking control of Mocha and advancing along the coast, the fighting in Taiz is important because the province is a junction between areas controlled by the government and allows forces and supplies to move.
To the east lies Marib, a longstanding strategic target for the Houthis and one of the most important remaining strongholds held by their rivals. Yemen’s main oil and gas fields are located there. A future takeover would harm the government’s economic base and give the Houthis a more independent source of income.
Their achievements also stem from the weakness of the Yemeni forces fighting them and from Saudi Arabia and its partners’ reluctance to become entangled again in a long war.
In this asymmetric conflict, the Houthis do not need to conquer Riyadh, sink the Saudi navy, or defeat its air force. They only need to survive and exhaust their opponents. The longer the campaign continues, the more it works in their favor.
That is the story behind the renewed war in Yemen.
Israel sees an opportunity in intelligence and defense cooperation
Israel has something to offer in this situation. For years, Israel sought to convince the Saudis that the shared threat from Iran was more serious than the disagreements between them. Now Iran and its proxy in Yemen are providing a practical demonstration of that argument.
In Jerusalem, the potential is easy to identify. Saudi needs meet areas in which Israel has a clear advantage: intelligence on the Houthis, operational experience against them, detection and interception systems, and years of experience connecting intelligence with long-range strikes.
For years, a regional alliance was discussed in ceremonial terms: leaders, flags, signatures and ambassadors. In practice, it could begin in a much less ceremonial way: a system that detects a threat, an alert delivered in time, tracking a target, and an interceptor launched into the sky.
The diplomats can come later.
Jerusalem should only be careful not to fall in love with its own thesis. In Israel, there is sometimes a tendency to view every security-related convergence of interests with Saudi Arabia as a step toward diplomatic relations.
Bin Salman can benefit from Israeli capabilities against the Houthis while at the same time managing his relationship with Israel according to a much broader calculation: the Palestinians, public opinion, his standing in the Arab world and the price he seeks from Washington.
Riyadh is not simply sitting and waiting for better conditions for a deal with Israel. In recent months, it has identified more risks than opportunities in normalization.
In a poll published in August 2025, 99% of Saudi respondents described establishing “normal relations and peace” with Israel as a negative step. The Saudi leadership has also stated that it will not establish diplomatic relations with Israel without a Palestinian state along the 1967 lines with east Jerusalem as its capital.
At the same time, improved relations with the Trump administration allow Riyadh to seek significant American benefits without paying for them through normalization.
A Houthi missile could change Riyadh’s security priorities. It does not erase the political calculation.
Even if the Saudis need Israeli capabilities, that does not mean normalization will advance with it. Bin Salman could receive intelligence, warnings, or operational coordination with American assistance in the future while keeping an Israeli embassy outside Riyadh.
For him, these are two different decisions with different prices.
Israel has become accustomed to thinking about security cooperation as a corridor that ends with normalization. The route may be longer and more complicated: the Saudis may work with Israelis where interests overlap, while publicly maintaining distance as long as domestic legitimacy and the ambition to lead the Arab world require it.
Even so, Israel can accumulate long-term assets in warning systems, intelligence, air defense and freedom of navigation. In the Middle East, security establishments have already found common ground long before leaders agreed to be photographed together.
But Israel’s interest in Yemen is broader than its relationship with Riyadh.
The Houthis have managed over time to harm freedom of navigation to Eilat. Direct commercial activity at the port was severely affected, and even after Israeli strikes in Yemen, major shipping companies have not returned to the route on a significant scale.
The threat to Bab al-Mandab has intensified as the Houthis expanded their control along the western coast.
Mocha, Taiz and Marib are also connected to Israel’s strategic map. The more the Houthis hold the coast and resources, the closer they come to a situation in which they can maintain a long-term threat to the southern gateway of the Red Sea and rely more heavily on their own revenues.
Marib and Mocha are thousands of kilometers from Eilat, but the strategic distance between them has narrowed significantly. Developments there affect the Houthis’ ability to finance forces, hold territory and pressure shipping routes connecting Eilat to the Indian Ocean.
The range of missiles and drones, together with Houthi control of the coast, makes the number of kilometers less reassuring.
Stable Houthi control over the coast, ports and resources could create a problem for Israel in the far south that resembles, in some ways, the challenge it has faced in the north: an armed organization backed by Iran but with its own interests and decision-making ability, holding territory, missiles and drones, and capable of applying pressure on an economic artery without defeating the IDF on the battlefield.
The Saudi story also offers Jerusalem a less comfortable lesson.
The rejection bin Salman received in Washington could increase the value of Israeli capabilities in his eyes, but it is also worth examining what happened between Riyadh and Washington.
The debate in Washington is not theoretical. The prolonged war with Iran depleted American interceptor stocks, and Saudi Arabia itself is now seeking missile-defense systems from its allies.
Opening another campaign against the Houthis would require the US to dedicate more aircraft, munitions, and defensive systems to a theater where it is currently attempting to remain behind the scenes.
And in November, Trump faces midterm elections.
Washington is assisting Riyadh and is currently avoiding taking responsibility for the war in Yemen. It can maintain that position as long as the Saudis contain the Houthis and the economic damage remains manageable.
A more serious disruption to oil routes and energy prices would make that choice more complicated.
Israel’s position in Washington is different from Saudi Arabia’s, as are the depth of its ties and its military capabilities. The differences are significant. Still, no American president decides to use force on behalf of an ally without calculating the American interest, the cost, the duration of the campaign, and the military’s other missions.
This week, Trump met in New York with leaders and representatives from Gulf states and other countries in the region, with Iran and the regional war at the center of the diplomatic agenda.
At the same time, Qatar is pushing for a regional security framework that would include Iran, while Saudi Arabia is advancing an idea for a regional nonaggression agreement with Tehran.
After months of war and disruptions in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, Gulf states are seeking protection from Iran while simultaneously trying to reduce the possibility of another confrontation with it.
Jerusalem and Riyadh are looking at the same map and seeing different things.
Israel views Iran and its proxies as a threat that should be weakened as much as possible. The Saudis must add a simple fact to their calculation: Iran will remain on the other side of the Gulf even the day after.
The détente with Tehran did not provide them with security, but the channel itself remains useful. Therefore, they can fight the proxies when necessary while continuing to speak with Tehran.
One battlefield, different calculations
Riyadh has operated this way for several years. It does not want to place all of its security in the hands of a single party, and it has no interest in living in a permanent confrontation with all of its rivals.
Bin Salman is maintaining the alliance with Washington, speaking with Tehran, and expanding his circle of partners so that he is not dependent on one actor.
In practice, each relationship serves a different need: America provides weapons and security, China is an economic partner and mediator, Turkey and Pakistan add military depth, and the channel with Iran is intended to lower tensions.
Israel may also have a place on that list in areas where it has capabilities that Saudi Arabia needs.
This gives bin Salman more options. The past few weeks have reminded him what those options are worth when he truly needs them.
Bin Salman is still searching for those who will protect Saudi Arabia. Israel could find itself part of the answer he assembles. However, Jerusalem should be at least as interested in understanding why he is forced to assemble that answer in the first place.

Photos published later by the channel show a massive flame in the distance.
Russian independent outlet Astra later claimed to have geolocated the attack, pinpointing it to the Ilsky oil refinery.

“The Seversky District was attacked by a drone. Sadly, there were casualties… Drone debris damaged a residential building. Fires have also been reported at two businesses in the district,” Kondratyev wrote.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.

Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.

The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.

FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.

Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.

People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.

Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.

A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.

The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.

DI describes the situation as serious and calls for closer cooperation between public authorities and the business sector.
Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.

Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

Denmark could become one of the four largest contributors to the Global Partnership for Education under a new funding plan running through 2030.
The government plans to provide up to 1 billion DKK to the global education fund, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a press release Wednesday.
The funding would begin with 250 million DKK in 2027 and reach a total of up to 1 billion DKK by 2030.
The money is intended to support education in developing countries.
“Education is one of the best investments we can make, both for the children who directly benefit from Denmark’s support, but also for Denmark itself,” Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said during the UN General Assembly in New York.
The funding is included in the government’s proposed 2027 finance bill. It is conditional on the proposal being passed and the funding being approved annually by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The announcement comes as the global education fund faces financial pressure, with several donors expected to reduce their contributions.
Rasmussen said better access to education could also support economic development.

The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.

Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.

Several Danish newspapers said Wednesday that Denmark and Greenland welcomed the new security and defense agreement, even as they raised questions about its consequences.
Berlingske called the deal a “triumph for wise and persistent diplomacy” in an editorial.
“If the agreement turns out to be worth the paper it is written on, foreign policy history was written in New York on Tuesday,” the newspaper wrote.
