Russia attacked Ukraine with 173 drones from various directions - how many were destroyed by air defenses
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of September 26, Russia launched 173 drones at Ukraine, including more than 50 jet-powered ones. Air defenses shot down or suppressed 134 UAVs.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 173 drones during the night of September 26; 134 of them were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of September 26 (from 18:00 on September 25), the enemy attacked with 173 Shahed-type strike UAVs (more than 50 of them were jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following areas: Oryol, Kursk, Millerovo, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Shatalovo — Russia; the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske.
How the air defense performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 07:30, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 134 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types.
Hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 19 locations, as well as the falling of downed targets (debris) at 8 locations.
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

Israeli scientists help solve genetic mystery linking hearing loss and gray hair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:14:36 UTC
14:14:36 KST

Imagine looking into a microscopic world where the slightest structural flaw can quiet the world entirely.
For an extended Palestinian family, a rare form of congenital hearing loss accompanied by silvery-gray-colored hair in children offered a profound genetic mystery.
An international team of researchers has now cracked the case.
By identifying a critical role for the FMN1 gene, scientists have uncovered how a single microscopic protein maintains the inner ear’s structural integrity, bridging the gap between human genetics and cellular mechanics.
The groundbreaking study by researchers from Bethlehem University, the University of Washington in Seattle, and Tel Aviv University (TAU) has just been published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences under the title “Formin-1 maintains cochlear microtubule architecture required for hearing in humans and mice.”
The study was conducted by Lara Kamal, who earned her bachelor’s degree at Jordan University of Science and Technology, then worked at Bethlehem University, and is now completing her doctorate at TAU.
The project team included Prof. Moien Kanaan (director of the Hereditary Research Lab in the Department of Life Sciences at Bethlehem University); world-renowned Prof. Mary-Claire King, Dr. Amal Aburayyan, and Dr. Suleyman Gulsuner of the University of Washington; and hearing expert Prof. Karen B. Avraham, Dr. Roni Hahn, and Dr. Shahar Taiber of TAU.
Having identified the FMN1 gene as essential for human hearing, they traced how a rare genetic variant disrupts Formin-1, a vital protein encoded by the gene essential for inner ear architecture and hearing.
By combining human genomics with decades-old mouse models, they proved that loss of Formin-1 disrupts the dynamic network of interlinking protein fibers that give the cell its shape and mechanical support, and helps transport materials in the organ of Corti – a sensory receptor organ for hearing located inside the cochlea, the hearing organ of the inner ear.
The discovery began with a Palestinian family in which four children, among three sets of cousins, were born with bilateral, moderate hearing loss accompanied by silver-gray-colored hair. The children are otherwise completely healthy.
The parents were not first cousins (consanguineous), but all are members of the same extended family.
Genomic analysis revealed that the affected children carried two copies of a rare variant in FMN1 that led to the loss of the protein Formin-1.
Genetic defects in other formin proteins have been linked with neurological, kidney, reproductive, and cardiac disorders, but the new discovery is the first in the world in which a human condition has been linked to a genetic defect in FMN1.
From mice to men
To investigate how loss of the protein causes hearing impairment, the team studied a mouse model that had no functional Formin-1. These mice were created in the early 1990s, but their hearing had not been studied before.
The authors found that these mice presented a hearing loss similar to that of the Palestinian family. The mouse could then be studied to discover the underlying cellular changes within the cochlea.
The mice’s abnormalities appeared soon after birth and continued with age. The structural disruption was accompanied by reduced auditory nerve activity and a lower number of auditory nerve fibers.
Formin-1 is also part of a molecular complex involved in transporting melanosomes (the pigment-containing organelles that contribute to hair and skin color), and the researchers hypothesized that the hearing loss and altered pigmentation could therefore arise through different biological effects of the same genetic defect.
“The discovery adds FMN1 to the more than 200 genes known to be essential for normal hearing and expands our understanding of the mechanisms underlying inherited hearing loss,” said Avraham, who is not only the senior author but also dean of TAU’s Gray Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences.
“This discovery provides additional evidence for understanding that hearing depends not only on sensory hair cells and auditory neurons, but also on precise organization of supporting cells to maintain the cochlea’s structure and mechanics,” she continued.
“As gene therapy for deafness becomes a reality, revealing the underlying genetic causes of hearing loss has become critical to treatment. Each new gene adds another part to our understanding of the complicated puzzle of auditory function.
“This work has shown that global partnerships can drive meaningful scientific advances, helping to pave the way for future genetic therapies and interventions.
“While the supporting cells are essential for the entire cascade of hearing to function normally, they do tend to be overlooked, as they are not the main cells leading to hearing function. But without them, the sensory hair cells cannot survive,” she explained.
The team members predicted a developmental window in which treatment would have to occur and perform gene replacement with the intact gene, delivered with an adeno-associated virus that might delay or prevent the hearing loss from occurring.
The pigmentation phenotype could actually provide a clinical clue for physicians to identify people with FMN1-related hearing loss, said Avraham.
“If high-throughput genetic screening is done, this discovery would allow the clinicians to first look for mutations in this gene.”
The team members have collaborated for almost 30 years.
“The work with the human family was conducted in Prof. Kanaan’s and Prof. King’s labs on different continents, while Lara Kamal worked in mine,” said Avraham.
“It has been a remarkable connection, with 24 co-authored scientific publications since then. The world seems to be disintegrating around us, but our scientific cooperation has been working well,” she continued.
“We are learning more and more about the mechanisms involving deafness that can help us put all the pieces together: hair color and deafness.”
Genetics and interconnections
In fact, Kanaan has worked with King and with Shaare Zedek Medical Center geneticist Prof. Ephrat Levy-Lahad for years to study breast cancer genes in Palestinian women.
King became renowned around the world for proving that inherited breast cancer is caused by mutations in a gene she named BRCA1. Her work transformed how scientists understand hereditary breast and ovarian cancers, leading to modern genetic testing and screening.
In 1984, she was acclaimed for her use of mitochondrial DNA sequencing to help identify Argentinian children kidnapped and illegally adopted during the Dirty War between 1976 and 1983.
“Our Israeli-Palestinian-American collaboration has led to fine science and to fine careers of devoted young scientists from all three populations,” King declared.
“We’ve shown that with persistence and confidence, good science can be carried out even in very difficult circumstances. There is a lot to be said for stubbornness on behalf of science,” she continued.
Breast cancer is a major health concern for women around the world, yet many populations lack the same genetic risk assessment as the general population, added Kanaan.
“Until recently, Palestinian women lacked access to genetic testing and cancer risk evaluation. The Middle East Breast Cancer Study the three of us conducted is changing that.”
Asked how certain they were that the FMN1 variant is responsible for the hearing loss, King noted that “we are sure because both the human family and the mouse with loss of function of FMN1 have the same hearing loss.”
“The mouse is from an inbred strain, and this is its only difference from the non-mutant strain, which has normal hearing,” she continued.
“The project involved studying the human family, working with the database created by Moien Kanaan for the Palestinian population, hearing deficits in the mouse, and functional evidence of abnormal supporting cells due to the mutation.
“This is the first time we encountered this particular FMN1 variant, which is not present in any public database or in the Palestinian genetic database created by Kanaan based on his studies of other inherited conditions in the Palestinian population.”
When asked why the lab mice created in the early 1990s had not been examined then for hearing loss, King explained that “these mice do not have problems of balance, so it can be difficult to recognize hearing loss in a mouse if balance is normal.
“And the geneticists who created the FMN1-mutant mouse were focusing on skeletal abnormalities during development, not on hearing. It apparently didn’t occur to them to evaluate their hearing.
“We think there are other people in the world carrying mutations in FMN1 whose hearing loss would very likely have been attributed to something else, because FMN1 has not previously been included in panels of genes surveyed for deafness.”
Kamal explained that she learned of the family at Bethlehem University: “My role was characterizing the family. The most difficult part is the responsibility of giving the family an answer; they already have two children with hearing loss.
“The children have hearing aids and have undergone speech therapy. I worked closely with them all.”
Kamal said that many genetic problems are caused by consanguinity in the Israeli Arab and Palestinian populations, but “fortunately, the rate is going down significantly; with the growth of better and higher education among the women, they are more aware of the problem of marrying close relatives.”

Using babies, Israeli study reveals why AI fails to truly understand animal calls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:14:02 UTC
14:14:02 KST

Humans have always wanted to talk with animals.
Dog owners try to understand their pets. At the same time, parents make great efforts to communicate with their babies before they start to produce words.
King Solomon is said to have done it, and so did Adam and Eve.
Others who accomplished it were a variety of fictional figures – Dr. Dolittle (Hugh Lofting’s physician who learned animal language from his parrot); Tarzan (Edgar Rice Burroughs’s iconic lord of the jungle who communicated with various jungle beasts); and Mowgli (Rudyard Kipling’s The Jungle Book hero who grew up with wolves).
“Talking with other creatures would not only make it possible to empathize with animals, learn about other levels of consciousness, and enrich our understanding of life. It would also have immense practical value,” suggested Prof. Yosef Yovel, who has worked in the zoology department of Tel Aviv University (TAU) for the last 15 years.
“Farmers might benefit from a machine that allows them to ask a cow about its health, though it might turn them into vegetarians,” he continued.
“Such a machine would also come in handy once we land on a planet inhabited by some simple alien life form, while if advanced aliens ever make it to Earth, they will probably already have such a machine.”
Even as artificial intelligence masters human language, a groundbreaking study he and his team conducted reveals a fundamental flaw in how AI decodes the animal kingdom: it hears the volume and pitch, but entirely misses the point.
The researchers have now discovered why AI is getting animal and human toddler communication all wrong.
For years, scientists have turned to AI to unlock the secrets of bird calls, bat chatter, and whale songs, but the new research published in Current Biology under the title “The challenge of decoding animal communication using AI” suggests our high-tech translators might be looking at the problem completely backward.
The TAU experts explained that while AI is a powerful tool, it needs a paradigm shift – moving away from raw audio analysis toward understanding neural and perceptual meaning.
The study was conducted by Mor Taub, Inbal Arnon, Amiyaal Ilany, Mirjam Knörnschild, and Yoav Ram, and it was supervised by Yovel.
The team also included scientists from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, the University of Edinburgh, the Natural History Museum-Leibniz Institute for Evolution and Biodiversity Science, and Humboldt University (both in Berlin).
Two sounds that look completely different on a spectrogram can carry the same message to a receiver, while the same acoustic sound can mean entirely different things depending on the context – proving that communication relies heavily on the receiver’s perception, not just the physical properties of the sound wave.
A spectrogram is a visual representation of the spectrum of frequencies of a signal as it changes over time. When applied to audio, it is essentially a picture of sound often referred to as a sonograph, voiceprint, or spectral display.
A standard 2D spectrogram uses three dimensions of data mapped onto a flat image.
Misleading communication system
The researchers found that acoustically similar sounds do not necessarily carry similar meanings, while sounds that appear different may convey the same information to the receiver.
Therefore, classifying sounds by their acoustic similarity, as most studies do, may create a misleading picture of the communication system and the meaning of the messages it conveys, Yovel added.
They discovered that humans listening to a toddler’s sequences perceive increasing urgency, apparently from subtle acoustic modifications. None of the tested AI models captured the ordering of those vocalizations according to urgency.
“In recent years, there has been growing excitement about the possibility of using AI to decode animal communication, but our study shows that these promises should be treated with caution,” said Yovel, who earned his bachelor’s degree in physics and biology and his master’s degree in neurobiology from TAU, followed by a PhD in biology from Germany’s University of Tübingen.
“Identifying acoustic patterns is not necessarily the same as deciphering meaning: to understand what an animal is ‘saying,’ we need to know how the animal receiving the message perceives it and responds to it,” he added.
“The path toward truly deciphering animal communication will require a combination of AI, behavioral observations, experiments, and research into the nervous system. Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool, but it is no substitute for the perspective of the animal itself.”
To investigate the problem, the team used a unique communication system – the vocalizations of human toddlers who have not yet fully developed speech.
Unlike animal vocalizations, in this case the researchers could try to know how the humans to whom the vocalizations are directed interpret them.
The recordings included vocalizations made in three contexts: distress, calling to a specific person (the mother or the father), and asking for food.
The researchers analyzed the recordings using a classical acoustic method and two state-of-the-art deep neural networks: one trained on animal vocalizations and another trained on adult human speech.
The models were asked to group the vocalizations according to their characteristics.
The results showed that the deep neural networks performed better than the classical acoustic method, but even they failed to classify the toddlers’ vocalizations by their meaning.
In some cases, they grouped together vocalizations carrying different messages; in others, they separated different vocalizations intended to convey the same message.
The models also failed to identify how a sequence of vocalizations expressed increasing urgency, a distinction that the human ear perceives naturally.
According to the researchers, reliably deciphering animal communication will require combining AI tools with behavioral observations, playback experiments, and sometimes measurements of brain activity.
Using context
Every species has its own unique perceptual world, and understanding what animals are “saying” therefore requires more than analyzing sound alone: it also requires examining how they hear the sound and respond to it.
“We cannot connect specific signals with meaning. The basic idea is that AI models will find the largest differences between the signals, but these are not necessarily the important differences for the brain,” Yovel explained.
“We can take an example from the stickleback fish during the breeding season. Males have a red abdomen and are very aggressive. The red color is, for them, the most important signal for detecting another male. They don’t care about the shape of the fish or how it moves.
“Researchers showed long ago that if they take a sphere and color code it in red, the fish will perceive it as another fish. AI models would never detect this unless we specifically ask them to pay attention to color.
“This is exactly the point with baby and other animal vocalizations. AI will look for the most significant acoustic difference, but these are not necessarily equivalent to the important differences for the brain.
“The human brain is using context. AI language models can learn to do this too with human language, but it’s far more difficult with non-human language.”
When asked why they chose pre-linguistic toddlers rather than an animal species whose communication they already studied, Yovel explained that “the reason was that we wanted to know something about the meaning, so we studied.”
“I thought I knew something about the meaning of their vocalizations. With bats, I needed to guess what they received, but my brain understood human toddler vocalizations,” he continued.
“I can’t be sure, but when my toddler calls for me, I am more certain what he wants. The sample size was small, but we only intended to use this as a case to highlight and exemplify the problem. We also used a data set of real human words and showed that the result was completely different.”
Asked if a toddler could produce acoustically similar sounds for completely different purposes depending on the context, he agreed: “This is exactly one of the big challenges in decoding animal communication because animals will do this as well.”
There has been enormous excitement about AI potentially decoding whales, bats, birds, and other animals.
“Nearly all of these studies are finding patterns in animal communication. That’s the first step, but we are very far from understanding meaning or even knowing how to do that exactly.”

US intelligence warns Saudi Arabia has not ruled out nuclear weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:11:04 UTC
14:11:04 KST

Classified documents provided to Congress include an assessment by the U.S. intelligence community that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out the option of developing a nuclear weapons program, The Washington Post reported Friday evening.
The report comes amid concerns raised by numerous experts over an agreement reached in July between the U.S. administration and Riyadh that would allow the kingdom to develop a civilian nuclear program under less stringent safeguards than are customary. Unlike similar agreements with other countries, the deal also opens a path for Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium domestically, potentially to the relatively high level of 20%.
The agreement, signed in July after years of negotiations between Washington and Riyadh, provides the legal framework for U.S. companies to operate in Saudi Arabia and develop nuclear facilities, including civilian power plants. Saudi Arabia, whose crown prince and de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman said in 2018 that the kingdom would pursue a nuclear weapon if Iran developed one, refused during negotiations with the United States to relinquish the ability to enrich uranium domestically or sign a stringent safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency, known as the Additional Protocol. The United Arab Emirates, by comparison, accepted such restrictions as part of its 2009 civilian nuclear agreement with the United States, which has since been regarded as the "gold standard" for agreements of this kind.
Instead, the July agreement includes U.S. safeguards that Washington has said will be sufficient to prevent Saudi Arabia from using its civilian program to develop nuclear weapons in the future. But details subsequently reported about the agreement have raised significant concerns among experts and Democratic lawmakers in Congress, who have sharply criticized it.
According to The Wall Street Journal, the agreement would not immediately allow Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium itself. Initially, as the United Arab Emirates does, it would have to import enriched uranium from abroad. During the first two years, however, the two countries would conduct a study examining the "economic feasibility" of enriching uranium on Saudi soil and the safeguards that would be required to prevent such a program from being used to develop a nuclear weapon, or at least the capability to do so. The Washington Post has also reported that the agreement calls for a two-year study into whether enrichment in Saudi Arabia is feasible and necessary.
The Journal reported that if the United States and Saudi Arabia determine that domestic enrichment is necessary, U.S. companies and their foreign suppliers would build a facility where enrichment would initially be limited to 5%. A further study would then examine the possibility of raising enrichment to 20%, a relatively high level. While experts note that uranium enriched to that level also has civilian uses, they say reaching 20% completes much of the technical work required to enrich uranium to weapons-grade levels of about 90%.
Experts have raised concerns about the possibility that some enriched material could be secretly diverted for military purposes. The Trump administration, by contrast, argues that the involvement of U.S. companies in the program would prevent that risk. Administration officials also argue that the agreement is important because it keeps Riyadh from turning to China or Russia for help developing its nuclear program. Under the agreement as described by people familiar with it, any Saudi enrichment would be controlled by U.S. companies using technology that would not be shared with the Saudis.
The Washington Post reported Friday that, in addition to the intelligence assessment warning that Riyadh has not ruled out developing nuclear weapons, the classified documents sent to Congress last month also included the State Department's assessment. People who spoke with the newspaper said the State Department appeared more confident in the safeguards established under the agreement and in assurances provided by the Saudi government.
The Saudi government did not respond directly to the Post's request for comment but referred the newspaper to an earlier statement by Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman, who said the kingdom's nuclear program would be peaceful and developed with the highest levels of responsibility and transparency.
President Donald Trump has said the agreement with Saudi Arabia will not take effect unless the kingdom joins the Abraham Accords and normalizes relations with Israel. The agreement has nevertheless already been submitted to Congress for review. Under U.S. law, Congress has 90 days while in session to review it. Lawmakers seeking to block the agreement would ultimately need sufficient support to overcome a presidential veto.
Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon told the Post that the United States should not rely on Saudi assurances on an issue of such importance.
"It’s bogus as hell," he said, arguing that Saudi demands to retain the ability to enrich uranium domestically indicate an ambition to develop a program that would not be entirely civilian.
"If they’ve given up the intent to develop a nuclear weapon, then they’d give up domestic enrichment and reprocessing power, right? They’d accept massive inspections from the IAEA," Merkley added.
Merkley and other Democratic senators sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday criticizing the agreement. They argued that the Trump administration was departing from precedent by accepting looser restrictions and agreeing to a process they said would almost certainly allow Riyadh to acquire uranium enrichment capabilities and potentially develop a nuclear weapon.

‘Godzilla’ El Niño to be the strongest in living memory. How can we prepare for the unavoidable?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:02:15 UTC
14:02:15 KST

El Niño can’t be stopped, but experts say better preparation and climate action could reduce the damage both now and in the future.
The ‘Godzilla’ El Niño is here, and it is already breaking records the world would rather have left unbroken.
Sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean have already surpassed the highest recorded during any previous El Niño, and the weather phenomenon is still strengthening. Between June 2026 and February 2027, experts estimate the extreme heat associated with it could contribute to 451,000 additional deaths.
The forecast has set off alarm bells among weather agencies, health authorities and governments around the world, including an unprecedented mobilisation by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) to prepare for the extreme weather ahead.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in early September. “The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”
But even as governments brace for what could be a devastating year of extreme weather, experts say there is still plenty that can be done to limit the damage – both now and in the future.
Why is this El Niño so concerning?
Records aside, many worry about what an El Niño of this strength could mean for weather around the world in the months ahead.
An El Niño event starts in the Pacific, but its effects can be felt around the world. When waters near the equator become unusually warm, they release heat into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures and changing where rain falls.
With ocean temperatures already at record highs, this El Niño could bring more intense heat, drought and heavy rainfall in vulnerable regions and push global temperatures to new highs – earning it the nicknames ‘Godzilla’ and ‘Super’ El Niño.
Some of those effects are already being felt. India has already experienced below-normal monsoon rainfall while southern Africa faces an increased risk of drought.
Even though Europe is unlikely to experience the most severe direct effects, El Niño can influence winter weather, and droughts or failed harvests elsewhere can disrupt supplies of foods imported into Europe.
The threat is already prompting governments to act around the world. This month, California Governor Gavin Newsom preemptively declared a state of emergency to prepare for potential flooding, landslides, coastal erosion and powerful winter storms.
How can we prepare for an unavoidable El Niño?
For all the preparations we make, one thing remains unavoidable: El Niño is a natural phenomenon. But even if we can’t prevent it, forecasts give us months to prepare.
“The key is to manage water and prepare for the changes in where and when rainfall occurs,” says Davide Faranda, research director at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and a lead author for the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
For example, he explains, governments can store and distribute water more carefully, better control how reservoirs and underground water are used, adjust farming schedules and irrigation practices, and prepare communities for droughts or floods.
The FAO has also offered concrete advice. Farmers, FAO officials say, can reduce losses by changing planting dates, irrigating at cooler times of day, storing water ahead of droughts and taking steps to protect their crops and livestock from extreme heat.
Some governments have stepped up with financial support.
The UK has pledged up to £15 million (€17 million) to help vulnerable countries prepare for this El Niño. The money will fund measures that range from vaccinating livestock before droughts to reinforcing homes before flooding and providing farmers with cash before harvests fail.
Climate action could limit future damage
Most El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C. While this is enough to trigger extreme weather conditions across the Global South, it is a fraction of the additional warming caused by climate change.
The burning of fossil fuels has pushed global average surface temperatures by approximately 1.3°C to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels, paving the way for Europe’s scorching summer that triggered mass droughts and wildfires.
El Niño’s impacts are therefore compounded by an already warming world. It’s why 2025 was the third warmest year on record – hotter than the El Niño year of 2016 – despite the naturally forming cool drag of a La Niña event.
Recent research suggests that climate change is turbocharging El Niño as well. A study published in August found that El Niños are 36 per cent stronger than before the industrial era, a trend researchers linked to human-caused warming.
If climate change is making El Niño stronger, then preparation will only go so far. But Faranda says cutting emissions can make a big difference over the long term.
A hotter planet means more extreme heat, more strain on water supplies and, in some places, more rainfall. Reducing emissions would not stop the natural climate cycle that leads to El Niños, he explains, but it would reduce the human-caused warming that is making those threats more severe.
That means the damage is not entirely beyond our control. “We cannot eliminate El Niño through climate mitigation,” Faranda says, “but we can reduce the extent to which climate change makes its consequences more severe.”

Ljubljana vs Zagreb: Which Central European capital should you visit next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:00:51 UTC
14:00:51 KST

The capitals of Slovenia and Croatia are overlooked in favour of lake and coastal destinations elsewhere – here’s why it’s time for you to change that.
Ljubljana and Zagreb are two seriously underrated capitals.
Both overshadowed by other destinations in their respective countries – Lake Bled for Slovenia, and basically anywhere along the coast for Croatia – these cities are more than overdue their time in the spotlight.
While people have slowly been waking up to the joys of Ljubljana, with its car-free city centre and fantastic creative scene, Zagreb next door hasn’t quite hit the mainstream just yet.
Hopefully we can change that.
(Plus, if after reading all this you still can’t decide between the two you can always “trip-maxx” and visit them both – you can travel between them by bus or train in just two-and-a-half hours).
Ljubljana
One of the things travellers comment on most when talking about Ljubljana is just how walkable it is.
Its centre has been closed to cars and other vehicles since 2007, and it makes the best parts of a European city break – walking around aimlessly and stopping in shops, cafés, and restaurants that catch your eye – infinitely better.
A good place to begin your wandering will be the Triple Bridge over the Ljubljanica River – not just because it’s incredibly central, but the bridges are UNESCO-listed as part of the works of Jože Plečnik in Ljubljana heritage site.
The Slovenian architect played a key role in the development of the city between the two World Wars, and you can see his works along the river embankments and at sites such as the National and University Library or the outdoor theatre Križanke.
For a closer look, you can visit Plečnik House, which offers a deep dive into his best-known buildings (both realised and not), and has his original furniture and tools amongst its collection.
If rambling has your stomach rumbling, head to Trubarjeva Street, which is dotted with independent shops, cafés and restaurants.
While I’ve obviously just spoken about the joys of meandering without a goal in sight, I do have to give a shoutout to Abi Falafel, which serves the best falafel I’ve ever eaten and think about constantly. High praise, given I live in Qatar which has plenty of great options to choose from.
Should you be in town on a Friday between March and October, you could also explore the Open Kitchen food market near the Central Market.
The city’s most iconic sight is, of course, Ljubljana Castle, which sits on a hill above the capital.
Originally built in the 11th century, much of the current structure is from the 15th and 16th century, and visitors can reach it via funicular railway.
Inside, you can learn about the fortress’ history, climb up the viewing tower, or buy a bottle of wine made with grapes on the slopes of the castle’s hill.
Ljubljana is also known for its alternative scene, the most famous of which is Metelkova Mesto, a cultural centre started from a squat in a former military barracks started in the 90s. Today, there are various art spaces here, and you can also attend club nights, the details of which are posted on the Metelkova website.
Zagreb
Croatia’s capital is also plenty walkable, with many of the main tourist attractions concentrated in the Upper Town, although you can also make use of the extensive tram network.
To reach the Upper Town, you’ll pass through the Stone Gate, which dates back to the 13th century.
While you’ll no doubt have been through plenty of medieval gates while visiting other historic cities in Europe, Zagreb is notable for its shrine to Mary, which survived a fire unscathed in the 18th century and now serves as the city’s patron saint.
Zagreb’s most notable – and most colourful – site has to be St. Mark’s Church. First founded in the 13th century, the historic building’s roof tiles show the Zagreb city emblem as well as the coat of arms of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia, the kingdom within the Austro-Hungarian Empire.
Time your visit to then pass by Lotrščak Tower for noon, when the Grič cannon has been fired daily since 1877.
An alternative to your bog standard history or archaeological museums, Zagreb’s Museum of Broken Relationships is a must-visit.
Featuring objects donated by the public from around the globe, you’ll find things inside like the “toaster of vindication”, taken cross country post break-up (“How are you going to toast anything now?”). Both depressing and hilarious, it’s proven so popular in recent years that a second location has since opened in Thailand.
Another popular attraction in the Upper Town is Zagreb Cathedral, but it should be noted that restoration works are still underway following the 2020 Zagreb earthquake.
While the Upper Town is all about medieval history, Zagreb’s Lower Town was built in styles popular in the Austro-Hungarian empire in the 19th and 20th centuries.
There’s plenty of greenery: The area is home to the Green Horseshoe, a U-shaped system of parks in the city’s squares, as well as the Zagreb Botanical Garden.
You’ll also find galleries and museums like the Archeological Museum, Ethnographic Museum and the Museum of Arts and Crafts, while those looking for restaurants, cafés and bars can head to the streets around Ban Jelačić Square.

Why are Norwegians buying more Chinese EVs despite growing scepticism?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

Electric cars account for more than 95% of new car registrations in Norway, the highest share in the world. About one in four new EVs registered there are from fully or partly Chinese-owned brands.
Chinese car brands are taking an increasingly large market share in Norway, even as their electric vehicles are being met with growing scepticism in the country, which leads the world in EV adoption.
According to a new survey by the Norwegian Electric Vehicle Association, conducted from 31 March to 3 May among nearly 15,000 EV owners in Norway, nearly one-third (31%) of Norwegian electric car drivers said they would avoid buying a Chinese brand for political reasons, compared with 23% a year earlier.
“New cars are, in practice, computers on wheels,” the association’s secretary general, Christina Bu, said in a statement.
“As data security and privacy receive more attention, it is only natural that more consumers become concerned about where the cars come from and how the data is handled,” she added.
A few years ago, Norwegian security researchers discovered that a car made by the Chinese maker NIO was transmitting data to China.
Other tests carried out on a bus from China’s Yutong revealed that the manufacturer had access to the vehicle’s control system and could, in theory, stop it or render it unusable remotely.
Sales of Chinese brands such as BYD, NIO and Dongfeng, and brands owned by Chinese companies like Volvo and Polestar, have nonetheless grown significantly in Norway, accounting for about 25% of new EV registrations in the first half of the year.
Back in 2019, they were virtually non-existent.
“This suggests that consumers weigh several factors against one another when they are buying a car,” Bu said.
“For some, factors such as price and technology are decisive, while others are influenced by moral dilemmas and uncertainty about data sharing and security issues,” she said.
Chinese-owned brands gain ground in Norway
In just a few years, Chinese-owned brands have gone from a negligible share of Norway’s new EV market to becoming its second-largest group by origin, according to an earlier report by the association.
The report suggested they could overtake European brands as soon as 2027 if current trends continue. It also said Norway could become one of the first European markets where Chinese EV makers gain a dominant position.
Gaining ground in Norway matters because the country leads the world in EV adoption. Electric cars accounted for 97.8% of new car registrations in the first eight months of 2026, according to the Norwegian Road Federation (OFV).
Norway remains far ahead of the EU, where electric cars accounted for 21.7% of new registrations between January and August, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA).
Chinese brands are gaining ground in the wider EU, too. Registrations across five groups with Chinese brands listed by ACEA rose by about 71% in August from a year earlier. Their combined share of the overall new car market climbed from 6.6% to 10.8%. This means that roughly one in nine new cars registered in the EU came from these groups. The figure includes brands with European roots, such as Volvo Cars, which is owned by the Geely Group.
In the EU, among the fastest-growing manufacturers were Leapmotor (up 211%), Chery (201%), BYD (129%) and Geely Group (24%). Registrations of cars made by US carmaker Tesla grew by 53%.
Tesla resistance falls
Political resistance to Tesla has fallen in Norway, too. According to the survey by the Norwegian Electric Vehicle Association, the share of respondents who said they would avoid Tesla for political reasons dropped to 24% from 43% last year. Musk’s political involvement and support for far-right leaders have drawn opposition to the brand.
“Last year, Elon Musk’s political involvement was highly visible and, unsurprisingly, provoked strong reactions,” Bu said.
“This year, there has been less attention on this, and that may have led to fewer people saying they would not have chosen Tesla,” she added.
Tesla remains Norway’s best-selling new car brand, with a 17.5% share of registrations so far this year, according to OFV data through 24 September.

And for us on the left, that means bringing our centre-left bloc back together,” she said. But she added that “includes some who have considered Reform as they have lost faith in the status quo”.
She said Labour would bring progressive voters who had turned to the Greens, SNP or Plaid Cymru back to trusting Labour over the coming months and years – saying they had not always seen Labour as the best chance to defeat right-wing politics. “I’ve always thought there was a clear majority in this country who didn’t want the kind of politics of Reform and that divisive blaming of others – they didn’t like it,” she said.
“The challenge has been that sentiment has not all come to Labour and the progressive coalition was very, very fragmented. And part of our task and challenge is to reunite that progressive alliance and that voter coalition.
“I think we can. We’ve got red shoots of hope coming through. There are a lot more choices for people [when it comes to political parties] … but the task is to rise above that and to be the leaders of the progressive change.”
Ahead of her conference speech, the education secretary said she will use her new role to announce an expansion of anti-harassment work in schools, having called in her deputy leadership race for Labour to be more explicitly progressive especially calling out racism and misogyny.
She will say schools must go further than the strategy announced earlier this year to tackle misogyny, where pupils will learn about deepfakes, image-based abuse and online harassment.
Powell said schools would be required to “embed healthy relationships and belonging into every part of school life, not just RSHE [relationships, sex and health education] lessons” and show they were helping to create real-world, authentic community.
“We simply cannot just teach our way out of misogyny,” she said. “Schools with strengthened RSHE teaching but no wider culture shift will not shift attitudes.”
She said Labour was now “on the front foot” and the party would talk more boldly about choices like workers’ rights and free childcare hours.
“Let’s not be embarrassed about that, that’s what we are,” she said. “We lift children out of poverty, we take the difficult decisions in order to do that. I think at times we’ve been a bit worried about the reaction rather than just being clear about why we’re doing that.”
“There was a real strong desire for that clearer political communication. Of purpose, of story, of values. Andy knew that that’s what he needed to do. That was what the moment required,” she said.
Powell said it would be obvious under Burnham what Labour’s values were – suggesting he would not make the same missteps on issues like welfare.
“If we’re not for pensioner poverty, and we’re not addressing that, and we are not supporting people who need the safety net, then what are we for?” She added that the government under Starmer had “lost sight of some of the politics and the purpose” once they came into power.
“We have to be clear-sighted about what we’re doing, who we’re doing it for and clearly articulate that every single day.”
“It’s really encouraging to see that people are coming back. Andy’s shown that we can win in places like Makerfield against Reform, and in some key council byelections we previously lost to the Greens in May.”
Powell declined to agree directly with the chancellor, John Healey, that Burnham’s government was offering “continuity”. “We are on the same manifesto, but look I think people want change. We have to seize that opportunity of that second hearing to really punch home with that Labour story and the underpinning of why we’re doing what we’re going.”
Powell said she wanted to use the social media ban for under-16s as a moment to think about how to help young people to build real life communities that would replace the online world “so that people aren’t just accessing all their content and all their thoughts from social media … We’ve kind of ended up with this highly connected world where actually isolation has become a bigger feature.”

Vast Casino Secrets leak exposes inner workings of offshore gambling firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

The secrets of thousands of online casinos have been laid bare in a vast leak of data that could have seismic consequences for offshore gambling firms, including some accused of illegally targeting consumers around the world.
The Casino Secrets leak reveals tens of thousands of previously confidential files stored by the gambling regulator on the Caribbean island of Curaçao.
The files detail the inner workings of some of the world’s largest online casinos, including the crypto-focused Everton FC sponsor Stake.com and the Santeda network, which was exposed in an investigation by the Guardian and Investigate Europe in April.
Some of the businesses appear to be owned or operated by British citizens, while others, such as the Leicester City FC sponsor BC.Game, have previously been accused of targeting UK customers illegally.
The leak has rocked Curaçao, whose opaque licensing regime has transformed the former Dutch colony into a thriving but sometimes controversial hub for gambling firms, hosting more than 8,000 casinos, one for every 20 people living there.
A Berlin-based hacker, Lilith Wittmann, claims to have obtained internal documents by accessing a database kept by the Curaçao Gaming Authority (CGA).
The CGA has confirmed it was subject to “unauthorised access” of its portal.
Data published in the leak includes information about the owners of some of the world’s largest offshore casinos and details including the source of their wealth.
Companies whose data has been published include Santeda International, the global casino network traced by the Guardian and Investigate Europe this year.
The investigation found that casinos owned by Santeda appeared to have targeted vulnerable UK gamblers who were trying to quit, despite it having no licence from the Gambling Commission, which is illegal.
The investigation also uncovered a digital paper trail leading to a business called Upgaming, which is owned and operated by a group of Georgian businessmen.
At the time, lawyers for Upgaming said their client denied operating the Santeda network but the Casino Secrets leak has raised new questions about this claim.
Information submitted by Santeda to the CGA names a Georgian called Onise Chimakhidze as its owner.
It also gives Upgaming email addresses as contact details, while a cache of files submitted to the CGA refer to Upgaming in their filenames.
Lawyers for Upgaming said their client could not “speculate as to why a third-party has listed their contact details without further information, or without having seen the documents”.
They said this could be because Upgaming previously had a business relationship with Santeda, which has since ceased.
A document submitted in 2025 described a man named Torniki Kapanadze as Santeda’s finance chief. A LinkedIn profile shows a Tornike Kapanadze works for Upgaming. Lawyers for Upgaming said this was a common name in Georgia and noted the difference in spelling.
Santeda also extended six loans totalling €15,590,000 (£13,420,000) to Buda Capital, a Luxembourg-based company owned by a group of Georgians who own stakes in or are directors of Upgaming. Upgaming did not provide an explanation for this loan.
The lawyers said Upgaming believed it was “subject to a targeted campaign by various parties, including with vested commercial interests of their own”, without providing further explanation.
The leak also reveals data about Oddsbet, a betting company focused on “VIP” gamblers that was owned until 2025, the data suggests, by Robert Bostock, from Goole in the East Riding of Yorkshire.
Documents submitted to the CGA by Bostock’s company claimed that the source of his funds derived from “long-term crypto currency investments” and a £100,000 loan from another person based in the UK.
He sold the business for $240,000 in 2025, the documents suggest.
Lawyers for Bostock said the £100,000 loan was never drawn. They said the business only served customers outside the UK.
BC.Game also appears in the leak. The company has previously been accused of accepting business from UK customers, even after surrendering its licence to do so. This would be an offence under the Gambling Act 2005.
The leak also reveals information about Stake.com, the vast online casino that pulled out of the UK in 2025 after a string of controversies.
Stake’s Curaçao-registered company, Medium Rare NV, gave its owner as Serbian national Mladen Vučković, who declared assets of more than $1bn to the regulator in 2024.
Regulators questioned whether he owned the business, after finding millions of dollars to companies tied to Stake’s founders, Ed Craven and Bijan Tehrani. Neither appeared on the licence application, according to the investigative journalism platform Follow the Money, which first reported the findings.
But the Curaçao regulator still issued a licence, one example among several that Follow the Money said indicated that it failed to act on red flags about applicants.
The UK Gambling Commission said it could not comment on leaks.
“Illegal activity linked to gambling is a threat that we take seriously, and we work closely with partners to identify and disrupt those seeking to operate outside the regulatory framework,” it said.
The CGA said it could not answer questions about an “ongoing, complex forensic matter”.
It said it was “committed to transparency” and would issue further updates.
The Guardian has approached BC.Game and Stake.com for comment.

Drones could speed up getting defibrillators to people having cardiac arrests, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

Drones could help cut the time it takes to get a defibrillator to people experiencing cardiac arrests when not in hospital, researchers have suggested.
In the UK alone, there are more than 30,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests a year where emergency medical services attempt to resuscitate the individual, according to the British Heart Foundation. However, fewer than one in 10 people survive such an event, and some who do are left with neurological problems.
One important factor that can affect survival is how rapidly victims get access to treatment – every minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of survival by 10%.
“We have an objective as EMS [emergency medical service] organisations and EMS physicians to help cardiac arrest patients get defibrillated as early as possible,” said Matthieu Heidet, a professor of emergency medicine at Henri-Mondor university hospital in Créteil, France.
Work by Heidet and colleagues has suggested drones could be used to increase access to the life-saving devices.
To explore the issue, the team analysed the number and location of 28,349 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occurred between 2011 and 2024 in administrative areas within the Greater Paris area. Central Paris was excluded from the analysis.
The team cross-referenced these events with the location of fixed automated external defibrillators (AEDs).
The researchers found accessibility of the 1,893 AEDs varied considerably across the area.
“Only 30% of all [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] cases occurred within the target 500-metre network distance of the nearest recorded fixed AED,” said Dr Hillary Minka, an emergency physician at the Lariboisière hospital in Paris and the first author of the work.
The team found an extra 910 fixed AEDs would be needed for 84.5% of the recorded cardiac arrest cases to have been within 500 metres of an AED, while 1,712 extra fixed AEDs would be needed for 100% coverage.
However, by using drones operating within a radius of 3,900 metres, coverage could be increased with fewer devices.
“As drone bases were introduced, the number of additional fixed AEDs required fell substantially,” said Minka, noting that with 100 drone bases and 26 additional fixed AEDs, more than 97% of the cardiac arrest cases would have been located either within 500 metres of a fixed AED or within approximately 4km (2.5 miles) of a drone base. The use of 200 drone bases and just four extra AEDs meant more than 99% of cases would have been covered.
The researchers also looked at the proportion of the cardiac arrest cases deemed close enough to an existing fixed AED that the device could be retrieved in a round trip within five minutes.
The results revealed only 30-40% of the cardiac arrest cases had access to current fixed AEDs within this time period using the ground transportation network.
Heidet added that this figure was optimistic. “In France, only 8% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients benefit from the application of a public AED before the arrival of the [emergency services],” he said, noting one factor is that a large proportion of AEDs are inaccessible, for example because they are housed in enclosed private spaces that are not open at all times.
By contrast, Minka noted that in a scenario involving 200 drone bases, 871 existing fixed AED sites and four additional fixed AED sites, drone delivery reached virtually all of the cardiac arrest cases covered by the model within five minutes.
The team’s models were based on drones being housed at sites ranging from current AED locations to fire stations and mobile intensive care units, and did not look at real-world deployment of such tech.
Heidet noted it is not the first time drones have been considered for the delivery of AEDs; the approach is already being used in parts of Sweden and has saved lives.
In real-world systems, Heidet added, drones are operated by trained drone pilots.
“Once an emergency call is received and an [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] is identified at the dispatch centre, the drone is activated by EMS dispatchers. It then takes off and follows an automated flight path, while the final approach and subsequent AED delivery are handled by the drone pilot. The entire process is conducted under the supervision of the emergency medical service,” he said. Once delivered, the AED can be used by members of the public at the scene.
Heidet added the cost of drones needed to be integrated into the evaluation of such technology, noting there may be a balance between the ideal model and the feasible economic model.
The study, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, is to be presented at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris on Saturday.

Schoolchildren without smartphones penalised with higher bus fares
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

Schoolchildren who do not own smartphones face paying hundreds of pounds extra in annual bus fares as cheaper travel passes are digitised.
Critics argue that by only making discounts available through an app, operators are undermining government guidance to keep mobile phones out of schools.
Adele Kightley’s 11-year-old daughter faces paying an extra £546 a year to get to school because a discount scheme launched by Derbyshire county council is only available via smartphones.
The b_line card caps single fares on trentbarton buses at £1.50 for those aged 18 and under. However, users have to register their card with an app to qualify.
“We made the choice not to give our daughter a smartphone, instead opting for a brick phone when she started secondary school this month,” Kightley said.
“In order to get trentbarton’s young person discount, a child has to connect their student card with the app. However, they can’t get the same discount by showing the same student card to the driver and paying by cash or card.”
Trentbarton said its ticketing machines are not configured to read the council-issued cards. “We are working at speed on developing a new physical card to provide the discounted b_line fare for under-19s,” a spokesperson for the bus company said.
“In the meantime, all young people, whether they have a smartphone or not, will continue to receive a range of discounts off our adult fares however they pay.”
East Midlands combined county authority said it sympathised with parents who did not want their children to have smartphones and would consider how young people accessed discounted fares as it developed the region’s fares and ticketing strategy.
The increasing use of digital-only passes is penalising poorer households as well as undermining efforts to restrict screen time for children, according to Daisy Greenwell, a co-founder of the campaign group Smartphone Free Childhood.
“There is now a huge movement of parents and schools trying to delay smartphones for children but, in many parts of the country, bus companies are making that much harder by charging smartphone-free children up to twice as much for exactly the same journey,” she said.
More than 200,000 parents have signed up to the campaign group’s “parent pact”, which promises to delay getting a child smartphones until at least 14, “yet essential services are still being designed around the assumption that every child has one”, Greenwell said. “For lower-income families in particular, owning a smartphone can effectively become the price of accessing cheaper bus fares.”
Other regional operators, including Stagecoach and Compass, also require children to have a smartphone to access the best discounts.
“My husband and I decided not to give smartphones to our children because of the overwhelming evidence that shows how harmful they are to developing brains,” Kightley said. “When our younger child starts secondary school, it will cost us nearly £1,100 a year more than it would if they had access to the discount through the app.”
A law banning the use of mobile phones in English schools came into force in June. Some schools prohibit pupils from bringing smartphones on site. However, the Department for Education said the legislation did not cover phone use during travel to school and that app-only fare discountswere a matter for individual bus operators.
The government’s stance is sending mixed messages, Greenwell said. “Bus fares shouldn’t be a barrier to schools choosing policies where smartphones aren’t brought on to site. Government and bus companies have a clear opportunity to fix this, so every child can access the same fare whether they carry a smartphone or not.”
Stagecoach and Compass were contacted for a comment.

The tricky tests awaiting Andy Burnham after Labour conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

1. The budgetThis is the most difficult event on the horizon for Burnham, set for 28 October, as the global economic picture continues to look bad in the face of the Iran war pushing up energy prices and wider inflation. Burnham’s chancellor, John Healey, has little room for manoeuvre, with government debt interest payments rising and his headroom shrinking. Big decisions on spending are likely to be put off until a bigger fiscal event in the spring, in the hope that the economic picture improves before then. But it will be difficult to maintain a mood of hope and optimism when Healey will have little good economic news to hold up. The best they can manage might be targeted help on the cost of living for those struggling the most with energy bills. A key date will be 25 November, when the energy regulator announces the next price cap for January, as there are warnings that prices could have to rise hugely in response to surging gas costs. The government will also have to decide whether to extend the freeze on fuel duty, which is due to finish at the end of the year. Some Labour MPs would like to see moves towards big wealth taxes to help plug the gap in the public finances, while Healey’s hands are tied by the manifesto promise not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT.
 2. The EU resetThis is an opportunity for Burnham to get some credit among pro-EU voters on the left and centre, if he can make some progress on closer ties with Europe. Building on work done by Keir Starmer’s administration, the UK is trying to break down more of the trade barriers caused by Brexit. However, there are still key sticking points in the relationship, including rows over Brussels’s “made in Europe” policy prioritising procurement within the bloc, which will disadvantage the UK and others such as Canada and Japan. There is no fixed date for talks but movement is expected this autumn, possibly in the first two weeks of November.
 3. The challenge of Zack PolanskiBurnham’s hopes of winning back more progressive voters lost to the Greens will be put to the test on 8 October in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Labour’s council leader candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, is pitted against Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, who lives in north London. The party hopes Burnham’s bounce in the polls will be enough for them to hold on to this traditional stronghold, the former seat of Starmer. However, the Greens hope voters will be tempted by a free hit to make the government take notice of leftwing concerns and the lure of having a high-profile figure on the left representing them. If Labour wins convincingly, it will be a sign that Burnham is starting to make progress with Labour-to-Green defectors over issues ranging from Gaza to benefit cuts.
 4. Oil and gas drillingBurnham’s government has repeatedly signalled that it is more open to allowing new oil and gas drilling under existing licences in the North Sea than the previous administration. His energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, looked set to approve the Jackdaw field and later Rosebank, but these decisions have been delayed – some would say so as not to cause a row at Labour conference or ahead of the Holborn byelection. When the green light comes through, expect widespread dismay from environmental groups and warnings that Burnham needs to take the climate emergency more seriously. He will get a chance to set out his thinking on the UK’s commitment to meeting its net zero target at the Cop31 climate change conference in Turkey in November.
 5. Disability benefits and wider welfare spendingOne of the trickiest subjects for any Labour prime minister is welfare spending, which is particularly sensitive after Starmer was forced by his backbenchers to retreat from £35bn in disability benefit cuts. This autumn, a review by the minister Stephen Timms concluded that the disability benefit known as the personal independence payment (Pip) was not fit for purpose, while Alan Milburn, the adviser on health, has also conducted his review on getting young people off benefits and into work. The government will decide in the coming months how to proceed with reforming the system, while trying not to antagonise either its MPs or voters. Burnham has signalled he is prepared to look at changes but in a “Labour way” that is aimed at helping people into work rather than making savings. At the same time, there will be pressure from the Treasury not to come up with any solution that leads to rising costs.
 6. Public control of servicesBurnham has made putting essential services under greater public control a key plank of his premiership but it remains to be seen whether his bold aims will survive the realities of office. The government will have to make a decision soon on what to do about Thames Water, which is due to run out of money this autumn. Full nationalisation could be expensive, especially if creditors challenge the terms of any government decision to tip the company into administration in order to take it over. The company, which has debts of £20bn, is now in effect being controlled by a group of 100 hedge funds and distressed-debt investors.
 7. The Chagos conundrumBurnham was sitting next to Trump as the US president laid into the deal to give up sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, claiming it was a disastrous idea to lose control of a strategically important military base. The US president suggested the UK would reconsider its agreement to relinquish and lease back the base, and Burnham did not demur. But that leaves the prime minister and the UK government in the uncomfortable position of having to renegotiate or scrap a draft deal agreed by Starmer. It may not be his most pressing problem but it is a thorny international one that is taking up attention.
 8. Small boats and migrationBurnham now has a wealth of data to show small boat arrivals and migration overall is reducing. But the issue is still going to be an extremely controversial one for the government this autumn, with Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, set to finalise her package of changes to settled status very soon. Under the plans, she wants to make migrants wait longer before being eligible for settled status in the UK, which allows them to claim benefits and access NHS services. The most difficult element is that she wants to apply these changes to people who are already in the country, alongside a series of other changes to the migration system, including forcibly deporting families who refuse to comply with removal orders. Mahmood has been consulting on some of her proposals and it is possible some of them will be watered down.

Henry Harris’ vegetarian recipe for French onion and parsley soup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

When I was a child, my mother often made onions in white sauce to serve with roast lamb. I loved their thick, velvety texture and how they brought richness, sweetness and even more savouriness to a good Sunday lunch. A similarly thick tangle of onions features in the classic soupe à l’oignon gratinée, which can’t really be mimicked without a deep, dark, beefy stock, so rather than even try, it’s best to introduce another layer of flavour entirely. The parsley here yields a very different end result that also proves to be rather comforting.
Onion and parsley soup
Prep 15 min
Cook 1 hr 15 min
Serves 4-6
125g unsalted butter
  6 large onions, peeled and finely sliced
Salt and black pepper
  2 bay leaves
  1 litre vegetable stock
  250ml double cream
  1 large bunch flat-leaf parsley, picked
75g emmental (suitable for vegeatarians), finely grated
4 tbsp croutons
Melt the butter in a large, heavy pan on a medium heat, then add the sliced onions. Season generously with pepper and a little salt, add the bay leaves, then cover and leave to cook gently for 45 minutes to an hour, stirring regularly, until the onions have sweated down to the softest vegetable mass – you want to take them to the point when, were you to squeeze them in your hands, they would turn to a pulp.
Add the stock, simmer for 10 minutes, then stir in the cream and cook for another five minutes. Taste and add more salt and pepper if needed.
At the very last minute, finely chop the parsley, stir it into the soup and ladle immediately into warmed bowls. Serve topped with the grated cheese and a few croutons.
- 
  Henry Harris is chef/co-owner of Bouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40. To order a copy for £36, go to guardianbookshop.com

Of course you can be English if you’re not white. So why can’t the right leave the question alone? | Jason Okundaye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:00:27 UTC
14:00:27 KST

Can you be English and non-white? It’s a question that keeps stubbornly resurfacing in our political discourse.
Last weekend, the former prime minister Rishi Sunak gave his view in a column in the Times, arguing that national identity should not be turned into a DNA test. After leaving office, Sunak, the UK’s first prime minister of colour, was subject to claims by a prominent podcaster that he was not English because he was a “brown-skinned Hindu”. Reflecting on this, Sunak described it as a “reverse Tebbit test”: the sociological concept measuring the loyalty of immigrants – and their children – in the UK depending on which cricket team they supported in international matches. “Once we say that this or that person isn’t really English or British because they are not white,” he wrote, “then we are on a very slippery slope. Some people will argue that English is an ethnic identity and British a civic identity. Though if you think those nuances are heard by most people, I fear you are being rather – perhaps even wilfully – naive.”
Sunak is right that this conversation isn’t really about nuanced distinctions between ethnic and civic identities. The questioning of one’s Englishness is deeply insidious, as it is not solely articulated through supposed “legitimate concerns” about the pace of immigration, crimes committed by migrants or ethnic minorities, or anxieties around jobs and access to public services. Instead, it is presented as a question of first principles: whether you are a “good” or “bad” minority, a citizen or non-citizen, your ancestry or skin colour means you will never truly belong. Your claim to belong in this country, and that of your descendants, will always be implicitly lesser than those who could, at least theoretically, trace their ancestry back to Oswald of Northumbria. That idea is deeply uncomfortable for many, rejected both by those who hold progressive views on immigration and community integration, and those who otherwise hold conservative views of national belonging and hardened borders.
There is growing concern among sections of the British right about increasingly “ethnonationalist” impulses emerging on its fringes and entering mainstream political debate. That has particularly gathered steam with the rise of Rupert Lowe’s hard-right Restore Britain. These beliefs belong to what the Financial Times’s Robert Shrimsley described as the right’s own “woke wing”, which fusses over “the great replacement theory and the betrayal of the west”. More moderate conservatives will want to distance themselves from these views as much as they will from the black-clad far-right mobs that descended on Portsmouth and Dover this summer.
There are indications that some of these views are gaining greater public legitimacy. An analysis by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) last year found that the percentage of those who believed “Britishness” was something you were born with had almost doubled in two years (from 19% to 36%). But there are reasons for those on the right to worry that the popularisation of these once-fringe views could alienate them from the majority, who still reject them. According to the IPPR analysis, only 3% of people believe that being a “good” British citizen requires having white skin, while at least 74% of English people believe that Englishness is not defined by ethnicity. The hard right’s attachment to a politics of ethnicity also threatens to upend a project that the broader conservative movement has been at pains to build over the years: a multi-ethnic coalition that can hold anti-immigration views without the Englishness or Britishness of its own members being called into question. That means maintaining a definition of national belonging that minorities can actually attain.
So it may feel curious to see the Tory traditionalist Jacob Rees-Mogg, no ally of Sunak, release a series of videos on X stating that “everyone who has a British passport is equally British or English” and positing that the English are “a mongrel people, not an Aryan master race”. But the desire to openly define Englishness, and Britishness, in exclusively ethnic terms remains relatively fringe, and it is not a politics that yet finds a broad coalition. Perhaps unsurprisingly, two of Sunak and Rees-Mogg’s lead opponents were minority politicians on the hard right: Reform spokespersons Suella Braverman, who insists that she cannot be English, and Zia Yusuf, who recasts the argument in familiar culture war terms about those who have “betrayed” our country, and insists that “people are furious about what Rees-Mogg and Sunak are saying”.
That preoccupation over ethnic nationalism isn’t purely a feature of the modern hard right; in 1701, the English writer Daniel Defoe wrote The True-Born Englishman, a poem to defend William III, born a sovereign Prince of Orange, from xenophobic attacks disparaging his lack of ethnic “Englishness”. Defoe wrote: “Thus from a mixture of all kinds began, / That het’rogeneous thing, an Englishman”, referring to the English, as Rees-Mogg did, as a “mongrel half-bred race”. That speaks to something that is worth remembering when questions about who gets to be English recur: it has never been a property passed down intact from one generation of ethnically pure Englishmen to the next. Instead, it has continually been remade through migration, assimilation, conquering, marriage, conversion and settlement.
Attempts to impose a simplified ancestry-based definition quickly become absurd, as Lowe saw when, in August, he could not answer whether or not he would consider King Charles, whose father was born in Greece and who has German and Danish ancestry, a “white Briton”. But even a more inclusive civic-nationalist definition of Englishness raises questions with no settled answer: is it defined simply through citizenship or through language, accents, behaviours, “values”, culinary preferences or sporting affiliation? For those who believe that it is an ethnic identity based on ancestry, how many generations back must you be able to trace your lineage?
Even if ethnonationalist views are stymied by more moderate voices on the contemporary right, the surfacing of these discourses is still deeply troubling for many ethnic minorities. Its traction may, for now, be limited, but it still risks contributing to a “common sense” assumption that there is something like a pure English ethnicity determined by race. Interestingly, ethnic-minority adults themselves are more likely to view Englishness as tied to heritage, and prefer an identification with Britishness. I can’t speculate on each individual’s reluctance, but it doesn’t displace a simple truth: there is no single, historically fixed population from which today’s “English” have descended. From the Celts, the Romans, the Anglo-Saxons, the Vikings, the Normans, the Huguenots, Jewish and Irish communities – England is ancestrally mixed. That waves of arrivals over the past century have been Caribbean, African and South Asian has only made this more observable.
For those who believe Englishness is threatened and marginalised by demographic change, it is precisely this process that has allowed it to endure: continued participation and attachment, not bloodlines and biological inheritance. Even if the ethnonationalist right wants to project a future based on a kind of racial nostalgia, English history itself offers very little support for it. It is a politics with nowhere to go.
- 
  Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian

Perth is now the only capital without a major writers' festival
