US Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use database to check voter citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:54:45 UTC
05:54:45 KST

The US Supreme Court has granted a Trump administration request to allow the use of a federal database to weed out potential non-citizens from the voter rolls.
A majority of the nine justices on the top court joined the unsigned opinion, providing a victory to President Donald Trump ahead of the November mid-term elections.
The three liberal justices on the conservative-dominated court dissented.
Trump has stated for years that many non-citizens vote in US elections and that mail-in ballots are vulnerable to fraud.
Friday's Supreme Court decision lifted a lower court order that had blocked the use of a Department of Homeland Security program known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) to verify the citizenship of individuals on the voter rolls.
SAVE is used to identify citizenship status to determine whether someone is eligible for benefits.
Ruling against the Trump administration in June, the lower court said, "States have partnered with the federal government to access the database and are actively removing United States citizens from voter rolls based on inaccurate information.
In its ruling, the Supreme Court said the federal government "has an obligation to respond to requests from state and local election officials seeking to verify the citizenship of voters."
The lower court order blocking the use of SAVE "prevents the Federal Government from using the programme it believes is best suited to the task."
“Victory for election integrity”
US Attorney General Todd Blanche welcomed the Supreme Court ruling as a "huge victory for election integrity," saying it will "allow states to clear the voter rolls of illegal voters."
Election experts, however, said the ruling is unlikely to have a major impact on the November elections because most US states ban purges of voters 90 days ahead of an election.
"Both the majority and dissent agree that this case is likely to have limited impact on the midterms," Rick Hasen, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, said in a blog post.
"Compared to the recent mail-in voting case, this one is not very important substantively."
Hasen was referring to a Supreme Court decision earlier this month that blocked a Trump plan that would have restricted the use of mail-in ballots.
Trump reacted furiously to that ruling, calling it "horrible" in a Truth Social post.

Sudanese army says it captured strategic North Kordofan city of Sodiri

Adel Abdelrheem, Rania Abushamala

The Sudanese army said Friday it had seized control of Sodiri in North Kordofan state after fierce clashes with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
“Our forces liberated the city of Sodiri in North Kordofan state today after fierce battles that inflicted heavy losses in personnel and equipment on the terrorist militia,” the army said in a statement, referring to the RSF.
The announcement followed accounts from military sources who told Anadolu earlier Friday that army troops and allied forces had entered Sodiri and taken control after intense fighting with the RSF.
Sodiri has been a key RSF stronghold in northern North Kordofan. It lies near Hamrat al-Sheikh and Umm Badr, close to the borders with North Darfur to the west and West Kordofan to the south.
Army personnel and members of allied armed movements also posted videos on social media that they said were filmed inside Sodiri after its capture. The footage showed destroyed combat vehicles they said belonged to the RSF.
The RSF had not commented on the developments as of 1845GMT.
The army’s reported capture of Sodiri follows a series of advances elsewhere in North Kordofan that have increased pressure on RSF forces in the state’s far northwest, particularly around Al-Mazrub, Jabra al-Sheikh and Umm Badr.
It also comes days after the army announced that it had captured 11 areas in North Kordofan, one of its largest reported advances in the state in recent weeks. On Sept. 6, the army said it had taken Hamrat al-Waz in Jabra al-Sheikh locality.
Since late July, the army has reported gaining extensive territory in North Kordofan, including the city of Bara and areas around Jabra al-Sheikh and Umm Sayala. It also said it had secured the main road linking Bara to Omdurman, west of the capital, Khartoum.
Sudan’s three Kordofan states — North, West and South — have witnessed continued clashes between the army and the RSF since last October.
The war between the two sides began in April 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

A Pakistani Muslim cleric honored by Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally has been accused of protecting an alleged extortion gang linked to abductions and torture, The Telegraph reported on Thursday.
The head of the Church of England withdrew an interfaith award from Tahir Ashrafi, Pakistan’s special envoy on interfaith harmony, last week, just six days after presenting it to him.
According to The Telegraph, Ashrafi’s brother allegedly leads a so-called “blasphemy gang” in Pakistan that entraps young men online and blackmails them with threats of prosecution under the country's blasphemy laws. The newspaper said the group was behind “a huge surge” in the number of people jailed for blasphemy in recent years. Blasphemy can carry the death penalty in Pakistan.
Ashrafi has publicly defended his brother and called a judge investigating the alleged gang a “dog,” according to the British newspaper.
Pakistan’s National Commission for Human Rights has said the group used women operating under pseudonyms to lure men into making blasphemous statements online. Those targeted were then frequently detained by “private individuals rather than law enforcement,” subjected to torture and denied access to legal assistance, according to the state human rights watchdog.
Relatives of alleged victims told The Telegraph they were “shocked” to see Ashrafi receive the British award. They claimed the cleric played the “good cop” while his brother acted as the “bad cop,” entrapping and rounding up victims. The newspaper said the relatives were granted anonymity because of fears of reprisals.
Ashrafi has denied any wrongdoing.
The controversy comes amid heightened scrutiny in Britain of crimes linked to gangs involving men of Pakistani heritage, following years of revelations about organized child sexual exploitation in towns and cities across the country.
An inquiry funded by Restore Britain MP Rupert Lowe reported in June that it had identified evidence of grooming gangs operating across 149 of the UK’s 317 local authority districts. The report determined that a “bare minimum” of 250,000 women and girls were raped by grooming gangs since the year 2000, and that senior politicians helped the gangs escape prosecution.

How Shadow Fleet Conceals Its Activities: Details of Such Vessels Revealed by USA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:52:50 UTC
05:52:50 KST

U.S. Coast Guard experts have revealed the technical methods that Russian shadow fleet vessels use to conceal their activities.
The presentation was given at the DEF CON 34 conference, and an analysis of it was prepared by the InformNapalm community.
These vessels actively use methods to spoof data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS).
Several transponders, tools for spoofing coordinates, means of remote access to ship computers, and tools for quickly forging documents were also found on board the vessels.
“One of the most revealing finds is the Russian program Stamp 0.62 for Windows. It allows for the rapid generation of images of ship seals in the event that the ship’s name or IMO number is changed in documents,” InformNapalm reports.
One of the main concealment tools is related to the AIS system, which vessels use to transmit their names, coordinates, and other data.
On some tankers, researchers have detected multiple transponders that can be switched between, as well as equipment and software for transmitting false GPS coordinates.
In simpler cases, the crew could physically restrict the antenna’s operation and thus stop the signal from being transmitted.
At the same time, the onboard IT infrastructure is often quite rudimentary.
Researchers found pirated navigation programs, software from torrent forums, and common remote access tools such as AnyDesk, TeamViewer, and ScreenConnect, which could operate without the crew’s authorization.
During some operations, external operators attempted to remotely erase data from the ship’s systems after the vessel had already been detained. They use off-the-shelf digital tools for this purpose, so changing a vessel’s name, flag, or identity may be accompanied not only by a false AIS signal but also by a corresponding set of documents.
Currently, vessels from Russia’s shadow fleet are being actively intercepted by European Union forces. Recently, the Italian Navy intercepted an oil tanker from Russia’s shadow fleet in the Mediterranean Sea.

Bahrain commits to joining US-led Falcon Strike task force, buying more air defense systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:42:50 UTC
05:42:50 KST

Rania R.a. Abushamala
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Bahrain has committed to joining the US Central Command’s Task Force Falcon Strike and purchasing additional US munitions and air defense systems, the US Embassy in Manama said Friday.
The commitment was made during a Military Consultative Committee meeting held Wednesday and Thursday co-chaired by US Deputy Assistant Defense Secretary Michael DiMino and Bahraini Defense Minister Lt. Gen. Abdullah bin Hassan Al-Nuaimi, the embassy said on US social media company X.
“Bahrain committed to join USCENTCOM’S Task Force Falcon Strike and purchase more U.S. munitions and air defense systems,” the embassy said.
The steps would strengthen Bahrain’s efforts to become “stronger, more interoperable, and more capable of providing for its own defense,” it added.
The US military’s CENTCOM announced the creation of Falcon Strike in August, describing it as the first multinational, multidomain task force for attack drones. On Aug. 13, it said US and allied personnel would operate one-way attack drones and unmanned systems in the air, on the sea surface and underwater.
Bahrain’s commitment comes amid efforts by the US and regional partners to strengthen defense coordination in the Gulf as tensions in the region rise.
Manama hosted a security dialogue involving 12 countries in July that addressed defense cooperation and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

The head of Yemen's governing body on Friday called for a general mobilisation to counter the Iran-backed Houthis, as the group ramps up attacks on government forces and their Saudi backer.
His call comes weeks after Yemen's fragmented government was dealt a major blow by the Houthis, who seized control of the country's entire Red Sea coast and are still fighting its forces in Yemen and attacking Saudi ships and territory.
"I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilisation and national mobilisation, to rally around their armed and security forces," Rashid al-Alimi, who heads the Presidential Leadership Council and is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a speech.

Anyone defecting from the Houthis to the government side will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty, he added.

We're getting hacked constantly. What can Australians do?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:39:16 UTC
05:39:16 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Hacking attacks have become so common that keeping data safe feels like an impossible task, with some cybersecurity experts saying the system is "fundamentally broken".
Mihai Lazarescu worked for years as a 'white hat' hacker finding vulnerabilities in computer systems, and says organisations simply don't have the resources to effectively manage the threats.
The cyber security consultant, who is an associate professor at Curtin University, says news this week that Australia's Medicare statistics portal was hacked — the first known hack of an Australian government website by an agentic AI agent — is another example of the challenges involved in keeping data secure online.
While no personal information was believed to have been accessed, it follows major data breaches involving businesses including Origin Energy, Optus and Medibank in recent years, in which personal data was accessed or stolen.
"My experience dealing with different organisations — ranging from small businesses to banks — is that they struggle to find enough resources to cover [cyber security]," Lazarescu tells SBS News.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Even if they have the funds to protect their systems, finding people with the right skills is difficult.
The reality is that if people want to get to your data [and] it is available, they'll probably find a way to do it.
Lazarescu says continuing to place data online at the same rate "makes no sense" and the system is "fundamentally broken".
"We can't protect things, and now you have this emergence of automatic agents, why do we keep going it?"
Lazarescu says consumers need to push for change.
"If there's no pushback, this is going to keep going."
Should we go back to paper records?
In recent years, there's been a trend towards putting everything online, but given the security risks, Lazarescu questions why it's necessary for businesses, especially telcos and power companies providing essential services, to store their customer data on the internet.
These businesses have millions of customers, which means a cybersecurity breach has the potential to impact significant numbers of people.
Almost 10 million people had personal information accessed in 2022 when Optus' system was hacked, and around 10,000 had their data published on the dark web.
The hack of Origin Energy in July impacted almost one million current and former customers.
The number of hacking attacks is rising, with the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner saying it received 1,205 data breach notifications in 2025, an increase of 8 per cent from the previous year.
Until a system is developed that enables information to be stored securely, Lazarescu says some businesses should consider returning to paper records, something that was functional in the past.
I've seen all kind of benefits being touted [to putting stuff online]. I haven’t seen yet any evidence that [it's] paying off.
Lazarescu points out the internet is essentially "unsecurable", arguing its underlying protocols were designed in an era when computers were primarily being used to link academics at different universities and assumed users were trustworthy.
"At the fundamental level [it] can't be secured unless we have an internet 2.0, and I can’t see anybody trying to do that," he says.
This makes putting stuff online a "comprehensively bad thing to do".
But Rahat Masood, a senior lecturer at the School of Computer Sciences and Engineering at the University of New South Wales, is sceptical about whether returning to paper records is practical.
She says technology has advanced and a significant increase in printing could also increase carbon emissions.
"The only solution I can see is public awareness and sharing less data, and companies collecting less data," Masood tells SBS News.
Rethinking data collection
While companies should be minimising the amount of personal information they hold, they often have limited incentives to delete data once it has been collected. Masood says many companies earn money from selling data.
It’s now common for businesses to ask for personal details from customers even when some of that information may not be essential to providing the service.
Masood points to Medicare card details being stolen during the recent Quest Apartment Hotels data breach.
Why do you need the Medicare [details to rent an] apartment?
The Quest hack raises questions about not only what information businesses collect, but also how long they retain it. Some impacted customers told the media they had last interacted with the business years ago.
Masood says data should only be stored when it is needed, and then deleted after a certain time period, including when a person dies.
While fines of up to $2.5 million for a person, and up to $50 million or other substantial penalties for a company, depending on the circumstances, can be issued for privacy breaches in Australia, Masood points out that laws are often not enforced.
She believes companies operating in Australia should be audited to ensure they are meeting the requirements of the Privacy Act 1988. This regulates how government agencies as well as some organisations, including those with an annual turnover of more than $3 million, handle personal information.
Changes should also be made so that people are given user-friendly and concise information about companies' privacy policies, instead of pages of terms and conditions they don't understand.
Masood says customers need simple information about what type of data is stored on business servers, how it is used, why it is needed, the potential consequences of this data storage, as well as who they can contact with issues.
"It's not a difficult task, it's just that companies don't want to do it."
More accountability needed
Jacqueline Boaks, a lecturer at Curtin University who specialises in business ethics, says there's often a sense of inevitability around AI and a sense of powerlessness that anything can be done to stop it, but she argues that societies have well-established laws to hold people morally and legally responsible for creating and releasing a product that does harm.
"We shouldn't forget that, just because something's digital and not physical," she tells SBS News.
We as a community and as the government need to have an expectation morally and ethically around who is accountable and who is responsible when [hacks] happen.
Boaks says it's impossible for individuals to oversee how their data is managed by companies or to opt out of services such as Medicare.
"[This] is a pretty vulnerable place to be, but it does seem to be exactly the kind of thing that we have a right to expect governments to protect us from," she says.
"That's one of their core roles."
But Boaks says there's often a disconnect between the level of harm done through these data leaks and the consequences faced by companies.
Lazarescu agrees the consequences are not serious enough for companies to change their practices.
What happens when you have a breach? Do you see anything in terms of people being held accountable? Organisations being held accountable?
Lazarescu, who grew up in Romania under Communist Party rule, is also sensitive to what could happen if more aspects of people's lives move into digital systems, particularly if governments can easily erase people.
"To me the biggest problem with putting stuff online is that you can also modify it online."
What can people do to protect their data?
Leaders such as United States President Donald Trump have rejected the need for stronger AI regulation, and Trump has also criticised Australia's plan for digital duty of care laws that would give residents the option to opt out of algorithmic feeds.
But Lazarescu says this doesn't mean every American agrees with the Trump administration's position.
People have a lot more power and they need to be engaged and tell the politicians enough is enough.
At an individual level, Lazarescu and Masood warn against sharing anything online unless it is absolutely necessary.
This includes posting on social media, which can allow companies to build detailed profiles of users, avoiding unnecessary sharing of documents such as passport copies, and not entering sensitive details into AI programs such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and other large language models.
"It's very crucial now," Masood says. "You need to be minimising the data yourself."

Extra cash for some Australians — and a card surcharge shake-up looms

Major Australian companies are sending billions of dollars to shareholders’ bank accounts as dividend payment season ramps up.
BHP, which is Australia’s largest listed organisation, delivered US$5 billion ($7.12 billion) in dividends to its investors on Wednesday.
That means its 450,000 retail shareholders may have received a fully franked final dividend of $1.38 for each share they hold in BHP.
It’s been a big year for the so-called “Big Australian” after copper became the company’s largest earnings contributor for the first time.
The nation’s most widely held stock is Telstra, though, with an estimated 1 million shareholders.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
On Thursday it delivered its final dividend of 10.5 cents per share, paying out $1.2 billion dollars over the last financial year.
Of course, not all shareholders elect to receive dividends into their bank account, with some opting to reinvest that payment instead.
Millions of Australians have exposure to shares like BHP and Telstra through their superannuation fund.
Credit and debit card surcharges are going
It might be worth paying closer attention at the checkout next week to see how businesses are handling new credit and debit card surcharge rules.
From 1 October, those surcharges will be banned, eliminating the fee that is added to the price of goods and services.
It means the advertised price of a product should be the price you pay at the checkout.
Right now, a $5 coffee, for example, might actually be $5.08 when a surcharge is applied.
While the RBA has reduced some background fees associated with card payments to help small businesses make the change, they’ll still incur an expense, which means many will be forced to decide whether to absorb it or pass it on to customers.
So, from 1 October, will that $5 coffee still be advertised as $5, or will it go up to $5.08 or more?
Sarah Megginson from consumer group Finder says some small businesses may look to other forms of payment to reduce costs.
“You can use PayID and bank transfers, which transfer instantly, so you might see small businesses turn to these more affordable ways to accept cash,” she told the SBS On the Money Podcast.
Some larger businesses are doing away with card payments altogether as a direct result of the changes.
DEFT, an online secure payment system used by thousands of renters and homeowners, no longer accepts debit or credit card payments, instead pointing customers to payment options like PayID, BPAY or Australia Post.
To fund the changes, banks are also making adjustments through rewards cards, annual fees and bonus points restructuring,
Not all fees and surcharges are disappearing with these new rules, though, because they don’t extend to weekend or public holiday surcharges, booking fees, or service fees.
Interest rates may still rise despite a higher jobless rate
Earlier this week, Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock warned the unemployment rate may need to rise to as much as 5 per cent to help ease inflation, which in turn could lower interest rates.
Fresh ABS data on Thursday revealed more people are now in the workforce or looking for work, which could be a sign of cost of living pressures, while of the near 40,000 jobs created last month, they were all part-time, suggesting many may have been related to Census workers.
The headline jobless rate has climbed from 4.5 per cent to 4.6 per cent, which is a near five-year high.
Westpac senior economist Pat Bustamante says the RBA is still likely to lift interest rates on Tuesday.
“We think a September hike is locked in and reflects the data we’ve already seen,” Bustamante said. “Going forward, particularly in November, if the labour market eases a bit more than what they’re expecting, we can see them pause and wait.”
Higher inflation will likely prompt the bank to pull the trigger, which is only likely to get worse, according to HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham, who has two more interest rate rises this year pencilled in.
Bloxham says this is because overseas factors are adding to inflation, like higher fuel prices from the Middle East war, unfavourable weather and El Niño driving up food prices, and the AI investment boom.

Russian historian Yuri Dmitriev, who uncovered mass graves of victims of Soviet repression, transferred to hospital with suspected stroke, rights group says
Historian Yuri Dmitriev, 70, was rushed from Penal Colony No. 18 in Mordovia to a prison medical facility in the village of Barashevo after a suspected stroke, the human rights group ZPCh reported.
A source for the rights group questioned whether the facility could treat him. “I doubt this prison medical facility has the equipment needed to diagnose and treat him. […] Yuri Alexeyevich needs to be transferred to a city hospital. His lawyer must also be allowed to see him immediately. On Saturday, September 26, the lawyer will try to visit Yuri Dmitriev, but I’m almost certain they won’t let him in over the weekend,” the source said.
Dmitriev is a historian and former head of Memorial in Karelia. In 1997, he found mass graves of victims of Soviet repression in the Sandarmokh forest. He also compiled memorial lists of Karelia residents who had been subjected to political repression.
Dmitriev has been in custody since 2016, when he was accused of producing pornography involving his underage adopted daughter, committing lewd acts against her, and illegally possessing a firearm part. The case stemmed from photographs of his daughter found in his possession. Dmitriev denied the allegations, saying he had taken the photos solely for medical reasons, to track the child’s development. In April 2018, a court acquitted him of two charges but sentenced him to three and a half years of restrictions on his movements for the weapons offense. Karelia’s Supreme Court overturned that ruling, and authorities opened another criminal investigation into sexual assault allegations against Dmitriev. He was sentenced to 13 years in a penal colony in that case. In December 2021, a court in Petrozavodsk combined the sentences and gave him 15 years in a high-security penal colony.
More than 150 Russian cultural figures and more than 400 foreign scholars signed joint letters in support of Dmitriev. Nobel Prize in Literature laureates Herta Müller and Svetlana Alexievich, along with Goncourt Prize winner Jonathan Littell, have also spoken out in his support. Memorial considers Dmitriev a political prisoner.

Thieves Stole ‘Nvidia’ Trailers. They Got 20 Tons of Sand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:30:40 UTC
05:30:40 KST

On Thursday morning, a top executive at self-driving truck developer PlusAI received an unexpected congratulatory text message from an acquaintance. “I have been proud of you for your adventure and success at Plus. Just saw two of your trucks near my work place! :)” the message said.
But PlusAI’s trucks weren’t supposed to be near this person’s office, in Newark, California. As of the last the company knew, the trailers were docked outside its warehouse, half a mile away. Soon, according to a police statement, cops were on the scene to help recover the two trailers, emblazoned with logos for PlusAI and Nvidia, the most valuable company in the world. The two companies are working together on AI software and autonomous truck technology.
That’s when PlusAI employees gave police a hint as to why whoever hooked their own cabs up to the trailers and drove away might have abandoned the whole thing after breaking them open: Each trailer was full of about 20,000 pounds of sand.
“PlusAI uses simulated loads in its trailers to assist with research and development testing,” says Lauren Kwan, a company spokesperson. The trailers were recovered with “40,000 pounds of sand intact.”
PlusAI’s tech-enabled truck cabs—where the driver typically sits and controls the vehicle—were parked inside its warehouse and weren’t taken, Kwan says. The trailers were secured with hand locks, which were broken.
The case is under investigation, and no arrests have been made, says Amy Gee, a spokesperson for the Fremont Police Department.
Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The incident comes at a time of rising theft targeting high-value computer equipment, especially chips and other electronics meant for use in data centers. In August, WIRED revealed two California incidents in which thieves deliberately struck the vehicles of security escorts that follow high-value tech loads to ensure they reach their destinations. The trucks involved were then driven to another destination. As of August, millions of dollars of data center equipment onboard had not been recovered.
This year, thieves have also targeted Tesla batteries and various bitcoin mining machines. Authorities have arrested suspects in some cases, but many crimes remain unsolved.
Some of the most common targets of cargo theft in recent months across the US include metals and enterprise-grade computer and networking equipment, according to Verisk CargoNet, an analytics and risk assessment firm.
This story has a happier ending. By Thursday afternoon, the sand trailers were back with PlusAI, the Fremont Police Department said.

Stunning free kick shows Irankunda's star is aligning for Socceroos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:29:50 UTC
05:29:50 KST

analysis
Nestory Irankunda's magical free kick against Brazil a sign of a special Socceroos star
With some players, there's always a moment in their career that, years into the future, you can look back on as a beacon of when they truly announced themselves.
Perhaps we will be able to point to a stunning free kick for the ages as that moment in the young career of Nestory Irankunda.
Neither, you suspect, will Chelsea wonder kid Estêvão.
The 19-year-old probably had the best view of anyone, lying at the base of the four-man wall looking back towards Hugo Souza.
He could see, with devastating precision, the ball fly over him and into the top corner, Souza skittishly crabbing across his line before admitting defeat.
It might be fun to wonder what was going through Estêvão's mind as he rolled onto his back to stare into the sky above the Townsville stadium.
Whatever he was thinking, Irankunda was already flipping towards the corner flag.
"I mean, good goal, good goal," he told Channel 10, the confidence of youth oozing from his voice as he was asked about his free kick.
"I've done it before and to do it again today against a top team in Brazil, it's amazing.
"Sometimes [when I try it], the ball goes outside the training ground. Sometimes I miss completely.
"For it to go in today, it felt good. You see there, beautiful."
Estêvão already had first-hand experience of Irankunda's slipperiness: on the half hour mark the Sporting forward showed brilliant balance to turn the Chelsea man and then exploded with power to dance away up field.
That, almost as much as the goal, was a moment worth remembering, an Aussie displaying the audacity to spin a Brazilian in the middle of the pitch.
"There were some big stars out tonight," Irankunda said on Channel 10, marvelling at the crowds that had come out to support both Australia and Brazil.
"But we've got some big stars too."
That is true, but already Irankunda deserves to be considered one that could burn among the brightest.
Having made the move to Portuguese giants Sporting from Watford in the off-season, Irankunda has not quite had time to make his mark yet.
Only once in five games has he started in the Portuguese Primeira Liga, and he is yet to provide an assist or score a goal.
But given this moment against Brazil, a team that still carries the romance of an illustrious past despite a 24-year-and-counting absence from the World Cup final, one wonders whether the ripples through the lusophone world may just nudge those in power at the Lisbon giants to afford him greater chances to prove his worth.
It certainly caught the eye of the club's social media team, who slapped a "GOLAÇO" label on it within three minutes of the net rippling 16,844 kilometres away.
Of course there must be caveats.
Brazil were most certainly off-colour, "average" according to Bruno Guimarães's damning assessment post-match.
In the first half at least, it was the Socceroos who were bossing the game, charging forward, rampaging through a fragile Brazilian midfield that still seems bruised from its last-16 defeat at the World Cup a few months ago, crafting the chances, delivering the crosses and winning the corners.
Of course Brazil started to turn it on. With the quality up front that they had, how could they not?
Endrick of Real Madrid. Raphinha of Barcelona. Estêvão of Chelsea. Vinícius Júnior of Real Madrid. Despite an atrocious pitch, which rolled up like a cheap carpet at a shabby motel, Brazil's bevvy of stars began to knock the ball around with the playful nonchalance of men who are all too aware of their own brilliance.
But it was their lesser lights, Flamengo pair Samuel Lino and Pedro, as well as Bournemouth's Rayan who finally made the breakthrough.
And it was Irankunda who provided the stand-out moment of the game.
It is his liveliness and confidence imbues in the Socceroos a dash of verve and belief in their own abilities.
Playing on the left, cutting back inside and posing a threat from set pieces, Irankunda has the sort of aura that few Socceroos players in recent years can command.
His ability to cut back inside and unleash with that right foot, just as he did inside the opening 10 minutes to force a fine save from Hugo Souza, is explosive.
Tony Popovic only made three changes from the side that started the game against Egypt in the World Cup but playing Irankunda left was so decisive, the pain of seeing him so wasted as a target man in Dallas surely enough to forever wipe that option from Popovic's mind.
Yengi played his part centrally as a willing runner and constant menace to an inexperienced Brazilian back four, while the Seleção's pitiful midfield was readily overrun by fullbacks Jacob Italiano and Aziz Behich, with Paul Okon-Engstler's driving runs from midfield the telling factor in winning the free kick that Irankunda so magnificently placed into the net.
Brazil may prove to be better in Brisbane.
A quiet night may have those who were singing Irankunda's praises on Friday bemoaning a lack of consistency by Tuesday.
But given he is showing himself repeatedly capable of such brilliance, it seems unlikely to be long before the next career-defining moment will come along.

Ukraine’s soldiers cracked problem US chased for 30 years: a drone that ferries combat robot deep into enemy rear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:29:02 UTC
05:29:02 KST

Ukrainian soldiers have built a drone that carries a combat ground robot into battle and drops it where needed, a trick the US has pursued but never fielded. The Alter Ego battalion of the 93rd Mechanized Brigade has paired a bomber drone with a purpose-built robot, the Desantnyk, and took it from idea to combat in 10 days, the Brave1 defense cluster said.
The system answers a problem that has long hobbled ground robots: getting them to the fight over mined, cratered terrain they cannot cross on their own.
A drone carries the robot dozens of kilometers behind the lines and drops it precisely, in a pairing engineers call a "marsupial", one carrier delivering another. The US worked on such systems for more than 30 years, Brave1 said.
And it is not alone: the 3rd Army Corps has been air-dropping robots behind Russian lines in its Vivaldi offensive.
A drone carries the robot in
The Desantnyk is a compact wheeled platform. Alter Ego built a way to release it accurately from a heavy bomber drone, dropping it well beyond the range a ground robot could reach on its own. It lands deep in the enemy rear and drives on to its target. The point is to spare the robot the most dangerous, exposed leg of the journey.
Confirmed kills follow fast
According to Brave1, just 10 days passed from the idea to its first combat use, and the Desantnyk has already carried out confirmed strikes: the unit used it to destroy Russian shelters and troops. Only a handful of Ukrainian units have mastered the tactic so far.
Brave1 moves it to production
The defense cluster, a state platform for scaling battlefield inventions, said it took notice of the Desantnyk and helped the battalion find a manufacturer to move it from prototypes to serial production and out to other units.

EU defense agency says Europe is rearming too slowly to be ready to defend against Russia by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:26:05 UTC
05:26:05 KST

EU defense agency says Europe is rearming too slowly to be ready to defend against Russia by 2030
The EU is not rearming quickly or effectively enough to be ready to defend itself against Russia by 2030, according to a summary of a report prepared by the European Defense Agency for the bloc’s leaders and seen by Reuters.
EU leaders commissioned the report last year to assess progress in strengthening Europe’s defenses. Amid concerns about Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Donald Trump’s calls for Europe to take on more responsibility for its own security, they set a goal of making Europe ready to defend itself by 2030.
But European countries’ current plans “do not seem to meet” the goal of closing gaps in areas including air and missile defense, ground combat, naval forces, ammunition stockpiles, and drones, the European Defense Agency says.
“Tackling the challenges of a contested and deteriorating security environment and the threat posed by Russia’s aggression requires moving further and substantially faster than now to reach defense readiness by 2030,” the report says.
The summary cites progress in EU defense spending, capability development, and industrial readiness. Even so, “the current momentum and increased investment do not yet translate into sufficiently deployable, sustainable and interoperable forces,” it says, and “critical capability gaps remain.” “What has been achieved so far, although unprecedented, is not yet enough,” the report’s authors say.
EU defense ministers are expected to discuss the European Defense Agency’s report in Brussels on Monday, September 28, before it goes to the bloc’s leaders for consideration.
Ukraine
Russia has stepped up strikes on Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications facilities, the Financial Times reports. The strikes have disrupted internet service in Kyiv and raised concerns among Ukrainian officials that Moscow is trying to undermine Ukraine’s digital economy.
In recent days, Russian forces have struck infrastructure belonging to the internet providers Pavutyna, Etherlink, Crazy Network, and Utels, as well as the hosting companies Cityhost and MiroHost. Data centers in Kyiv have also come under attack. One was in a complex that housed Volodymyr Zelensky’s campaign headquarters in 2019.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces struck the “Kyivstar” and “Parkovyi” telecommunications centers overnight on September 24, claiming they provide “communications services and computing capacity for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
According to Ukraine’s Digital Transformation Ministry, strikes on September 23 and 24 temporarily left about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region without internet access.
Ukraine’s national communications commission warned of “temporary disruptions to networks and access to telecommunications services.” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the strikes had also disrupted attack alerts sent to mobile phones.
Ukrainian officials and company executives warn that Russia may be trying to cause wider outages that could threaten the digital infrastructure used by banks, online payment providers, businesses, government services, and the military.
The Financial Times notes that, unlike strikes on individual communications networks, an attack on a data center can affect large numbers of users at once if a single facility is damaged.

Neale the common thread in Fremantle and Brisbane's eerie shared history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:15:47 UTC
05:15:47 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
analysis
As Fremantle and Brisbane meet in AFL grand final their most common thread is Lachie Neale
When Fremantle coach Ross Lyon activated his sub in the fourth quarter of the 2013 grand final against Hawthorn, he scarcely could have believed the impact that player was going to have.
On the odd occasion, the sub would come in and make a serious impact, acting as a spark plug, while on other days, their impact would be negligible.
Fremantle's sub that day came on to replace ruckman Zac Clarke and picked up seven disposals, but it was ultimately in vain as an experienced Hawthorn side held the Dockers at bay.
Fremantle's sub that day was Lachie Neale.
Neale, then 20, would not have believed that he would have to wait 13 years to see the Dockers in another grand final.
He also would not have believed he'd be playing against them in Brisbane colours, looking for a third straight premiership.
It is funny how time works.
Fremantle and the Brisbane Lions both entered the AFL in the mid 90s as the league was undergoing an expansion boom into states outside of Victoria.
Brisbane's entry occurred as the Bears back in 1987 alongside Fremantle's WA rivals West Coast, and while the Eagles found themselves in a grand final within four years and holding the premiership cup within five, the Bears struggled.
The Lions were eventually formed in 1996 when the Bears merged with the Fitzroy Lions, another club that had been haemorrhaging money for years.
West Coast's success saw the AFL expand further into WA with Fremantle chosen as the state's second team with its inaugural season played in 1995.
It is somewhat poetic that the Dockers and Lions are playing against each other in this year's grand final when you consider how closely they are tied together right at the inception of both clubs.
Fremantle's first ever win in the AFL came against the Fitzroy Lions in round 3, 1995, while Fitzroy's last ever AFL win came against Fremantle in round 8, 1996.
Fitzroy's last ever AFL game? You guessed it, against Fremantle in Perth in round 22 of the 1996 season.
Over the three decades that have followed, both Fremantle and Brisbane have had periods of dominance, but never really at the same time until recent years.
Leigh Matthews's arrival as Brisbane's coach at the end of 1999 immediately turned the Lions into a force to be reckoned with.
Matthews masterminded Brisbane to three straight premierships and four straight grand final appearances between 2001 and 2004 before his departure and the aging of that era of Brisbane players left the club in AFL purgatory for the best part of 15 years.
Fremantle had to wait until its ninth season in the AFL to make a finals appearance, and then had to wait another three seasons before it won a final.
Since 2000, Brisbane has made the finals on 14 occasions, while Fremantle has registered 10 post-season trips, yet Brisbane has five premierships to Fremantle's zero.
And tying them together through the last 13 years has been Neale, once the best midfielder for both clubs.
Neale was drafted 58th overall by Fremantle in the 2011 draft.
He was Fremantle's fourth selection that night. The three players selected before him — Tom Sheridan, Hayden Crozier and Alex Forster — played a combined 226 games.
The grand final will be Neale's 321st appearance.
His arrival coincided with Fremantle's first real period of contention under Lyon in the early 2010s.
In Neale's first four seasons, Fremantle won the third-most home and away games in the AFL behind Hawthorn and Sydney.
In that period, the Hawks won three premierships and played in four grand finals, while the Swans played in two grand finals and won one.
Fremantle came away with the one unsuccessful grand final appearance.
While Fremantle was knocking on the door of its first premiership, Brisbane was going through one of the worst periods of its existence.
By 2012, Neale's debut season, just two of Brisbane's triple premiership-winning players — Simon Black and Jonathan Brown — remained on its list.
Memories of Brisbane being one of the AFL's most feared sides were disappearing fast and players on the list originally from outside Queensland wanted to be anywhere but at the club.
Even Brisbane's logo on its jumper had changed, going from the traditional Fitzroy passant lion to a lion with a front-facing head, infamously nicknamed 'The Paddle Pop Lion'.
Fremantle won the first minor premiership in club history in 2015, with Neale becoming one of its most indispensable players, but the Dockers were again denied by Hawthorn, this time in a home preliminary final.
The Dockers cratered spectacularly the following season, dropping from first to third-last, and would not make it back to the finals for another seven seasons.
In dire need of some stability, Brisbane turned to one of the figureheads behind Hawthorn's triple premiership dynasty, Chris Fagan, to be its head coach.
The Lions struggled in Fagan's first two seasons in charge, but Neale had seen the vision and requested a trade to the then-cellar dwellers.
Had Fremantle known what he was about to become, they'd have asked for double what they received in return for him from Brisbane.
Neale's move to Brisbane put him up in lights on Broadway.
The All-Australian jackets, the Brownlow Medal wins and eventually premierships all arrived, leaving him with a resume that undoubtedly has him in the conversation as one of the best players of his generation.
His departure from Fremantle, which looked like someone getting the last life raft out of a sinking ship, proved to be a pivotal moment in the Dockers' trajectory to the grand final as well.
The following year's draft proved to be a watershed moment for Fremantle, as it supercharged its rebuild with the selections of Hayden Young and Caleb Serong.
Having seen Brisbane supplement its young core with shrewd recruitment of seasoned players such as Neale, Charlie Cameron, Josh Dunkley and others, Fremantle has done the same, adding Luke Jackson and Shai Bolton.
For both clubs, the addition of star talent from rival clubs has resulted in an immediate uptick in on-field fortunes.
All of it leads us here, to two teams inextricably linked from their inceptions and still connected by one man.
Now that he has been freed to play, don't be surprised if that one man, Lachie Neale, has a big say in who holds the premiership cup.

The big 'what if': Do those chanting 'from the river to the sea' really mean it? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:15:36 UTC
05:15:36 KST

What if they mean what they are saying?
How many times must we hear “Free Palestine from the river to the sea” at concerts, on university campuses, and city streets?
How many politicians, celebrities, and people of influence must repeat those words before we confront the question hiding in plain sight: What if they actually mean it?
Between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea live approximately seven million Jews. Let us be clear: a Palestinian state replacing Israel across this entire territory is not suggesting a two-state solution.
What happens to the Jews who live there, some for generations?
Where do they go? Who protects them? And what happens if they refuse to leave?
These are not hypothetical questions about a distant future. They concern the survival of a people whose history includes persecution, expulsion, and attempted annihilation.
Yet the international debate increasingly treats Israel’s elimination as a legitimate political aspiration without demanding an explanation of its consequences.
Consider the regional realities.
Israel is surrounded by Arab states that are not liberal democracies. The Palestinian Authority has not held a presidential election since 2005. Hamas, which seized control of Gaza in 2007, perpetrated the October 7 massacre.
In September 2026, the US again denied Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas an entry visa for the UN General Assembly, citing objections to Palestinian leadership conduct. Abbas has also made statements widely condemned as Holocaust denial.
The PA and Hamas are the political institutions and movements against which promises of coexistence must be evaluated.
Israel withdrew its settlements and permanent ground forces from Gaza in 2005. Rather than creating a peaceful model of Palestinian governance alongside Israel, Hamas built military capabilities and ultimately launched October 7.
What credible guarantees would protect seven million Jews suddenly transformed from a sovereign majority into a vulnerable minority?
October 7 was not the whole plan
Evidence uncovered since October 7 makes this question considerably more urgent.
Hamas documents examined by The New York Times revealed that Yahya Sinwar sought to enlist Iran and Hezbollah in a broader assault against Israel.
In July 2023, a senior Hamas official discussed the planned attack with an Iranian Revolutionary Guard commander. According to the reported documents, Iran and Hezbollah welcomed the plan in principle but needed more time to prepare.
Sinwar proceeded.
Meanwhile, Israel subsequently exposed Hezbollah’s preparations for its own invasion of the Galilee.
The IDF reported discovering underground compounds, tunnels, weapons, motorcycles, and operational infrastructure intended to support attacks and military operations on northern Israeli communities.
How can anyone assess the foreseeable consequences of Israel’s elimination while ignoring the intentions and conduct of armed organizations seeking its destruction?
Three choices for seven million Jews
The first choice is departure, but to where?
At the 1938 Évian Conference, most participating countries refused to expand immigration opportunities for Jews fleeing Nazi persecution.
In 1939, the St. Louis, carrying more than 900 Jewish refugees, was denied entry to Cuba and the US. Forced back to Europe, many passengers subsequently perished in the Holocaust.
The second possibility is remaining under Palestinian sovereignty.
Would Hamas protect Jewish religious freedom? Would the PA guarantee Jewish property rights? What independent judiciary, police force, or military would protect Jewish communities against extremists?
The third possibility is resistance.
Millions of Israeli Jews could refuse to surrender their country and fight.
The consequences could include regional war, mass displacement, and catastrophic loss of life.
If a movement knowingly pursues a political objective whose implementation entails mass expulsion or destruction, can its proponents avoid scrutiny simply by calling their objective liberation?
Apply the same genocide standard
Israel has faced accusations of genocide in Gaza. Amnesty International’s December 2024 finding relied on officials’ statements, patterns of conduct, and cumulative consequences. Israel rejects the accusation.
The Genocide Convention requires specific intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part. That intent may be inferred from evidence; it need not be announced explicitly.
Now, apply the same methodology to a movement demanding Israel’s elimination.
Examine its rhetoric and the conduct of organizations pursuing that objective. Examine historical context, foreseeable consequences, and the willingness to accept mass harm.
If the intended outcome of “Free Palestine from the river to the sea” is the forced departure of seven million Jews, the issue is ethnic cleansing.
If the intended outcome includes killing Jews who refuse to leave, or deliberately imposing conditions calculated to destroy them as a group, the issue becomes genocide.
And if advocates knowingly accept such consequences, their declared objective of liberation cannot automatically absolve them of responsibility.
Intent cannot require inference when Israel is accused but suddenly require an explicit confession when Jews are the prospective victims.
Not every demonstrator intends genocide. But those demanding Israel’s elimination must explain how their objective could be implemented without mass expulsion, persecution, or killing.
Why does the Palestinian refugee problem endure?
Following the Holocaust, Jewish survivors were resettled, including in the newly established State of Israel.
Approximately 850,000 Jews left or were expelled from Arab countries and Iran in the decades surrounding Israel’s establishment. Many were absorbed by Israel despite enormous challenges.
The Palestinian refugee question followed a different trajectory.
UNRWA began operations in 1950, serving approximately 750,000 refugees. Today, approximately 5.9 million people, including descendants, are eligible for its services.
Why has a permanent solution proved so elusive?
Could the enduring refugee problem itself have become a strategic instrument in the long-term struggle against Israel?
Harder to understand is why so many in Europe and America have embraced demands framed around eliminating the one Jewish state among a multitude of Arab states.
Diaspora Jews
The danger does not stop at Israel’s borders.
Israel has sovereign institutions, intelligence services, and an army. Diaspora Jews depend on their host governments for protection.
In America, the warning signs are unmistakable.
According to the American Jewish Committee’s 2025 survey, published in February 2026, 91% of American Jews said violent antisemitic attacks had made them feel less safe. Thirty-one percent reported personally experiencing antisemitism during the preceding year.
CNN’s July 2026 analysis found that Israel’s average net favorability had fallen from plus 51 during Trump’s first term to minus 16, a staggering 67-point reversal.
Among Democratic voters, sympathy for Palestinians now exceeds sympathy for Israelis by 60% to 16%.
For Israel, the implications extend to its diplomatic relationships. For American Jews, already confronting rising antisemitism, the changing environment raises additional questions about their security and place in American society.
History has repeatedly demonstrated what happens when Jews become politically powerless, and societies cease to protect them.
The Holocaust is not ancient history. October 7 was less than three years ago.
At the UN this month, the world is being asked to normalize political demands whose implementation could place millions of Jews in existential danger.
Those advocating peaceful coexistence must explain how to achieve it. Those advocating expulsion or destruction must be judged by the same standards applied to anyone threatening a protected population.
And those who chant without considering the consequences must confront the genocidal implications of their words.
Because the concern is no longer just simply what the slogan’s genocidal meaning is.
The concern is what happens if someone attempts to turn it into reality, as Iran and Hamas tried on October 7.
For those of us who laughed at the many demonstrators who couldn’t tell you which river and which sea, perhaps laughing was a very inappropriate response.
What if some of them really mean what they are saying?

The EU lifted sanctions on Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman but extended restrictions on more than 3,000 others for three years. Here’s how that deal works.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:12:51 UTC
05:12:51 KST

The EU lifted sanctions on Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman but extended restrictions on more than 3,000 others for three years. Here’s how that deal works.
What happened?
On September 22, EU countries agreed to remove two Russian billionaires from the sanctions list: USM Holdings founder Alisher Usmanov and Alfa Group co-founder Mikhail Fridman.
They also agreed to extend the broader list, which covers more than 3,000 people and entities, through September 22, 2029. Previously, the list had been reviewed every six months.
Removing Usmanov and Fridman was a key political condition for such a lengthy extension. France demanded Usmanov’s removal and, in return, secured a pardon for one of its citizens in Azerbaijan. Luxembourg demanded Fridman’s removal; the businessman had filed a $16 billion lawsuit against the country.
Why did the whole EU have to heed France and Luxembourg’s demands?
Because EU sanctions decisions require unanimous approval from all 27 member states. Each country has a veto.
That rule also delayed the extension. EU countries failed to reach an agreement in time and, facing the prospect that the entire list could expire, extended it for just seven days — through September 22. That bought them time to negotiate.
The sanctions list was originally due to expire overnight on September 15. On September 14, a day before the deadline, the EU countries’ permanent representatives took the emergency step of extending it temporarily. Usmanov’s case sparked fierce disagreements within the bloc: Slovakia, followed by France, issued an ultimatum demanding that sanctions against him be lifted. The other 25 countries blocked the proposal. Tensions rose further when Luxembourg made a similar demand concerning Fridman.
By September 22, Latvia was the only country still opposed to a compromise. At the last moment, it relented, lifting its veto through a diplomatic procedure known as “constructive abstention.”
As Alyona Vandysheva, executive director of Transparency International Russia, told Meduza, removing the two Russian billionaires from the list was, under the circumstances, the only way to keep all the other sanctions in place:
Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/2161 of September 22, 2026, both extended the entire individual sanctions regime and provided the basis for removing Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the list. There was no separate vote on them. If, say, Estonia had voted against it, the entire sanctions package would have failed.
Has anyone else secured removal from the list this way?
Yes, though other cases aren’t entirely comparable to Usmanov’s and Fridman’s.
Vandysheva said every case is unique, though some share certain features: “There haven’t been many decisions like this in Europe, and they [mostly] concern businesspeople for whom there is no evidence that the grounds for sanctions still apply.” Restrictions can also be lifted if it emerges that there was not enough evidence to justify them in the first place.
What are some specific examples?
In September 2022, the EU lifted sanctions against Usmanov’s sister, Saodat Narziyeva, and Fridman’s former wife, Olga Aiziman. Vandysheva told Meduza that this happened during a regular review of the sanctions list, without a court ruling. According to Narziyeva’s representative, the sanctions had been based on false allegations that were later disproved. But the EU Council did not disclose its specific reasons for removing them, Vandysheva said:
That’s what happens in most cases. The specific reasons for removing Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list were not made public either. The European Commission’s website stresses that sanctions discussions are strictly confidential, so individual member states’ positions are not disclosed.
Sanctions have also been lifted against other relatives of sanctioned businesspeople, Vandysheva said: “For example, Yevgeny Prigozhin’s mother, Violetta Prigozhina, and the son of prominent businessman Dmitry Mazepin. The allegation against Nikita Mazepin was that his Formula One career had been financed through Uralkali. The court found that a family connection to a sanctioned person alone cannot be considered sufficient evidence.”
In some cases, people were removed after court proceedings. That happened with former Sistema vice president Sergey Mndoyants and former Ozon CEO Alexander Shulgin. After sanctions were imposed, Shulgin stepped down as Ozon’s CEO and left its board of directors. In September 2023, an EU court partially upheld his challenge, and a few days later the EU Council did not renew the sanctions against him.
Arkady Volozh’s case was similar: he publicly called Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine “barbaric,” distanced himself from Russia’s Yandex, and initiated the separation of Yandex NV from its Russian assets. In March 2024, the EU Council did not renew the sanctions against him. In this case, however, Vandysheva said the decision was influenced by “confidential discussions” within the Council, not by a court.
Leaving Russian business does not always lead to sanctions being lifted
Dmitry Pumpyansky is one example, Vandysheva said. He stepped down from management roles at TMK and Sinara, after which a court annulled several decisions extending sanctions against him. The EU Council subsequently supplemented its evidence and kept the restrictions in place. As of 2026, Pumpyansky remains on the sanctions list.
So sanctions do get lifted, for a variety of reasons.
How does someone get removed from the sanctions list?
There are several ways.
First, the EU Council can remove a person or company when it reviews the list. It can decline to renew sanctions if it believes the grounds for them no longer apply or are no longer convincing enough. Or it can make the decision for political reasons, as it did with Usmanov and Fridman.
Second, a person can petition the General Secretariat of the EU Council for removal. According to Vandysheva, this procedure applies if “the criteria for inclusion on the sanctions list are no longer met” — for example, because circumstances have changed.
Finally, sanctions can be challenged in court. Such cases are heard by courts in EU member states and by the EU General Court in Luxembourg. If a court finds that the Council failed to show that a person met the sanctions criteria, relied on outdated information, or made an error in its assessment, the decision to impose or extend the sanctions can be annulled.
The EU Council makes the final decision on sanctions. Political support from the European Commission also plays a significant role, Vandysheva said.
So sanctions can be lifted without a court ruling — and without a transparent process?
Essentially, yes. Vandysheva said this raises questions about the process’s transparency and casts doubt on how effective sanctions are as a tool:
For the EU, lifting sanctions is a way to show that sustained support for Ukraine and a refusal to cooperate with the Kremlin offer an effective path out of sanctions. But that reasoning is far from clear in every case. The logic is especially hard to follow when the EU Council removes someone after closed-door discussions without explaining why. This weakens the deterrent effect of sanctions and the incentive to comply with them, and it provides an opening for political point-scoring.
Let’s return to Usmanov and Fridman. Did they try to get the sanctions lifted in court?
They did.
In April 2024, Mikhail Fridman and Pyotr Aven won an EU court ruling annulling the sanctions decisions that had applied to them from February 2022 through March 2023. The court found that the EU Council had not provided enough evidence that Fridman and Aven “supported actions undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity, provided material or financial support to Russian leaders, or benefited from them,” Vandysheva told Meduza.
Fridman did not come off the list at the time: the EU Council continued to renew sanctions against him every six months. The court had annulled decisions covering a specific period, while later decisions remained in force.
Alisher Usmanov also challenged the sanctions in an EU court, but lost in February 2024. The court found that the EU Council had enough evidence to keep him on the list.
Usmanov also challenged claims in European publications that had been used as evidence for the sanctions, taking the matter to national courts. In January 2024, the Hamburg Regional Court barred the circulation of a Forbes claim that Usmanov had “fronted” for Putin and handled his business affairs. In January 2026, the same court barred FAZ from repeating several claims about the billionaire’s ties to the Russian authorities and his interference in Kommersant’s editorial policy.
“His lawyers explicitly linked these cases to an effort to undermine the evidence on which the EU sanctions were based,” Vandysheva said.
I see. Could they be put back on the sanctions list?
Yes, that’s likely, with some caveats.
Vandysheva said lifting the restrictions on the two billionaires on September 22 “does not give them any legal immunity”:
The EU Council can put them back on the sanctions list if new circumstances arise or sufficient evidence emerges that they meet the sanctions criteria. And a new listing decision can likewise be challenged in an EU court.
But this time, the EU Council itself removed Usmanov and Fridman from the sanctions list. In theory, that would make putting them back on the list harder: the Council would have to present new, legally sound grounds instead of simply repeating the old allegations.
What can Fridman and Usmanov do now? Travel to Europe? Do business there?
Officially, they can now do the following in the EU:
- Regain control of money and property frozen under EU sanctions. Their accounts at European banks, frozen since 2022, should be unfrozen. They can once again freely own and manage their villas, yachts, aircraft, and investment portfolios in the EU.
- Travel freely within the EU. They can enter the Schengen Area without restrictions, obtain visas, stay in European countries, and transit through them.
- Open new accounts and do business. They can register new companies, open bank and brokerage accounts with EU banks, and hold executive positions at European corporations.
- Buy any goods and hire professionals. European companies can now legally accept their payments for goods, including luxury items, and for services such as building houses.
But they still won’t have “complete freedom”:
- First, restrictions do not disappear instantly — databases take time to update. So “phantom” sanctions may remain in effect for now.
- Second, some countries have announced plans to impose national sanctions on the billionaires, including Latvia and Estonia. “That means restrictions will remain in place in countries that put Usmanov and Fridman on their national lists,” Vandysheva said. Other sanctions lists remain unchanged. The United Kingdom, in particular, has no plans to review its sanctions against them.
Where sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman remain in place
Mikhail Fridman
- 🇺🇸 U.S.
- 🇬🇧 United Kingdom
- 🇨🇦 Canada
- 🇦🇺 Australia
- 🇳🇿 New Zealand
- 🇺🇦 Ukraine
- 🇨🇭 Switzerland
- 🇲🇨 Monaco
🇵🇱 Poland
Alisher Usmanov
- 🇺🇸 U.S.
- 🇬🇧 United Kingdom
- 🇨🇦 Canada
- 🇦🇺 Australia
- 🇳🇿 New Zealand
- 🇯🇵 Japan
- 🇺🇦 Ukraine

- 🇲🇨 Monaco
- Third, reputation matters, and it cannot be restored quickly. Having been placed on any sanctions list remains a red flag in bank background checks and other compliance reviews, even after removal. Unfreezing existing accounts may also take a long time: large financial institutions will conduct lengthy internal reviews because they are concerned, for example, about possible secondary sanctions from the U.S.

Bill Gates called on governments to regulate AI through legislation because of the risk of abuse. He considers self-regulation by technology companies insufficient.
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates stated that artificial intelligence is powerful enough to contribute to events that could result in the deaths of a billion people. UNN reports this with reference to Axios and Forbes.
He called for statutory regulation of the technology, emphasizing that companies’ self-regulation is insufficient.
Details
In a conversation with television host Kristen Welker, Gates drew attention to the danger of people with malicious intentions using the latest artificial intelligence tools.
"AI is certainly powerful enough to lead to events that, you know, will cause a billion deaths," he said.
According to the Microsoft co-founder, the combination of modern AI’s capabilities and people’s malicious intentions creates an unprecedented threat. Gates also spoke in favor of the government’s involvement in establishing rules for artificial intelligence developers. In his view, policymakers and law enforcement agencies should participate in determining mandatory protective and monitoring measures.
He emphasized that voluntary restrictions imposed by technology companies themselves are insufficient. When asked whether appropriate legislation was needed, Gates answered in the affirmative.
Context
In August, Gates published an essay on his website about the risks of artificial intelligence development. Among the threats, he listed job losses, the spread of fraud and disinformation, the facilitation of cyberattacks, and growing bioterrorism risks. He also warned that the technology could exacerbate inequality if its benefits were concentrated in the hands of a limited number of people.
At the same time, the Gates Foundation announced its intention to direct at least $1 billion over two years toward expanding access to AI. The funds are intended for projects in education, healthcare, agriculture, and digital infrastructure development.

Lions list changes but machine the same ahead of fourth grand final
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:02:47 UTC
05:02:47 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
analysis
Brisbane Lions face fourth straight AFL grand final with different players, but same look
On Saturday the Brisbane Lions will march out for their fourth straight grand final appearance.
From the outside it's yet another chapter for the relentless, exciting machine that has taken the league by storm over the past half decade.
Under the hood, though, pieces have been slowly changing.
Like the Ship of Theseus, the Lions have slowly been transforming as they have sailed the premiership waters.
The Lions will have fielded 35 different players across their four years in the grand final by the time they run out on Saturday — almost enough for two distinct teams of 18.
Just 11 players have hit the field in all four games — less than half of their 23 man side.
This is no different to all football teams over a long enough period of time. Players come, players go. Styles change, emerge and alter as the clock ticks. But these Lions have shifted more than most dynasties.
For example, Brisbane had just 29 players feature over their four straight grand finals at the turn of the century.
These Lions are turning their ship over faster, but the look is largely the same.
Of the constants remaining, perhaps the most important is the steward of the ship.
Coach Chris Fagan's distinctive style has been key to ensuring that the Lions can both retool and stay in the premiership hunt.
The 2026 Lions remain a force to beat — even if that force is different to that posed in 2023. If they can capture the flag on Saturday they will become the seventh VFL/AFL side to win three premierships in a row.
"It's very exciting to be in the position where we could achieve something like that," Fagan said after their thrilling win over Hawthorn.
"But it's not worth thinking about that — if you know what I mean — because you (can) get caught up in thinking the wrong way."
In the path of their greatness stands the side best over the course of the year, and a new challenger to the Lions' crown.
This year's Lions — an increasingly homegrown side — stand on the cusp of history.
Only a Purple Haze stands in their way.
The Lions' Den
So if the pieces have changed, what about the Lions' identity and style of play, has it stayed the same? Plenty, it turns out.
The Lions kick the ball more than any other side in the competition and have done so since 2024.
The Hawks and Lions handballed the ball just 92 times a piece last weekend, only the fifth time since 2008 that both teams have taken fewer than 100 handballs in a game.
Instead the Lions control the ball by making sure they find marking targets by foot.
No team has taken more marks than the Lions. They also defend against opposition marks exceedingly well.
Much like Roger Federer in his prime, the Lions beat the opposition by making them run while remaining in control themselves.
It's somewhat reminiscent of the style of the 2013-2015 Hawthorn sides which Fagan ably served.
The opposition can't score when you have the ball, and you can use the advantage of control to pressure the opposition.
Helping get the ball first helps as well. In the last four years the Lions have ranked in the top two for clearance difference in each season.
Brisbane boast arguably the best group of ball winning midfielders in the competition.
The Lions boast an enviable midfield group, boosted by the freeing of Lachie Neale from suspension in what may be his last game for the club.
Their second layer and rotation midfielders would be the first choice across much of the rest of the league.
If Neale, Dunkley and Hugh McCluggage don't beat you, Zac Bailey and the Ashcrofts will. Even the likes of former number one draft pick Cam Rayner can break games open as a change of pace option.
This helps to generate attack for the Lions — who aren't short on that front.
The Lions can score from all parts of the ground, but are especially adept when keeping the ball in their own forward half.
The Lions have long boasted a dynamic forward line but this year might be their best combination yet come finals time.
The Lions have found a group that can all do damage on their own but are also willing to sacrifice their own games for the greater good.
All seven core Brisbane forwards average more than a goal a game, along with Zac Bailey. Almost no other side boasts that kind of widespread firepower from such a variety of different sized players.
Prize recruit Oscar Allen has been able to slot quietly into the mix as he pursues his first premiership, essentially replacing Joe Daniher.
The surprise positional switch of veteran Irishman Conor McKenna has been equally seamless.
The Lions are even deadly from the usual safe sanctuary of the boundary line or the umpire's arms. No side is better at scoring from stoppages inside 50 — meaning that opposition sides can't just kill contests.
That increases the pressure on opponents to exit cleanly, otherwise cricket scores are likely to follow.
But maybe part of the reason why they score heavily is that they have to do so to win games.
The shaky defence
Unlike previous years the recipe to beat the Lions has become increasingly clear.
Teams have taken to putting the Brisbane defence under pressure as swiftly as possible, going in straight lines at speed.
The Swans were able to capitalise in their qualifying final win, moving the ball more directly than any other point of their season.
Last week the Hawks tried similar and were nearly successful.
So far this finals the Lions have conceded more points than any other team to ever make the grand final.
Every other team to concede more than 100 points per game before making the grand final went on to lose the decider.
As the year has progressed the Lions have struggled to defend against transition.
They can get overwhelmed by teams with multiple tall options and crafty small forwards — something that the Dockers have in numbers.
But the defence still believes that it can do the job when it matters most.
"We've proven in the previous couple of grand finals and throughout the year — and the past few years — that we can keep teams to a limited score. We certainly don't go into the game going we need to kick 120 (points) to win," defender Ryan Lester told the media this week.
That defence shapes as a critical factor in the game ahead.
In their round 12 loss to the Dockers their defence was shredded when tasked with defending the full field.
That loss happened in the Lions typical mid-season swoon. It was also one that didn't have Fagan as concerned as many would think from the outside.
"The last time we played them they beat us by four goals at the Gabba. There was a bit to like about that game (actually)," Fagan said last week.
Brisbane did what they typically need to do to win that game — namely win clearances and dominate field position.
But they failed to execute in front of goal and failed to keep Fremantle at bay up forward.
It's easy to see how Brisbane turn it around on Saturday — mainly because they've done it so many times before.
Regardless of the personnel, or the opponent — the Brisbane ship always seems destined for success.
