Iraqi airports halt Iranian flights after new US aviation sanctions
Baghdad, Najaf, Erbil, and Sulaimaniyah airports suspend flights as US ramps up pressure on Iran’s aviation sector.
Four Iraqi airports have suspended all flights to and from Iran days after the United States announced new aviation sanctions on any global companies doing business with Iranian airlines.
It is the latest ramping up of sanctions since the US launched Operation Economic Outcast in August in an effort to isolate Iran from the global economy.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran threatens countries enforcing US airline sanctions
- list 2 of 3US aviation sanctions disrupt Iran flights, push travellers overland
- list 3 of 3Why is Iran threatening regional airports, and what could be the impact?
Iraqi state media said flights will no longer be operating from Baghdad, Najaf, Erbil and Sulaimaniyah airports.
Iraq was one of the top destinations for Iranian airlines, especially after Iraqi airlines stopped flying to Iran at the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.
Passengers travelling between Iran and Iraq will now be forced to make a land journey of at least 12 hours, depending on the destination.
Najaf airport
Iraq’s state news agency reported the suspension at Najaf international airport earlier on Friday.
Airport director Hussein Muhanna told the AFP news agency that “all flights were halted between Iran and Najaf airport following a directive from the prime minister’s office to the governor” of Najaf.
Iraq and neighbouring Iran are both Shia-majority countries, and flights to and from Najaf carry Iraqi Shia Muslim pilgrims to Iran’s holy cities or Iranians visiting sacred sites in Iraq.
In a post on X, the Iranian Consulate in Najaf responded to the suspension of flights to and from Iran, saying “Najaf international airport, the shrine of the first Imam of the Shia, and the capital of their last Imam, is closed to the largest Shia country in the world?!”
An Iraqi employee of an Iranian airline at Najaf airport told AFP Iranian carriers usually operate at least 20 daily flights, but after the suspension, only four flights to other destinations remained scheduled on Friday.
Several other regional countries, including the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, have either cancelled or restricted flights to Iran to enforce US aviation sanctions.
That is despite the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council warning neighbouring nations against imposing a US flight ban.
Iranian airlines are now relying on a few reduced routes, including Turkiye, Russia, China and Armenia, to remain operational.
“We cannot say that Iran is totally cut off from air traffic, but shrunk considerably,” said Al Jazeera’s Sinem Koseoglu, reporting from Tehran.
Reporting from Baghdad, Al Jazeera’s Jack Hewson said Iraq’s central government has made no statement about the flight suspensions, likely because it “doesn’t want to antagonise” pro-Iranian factions in Iraq’s parliament.
Explaining the country’s decision to comply with the US move, Hewson said: “Companies providing ground services, like refuelling, baggage, it appears, are not willing to risk secondary sanctions and being frozen out of the international US dollar system.”
“Iraq’s in a very difficult position,” Hewson added. “It’s tied to the US, but it’s also tied to Iran. And at times like these, it’s squeezed between the two.”

====================================================================================================

From The Beatles to psychedelia, discover how 1966 changed music forever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

When you think about the biggest albums of 1966, two records stand head and shoulders above the rest.
The Beatles' Revolver and The Beach Boys' Pet Sounds have tended to overshadow everything else released that year.
But the mythology surrounding the albums has also overshadowed the actual music on the records themselves.
So, let's dive into the sounds of 66 to get a better understanding for where music was at 60 years ago.
Oh, I almost forgot the obligatory historical context of 1966: Harold Holt was sworn in as prime minister in January (almost two years before his fateful swim), Australian currency went decimal, The Sound Of Music and Doctor Zhivago dominated the Oscars, England clinched its only FIFA World Cup, and St Kilda won its lone AFL/VFL grand final.
The big two of 1966
While there was much more to the music of 66 than just Revolver and Pet Sounds, you can't ignore these records. They literally changed music.
In his detailed day-by-day breakdown titled The Complete Beatles Chronicle, Mark Lewisohn wrote: "In 1965 the Beatles' recordings had been progressing quite nicely, but here was a quantum jump into not merely tomorrow but sometime next week."
He was writing about Revolver, but specifically Tomorrow Never Knows, the album's insanely adventurous closing track which, Lewisohn wrote, displayed "an unrivalled musical progression [and] The Beatles' willingness first to observe the boundaries and then smash right through them".
Revolver was a pioneering example of using the recording studio as a musical instrument itself, and nowhere better exemplified this than Tomorrow Never Knows, a whirling hallucinogenic groove unlike anything ever heard before.
The Beatles weren't always the first to use particular recording techniques attributed to them, but they typically popularised them by combining little-known studio tricks with the canny songwriting skills of Lennon, McCartney and Harrison.
On Revolver they used such unheard-of or rarely used ideas as tape loops, artificial double tracking, backwards tracking, sampling, varispeed recording, plugging the bass directly into the mixing desk to record it, and the bold move of putting microphones as close as possible to the instruments and amplifiers (something that caused conniptions among the lab-coated technicians at Abbey Road Studios).
All this made Revolver sound unlike any other record, but it meant nothing without the tunes to back it up.
Taxman, Eleanor Rigby, Yellow Submarine, I'm Only Sleeping, Here, There & Everywhere, She Said She Said, Got To Get You Into My Life and Tomorrow Never Knows are all among the best songs The Beatles ever recorded (and that's not to mention Paperback Writer and Rain, which were recorded during the Revolver sessions but carved off for a standalone single).
Revolver pointed the way towards so many new musical styles by incorporating psychedelia, Indian music, and sampling, and pushed the recording studio to new extremes.
It also just so happens to be a collection of damn fine songs from a band that was quite rightfully the biggest on the planet 60 years ago.
The story goes that The Beach Boys' Brian Wilson heard The Beatles' late 1965 record Rubber Soul and decided to top it with Pet Sounds.
A work of unrivalled beauty in pop music at the time, Pet Sounds saw the band ditch their surf rock roots and beach party vibes for something deeply introspective and hymnal.
Wilson worked closely with lyricist Tony Asher (and, occasionally, bandmate Mike Love) to compose a suite of songs that hinted at Wilson's increasingly fragile, questioning and insecure state of mind; That's Not Me, I Know There's An Answer, and I Just Wasn't Made For These Times are two key examples.
Elsewhere the album is an ode to love.
Wouldn't It Be Nice, You Still Believe In Me, Don't Talk (Put Your Head On My Shoulder), and Let's Go Away For A While are all paeans to devotion, affection and connection, illuminated by the beautiful melodies, harmonies and accompaniments that go with them.
But perhaps best of all is God Only Knows, generally (and rightly) regarded as one of the greatest songs of all time.
Like other songs on the record it combines typical rock and orchestra instrumentation, plus some unusual ones such as harpsichord, accordion and sleigh bells, all working in service of Carl Wilson's angelic vocal performance, and Brian Wilson and Asher's tender heartfelt lyrical ode to eternal undying love.
Wilson would later use the term "teenage symphony to God" when describing his unsuccessful and unfinished follow-up Smile, but the words fit just as beautifully as a descriptor for Pet Sounds.
Painstakingly crafted, the songs remain among the most harmonically and melodically rich of not just the 60s, but any era in music.
While Pet Sounds sounds decidedly square compared to the likes of The Beatles, Dylan and The Rolling Stones, it set a benchmark for beautiful pop music and was an important step in its evolution.
As Paul McCartney put it, "no-one is educated musically till they've heard that album".
Rockin' in the USA
The mid-60s were a strange time in music, particularly in America.
Jazz was still big, the crooners (Frank, Tony, Dean and co) still held some sway, and one of the biggest bands in America was Herb Alpert & The Tijuana Brass.
Meanwhile rock music was 10 years old, the invasion of British bands had started to peter out, folk music was still popular though morphing in new and strange ways, and everyone still wanted to be The Beatles three years on from their worldwide explosion.
Seriously, it's crazy how many albums from 1966 featured a Beatles cover.
But the end result in the US was a wild melting pot of sounds, perhaps best exemplified by these six albums.
The folk duo of Paul Simon and Art Garfunkel had effectively broken up in mid-1965.
But then a forgotten song on their 1964 debut album Wednesday Morning, 3AM became a belated surprise hit.
The Sound Of Silence, with new added rock'n'roll overdubs, went to number one and became the title track of a thrown-together follow-up album released by the hastily reunited Simon & Garfunkel in January 1966 to capitalise on their new-found success.
But it was the follow-up album Parsley, Sage, Rosemary & Thyme, released in October 1966, that really showed the breadth of the duo's talent and fittingly catapulted them to fame.
From the haunting medieval beauty of Scarborough Fair/Canticle to the jazzy The 59th Street Bridge Song, from the pretty For Emily, Whenever I May Find Her to the sad longing of Homeward Bound, it's an album that packs a lot into its 29 minutes.
Just about every rock'n'roll trope can be found in the short but influential career of The Mamas & The Papas.
Drugs, affairs, dodgy record deals, infighting, studio obsessing and sackings are all part of the folk-pop group's story.
But more importantly, their first album helped shape the California sound and the following year's Summer of Love with its sunshine harmonies, jangly folk guitars, beat rhythms and teen-targeted lyrics about "somebody groovy" and hanging with the "in" crowd.
The big singles are Summer of Love anthem California Dreamin' and the Grammy-winning Monday, Monday, both of which helped propel If You Can Believe… to number one in the US and top five on the NME and Melody Maker charts in the UK, but in between are decent Beatles homage Straight Shooter and the freewheeling Go Where You Gonna Go.
By his seventh album, Dylan had well and truly gone electric. He'd also dispensed with his spokesman-for-a-generation mantle and was deep into building his own mythology.
Blonde On Blonde is stacked with material that's kept Dylanologists busy for 60 years, as he paints incredible lyrical images and dips in and out of his own relationships from one song to the next.
Featuring the much-acclaimed Visions Of Johanna, the aching Just Like A Woman, the high-as-a-kite Rainy Day Women #12 & 35, and the epic romance of Sad Eyed Lady Of The Lowlands, this hefty double album is one of Dylan's best, capping off an incredible trilogy of rock records after Bringing It All Back Home and Highway 61 Revisited.
Buffalo Springfield's rise was rapid and fascinating.
Within five days of meeting they were playing at a top Hollywood club. Within a few weeks they were the house band at Whisky A Go Go. Within a few months they had a record deal. Within six months they had released their first album. And within a couple of years they were no more.
Neil Young and Stephen Stills would go on to even greater success, but their self-titled debut is a solid and influential effort featuring groovy rocker Sit Down I Think I Love You, the jangly Burned, and Young's early psychedelic gem Out Of My Mind.
But the best track was recorded on the day the album came out and only added to the track listing months later when it became a hit single: For What It's Worth (aka Stop, Hey What's That Sound) became not only Buffalo Springfield's defining song, but a defining song of the 60s.
Of all the bands trying to ape The Beatles, none did it as successfully as manufactured TV show band The Monkees.
Its self-titled debut was the first of four consecutive US number-one albums released in just 13 months.
While The Monkees had no creative control over their first two records and were largely forbidden from playing instruments, Mickey, Davy, Mike and Peter nonetheless became the biggest thing since John, Paul, George and Ringo.
The only single off their self-titled debut is the iconic Last Train To Clarksville (easily among their greatest tracks), but there's also the similarly Beatlesy Saturday's Child, Let's Dance On, and Tomorrow's Gonna Be Another Day.
However tracks like This Just Doesn't Seem To Be My Day and Sweet Young Thing are among the more interesting numbers here.
Frank Zappa released 62 albums in his lifetime (and another 70 and counting since his death).
But Freak Out! is the first and one of his most important, kicking off a career that was one of the most fascinating and vital in American music.
Considered one of the first double albums and concept albums by a rock band, Freak Out! was a biting satire on American society and unlike anything else released at the time.
A lot of the songs are spot-on parodies of the inane presentation of teen culture in pop music (Go Cry On Somebody Else's Shoulder, How Could I Be Such A Fool, and You Didn't Try To Call Me), while much of the rest of the album is an excoriating take-down of the United States.
Check out songs such as Who Are The Brain Police?, Hungry Freaks, Daddy, and the blistering attack on America's systemic racism Trouble Every Day (key line: "I'm not black, but there's a whole lotta times I wish I could say I'm not white").
After the invasion
The Beatles had kicked open the door to the US for English acts, and every Tom, Mick and Eric was clambering to follow suit.
But the so-called British Invasion, which saw the US Billboard charts successfully infiltrated by UK bands, had started to wane by 1966.
Regardless, some fascinating sounds were continuing to emerge from the British Isles.
Some of the soon-to-be-biggest bands in the world were taking interesting steps in some intriguing directions.
It's not the greatest Stones record, but Aftermath is an important step forward for the band nonetheless.
It hasn't aged well. Some of the album's more misogynistic lyrics were bad enough in 1966, let alone 60 years later.
But The Rolling Stones' fourth album was the first to feature nothing but Jagger-Richards compositions, and sees some musical experimentation yielding two of their best early tracks — Under My Thumb (sadly, one of the worst lyrical offenders) and Out Of Time — as well as the intriguing tale of suburban drug use Mother's Little Helper and the medieval Lady Jane.
Aftermath is the sound of The Rolling Stones stretching out and occasionally finding gold, but is ultimately a stepping stone towards bigger and better things.
The blues came back in a big way in the UK in the 60s, led by the new wave of rock'n'roll bands like The Rolling Stones and The Yardbirds, who tapped into their love of everyone from Muddy Waters to Robert Johnson.
Eric Clapton had experience with the new blues-rock sound via The Yardbirds and a short stint with John Mayall's Blue Breakers, but took the idea to new levels by teaming with Jack Bruce and Ginger Baker to create Cream.
Fresh Cream, the first of four albums in four years for the short-lived, volatile band, is as good an example of what they did: loud, rocking, jammy blues that's a cornerstone for fans of the genre.
Outside their gorgeous 67 single Itchycoo Park, Small Faces' impact in the US was minimal.
But to those in the know, their debut record is a fantastic album that provides a bridge between the Beatlesy rock'n'roll of the British Invasion bands and the harder/heavier rock sound that would follow in the UK in the late 60s and 70s.
Led Zeppelin certainly owe a debt; Whole Lotta Love steals outright from You Need Loving, which was a Willy Dixon song Small Faces nicked via a Muddy Waters cover.
But right from the opening chord of Shake, Small Faces brought distortion, pace, attitude and the powerful wail of Steve Marriott to the masses.
The Kinks used their fourth album to change gears.
One of the great UK bands of the 60s, Face To Face saw them go from being an awesome beat band to a songwriting powerhouse.
Led by the immense songwriting talents of Ray Davies, the band turned out an incredible group of songs on Face To Face; character-driven pieces, sometimes satirical, that showcased British life, warts and all, and didn't just ape American musical trends and styles.
Sunny Afternoon was the big hit on an album of great songs. The whole thing preceded such "Kinks klassics" as Dead End Street and Waterloo Sunset by mere months, kicking off a new golden era for a band already known for killer rock singles like You Really Got Me, All Day And All Of The Night, and Tired Of Waiting For You.
There are differing opinions on which line-up of The Yardbirds was the greatest.
The blues rockers featured three of the greatest English guitarists of all time (Eric Clapton, Jeff Beck and Jimmy Page) at various points in their existence, and Roger The Engineer is considered the peak of Beck's time with the band.
It was the band's third proper studio album, and many would argue it remains The Yardbirds' greatest non-live record.
Amid the R&B rave-ups, there are basic bar-room boogies (The Nazz Are Blue), hypnotic exotic riffs (Over Under Sideways Down), and fun experiments (Hot House Of Omagararshid, Turn Into Earth), but the greatest moment has to be Jeff's Boogie, in which Beck pulls out every guitar trick in the book inside two and a half minutes.
In 66, The Who were on their way to becoming one of the biggest bands in the world.
Much like The Rolling Stones' Aftermath, The Who's A Quick One was a stepping stone. While it lacked a hit single to match the heights of My Generation or Substitute, it contained hints of things to come.
The closing six-part suite — A Quick One, While He's Away — is a taste of the rock operas to come (such as Tommy and Quadrophenia).
Album opener Run, Run, Run is a hard rocker before such things really existed, Boris The Spider and Cobwebs & Strange showed their diversity and kookiness, while So Sad About Us is a ripping piece of power pop that should've been a hit.
Soul music
Pop, rock, gospel, and rhythm and blues were shifting and swirling together in black communities in America to make something new in the 50s.
By the 60s, it had become soul music and was a juggernaut that dominated black music charts (euphemistically called the R&B charts) and seeped into the white music charts (the "pop" charts), such was its popularity.
Here are three of the big non-Motown soul records of 66 (we'll get to Motown in a minute).
Otis Redding crammed a lot of incredible music into a short but magical life.
He released six studio albums before his untimely death in a plane crash, aged 26, including this collection, which was his fifth studio album.
His signature song (Sittin' On) The Dock Of The Bay wouldn't be released until after his death, but Complete & Unbelievable boasts a handful of great Redding moments, including Try A Little Tenderness, Fa-Fa-Fa-Fa-Fa (Sad Song), and his wild cover of The Beatles' Day Tripper.
Not only is the album a highlight of Redding's too-short career, but the arrangements and playing are top-shelf, provided by Stax house band Booker T & The MGs, as well as the famed Memphis Horns, and a young piano player by the name of Isaac Hayes.
Tina Turner was an icon with a voice like no other.
While Ike Turner's horrific treatment of Tina casts a sad shadow over their musical output together, nothing can take the shine off the title track of this soul classic (not even the participation of convicted killer Phil Spector).
Turner's vocal performance on the opening track is one for the ages, as her voice goes from impassioned scream to beautiful sweetness and back again in a heartbeat. It's so incredible it overshadows the rest of the album.
But don't sleep on the rest of River Deep, Mountain High like American labels and audiences did in 66.
Tracks like I Idolize You and A Fool In Love are stone-cold soul groovers, while a gender-flipped Save The Last Dance For Me is also a highlight.
Wilson Pickett was a prodigiously voiced and gifted performer.
This helped make him one of the biggest stars of 1966, which would end up being the peak of his career before a sad decline.
Capitalising on the success of his previous record, Pickett's third album saw him re-team with some of the classic Stax house band players (who would become Booker T & The MGs) as well as the equally awesome players from Fame Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama.
There are the obvious soul classics here — Pickett's renditions of Land Of 1,000 Dances and In The Midnight Hour are among the greatest songs of all time — but don't sleep on tracks like Something You Got, Ninety-Nine & One-Half, Danger Zone, and Mercy, Mercy.
Psychedelia
As the late great comedian Bill Hicks pointed out, "the musicians that made all that great music that's enhanced your lives throughout the years [were] real … high on drugs".
That's most evident in the emergence of psychedelic rock, strongly influenced by the use of LSD, which was banned in California and Nevada in mid-66, but already had a foothold in the arts, music and "counter-culture" communities.
Some historians point to The Beatles' album Rubber Soul (December 1965) and B side Rain (May 66) as precursors to psychedelic rock, and they were certainly among the musicians letting LSD ooze into their music.
While key Californian acid-soaked bands like The Grateful Dead and Jefferson Aeroplane weren't quite there in 1966, plenty of others were already turning on, tuning in and dropping out to make a groovy new sound.
Pinpointing the sound of psychedelic music can be hard (it's all about the vibe, man).
But Scottish singer-songwriter Donovan was definitely an early proponent with his third album, which came out in August 66 in the US (and later, for legal reasons, in the UK).
The album's mesmerising title track (sampled extensively for Imani Coppola's Legend Of A Cowgirl) referenced LSD and combined sounds new and old, making it one of the first truly psychedelic pop songs. Having a B side called The Trip certainly helped.
The album melds folk, jazz and blues with sitar, bouzouki and bongos, with Donovan's lyrical eye and melodic ear making something truly new on tracks such as Three King Fishers, Ferris Wheel and the two-chord apocalyptic pop of Season Of The Witch.
The debut album from this New York five-piece was at the cutting edge of psychedelia.
A true forgotten gem, it was among the first records to use the P word in its title.
The band broke up four years after Psychedelic Lollipop, which was their only record to crack the top 25 in the US.
While the lyrics leave something to be desired, the musicality and harmonies are strong, and the record boasts some incredible moments: a startling cover of Tobacco Road, a trippy tape effect that sends Love Seems Doomed into another dimension, the Animals-esque Sometimes I Think About, and their garage rock hit single (We Ain't Got) Nothin' Yet.
The first truly psychedelic band, these madcap Texans took LSD and sure as hell sounded like it.
Easily recognisable for the fluttering staccato electric jug playing of Tommy Hall, the Elevators peppered their songs with trippy lyrics, dark atmospheres and Roky Erickson's howling vocals.
To call their debut album ahead of its time is an understatement.
Hypnotically dreamy tracks like Rollercoaster and The Kingdom Of Heaven are the very definition of psychedelic, but killer tunes like You're Gonna Miss Me and Splash 1 were dark-horse hits dressed in tie-dyed shirts, hippy beads and rose-coloured glasses.
Few albums are more obvious stepping stones into psychedelic rock than this.
The third album from Los Angeles folk-rockers The Byrds followed the departure of chief songwriter Gene Clark, which pushed the band in new directions.
This included adding Indian influences ("raga rock") and psychedelic guitar solos (inspired by John Coltrane) to their jangly guitar sound and beautiful harmonies.
Eight Miles High is the obvious psych highlight, but 5D (Fifth Dimension), What's Happening?, and I See You are equally LSD-tinged.
The album's influence extends beyond the psychedelic. For example, I Come & Stand At Every Door sounds almost exactly like REM, just 20 years earlier, while their cover of Hey Joe hints at punk and garage rock.
Another of the first records to adopt the word "psychedelic" to describe their sound (some accounts say the first). However this one-off studio experiment is one of the albums that lives up to that adjective the most.
The brainchild of New York musician Rusty Evans, Psychedelic Moods was recorded by a throw-together band in the space of a couple of days, with the musicians sleeping in the studio in between LSD-fuelled recording sessions.
At least, that's what the legend says. How much of that is true is up for debate, as is whether or not the album was recorded as a joke or as a serious tribute to its subtitle of "A Mind-Expanding Phenomena".
Either way, its heady tunes "actually capture the fuzzy off-balanced mind-bending experience", as one reviewer put it, blending wiry guitars and woozy rhythms with trippy lyrics and out-there sound effects.
Garage rock
Rock'n'roll, or beat music as it was sometimes called, began to diversify and evolve even before anyone coined the term rock'n'roll.
Blues-rock, country-rock, rockabilly, swamp rock — all of these subgenres were getting thrown around long before 66.
But it was only in hindsight that the term garage rock came about, as people tried to find a name for the dirtier rock sound of the mid-60s that would become a bridge to punk, metal, grunge, hardcore, post-punk and a bunch of other alt-rock subgenres.
1966 is littered with great singles and bands that were overlooked in their day. Indeed, without Lenny Kaye's compilation series Nuggets (1972 onwards), many would have been forgotten.
But here are some of the key acts that helped give rock'n'roll music a grittier sound and a tougher attitude.
Little known outside the US, this Boise, Idaho band were a big deal.
So big, in fact, that their fifth album, Midnight Ride, was one of just three US top-10 records the group released in 1966 alone.
Best remembered for the pop hit Kicks and the killer tune I'm Not Your Stepping Stone (a later hit for The Monkees), this record is also important for its reputation as a seed of garage rock.
Up-tempo tracks like There's Always Tomorrow and Ballad Of A Useless Man boast the slightly grittier sound of the subgenre, though it's I'm Not Your Stepping Stone that is the true signpost; the Sex Pistols cover released over a decade later shows where the band was pointing.
The loudest of the garage rock bands, Seattle's The Sonics released just three albums with their original line-up before temporarily combusting, however they're the best examples of what garage rock was all about.
While their 1965 debut Here Are The Sonics contains their best-known track (a cover of Richard Berry's Have Love Will Travel), the follow-up Boom has plenty of fast-paced fuzzed-out rockers that lay the groundwork for punk, such as Cinderella, He's Waitin', a fantastic cover of Louie Louie, and the killer closer Shot Down.
They never sold many records, but The Sonics inspired everyone from The Stooges and The Hives to Nirvana and The White Stripes.
Californian band The Seeds were led by Sky Saxon, the self-proclaimed "King of Garage Rock".
Saxon's band put out two rock albums in 1966: their self-titled debut and follow-up A Web Of Sound, which not only paved the garage rock road but also pointed towards psychedelia.
The former contains their two biggest hits, Can't Seem To Make You Mine and Pushin' Too Hard, and both feature Saxon's strangled vocals, which were surely a precursor to the punk howls of singers like Iggy Pop.
The scuzzy riffs of Evil Hoodoo, the agonised howls of Girl I Want You and Try To Understand, and the anti-authority sentiments of Pushin' Too Hard make this a true garage rock touchstone and go some way towards backing up Saxon's claim to the garage rock throne.
Nailing down the "first" punk record is impossible, but a lot of people like to point to this album as a kind of birth of punk, and it's a compelling choice.
The Monks were five US soldiers stationed in Germany who got monk tonsure haircuts and inadvertently invented a new genre on tracks like Monk Time, Shut Up, Higgle-Dy-Piggle-Dy, and I Hate You, accidentally influencing countless musicians who liked the idea of music being a ferocious, wild and weird parent repellent.
The one and only album by The Monks combines fuzz bass, driving rhythms, bursts of noise, and an anti-establishment attitude (oh, and banjo!) to get closer to punk than any other garage rock band of the day.
"Wild thing, you make my heart sing…"
It's the speak-sung, three-chord jam that sparked a thousand backyard bands, and if you're looking for a garage rock song to tag as the genesis of punk rock then this is as good as any.
UK band The Troggs are still (sort of) touring to this day and released albums into the 90s, but their halcyon days lasted just 18 months, starting with their cover of Wild Thing in April 66 and ending with the sublime Love Is All Around in October 67.
Their debut album From Nowhere opens with Wild Thing, also includes the under-rated With A Girl Like You, and reissues also excellent garage rock hits From Home, I Can't Control Myself, and their version of Louie Louie, the latter containing the dirtiest guitar sound of the era.
Love was a band like no other.
Led by the melodic magic of multi-instrumentalist Arthur Lee, the Los Angeles group released three incredible albums between March 66 and November 67 that touched on garage rock, psychedelic rock, jazz, folk-rock and symphonic pop.
Their self-titled debut is their most garagey and it rocks hard; Lee's voice cracks and shreds on My Flash On You, their version of Hey Joe moves at breakneck speed, while Can't Explain is one of the great rock songs of the era.
This line-up of Love would never be this proto-punk again. Follow-up album Da Capo is more psychedelic and the cult classic Forever Changes is a pop masterpiece that sounds like nothing else, but across all three albums they would leave a huge influence on bands across a wide range of genres.
The sound of Australia
Pop music in Australia in the 50s and 60s was largely content to copy the sounds of the UK and US.
As a result, the albums, songs and acts that endured in the cultural memory are the ones that had something truly special.
Here are three Aussie bands with big albums in 66 that we still talk about today.
Pitching the sound of the British Invasion back to Britain may have seemed a bit like selling sand at the beach, but that's what The Easybeats did, becoming Australia's first successful original rock band in the process.
1966 was a prolific year in which the band released two albums (It's 2 Easy and Volume 3) and two EPs (Easy As Can Be and Easyfever), relocated to England, and put out one of the greatest Aussie songs of all time, Friday On My Mind.
While they were always more of a singles band than an album band (the book The 100 Best Australian Albums features the compilation The Best Of The Easybeats at number six rather than a studio album), It's 2 Easy is a fascinating document.
It precedes Friday On My Mind, but the best tracks on it hint at the driving rhythms and attitude of that incredible single: Women, I Can See and Wedding Ring are great songs, though the album lacks a real killer hit.
Born in the UK, the brothers Gibb spent eight and a half formative years in Australia, but it was the lack of success for Spicks & Specks, their second album, that sent them back to the UK.
While the record didn't set the charts alight, it's filled with charm and the Gibb boys' tight three-part harmonies with highlights including How Many Birds, and the Beatlesy tracks Big Chance, I Don't Know Why I Bother With Myself, and Where Are You.
And then there's the title track, one of the greatest Australian pop songs of all time, containing a stomping piano rhythm, two key changes, a beautiful trumpet outro, and the sadness of nostalgia in three powerful minutes.
The Seekers' career arguably peaked about six months after the release of this album.
That was when the Aussie quartet played to an unfathomably huge world-record crowd of 200,000 people at Melbourne's Sidney Myer Music Bowl.
Come The Day took the band to heights no Australian band had ever reached. The Seekers had hit singles around the world prior, but this album (their fifth) was the first to crack the top 10 in Australia, the UK and the US.
Capped off by sparkling single Georgy Girl (which leant its name to the US version of the album), Come The Day showcases the band's strengths, particularly on songs such as the title track, where the lush harmonies and folk-pop playing perfectly accompany Judith Durham's flawless vibrato.
Motown
In its early years, Motown Records operated out of a two-storey home in Detroit dubbed Hitsville USA, which was more than fitting; from 1961 to 1971, the label produced 110 Billboard top 10 hits.
Throughout the 60s and 70s, the label pumped out an insane run of world-changing music, and the genres of soul, pop, R&B and funk wouldn't be the same without Motown and its famed backing band, known fittingly as The Funk Brothers.
Here's a taste of just some of the remarkable music that emerged from the Detroit label in 1966.
Between August 64 and November 72, The Supremes released an astonishing 25 albums.
Amid that incredible run were 12 US number-one singles, most of which were the work of Mary Wilson, Diana Ross and Florence Ballard.
While their other 66 album I Hear A Symphony is adventurous and interesting, especially the dazzling title track, A' Go-Go was led by two stellar singles: the top-10 hit Love Is Like An Itching In My Heart, and the Motown classic You Can't Hurry Love, which stands as one of greatest songs of all time.
The rest of the record is a calculated collection of dancefloor-ready covers of chart-toppers previously done by the likes of The Four Tops, The Temptations, Martha & The Vandellas and more, helping make this the first Supremes album to hit the top of the US Billboard 200.
This is 16-year-old Stevie Wonder's sixth album (and second of 1966).
Down To Earth saw Wonder trying to establish himself as a serious musician rather than just an angelically voiced child prodigy.
Much like its predecessor Up-Tight (the title track of that record is Wonder's first truly killer tune), Down To Earth is an eclectic mix of covers, ranging from Merle Travis's 16 Tons to Bob Dylan's Tambourine Man, and songs penned by Wonder, Henry Cosby and Sylvia Moy.
But on tracks such as soulful swinger A Place In The Sun and dancefloor banger Be Cool Be Calm, you can hear a superstar starting to emerge.
The Four Tops formed in 1953 as part of the vocal group boom, however the band didn't release its first album until 1965, three years after joining Motown.
They quickly became hit machines who, along with label-mates The Supremes, took some choice material from the songwriting powerhouse of Holland-Dozier-Holland to the top of the charts.
On Top, the third of five albums released in the space of just three years, isn't laden with hits — its biggest song is Shake Me, Wake Me (When It's Over) — but shows the band's sound growing, with its nod to the past (a Cole Porter cover) and to the present (a Beatles cover).
Gettin' Ready is the second of seven consecutive Billboard top-20 albums for The Temptations.
The vocal group was one of the core hit-making vocal groups for Motown in the 60s. The two big hits on Gettin' Ready are Ain't Too Proud To Beg and Get Ready, both of which went to number one on the US R&B charts and remain soul classics.
Still performing with 84-year-old founding member Otis Williams, The Temptations would develop their sound after this by adding tastes of psychedelia and funk, and continued to have hits even into the 90s.
The Supremes were on the rise in 1966, but Martha & The Vandellas were already on top.
Watchout! is Martha & The Vandellas' fourth studio record, and while it doesn't contain anything as legendary as previous hits Dancin' In The Street or Nowhere To Run, it does boast two top-10 hits: I'm Ready For Love (which sounds an awful lot like The Supremes' You Can't Hurry Love) and Jimmy Mack.
The latter would be their final top-10 hit and the band would start to fracture in the following years, just as the Motown label also began to hit tough times.
But Watchout! marks the last great album from one of Motown's definitive acts.
Gaye had 10 top-50 singles on the Billboard charts prior to this, his seventh album, but none had cracked the top 100.
Moods was his best effort to date but still fell short, peaking at 118.
It was an attempt to present Gaye as a serious artist and not just a pop star.
Armed with a strong line-up of songs from Motown's in-house songwriters (including Holland-Dozier-Holland), the album didn't achieve its aim, yet still produced another five top-50 singles including Ain't That Peculiar, Take This Heart Of Mine, and I'll Be Doggone.
And three more …
This article wouldn't be complete without these world-changing albums.
Surprisingly, Simone's 14th album was thrown together from session leftovers.
But it doesn't feel like an afterthought, rather a distillation of her many voices and styles.
Simone is brassy on Break Down & Let It All Out, then on the very next track (Why Keep On Breaking My Heart) she coos in sweet agony, while on her own song, Four Women, she brings all the rage and violence required to tell such a tale of racism, slavery, rape and misogyny.
An influence on Jeff Buckley, David Bowie, Aretha Franklin and more, Wild Is The Wind is perhaps the definitive Simone album, more than earning its place on many a best-ever-albums list.
Jazz was leaving rock behind in the experimentation stakes of 66.
The likes of Sun Ra, Ornette Coleman and John Coltrane were among those taking the genre to wild new places.
Ascension is one of Coltrane's last studio albums (he died in July 1967). It's a hugely influential, free-jazz experiment that has an organised structure behind it.
Coltrane released the slightly easier-to-digest Meditations in 1966 too, but Ascension is often considered one of his greatest works, though, as music mag Mojo once put it, the album "has been found useful in clearing the room of squares", such is its chaotic and free nature.
Nothing sounds like cowboys, deserts and Mexican stand-offs quite like this.
Italian composer Ennio Morricone's transcendent score for the spaghetti western The Good, The Bad And The Ugly spent more than a year in the Billboard charts, keeping Sergio Leone's film in the cultural consciousness long after it had left cinemas.
The sunburnt trumpets, the mirage-shimmering guitars, the haunting whistle — these are the sounds that stand out in the memory.
But there are so many more, including ocarinas, organs, an amazing orchestra and so many weird voices.
It may have had Leone scratching his head, but it works a treat.

A week of warnings reveals Europe's dangerous new reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

analysis
European leaders warn of imminent Russian threat to their countries
One after the other they lined up to speak: national leaders warning of increasing imminent danger to their countries.
World leaders spent this week bemoaning the big challenges facing the world in speeches to the United Nations General Assembly.
But the more extraordinary line up of warnings has been coming from Europe over the past week.
Last weekend, France, the Netherlands, Finland, Lithuania, and Switzerland all individually warned their citizens of increased threats from Russia.
'No one is safe'
This followed Polish prime minister Donald Tusk, citing intelligence assessments, telling the Polish parliament last week that Russia could launch "hybrid drone and missile strikes" against Poland and other NATO countries supporting Ukraine, while portraying them as accidental.
Such attacks could form part of a Russian effort to test NATO's resolve, he said, and cast doubt on whether the alliance would invoke Article 5, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
"These possibilities have been discussed for some time, but the information is now highly consistent and, unfortunately, convincing," he added.
"I want to present the public with the most likely scenario for the next few months, because it is one that envisages serious events and requires focus, seriousness and the mental readiness to face difficult tests," he said.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, followed by calling the leaders of France's political parties — and 2027 presidential candidates — to an emergency briefing at the Elysee Palace to discuss Ukraine, Iran and the growing energy crisis.
He called Tusk's warnings "sound and well-documented" as he announced a new critical infrastructure protection plan.
Guillaume Lacroix, leader of the Radical Party of the Left, left the meeting saying: "At the age of 50, I have rarely felt such vertigo."
"No one is safe," Macron said.
Then, on Thursday, the Danish government's defence intelligence service released an assessment that concluded Russia would increase its threats to NATO nations, "with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past" of hybrid war and sabotage.
Underlying all these assessments of changing threats are not just warnings of greater cyber interference, or the occasional drone over NATO airspace.
The concern is that Russia may be planning to target critical infrastructure as it concentrates more on civilian targets in countries supporting Ukraine.
Several railway lines in the Netherlands and France have recently been sabotaged, for example, with at least one causing many injuries. There have been suspicious fires near explosive manufacturing plants.
Le Monde reported this week that ''more and more experts argue that it is time to abandon the term 'hybrid warfare' and simply call it war".
It is not that European leaders are worried about the threat of an imminent land invasion. It's more the spectre of finding themselves in the same situation as the Gulf countries that have been enduring months of Iranian missile and drone attacks on military and civilian targets as the stalemate between Iran and the US continues.
Germany's lame duck
The European warnings came as the far right, pro-Russian Alternative for Deutschland (AfD) party made more gains in state elections in Germany last weekend and support for the centre right party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz collapsed.
Merz's leadership of the country was left on life support amid agonising over how he could be removed (apparently not as easy as it is in Australia).
In the meantime, there is a sense of the lame duck around German politics which is just what Europe doesn't need from its biggest economy just now.
The AfD is pushing for Germany to buy more oil and gas from Russia ahead of an expected cold winter — and generally become more friendly towards Moscow.
Given the German industrial base is undergoing its biggest transformations in a century — from car manufacturing to weapons and defence material — it's hardly surprising that some of its neighbours are watching developments with alarm.
However, it turns out that the AfD is not the only group wanting to buy Russian oil.
The Financial Times reported this week that the US government and Gulf powerbrokers with ties to the Trump family are backing a bid for the international assets of the Russian oil company Lukoil — put up for sale after it was hit with US sanctions last year.
Lukoil's international assets were originally due to be sold to the US private equity group Carlyle. But that deal "has stalled in Washington awaiting final US approval".
"Lukoil's overseas assets, valued at $US20 billion ($28 billion) when they were written off in March, include oil and gas fields from central Asia to Mexico, thousands of petrol stations and a large European refining portfolio," the Financial Times reported.
"The sale of the assets presents a rare opportunity to snap up more than 3 billion barrels of proven and probable reserves, as well as some of Bulgaria and Romania's biggest refineries."
The proposal "would put the US government in the unusual position of simultaneously bidding for the assets while another part of the administration decides their fate," the Financial Times noted with some understatement.
"The proposal raises the question of whether Carlyle would be disadvantaged if pitted against a consortium involving the US government and investors with ties to the administration, in a decision made by the White House. One person familiar with the process said: 'Yes, there is that concern'."
Loading
No action on Gaza at UN
The Trump family's business interests continue to plough on apace, it seems, even as President Donald Trump's power base seemed to be diminishing in inverse proportion to his boasts at the UN General Assembly.
"I have a big decision to make,″ Trump had told the UN on Tuesday.
To make a deal with Iran, or "annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again".
If only the threat was unique enough to be truly, truly shocking.
Yet few other world leaders gave it much credence. It was striking that in the addresses of others, the US/Israeli war on Iran seemed to feature relatively little in speeches, except perhaps from the Gulf states, with more (rhetorical) focus notably on Israel and its actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
Trump's speech seemed particularly directed at his ebbing political support in the US, ahead of mid-term elections.
He boasted he was "reasserting American power" and its "unmatched military might": boasts that sounded particularly hollow after a weekend in which he had been building up to join the attack on the Houthis in Yemen, only to pull out at the last moment, reportedly amid concerns from military advisers about the perilous state of US weapons stocks.
Despite almost criminal overuse of the words "pomp, and pageantry and red carpet", the media coverage of the state visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping was all framed in terms of the Chinese leader's better tactical hand on AI and other issues.
Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was also using the platform of the UN to appeal to a domestic audience back home ahead of an imminent election, attacking the many detractors who had used the same podium this week to accuse Israel of genocide in Gaza.
For the second year in a row, he faced a walkout of delegates from more than 70 countries.
Loading...
"Shame on you," he declared to all those he said were spreading lies about Israel.
Earlier in the week, Macron had used notably similar language about the world's failure to act on Gaza, after a dozen countries — including France and Australia — last year used the same forum to formally recognise Palestine.
"What credibility do we have if we continue to remain inactive in the face of Gaza?" he said
"Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all? Never!"
Netanyahu attended the meeting despite an International Criminal Court warrant calling for his arrest, while the Trump administration denied a visa for Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas.
Despite leader after leader stepping forward to speak about Gaza this week, there was no more action from the UN on the issue.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

Eggs, sugar, and meat are becoming more expensive: how food prices changed in September
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:27:34 EEST
03:27:34 KST

Eggs, sugar, and meat are becoming more expensive: how food prices changed in September
Kyiv • UNN
In September, egg prices rose by up to 41.6%, sugar by 18%, and rice by 13.5%. Experts cited the reasons for the price increases.
In September, staple foods—eggs, sugar, buckwheat, rice, sunflower oil, and meat—increased in price by 1.25%. According to economic experts, there are several reasons: from strikes by the russian armed forces on warehouses and logistics, which increase business costs, to seasonal factors and a shortage of domestic supply.
Which products rose in price the most during the first month of autumn, and how much Ukrainians will have to pay for them, was determined by UNN.
How much can eggs be bought for in Ukraine
Eggs saw the biggest price jump over the month. Currently, a standard tray of 10 eggs of the Kvочка brand, category C1, costs an average of UAH 80. Eggs of the Yasensvit brand in the same category are even more expensive: they cost UAH 84.25. For comparison, in August they cost UAH 57.12 and UAH 59.49, respectively. As we can see, the product became 38.3–41.6% more expensive, respectively.
Currently, the cheapest place to buy eggs is the Varus supermarket chain: at a promotional price, they cost UAH 75.50 there. ATB offers them at a slightly higher price—UAH 78.90 for 10 category C1 eggs of the Kvochka brand. If you buy this product at Silpo supermarkets, you will have to pay UAH 84.52.
Yasensvit eggs can be bought more cheaply: from UAH 63.80 at the Varus chain (although this is a promotional rather than a regular price) to UAH 79.90 at ATB stores.
What is happening to sugar prices
Sugar ranked second in the price anti-rating. It became 18% more expensive over the month. Currently, a kilogram of granulated sugar can be bought for an average of UAH 35.82, whereas in August it could be purchased from store shelves for UAH 30.22, despite the preservation season.
As of September 25, Auchan and Metro hypermarkets offer sugar at an advantageous price: UAH 34.90. Sweet purchases at Novus will cost a symbolic nine kopecks more, where a kilogram of sugar costs UAH 34.99. The highest price will have to be paid at the Megamarket chain, where a kilogram of granulated sugar already costs UAH 38.50.
The cheapest place to buy a kilogram of white sugar now is Silpo: it costs UAH 32.99 there. Purchases at ATB and Varus will be slightly more expensive: UAH 34.90 and UAH 39.50, respectively.
Is buckwheat currently affordable for Ukrainians, and where can it be bought most cheaply
Unlike other popular foods, buckwheat rose only slightly in price in September—by 5.1%. While a kilogram of the grain could be bought for UAH 74.63 in August, in September it already costs UAH 78.45.
The most advantageous place to stock up on this grain now is Silpo: there, a kilogram of buckwheat is offered at a promotional price of UAH 54.99. At ATB and Metro, it already costs more—UAH 69.90. Auchan offers customers a kilogram of the grain for UAH 74.90. Novus is at about the same level, with buckwheat priced at UAH 74.99 per kilogram. The highest prices are currently at Varus (buckwheat costs UAH 97.30 per kg) and Megamarket (the price is set at UAH 99 per kg).
How much does rice cost and why has its price skyrocketed
Round-grain rice, unlike buckwheat, rose in price by 13.5% over the month, increasing from UAH 54.71 to UAH 62.07 per kilogram.
Auchan has currently set the lowest price for it—UAH 53.90 per kilogram. It is also выгодно to buy rice at the ATB supermarket chain and Metro hypermarkets, where it costs UAH 54.90 per kg. You will have to pay more at Megamarket—UAH 58.50 per kilogram of rice. Varus offers it for UAH 74.50. Novus set a higher price, where the popular grain already costs UAH 80.99. The highest price for rice is currently at Silpo: there, rice under its own
Premiya brand costs UAH 92.49 per kg.
How much did oil rise in price in September
Prices for sunflower oil rose by approximately 6.6% over the month. While 850 ml of Oleina sunflower oil cost UAH 100.68 in August, by the end of September the price on the shelves of popular supermarkets had been set at UAH 107.30.
The lowest price is currently offered by the ATB supermarket chain: the oil costs 99.85 UAH here. At Varus, the price of Oleina also remains affordable: 99.90 UAH per bottle. A few kopecks more — 99.99 UAH — is the price of a bottle of oil from this brand at Novus. And you will have to pay 101.50 UAH at the checkout in Auchan for refined oil. The highest prices for sunflower oil have currently been set by Silpo and Megamarket: 109 UAH and 112.50 UAH, respectively.
Where it is most выгодно to buy meat in September and how much it costs
As for meat, its price also rose in September. In August, Ukrainians bought a kilogram of pork neck for 314.38 UAH, while in September they already have to pay 346.45 UAH for it. Thus, the price increased by 10.2%.
Despite this, meat can still be bought at a good price. At Silpo, the promotional price for a kilogram of boneless pork neck is currently 279 UAH. Novus and Metro offer a kilogram of this meat for 309 UAH. At Varus, a piece of pork costs 324.90 UAH, while at Megamarket it costs 379 UAH.
Why food prices have increased in Ukraine
First of all, the damage to warehouses and refrigeration equipment, as well as the loss of stock, make storage and delivery more difficult.
Economist Andrii Zablovskyi explained at the beginning of September that switching to small supply batches costs more than transporting large consignments by trucks and refrigerated vehicles.
Meanwhile, Deputy Chairman of the All-Ukrainian Agrarian Council Denys Marchuk links the autumn price pressure to seasonal changes in supply. For milk, this is due to a further decline in milk yields during the cold season; for eggs, it is due to a combination of seasonality, energy and logistics costs.
Pork, in turn, has become more expensive for Ukrainians because of a shortage of domestic supply. In other words, the reason lies in an internal shortage of livestock.
Buckwheat, meanwhile, has faced an older problem with production volumes. Back in the spring, Serhii Hromovyi, executive director of the International Buckwheat Association, explained the high prices by reduced acreage and the small harvest of the previous season.

US Army Reserve assessing troop readiness for potential military operation in Cuba
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
18:22:07 UTC
03:22:07 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
The US Army Reserve is assessing whether it can provide medical, military police and other support units to US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) within 90 to 120 days amid military planning for potential action in Cuba, according to US officials.
The officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the message does not constitute deployment orders. They also said President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on launching a military operation.
The internal directive asks subordinate commands to assess the availability of six types of formations that could be placed under SOUTHCOM within 90 to 120 days.
The requested assets include medical brigades, forward surgical units, military police, engineer battalions and sustainment command units.
The message itself does not mention Cuba. However, multiple US officials told local media that the request is part of continued military planning concerning possible action against Cuba.
Officials stressed that readiness assessments can be conducted for contingency planning and do not necessarily indicate that military action will take place soon.
The assessment comes amid heightened political and economic pressure from the Trump administration on the government of Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel.
On Sept. 17, the Treasury Department announced Cuba-related sanctions, including measures targeting Cuban military-linked entities and officials.
Diaz-Canel previously said Cuba would be prepared to resist any US aggression, while also denying that Havana poses a military threat to Washington.
The latest Army Reserve assessment follows earlier reports that US military planners have examined possible operations involving Cuba.
In July, CBS News reported that Pentagon officials had considered several military options, while stressing that such planning did not mean a decision had been made.
The Army message provides no indication that troops have been ordered to deploy or that an operation is imminent.
SOUTHCOM has not publicly disclosed any operational timeline related to Cuba.

The enemy attacked a lyceum near Kyiv with a drone, sparking a fire

Failures at Manston asylum centre linked to decisions at Number 10, inquiry hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
18:15:31 UTC
03:15:31 KST

A catalogue of failures including racism, use of force and chronic overcrowding at a Home Office processing site for people who arrive on small boat were linked to decisions made at the highest level of government, an independent inquiry has heard.
The government commissioned the Manston independent inquiry to look at problems under the Conservative government between 1 June and 22 November 2022 at the facility in Kent.
Almost 200 asylum seekers detained at Manston are participating in the inquiry along with the former home secretaries Suella Braverman and Priti Patel, several government departments including the Home Office, Treasury, Ministry of Justice and Ministry of Defence, and HM Inspectorate of Prisons and the UK Health Security Agency.
The problems began when the site became vastly overcrowded. Manston was designed to hold a maximum of 1,600 new arrivals for no more than 24 hours as there are no proper sleeping or other facilities there. But after decisions by ministers to pause transfers of many of the asylum seekers to other accommodation such as hotels the site became dangerously overcrowded.
Up to 4,000 people were accommodated there unlawfully for several weeks at the peak of the crisis, most of them sleeping on the floor in profoundly insanitary conditions.
There were outbreaks of infectious conditions including scabies and diphtheria, the latter of which can be fatal in approximately 30% of cases in unvaccinated populations. There were also reports of assaults and drug use by guards, racist abuse from guards, and the death of a man after contracting diphtheria.
The inquiry, chaired by Sophie Cartwright KC, heard that two former prime ministers, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak, who were both in post at different points in 2022, were involved in decision-making about the Manston site.
Laura Dubinsky KC, representing some of the participants, told the inquiry that the decision to pause sending many asylum seekers on to hotels was in line with the thinking at No 10.
“No 10 clearly did play a decision-making role,” she said. Patel has provided evidence to the inquiry that funding was deemed inadequate to address the small boats issue, including funding for Manston and onward accommodation.
The inquiry heard that events in Manston “raise very serious questions for ministers”.
Clair Dobbin KC, counsel to the inquiry, said it was taking place in a “crucible of hostility” at a time when the arrival of small boats remains a significant issue.
She added that “to put it bluntly” the inquiry would look at whether at certain points “the entire operation at Manston was outside the law”.
One senior Home Office official wrote a report saying: “To be frank, I’m struggling for words,” after observing what he said were “the worst conditions I have observed working in this environment”.
Hussein Haseeb Ahmed, 31, was taken to Manston after arriving in a small boat. He died in hospital after becoming ill with diphtheria. He was belatedly admitted for care and was kept in handcuffs as he lay dying. The handcuffs were only removed two and a half hours before he died. According to the inquiry, evidence about his death suggests “a succession of missed opportunities”.
The inquiry also heard that “very racist language was used towards detainees by some staff”.
Sixty families were crammed into 11 rooms in a barracks building with no hot water, showers or clean clothes for nine days with one toilet for 81 people, and no soap or sanitiser available.
Some used toothpaste to soothe bites and one used a croissant wrapper to dress wounds.
Questions were raised about whether some unvetted staff were working legally at Manston.
Shu Shin Luh, one of the lawyers representing participants in the inquiry, said: “Why were people treated as less than human?”
Stephanie Harrison KC, also representing some of the participants in the inquiry, accused the Home Office of presiding over “an institutional culture defined by impunity with widespread illegality and non-compliance with the law”.
Future dates for inquiry hearings have not yet been confirmed.

25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Months after Saudia Arabia and the US signed a bilateral civil nuclear pact, classified intelligence assessments recently provided to the US Congress conclude that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons program, The Washington Post reported Friday.
US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that the evaluation forms part of intelligence documents submitted to lawmakers alongside material from the US State Department, which expressed greater confidence in Riyadh's commitments and the agreement's oversight safeguards.
"With this deal, the Trump administration is departing from precedent, adopting looser restrictions, and caving to Saudi demands by agreeing to a process that is all but certain to allow Riyadh to acquire the means to enrich uranium and possibly develop nuclear weapons," a coalition of Democratic lawmakers, led by US Senators Ed Markey and Jeff Merkley, wrote Friday to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a former Republican senator.
The US State Department defended the arrangement, maintaining in a statement to the Post that Washington "does not and will not support a Saudi nuclear weapon program."
Abdulaziz bin Salman, the Saudi energy minister, said earlier that the civilian effort remains "peaceful" and operates under "the highest levels of responsibility and transparency."
Under the bilateral civil nuclear pact signed this July by Abdulaziz and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Washington agreed to supply technology and fuel while granting a conditional pathway to domestic enrichment, limiting levels below 5% before potentially authorizing up to 20% following additional review.
The agreement sits under a 90-session-day congressional review timeline following its August submission, facing a Joint Resolution of Disapproval introduced by House Democrats over non-proliferation concerns.

alexandre arrechea grows a playable tree of basketball hoops in toronto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
18:10:41 UTC
03:10:41 KST

At the entrance to Toronto’s Biidaasige Park, a bright red trunk splits into a canopy of basketball hoops. More than twenty rims sit at the ends of curving steel branches, some low enough for an easy shot and others hovering overhead. Alexandre Arrechea’s Orange Functional translates a piece of familiar court equipment to suggest an oversized fruit tree, and anyone arriving with a basketball can play it. The sculpture currently stands in the plaza of Old Firehall 30 as part of the Lassonde Art Trail.
The basic idea predates its Toronto setting by well over a decade. Arrechea developed Orange Tree in 2010 as a branching structure whose ends terminate in basketball rims, with balls gathered below like fallen fruit. The artist’s archive dates the work to 2010, while contemporary documentation describes versions reaching roughly twenty feet high. Those earlier sculptures established the strange image at the center of the project: a basketball hoop multiplied until the game itself becomes difficult to recognize.
A major change for Alexandre Arrechea’s Orange Functional came in 2022. Produced as a commission for Art Omi in Ghent, New York, the steel sculpture was designed so people could actually shoot into its branching hoops. Art Omi describes it as the artist‘s first functional basketball sculpture, built from steel with basketball nets and a painted finish. The formal joke suddenly became playable.
Once a ball leaves someone’s hands, the familiar geometry of basketball starts to break apart. A player can aim for a high rim and watch the missed shot drop through one below it. The branches create several possible trajectories at once, so a clean miss can unexpectedly become a basket.
The concept of instability has followed Arrechea’s basketball works for years. The court is one of the artist’s recurring subjects, used as a recognizable system with boundaries and agreed ways of moving through space. Here, the standard hoop is still legible, yet multiplication scrambles its purpose. There is no single basket to defend or obvious direction of play. The object remains familiar enough that people instinctively know what to do with a ball, then asks them to invent what happens next.
The tree analogy becomes clearest once the shooting starts. Balls rise into the branches and drop back toward the pavement like oversized orange fruit, a movement built into Arrechea’s description of the work from its 2022 functional version onward. Toronto gives that image a particularly literal setting: the sculpture sits among the new plantings of Biidaasige Park, its red steel canopy standing above younger trees nearby.
after paris and new york, the evolving sound installation arrives in athens, where water, porcelain, architecture, and the weather become part of the composition.
the swiss artist turns industrial mesh and raw concrete into a temporary painting for audemars piguet contemporary, shaped by architecture, movement and the changing city.
naïve my love: ukrainian folk art of the 20th century brings together paintings, textiles, decorative objects, and other works gathered through years of research across ukraine.

US Supreme Court revives expanded voter citizenship verification system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
18:10:34 UTC
03:10:34 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
The US Supreme Court on Friday granted the Trump administration’s request to temporarily revive an expanded federal voter citizenship verification system while litigation over the program continues. 
In a per curiam order, the justices stayed a June 22 ruling by a federal district court in Washington, DC, that had set aside and vacated modifications to the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, program. 
The case, Department of Homeland Security v. League of Women Voters, involves changes made to SAVE in 2025 that expanded the records available for citizenship verification and allowed state and local authorities to conduct searches involving multiple individuals at once. 
The modified system incorporated records from the Social Security Administration, including Social Security numbers, and allowed election officials to submit identifying information through the SAVE portal. The system could then return information concerning an individual’s citizenship status. 
The justices granted the Justice Department’s request to pause the lower-court ruling, which had barred state officials from using Social Security numbers and other federal records to conduct broad citizenship checks of registered voters. 
The administration’s expanded voter-verification efforts are part of a broader push to boost the federal government’s role in election administration ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, while states traditionally have primary responsibility for conducting and overseeing elections under the US Constitution. 
Attorney General Todd Blanche praised the Supreme Court's decision. 
"Huge victory for election integrity!" Blanche said on US social media company X. 
Blanche said the Supreme Court granted the Justice Department’s stay in revamping the SAVE citizenship verification database, which will allow states to clear the voter rolls of "illegal voters." 
"The modified SAVE system allows state and local officials to conduct citizenship verification of registered voters to keep aliens from voting," he said, adding the Justice Department will continue fighting in court for secure elections. 
The decision was a victory for the Trump administration after a series of judicial setbacks. 
Trump is not on the ballot for the midterms, but if Democrats make sizeable gains in Congress, as most current polls predict, Trump’s ability to govern in the rest of his term could be significantly hindered.

Poland boosts air defence after ‘Russian provocations’ amid Ukraine war

Poland boosts air defence after ‘Russian provocations’ amid Ukraine war
Alleged incursions put NATO nations on alert as Ukraine launches strikes on Russia during parliamentary voting.
Poland has heightened its air defence posture, following repeated alleged incursions into its airspace in recent weeks.
The Polish Air Force launched preventive air patrols on September 17 aimed at securing the eastern part of Polish airspace.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items

- list 2 of 4Russian attacks kill eight people across Ukraine as US steps up diplomacy
- list 3 of 4Russia attacks Ukraine while Zelenskyy speaks at UNGA

Warsaw officially blamed Russia, but Moscow has denied allegations that it is targeting NATO nations.
“Following the latest Russian provocations and acts of aggression, I have made the decision to expand the protection of our airspace. We are increasing the activity of our air forces, including F-16 aircraft and helicopters,” wrote Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz on social media.
Those patrols came with a political warning.
“I want to present to the public the most probable scenario for the next few months, because it is a scenario that assumes serious events and requires focus, seriousness and the mental readiness to pass difficult exams,” said Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
“According to intelligence, the Russian plan also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” he said in parliament. “These possibilities have been mentioned for a long time, and today the information is very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing.”
He said the aim of suspected Russian incursions was “to weaken the motivation of NATO countries to apply NATO regulations in the event of aggression against any member state”.
Days later, on September 23, Poland said an Mi-8 helicopter entered Polish airspace from Kaliningrad for 42 seconds.
“Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence,” said Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command.
The most serious Polish claim of a violation was by a Russian Su-24 reconnaissance aircraft in the Baltic Sea in February 2025, an incident Russia reportedly acknowledged.
During the past week, suspected Russian drones were shot down twice in Moldova, and once in Romania on September 24, observers said.
Poland and Romania are two NATO members immediately bordering Ukraine through which military supplies and Western officials have reached Ukraine. Hungary is also a NATO member bordering Ukraine, but has not allowed military supplies through its territory.
The latest alleged airspace violations have again raised the spectre of an open Russian attack on NATO territory, a prospect European intelligence chiefs have been warning about since January 2024.
Czech intelligence chief Michal Koudelka this week told The Guardian that a Russian attack, which “could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, [or] a massive influence campaign”, might come in a matter of “months, not years”.
Russian information, and reality
During the past week, Russian officials made claims to have captured towns in the eastern Ukrainian Donetsk region.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on September 19 Moscow’s forces had seized 5,300 square kilometres (2,050 square miles) and more than 220 settlements in Ukraine since the start of 2026.
Moscow launched drone strikes against Ukrainian cities every night of the week, and combined them with missiles on September 19, 22 and 24, killing at least eight people and injuring dozens. One of those deaths was a cleric at a monastery in Kherson. Two were killed when Russia launched three waves of ballistic missiles at Kyiv, including a maternity clinic.
“Since the beginning of this year, Russia has used more than 2,100 missiles of various types against Ukraine. More than 950 of these were ballistic missiles,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly. During the same period, Russia launched 63,000 drones into the country, he said.
“We need to slow it down before we move to the next stage,” he said. “Because next year, there is a real possibility that AI – not just humans – will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield.”
According to the Institute for the Study of War, which assesses territorial changes using geolocated open sources, Russian claims of a serious advance are vastly overstated.
It estimates that Russia has captured a net 147.7sq km (57sq miles) in the first eight months of 2026, its worst performance of the war by far. Ukrainian forces had liberated at least 972.56sq km (375sq miles) from Russian occupation during the same period, it has found.
Those counteroffensives have come near Oleksandrivka, straddling the Donetsk-Zaporizhia border, and around the town of Lyman in northern Donetsk.
The Lyman operation, codenamed Vivaldi, saw 50sq km (20sq miles) liberated in a second phase of the operation in recent days, Ukrainian officials said.
“Artillery and drone systems targeted enemy command posts, communication hubs, logistics, crossings, and reserves. Air defence and electronic warfare systems created a protective shield over the area of combat operations. The blinded enemy was unable to decipher the plan of the operation, and our units consolidated on the liberated lines,” said an announcement from the Third Army Corps commanded by Andriy Biletsky.
Russia’s vote, a referendum on the war
Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia Party triumphed in the Duma elections, raising its majority from 315 seats in the 450-seat body to 355.
Russian officials prejudged the result as a positive referendum on Putin’s war in Ukraine.
“I have no doubt that the result will confirm the commitment of all our parties and voters to the course the president has set both domestically and for our foreign policy,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters ahead of the election.
“We will continue to ensure support for our president’s course and bring victory over the enemies of the Fatherland closer,” deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev wrote on Russian social media.
Ukraine launched its biggest combined air strike of the war on the final day of Russia’s parliamentary elections.

Some got through, putting Moscow’s oil refinery out of action for the second time this year. Videos posted online showed several fires, suggesting a number of successful strikes.
