02:37:21 KST

Mining company Ferrexpo, which owns assets in Ukraine, ended the first half of 2026 with a net loss of $14.9 million, 13.2 times lower than the figure for the first half of 2025, according to the company's report published on Friday.
According to the report, revenue fell 2.3 times to $196 million due to lower sales volumes, while EBITDA was negative at $4 million, compared with positive EBITDA of $4 million in the first half of 2025, reflecting the combined impact of lower sales volumes and selling prices, as well as higher production costs.
Ferrexpo said it deliberately reduced capital expenditures (CapEx) to $10 million from $28 million in January-June 2025, allocating 88% of these expenditures to projects necessary to maintain operations and just 12% to development projects.
Due to a prolonged delay in VAT refunds and the resulting decline in financial liquidity, the group was forced to reduce production volumes to a single pellet production line, the report said.
Total commercial production in the first half of the year amounted to 1.556 million tonnes, down 40% from the previous half-year period (which ended on Dec. 31, 2025) and 54% from the first half of 2025.
The production mix in the first half of 2026 consisted of 89% pellets and 11% commercial concentrate, compared with 61% and 39%, respectively, in the first half of 2025, when the higher share of concentrate production provided additional market opportunities during a period of lower demand for pellets and lower market premiums, Ferrexpo noted.
Interim Executive Chair Lucio Genovese recalled that in early September the company had a successful $100 million equity raise, which materially strengthened the group's liquidity position, providing additional financial resilience and greater flexibility to manage the continuing operational and financial pressures facing the business.
"The additional capital does not however remove the underlying challenges as a result of the continued withholding of VAT refunds, the war in Ukraine, constraints on logistics and energy infrastructure, and the need to maintain disciplined management of cash and working capital," he said.

Mongolia’s New Government Set Ambitious Goals. But Are They Realistic?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:36:00 UTC
02:36:00 KST

On September 15, Mongolia’s parliament, the State Great Khural, began its autumn session – and it started full throttle. The incumbent government headed by Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor has an ambitious agenda that saw it propose one of the largest state budgets. Among its goals: establishing a sovereign wealth fund, securing energy from China, and building data centers. Parliament will likely scrutinize many of these big initiatives.
The State Great Khural has much to decide, but it is operating within a highly politically divided environment. Mongolia is still wrangling with government instability that began with the ousting of Oyun-Erdene Luvsannamsrai’s administration in June 2025. Uchral’s government only took office on March 31 of this year – less than six months ago.
When parliament convened on September 15, the new government revealed one of the largest state budget proposals in Mongolia’s history, asking for 41.3 trillion tugrik, with a deficit of 2.3 trillion tugrik. Economists and skeptics worry that, with inflation standing at 12.5 percent, such a large deficit will only increase Mongolia’s debt, forcing the government to increase taxes on businesses and individuals. The state budget proposal has already faced massive scrutiny within the parliamentary committees. In a warning sign for Uchral’s government, parliament failed to reach the required quorum last week.
One of the major issues with the 2027 state budget proposal is the 2.3 trillion tugrik deficit. One of the solutions the Uchral government proposed is to utilize the increased Oyu Tolgoi dividend.
On September 11, Mongolia and Rio Tinto agreed to amend the Oyu Tolgoi contract, the Shareholder’s Agreement that was first established 17 years ago. The amendment will allow Mongolia to receive 13 trillion tugrik, approximately $3.6 billion. Uchral also announced that Rio Tinto agreed to reduce operational costs by approximately 30 trillion tugrik, an equivalent of $8.4 billion.
While the Mongolian parliament has to review another state budget amid the constant changes of government, a second issue that will face major scrutiny is the establishment of Mongolia’s Sovereign Wealth Fund. Under the Oyun-Erdene administration, in 2024, the Parliament of Mongolia passed new laws on a Sovereign Wealth Fund. In February 2026, just before it was forced from office, the Zandanshatar Gombojav government signed a preliminary agreement with companies to allocate 60 percent of the benefits from Mongolia’s strategic deposits to the Sovereign Wealth Fund as a new profit-sharing mechanism meant to benefit the public.
The current trajectory and the goal of the Sovereign Wealth Fund, however, may have pivoted from Mongolia’s welfare system, which would have directly benefited the public. The fund is now leaning more toward a corporate governance structure.
The initiative is now part of a larger reform in Mongolia’s state-owned companies. To support this reform, on September 10, Mongolia signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the U.S.-based BlackRock Financial Markets Advisory. BlackRock and the Mongolian government outlined a general framework that looks to explore selling shares in state-owned enterprises in both domestic and international capital markets.
After the MoU was signed, critics asked whether BlackRock’s corporate model – the restructuring of Mongolia’s state-owned enterprises – aligns with the country’s semi-welfare system. The government will need to have access to those funds to provide public assistance to the elderly, the disabled, children, the poor, and for public education and health. These welfare systems are indeed at the heart of Mongolian society today.
In 2025, Mongolia experienced intermittent protests and strikes from educators and medical workers, demanding a pay raise. If the Uchral government fails to deliver these promises, this wealth fund policy and priority changes will have a great impact on the Mongolian people who depend on these funds.
Beyond the financial wrangling, the issue of energy security looms over Mongolia. The Iran-U.S. war has roiled global energy markets, as have repeated Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Mongolia is uniquely dependent on Russia for fuel, importing over 95 percent of refined petroleum products from its northern neighbor. When Russian supply dwindled, Mongolia felt the pinch. In the summer and fall of 2026, nationwide fuel shortages highlighted the country’s vulnerability and pushed policymakers to seek an additional source: China. In September, delegates from the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources held bilateral meetings with China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) to discuss importing 10,000 tonnes of refined petroleum, 4,000 tonnes of jet fuel, and 3,000 tonnes of diesel.
Moreover, China is currently financing one of Mongolia’s first hydropower plants, Erdeneburen Project in Khovd province. With a Chinese soft loan line of approximately $288 million, the construction contract was awarded to Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) and PowerChina in 2023.
In mid-September, Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa and officials inspected the progress on the construction of the Erdeneburen Hydropower Plant. The Office of the President announced that the project is now 40 percent complete. When finished, the plant will have the capacity to supply reliable electricity to five provinces, including Khovd, Bayan-Ulgii, Uvs, Zavkhan, and Govi Altai.
Considering Mongolia’s energy infrastructure, combined with the landlocked challenges, full energy independence may not be in the cards as a short or medium term goal. That said, managing fuel shortages by reaching out to diverse global partners is in the national interest. Even prior to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Mongolia experienced intermittent energy shortages, which motivated the government to seek third-neighbor investments and diversify energy sources.
In August, Mongolia’s Deputy Prime Minister Dorjkhand Togmid announced Mongolia’s interest in building data centers in connection with accelerating Mongolia’s renewable energy sources. While the initiative is an attempt to kill two birds with one stone, even before discussing investment opportunities, Mongolia will need to decide how to handle data centers’ demand not only for energy, but for water.
According to the Brookings Institution, “A typical data center uses 300,000 gallons of water each day… but large data centers can use an estimated 5 million gallons of water each day.” The study warned: “Building a new facility and pledging economic impact mean little without sustainably incorporating water resources into ongoing operations.”
In 2025, an OECD study on water resources highlighted Mongolia’s water scarcity. Mongolia’s geographic disparities as well as surface water distribution make constructing – let alone maintaining – data centers a highly questionable endeavor.
The Uchral government is viewing China’s data centers in Inner Mongolia as a template and following the global trend. However, despite the similarities in wind and solar capacity and the cold climate, the water issue is one of the most important areas that needs to be scrutinized before Mongolia moves forward.
The State Great Khural has entered another highly politicized season with much to resolve. Unfortunately, the internal feud within the Mongolian People’s Party (MPP) will continue to weaken the parliament’s function. The MPP, the nominal ruling party with 68 total seats, is now effectively divided into two blocs of 30 and 38 legislators.
The Uchral government’s proposals are supposed to bring Mongolia economic prosperity and development, but without truly addressing the long-standing challenges of corruption, air pollution, water shortages, and energy security, the people’s confidence in governance remains extremely fragile. What the Mongolian people need is lawmakers and a government that prioritize the well-being of its citizens – not political vendettas.

Netanyahu just incited genocide in his UN speech. Here’s what you missed.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:35:12 UTC
02:35:12 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu spoke at the UN General Assembly yesterday in New York. Hundreds of protesters blocked access roads to the UN, and about a hundred were arrested for demanding Netanyahu’s arrest — among them actors Susan Sarandon, Hannah Einbinder, and Debra Winger.
Inside the hall, as Netanyahu took to the stage, a walkout of many dozens ensued for about 1.5 minutes, as Israel’s cronies chanted “Am Yisrael Chai” (‘the nation of Israel lives’).
The speech itself was a potpourri of lies and incitement, vacillating between condemnations of Zohran Mamdani and Hassan Piker to recounting Israel’s standard October 7 atrocity propaganda and shamelessly repeating the line about Israel having the “most moral army in the world.”
But then, the Israeli Prime Minister chose to end his speech with a seemingly obscure verse from the Bible: “Nezah Israel lo yeshaker,” or “the eternity of Israel will not falter.” The line is sometimes translated as “the eternal one of Israel shall not lie.”
Either way, readers unversed in the Bible will no doubt find all of this vague. But Netanyahu’s followers in the national-religious camp know exactly what he’s referring to — and it’s a genocidal dog whistle.
It’s important to remember that Israeli elections are only a month away (October 27), so his speech is in large measure aimed at this constituency.
So here’s the context.
The phrase, which comes from Samuel I, 15:29, relates to the genocide of Amalek, or the Amalekites, the bitter enemy of the Israelites. It’s a biblical reference that Netanyahu has applied numerous times to modern-day Palestinians, most infamously at the start of the Gaza genocide.
King Saul was admonished by the prophet Samuel for failing to completely eradicate the Amalekites. Saul had spared their king Agag and “the best of the sheep and cattle,” which the Israelites “were unwilling to destroy completely.” According to the Bible, this level of annihilation was insufficient and betrayed King Saul’s supposed weakness. That is why the Prophet Samuel admonished the biblical king:
“The Lord anointed you king over Israel. And he sent you on a mission, saying, ‘Go and completely destroy those wicked people, the Amalekites; wage war against them until you have wiped them out.’ Why did you not obey the Lord? Why did you pounce on the plunder and do evil in the eyes of the Lord?”
Saul sought to defend his actions, but Samuel delivered an uncompromising message:
“You have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord has rejected you as king over Israel!”
Saul asked for forgiveness, but Samuel delivered the unrepentant message:
“The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to one of your neighbors — to one better than you. He who is the Eternal One of Israel shall not lie or change his mind; for he is not a human being, that he should change his mind.”
The context for the phrase is crucial. Transposed to the Israel of today, Netanyahu is telling his followers: they must go all the way in the annihilation of today’s Amalek. Anything short of that would be to reject the word of God.
It wasn’t the first time that Netanyahu had deployed precisely this phrase. In May 2024, when the ICC Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan announced that he was seeking an arrest warrant for Netanyahu, among others, for war crimes and crimes against humanity, Netanyahu responded with two videos, one in English and one in Hebrew. He called the whole thing a “blood libel” and compared Khan to a Nazi judge. While the English version of the rant ended with “never again is now”, the Hebrew one ended with the same line: “Netzah Israel lo yeshaker.”
The quote was also applied by Netanyahu in 2017, when he delivered another UN speech, but it was reserved for the Hebrew transcript.
Netanyahu’s use of Biblical messaging isn’t arbitrary. It’s a message he sends to his constituency, and today that message reads: genocide to the end.
In yesterday’s UN speech, he summed it all up like this: “And the reason is simple. We have no other choice. Thank you all. Chag Sameach le’Am Yisrael,” or “happy holidays to the nation of Israel.”
In other words, we have no choice but genocide.
It’s possible to mention many more things about his speech, which also included the standard kitsch-bravado stories about his brother Yonatan (Yoni), who was killed at the Entebbe operation in 1976, but we must not lose sight of the main point: a wanted war criminal got onstage at the UN to incite continued genocide — another nadir for the crumbling institution.

Kanyshai Butun
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
The Russian Foreign Ministry said Friday that negotiations on the Eurasian Charter of Diversity and Multipolarity in the 21st Century had officially begun.
According to a joint statement published by the ministry, the process will be open to all interested Eurasian states and based on sovereign equality, inclusiveness, transparency and equal participation.
A ministerial meeting was held on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York and was co-chaired by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and Belarusian Foreign Minister Maxim Ryzhenkov at Russia’s UN mission.
The two officials said negotiations on the charter would help build trust and establish common approaches to security issues across Eurasia based on balancing the interests of all countries involved.

The officials said the charter would promote economic cooperation and connectivity, humanitarian ties, civilizational dialogue and mechanisms for equal decision-making among Eurasian countries.
Representatives of several Eurasian states welcomed the Belarusian-Russian initiative and expressed interest in joining the negotiations.
The meeting concluded with representatives from Belarus, Vietnam, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Laos, Myanmar, Russia and Tajikistan adopting a joint statement launching the negotiations and approving rules for a working group tasked with drafting the charter.

Sukkot 2026: What the sukkah and Four Species teach us about Israeli unity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:34:18 UTC
02:34:18 KST

Sukkot has two particularly distinctive mitzvahs that make the holiday even more special and colorful: the sukkah itself and the Four Species.
The sukkah is where we spend much of our time over the holiday, eating our meals, and many sleep in the sukkah when conditions and weather allow.
The Four Species – the lulav (palm branch), etrog (citron), hadassim (myrtle), and aravot (willow) – are central to the holiday's prayer and practice.
From a different perspective, the sukkah is our physical home during Sukkot, and the Four Species serve as a form of spiritual focus.
In addition to these distinct thematic differences, there is a clear halachic distinction between these two mitzvahs.
On the first day of Sukkot, the Torah commands us to take up the Four Species (note that this is when the first day doesn’t fall on Shabbat, as it does this year).
The Torah makes this a very personal mitzvah, whereby one must own their own set rather than rely on someone else’s. This means that not only can one not steal someone else’s Four Species, but even borrowing them for the purpose of the mitzvah would be problematic.
The halachic origin of this comes from the verse “V’lakachtem lachem,” And they shall be taken for you, with an emphasis on the word “you.” The seemingly extraneous word “you” led commentators to explain that every individual needs to have personal ownership of their set of Four Species.
This individual commandment, however, does not apply to the sukkah, where a person can certainly use and enjoy someone else’s structure to fulfill the mitzvah. This understanding comes from the verse “Kol ha’ezrach b’yisrael yeishvu basukkot”, meaning “every citizen of Israel should sit in sukkot.”
The use of the plural form of sukkah and the absence of the word “your” or “their” were interpreted as conveying a fascinating teaching: “it would be fitting for all the people of Israel to sit in one common sukkah.”
Certainly, this isn’t meant to be understood in a practical sense but is designed to highlight the communal aspect of the mitzvah and to show that going into someone else’s sukkah is a full realization of the mitzvah.
So what can we learn from the fact that one mitzvah is designed to be so individualistic and the other so communal? And how do these distinctions relate to our world today?
Sages compared the Four Species to different types of people
ON NUMEROUS OCCASIONS, the Sages compared the Four Species to different types of people. For example, the etrog is represented by its positive, inviting scent and taste, connoting people who are accessible, welcoming, and sociable.
On the other hand, the arava has no smell or taste, reflecting less personable figures in society.
But these traits described by the Sages should not be limited to the physical or behavioral; they also reflect the spiritual aspects that shape who people are and how they relate to God and their surroundings.
This is perhaps why every person needs to purchase their own lulav set.
Spirituality and religiosity are deeply personal values, and what is right for me should never be perceived as what is right for my friend or neighbor, or even my fellow family member.
In Judaism, we are taught to encourage people to follow individual paths to attain spirituality, and that our diversity and differences contribute to making the Jewish people the remarkable nation it is.
But alongside individualism, we also have communal institutions and organizations that need to be shared and embraced collectively, and this is the symbolism of the sukkah.
As a nation, we cannot have separate “sukkot” for every group with its individual interests. We cannot create individual armies, political parties, law enforcement agencies, medical services, etc., for every splinter group and way of thinking within the greater society.
Yet, even while accepting this inherent value of communal, shared ideas and institutions, any citizen of a modern nation knows that it is certainly not easy to live together in one “sukkah.”
Taking our metaphor to another level, we know that sitting alongside one another in the sukkah are those who want to sing certain songs, people who sing aloud into the wee hours of the night, while others demand quiet and more subdued expressions of spirituality.
Some think the answer is simply to build multiple sukkot and perhaps that will work best. But if history has taught us anything, it is that no society or nation will survive and thrive when every person is given the opportunity to create his or her own institutions. Candidly, that would be the recipe for social and national disaster.
This dynamic metaphor brings us to our current times as the people of Israel prepare to participate in a critical, and likely deeply divisive, election. The vote comes after three years of pain-filled war, which followed one of the most complex social crises in our nation’s history surrounding the question of judicial reform.
Even in the best of times, election cycles tend to create internal walls within society and lead to the formation of multiple camps directly opposed to the concept of “one sukkah,” which we described as so critical to national success.
Campaign strategists try to make it seem as though the divisions are greater than they actually are, and that the black-and-white choice therefore is for their particular party.
A different path forward is possible
AS A NATION and society that has achieved so much and overcome so much pain and loss, we cannot fall victim to that desire by political and media forces to expand the gaps between us.
Our national and Jewish responsibility demands that we say, very simply, that a different path forward is possible.
I would humbly suggest that several fundamental ideas must be embraced if we are to succeed in building the communal national sukkah we so need at this time.
The first is to remember that a family is a family in both good and bad times. Certainly, we have our physical, behavioral, and even religious differences. But at times like these, we need to remember what unites us: we share one father, and we all belong to the same Jewish family.
Remembering this truth is so important today when people begin to think that ideologies or characteristics, like who we vote for, where we pray, or how we define ourselves as Jews, make us any less of a family.
No family is without its fights, bitter debates, and, tragically, even moments of estrangement. But we are all witnesses to countless stories where those divisions were overcome when we remembered that the power of one nation is perhaps one of the greatest emotional forces the world has ever known.
The second fundamental ideal for creating a more cohesive society during these deeply fragile times is to accept that as bitter as our internal divides might be, we need to set aside the fear that one side is intent on destroying the other.
As someone who is committed to working and speaking with diverse elements of Israeli society, I know this fear exists among most camps.
A study conducted by Tzohar last year found that a majority of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) respondents believe that one of the main reasons secular Israelis want haredim to enlist in greater numbers and to expand haredi education into new areas is to create greater exposure to secular values and, ultimately, weaken the haredi community.
Conversely, the same survey found that a majority of secular Israelis are concerned that placing a greater emphasis on Jewish studies in secular schools could have a similar effect of exposing young minds to religious perspectives in ways that could influence their approach to Jewish practice.
So it turns out that we are a nation instilled with fear. Not just fear of annihilation from enemies like Hamas and Iran, but spiritual destruction from the fellow Jew often living just across the hall or on the other side of town. And amidst a world of fear and suspicion, it will be nearly impossible to build the communal sukkah we so need.
Finally, and perhaps most critically, we need to find ways to embrace a new and original vision and look towards a common and better future.
Our commitment to building a better society cannot be predicated solely on physical survival or national defense. Certainly, the experiences of the last three years, and more broadly, our entire national history, have proved that we are more united in times of stress and under the threat of external destruction.
But that cannot be the main source of our national unity or peoplehood. Rather, the time has come to create new paths of thinking that rely on common values, acceptance of the other, and a community that highlights and celebrates our differences while allowing us to thrive as a people despite moments of disagreement.
Once we accept these truths and find the path to work towards them, with God’s blessing, we will merit the chance to finally all live together under one sukkah.■
The writer is the chair of the Tzohar Rabbinical Organization and the chief rabbi of Shoham.

Sukkot 2026: Yom Kippur reminds us life is short - Sukkot asks what we do with it - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:34:13 UTC
02:34:13 KST

There are moments in the Yom Kippur prayer book when a familiar line suddenly refuses to remain familiar.
This Yom Kippur, somewhere in the long hours of prayer, I found myself looking at the words: “Man is founded in dust and ends in dust.” I have said those words many times. This year, however, it was the commentary alongside them, by the late Rabbi Lord Jonathan Sacks, that stopped me.
He writes about the extraordinary brevity of human life. Against the history of the universe, even a long life is barely a microsecond. Therefore, perhaps the greatest decision we ever make is how we use our time.
It is an obvious thought, but sometimes the obvious thoughts are the ones we most successfully avoid. Almost everything else we possess can, at least theoretically, be replaced. Lose money, and you may earn it again. Lose a possession, and you may buy another. Lose a job, and another opportunity may appear. Even damaged relationships can sometimes be repaired.
But an hour cannot be recovered. Yesterday cannot be bought back.
Time is the one currency we are all spending constantly, whether we realize it or not. Rich and poor spend it at precisely the same rate. And none of us knows the balance remaining in our account.
Perhaps that is why Judaism is so preoccupied with time. We sanctify days. We count days and weeks. We welcome Shabbat and reluctantly escort it away. The first thing in the Torah that God declares holy is not a place or an object. It is a day.
Judaism asks us not merely to pass through time, but to sanctify it. And that thought takes us directly from Yom Kippur to Sukkot. On Yom Kippur we spend an entire day pleading for life. “Remember us for life. Inscribe us in the Book of Life.”
There is a story I once heard about a man walking along a beach who saw a child struggling in the sea. The child was clearly drowning. Without hesitation, the man ran into the water, fought his way through the waves, and dragged the child safely back to shore.
'A life worth saving'
When the boy had recovered his breath, he looked at his rescuer and said, “Thank you. You saved my life.” The man replied: “Then make sure it was a life worth saving.”
I have no idea whether the incident actually happened. Perhaps it is simply a parable. But its message has stayed with me.
On Yom Kippur we asked God to save our lives. Sukkot begins only a few days later. Perhaps Sukkot is God’s answer: Now make sure your life was worth saving.
This Friday evening, Jews throughout the world will leave their solid houses and move into structures that are deliberately temporary. The sukkah is a house that makes no pretense of permanence.
We spend enormous amounts of our lives building security. We acquire homes, pensions, investments, possessions and insurance policies. None of that is wrong. Responsibility requires us to plan for the future.
But then, once a year, the Torah says: leave the house. Go outside. Sit beneath a roof through which you can see the sky. Remember that ultimately you are only passing through.
And strangely, the festival that forces us to confront impermanence is specifically described as a time of joy. Perhaps that is because knowing that something will not last does not make it less precious. It can make it more precious.
A parent holding a newborn child may not appreciate how quickly those years ahead will disappear. A grandparent does. We watch our grandchildren running around the table and know that these moments will not last forever. We sit with aging parents and gradually realize that an ordinary cup of tea together is not ordinary at all.
Impermanence can teach us gratitude. It can also teach us urgency.
Perhaps the purpose of our brief stay on this earth is actually remarkably simple: to leave the world a little better than we found it. Not necessarily to change the whole world. Very few of us will. But perhaps to change our corner of it.
To have brought more kindness than cruelty into the world. To have healed rather than hurt. To have taught someone something they did not know before. To have helped someone who needed us. To have raised children with values. To have comforted someone who was lonely. To be able to say that because I passed through this world, something, somewhere, is better than it would otherwise have been.
That seems an extraordinarily Jewish ambition.
We are not asked simply to believe. We are asked to act, give charity, visit the sick, comfort mourners, teach our children, welcome strangers, and pursue justice. To repair what we can.
We cannot control how much time we are given. We can control what we do with it. And perhaps this is where Yom Kippur and Sukkot, apparently such different festivals, meet.
On Yom Kippur we asked to be written and sealed in the Book of Life. Sukkot asks the harder question: What are you going to do with the life you have just prayed for?
Another argument that really does not matter? Another evening scrolling through things we will not remember tomorrow? Another year postponing the telephone call, the apology, the visit to an elderly relative, or the conversation with a child or grandchild because there will always be another opportunity?
Except that one day may not come.
There is a profound difference between filling time and using time. A full diary is not necessarily a full life.
This Friday night, when we enter the sukkah, perhaps we should look through its fragile roof at the sky and remember the message that caught my attention on Yom Kippur.
Our houses are temporary. Our possessions are temporary. We are temporary. But the consequences of what we do need not be.
The kindness we show, the children we raise, the people we help, the wounds we heal, the love we give, and the difference we make can remain long after we have returned to the dust from which we came. “Man is founded in dust and ends in dust.”
We prayed on Yom Kippur for another year of life. Now comes the challenge. Make sure it is a life worth saving.
Chag sameach.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman

Supreme Court restores Trump's mass voter verification system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:33:59 UTC
02:33:59 KST

The US Supreme Court revived on Friday an expanded immigration database that President Donald Trump's administration said aims to combat voting by noncitizens, but critics contend could disenfranchise eligible voters.
The justices granted the Justice Department's request to block a judge's order that had stopped state officials from using Social Security numbers and other information to conduct sweeping checks of the citizenship status of registered voters against federal records.
The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Its three liberal justices dissented from Friday's order.
The majority said the plaintiffs' arguments likely fail because federal law expressly authorizes the Department of Homeland Security to request and receive information relating to citizenship and immigration status from other agencies, including the Social Security Administration.
The administration's data-sharing arrangement is one in a series of actions boosting the federal government's involvement in voting ahead of November's midterm elections in which Trump's fellow Republicans seek to maintain control of Congress. The US Constitution gives individual states the primary authority to run and administer elections.
Gaining political advantage by narrowing the electorate
The Department of Homeland Security last year redesigned a federal database known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, used to verify a person's citizenship and immigration status. The revamp allowed users to search many records at a time and to conduct searches using individuals' Social Security numbers.
Since then, several Republican-led states have compared their voter lists to the database, and some voters flagged as potential noncitizens have had their registrations canceled.
Critics say such election-related actions by Republicans are driven less by concerns over election security than by an attempt to gain political advantage by narrowing the electorate, risking the disenfranchisement of eligible, often Democratic-leaning voters.
Trump has carried out hardline policies toward immigration and has made false claims of widespread voting fraud, including in his 2020 election loss to Democratic former President Joe Biden.
Advocacy groups that sued to block the revised SAVE system said that the new approach has resulted in people who were wrongfully identified as noncitizens being kicked off voter rolls. They have argued that SAVE can be outdated, meaning immigrants who have become naturalized US citizens and are thus eligible to vote are sometimes labeled as noncitizens.
The modified system's overall error rate is not publicly known. The Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice did not provide that information when asked.
Court's decision puts Americans 'at risk'
Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, which represents the plaintiffs, called Friday's decision "profoundly disappointing," saying it puts Americans "at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration's unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections."
In a dissent on Friday that was joined by her two fellow liberal justices, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that "the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take."
In their Supreme Court filing, the advocacy groups cited a Travis County, Texas, election official who said 25% of the system's noncitizen matches there involved people who had already proven their US citizenship, and news reports finding that at least 81% of the system's responses in St. Louis County, Missouri, were erroneous.
The voting rights group League of Women Voters and privacy rights group Electronic Privacy Information Center sued in September 2025 to block the Trump administration's modified system. They said that the revamp violated federal privacy and other U.S. laws.
In a June ruling blocking the revamped database, US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan in Washington, DC, said the system was haphazardly assembled and contained unreliable citizenship data.
"All in all, the federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote," Sooknanan wrote. "This court cannot stand idly by while that happens."
The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in a 2-1 ruling on September 4 declined to halt Sooknanan's ruling, prompting the administration's request to the Supreme Court.
In a Supreme Court filing, Justice Department lawyers called the judge's order "indefensible," arguing that it "threatens the integrity" of the midterm elections.
Texas, which intervened in the case in support of the administration, has disputed claims that the system is unreliable.
Due to separate litigation in Florida, the Trump administration has been able to continue using its modified SAVE system in the Republican-led states of Florida, Iowa, Indiana, and Ohio.

Iran has sent a new proposal to Washington that it would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program in seven days if the US lifted its naval blockade, waived oil sanctions and observed a ceasefire that includes Lebanon, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told a private gathering on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Thursday, according to the Associated Press.

Accusations against 'certain European nations'

Also on Friday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian held talks with Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani in New York, as Qatar presses on with its efforts to mediate between US and Iran, including during hours of indirect Iranian-US talks at the UN this week.
Do not mistake Tehran's position for 'stratregic retreat'
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said that the two leaders discussed “the latest developments in the region, along with efforts to de-escalate tensions and create a conducive environment for dialogue, thereby contributing to the enhancement of regional security and stability.”
Former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department Danny Citrinowicz said in a post on X that “Tehran appears to believe that a political window is opening in Washington,” and that “with the US midterm elections approaching and President Trump facing strong incentives to bring down oil prices, Iran sees an opportunity to test whether economic and political pressure can translate into American flexibility.”
“But Tehran’s position should not be mistaken for a fundamental strategic retreat,” Citrinowicz added.

Iran offers Hormuz reopening, nuclear talks in conditional US deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:27:00 UTC
02:27:00 KST

Iran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations over its nuclear program within seven days if Washington lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, grants waivers for Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire extending to Lebanon.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi detailed the proposal in a private gathering on Thursday on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, according to one attendee.
Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute think tank, said Araghchi suggested that a speedy agreement would help U.S. President Donald Trump ahead of November's midterm elections. The arrangement would also relieve enormous economic pressure on Tehran as the U.S. piles on additional sanctions.
Iran's disruption of the strait - through which a fifth of the world's traded oil and gas transited before the war - has emerged as its main point of leverage. The effects have been felt far beyond the Middle East.
There was no immediate comment from Iran's U.N. mission or other Iranian officials. A person familiar with the matter, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss private deliberations, told The Associated Press that Saudi Arabia was skeptical of the latest push for a deal.
The White House did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment on Iran’s proposal.
The proposal, conveyed to the U.S. by mediators, strongly resembles the so-called Memorandum of Understanding reached in June, but with an accelerated timetable. The earlier agreement, which called for a 60-day interim period, quickly collapsed as Iran resumed attacks on shipping in the strait.
Trump has said he is in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hard-liners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates like President Masoud Pezeshkian.
"If Trump calculates this arrangement is worthwhile and can bring political benefit before the midterms and reduce gas prices, perhaps we'll see flexibility not seen in previous weeks,” Parsi said. But he noted "deep suspicion,” especially around the prospect of Iran merely buying time to ship out more of its oil and ease its economic pain.
In the latest sign of diplomatic movement, Pezeshkian hosted the prime minister of Qatar early Friday. Qatar has been a key mediator, including during hours of indirect Iran-U.S. talks at the U.N. this week.
It was not clear how long Pezeshkian and Araghchi would stay in the U.S. after Pezeshkian addressed the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders on Wednesday, ending his speech by saying Iran remained open to diplomacy.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on the same day, said "if there’s an opportunity to exchange ideas and messages, we will.”
After multiple failed attempts at a deal, however, suspicion is high on both sides. The U.S. and Israel have attacked Iran twice while it was engaged in nuclear talks, and the U.S. and Iran accuse each other of having swiftly violated the June agreement.
"The Iranians already know that the chances of this not being accepted by Trump are much higher than the opposite,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote on X.
"They want to show that they were ready for diplomacy and that it was the United States that, for the third time, decided to attack in the middle of a diplomatic track - something that people within (Iran’s) strategic community have been anticipating over the past few days.”
The proposal would include Lebanon, where Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah have been mostly observing a ceasefire. It's not clear, however, if it would include the revived conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia, which has put even more pressure on global markets.
Iran appears to think the Houthis' newly enhanced ability to threaten the Bab el-Mandeb strait on the Red Sea - another trade chokepoint on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula - could push Trump to make a deal.
Maj. Gen. Yahya Rahim Safavi, a military adviser to Iran's new supreme leader, told state television that the Americans "face a new problem called the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.”
He added: "I think the process that is unfolding is in our favor, and the Americans will be forced to accept Iran’s conditions.”
With the Houthis' latest surge in attacks, Saudi Arabia was skeptical of Araghchi’s latest push for a deal with the U.S., according to the person familiar with the matter.
The kingdom, along with other Gulf states, had advocated over the summer for a return to negotiations, saying they could live with an agreement that gave Iran a temporary role in managing the Strait of Hormuz, the person said.
But the Saudi calculations changed as the Houthis seized Yemen’s strategic Red Sea coast from pro-government forces and a vital Saudi pipeline came under attack .
Earlier this month, Gulf leaders planned to gather in Oman to discuss an emerging agreement between Oman and Iran on the Strait of Hormuz, which runs between the two countries. But the meeting was canceled after Saudi Arabia called for amendments, only some of which were accepted by Iran, the person said.
Iran's leaders have sought to project unity, but some hard-liners want to continue or escalate the war to secure bigger U.S. concessions and have criticized Pezeshkian and Araghchi's diplomatic steps this week.
Firebrand lawmaker Ebrahim Rezaei wrote on X that merely meeting with "the aggressor enemy” showed weakness. Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a panel of Shiite clerics who appoint the supreme leader, said "there is no path other than resistance.”
The head of Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guard, Brig. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, highlighted the U.N. speech by "the esteemed president” while focusing on Pezeshkian’s comments that Iran doesn’t fear war.
Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, who served as chief negotiator in earlier talks with the United States, provided a rare public acknowledgment of the internal divide.
"There is a view that speaks of war but offers no prospect or mechanism for bringing it to a powerful conclusion,” he wrote on social media. "At the opposite end is a current that makes the error of underestimating national capabilities.”
He added: "The first error keeps the country in a state of permanent crisis, while the second hands national resources and dignity over to the enemy.”

US university ends cadaver transfers for Israeli military training

The University of Southern California has ended an arrangement involving the transfer of donated human cadavers for medical training provided to Israeli military personnel, according to USC's Annenberg Media.
The university concluded the agreement between its Keck School of Medicine and the U.S. Navy on Thursday, ending a program that spanned more than five years and generated more than $1 million for the university.
Officials at the medical school said the decision did not stem from recent student demonstrations sparked by media disclosures of the initiative. Instead, the school confirmed the agreement ended because the University of California San Diego (UCSD) declined to continue supplying donated bodies for the venture.
The University of California Health Communications team explained that UCSD ceased transfers because the receiving surgical skills lab failed to satisfy regulations requiring courses with human remains to take place in specialized surgical facilities. The Keck School noted that USC did not profit from the donated remains.
There was previously no indication of what purposes bodies could serve following donation, and donor families got no prior notice that their relatives' remains could be utilized by the U.S. military, according to the report.
The Greater Los Angeles Area office of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR-LA), Southern California's largest Muslim civil rights organization, welcomed the contract termination.

Lebanon PM stresses need to avert 'vacuum' if UN force leaves
Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam stressed at the UN Friday on the need to "avert the vacuum" that would be caused by withdrawing the UN peacekeeping mission deployed in the country's south without a viable replacement.
Under US pressure, the UN Security Council decided last month to fix December as the end of the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which has been deployed since 1978.
"What we wish to stress here and today is the need to avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it," Salam said in a speech to the UN General Assembly.
UNIFIL currently has 7,500 peacekeepers from around 50 countries.
They are deployed in southern Lebanon along the Blue Line, which stretches for 120 kilometers (75 miles), marking a de facto border between Lebanon and Israel.
Salam also stressed the need for Israel to fully withdraw from Lebanese territory and for Beirut to move forward in extending state authority over its entire territory, ensuring "weapons (are) held by the state alone."
Hezbollah, backed by Tehran, has so far opposed disarmament.
Lebanon and Israel concluded a framework agreement in June under US auspices, providing for the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces and the disarmament of Hezbollah, but its implementation has stalled.
It is intended to end a conflict that has lasted for decades.
The UN force reported extensive Israeli military ground activities in its area of operation and repeated violations of Lebanese airspace and territorial waters, between Monday and Thursday.
The peacekeepers recorded 195 airspace violations involving Israeli drones, fighter aircrafts and helicopters, according to UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric.

Indonesia on Thursday commissioned its first aircraft carrier, KRI Sriwijaya-100, into the Navy at Tanjung Priok Port in North Jakarta, according to Jakarta Globe.
The vessel, formerly the Italian Navy’s Giuseppe Garibaldi, was formally inducted after being acquired by Indonesia. Italy retired the ship in 2024 after more than four decades of service.
Col. Mochamad Fuad Hasan was formally appointed commander of the vessel.
The 180.2-meter-long (591-foot-long) vessel has a displacement of about 13,850 tons and a flight deck capable of operating helicopters and short-takeoff and vertical-landing aircraft.

The Navy hopes eventually to equip the carrier with vertical-takeoff combat aircraft, although no acquisition has been announced. The ship previously operated AV-8B Harrier II jets with the Italian Navy.
KRI Sriwijaya-100 will also serve as a maritime command platform and support disaster response, humanitarian aid and efforts to combat forest and land fires.

U.S. appeals court upholds Pentagon designation of Anthropic as supply chain risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:19:19 UTC
02:19:19 KST

A federal appeals court panel in Washington, D.C., on Friday upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic, dealing a blow to the artificial intelligence company in its months-long battle with the Trump administration.
The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional.
"The Department had ample support for its conclusion that the continued integration of Claude into the Department's information systems, by the Department or its contractors, presented a statutorily covered national-security risk," Judge Gregory Katsas wrote in the majority opinion for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, which Judge Neomi Rao joined. Katsas and Rao were appointed by President Donald Trump.
Judge Karen LeCraft Henderson, who was appointed by former President George H.W. Bush, dissented.
In March, the DOD labeled Anthropic a supply chain risk, meaning the company purportedly threatened U.S. national security, after negotiations about how the military could use its Claude AI models spiraled out of control. The designation prevents the U.S. military from using Anthropic's models and blocks defense contractors from using them in their work with the agency.
Anthropic's relationship with the Trump administration has been fraught ever since, and Trump has repeatedly slammed company's CEO Dario Amodei on social media. Amodei recently drew Trump's ire by calling for an industry wide slowdown, and he was not invited to the glitzy state dinner the White House hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
"The Trump Administration has stopped AI "people" from doing bad, or potentially bad, "things," like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a "perfect little angel" - and we will continue to do so!," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social on Monday.
Anthropic sued the Trump administration in U.S. District Court in San Francisco and in the D.C. Circuit Appeals Court in March, seeking to reverse its blacklisting. The DOD relied on two distinct designations to justify its supply chain risk action, which meant they had to be litigated in two separate courts.
A San Francisco federal judge ruled last month that one designation was illegal. The ruling Friday by the D.C. appeals court upheld the second designation.
"We respectfully disagree with the court's decision," an Anthropic spokesperson told CNBC in a statement. "Another federal court has already held the government's parallel designation unlawful. We remain confident in our position and are considering all options, including further review."
The appellate panel said it would delay the decision from taking immediate effect to give Anthropic time to petition the same panel for a rehearing or to seek an en banc rehearing of the case, by all of the judges on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals. Anthropic could also ask the Supreme Court to take the case.
Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed.
The DOD wanted Anthropic to grant the military unfettered access to its models across all lawful purposes, while Anthropic wanted assurance that its technology would not be used for fully autonomous weapons or domestic mass surveillance. They were unable to come to an agreement, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of attempting to "to seize veto power over the operational decisions of the United States military."
Katsas said Friday that Hegseth raised the "deeply sobering" idea that "overly constrained" AI models could shut down unexpectedly, as well as the potential that Claude might be "subject to manipulation." While Anthropic refuted those claims, Katsas said decision-making authority ultimately rests with Trump and Hegseth.
"In our Republic, it is the President and the Secretary of War who must determine how best to balance the competing risks," Katsas wrote. "In doing so here, the Secretary did not transgress any limits on his authority under the Supply Chain Security Act or the Constitution."

Ukraine is trading access to 5 million frames of real combat for British AI technology: they use the data inside locked platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:17:47 UTC
02:17:47 KST

Ukraine is opening its battlefield data to British weapons makers so they can train their AI on a war no one else has fought. Up to 12 British defense companies will join Avengers Labs, Ukraine's platform for training AI models for drones and robots on real combat data, the Defense Ministry said.
Ukraine's combat data is a resource no other military has access to. British firms get to build and test their AI on battlefield data they could not access elsewhere, while Ukraine gets their technology and joint development of AI for unmanned systems.
What is Avengers Labs?
More than 30 Ukrainian companies already use the Avengers Labs, and three of their systems have reached the battlefield. It is part of the AI push former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov built around Ukraine's data.
The terms are built around control. The British companies can develop and test their own AI models within Avengers Labs, the ministry said, but the data remains within the platform's protected environment, with no way to download it or take it out. That lets Ukraine share the value of its war experience, the annotated record of real combat, without surrendering the record itself.
The platform was developed by the Center for Innovation and Development of Defense Technologies, the team that created the DELTA combat system. At the core of Avengers Labs is an annotated dataset of 5 million frames collected on the battlefield. Most of this material comes directly from the DELTA combat system and is continually supplemented with new data of practical value in combat conditions.
Britain trains for a real war
In March 2026, Ukraine announced the establishment of a system of military technology competence centers. The first in the network was intended to be the Defense AI Center "A1," which would focus on AI solutions.
The AI center is being launched with support from the UK. Its main tasks were planned to be:
analysis of combat data;
forecasting enemy actions;
development of autonomous systems;
new management/control tools
A separate center was said to have been established for each key direction of the war: drones, mid-range strike, deep strike, artillery, and others.

The Oligarch Part 4: This man made billions in Ukraine, befriended Soros – and bought a place at the West’s table

The Oligarch Part 4: This man made billions in Ukraine, befriended Soros – and bought a place at the West’s table
Late August brought news that the Victor Pinchuk Foundation is partnering with America’s prestigious Yale University to launch an international leadership development program for Ukrainian veterans of the NATO proxy war against Russia. Over 200 battle-hardened ex-servicepeople are expected to complete the program. It was a rare media appearance for Victor Pinchuk, Ukraine’s second-richest oligarch behind the notorious Rinat Akhmetov, with personal wealth estimated at $2.8 billion. Pinchuk has remained largely in the shadows throughout the proxy war. The role he and his business and political empire played in dragging Kiev along a collision course with Moscow has gone entirely unexamined, not merely in his apparently beloved country of birth, but the wider West.
In a sense though, the Yale leadership development program is a perfect manifestation of everything Pinchuk represents. Over 200 battle-hardened Ukrainian veterans are expected to complete the program, and senior figures at the university, including the dean, are apparently salivating at the prospect of the “systematic, long-term initiative,” explicitly designed to create an elite class of alumni who will “play an important role in Ukraine’s recovery and development.” Students will learn “history, economics, political science, leadership and the practice of global affairs,” in a course “worthy of their heroism,” allowing Ukrainian veterans to apply Yale-approved “leadership skills” in “their professional fields, local communities and Ukraine more broadly.”
Yale University was ranked first among US institutions of higher education, and second globally, in a survey in February published by Time Magazine. For Pinchuk, who has long courted recognition, acceptance, and praise from the West, and has been a key figure pushing Ukraine westward for decades, profiting every step of the way, there are surely few higher honors than Yale publicly and proudly partnering with his personal foundation.
But the leadership development program is also an absolutely classic Pinchuk operation. He pioneered a tactic known as “invisible appointments.” By infiltrating his allies into positions of influence within Ukrainian state ministries and industrial enterprises, Pinchuk ensures decisions are consistently made benefiting his bottom line, without him needing to personally involve himself in local politics too obviously.
As RT’s The Oligarch series has shown, historically, it doesn’t pay for Ukraine’s ultra-wealthy classes to take sides, and the West’s proxy war on Russia has imposed ever-stricter and constantly changing ‘rules’ by which they are expected to play. If they don’t fall foul of the US-funded National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), the troubled administration of Vladimir Zelensky could turn on them at any moment – whether for political reasons, or personal enrichment. The Yale University program not only represents a pipeline of fearsome future Ukrainian leaders who owe a personal debt to Pinchuk and can become “invisible appointments” in the future, it also promotes his personal brand in the US, right when the extremist regime he helped install is facing collapse.
How did Pinchuk get so filthy rich?
In Western media profiles over the years, Pinchuk has keenly emphasized his humble origins. Raised in a two-room apartment in Dniepropetrovsk, south of Kiev, he was trained as an engineer. In 1990, as the Soviet Union teetered on collapse and capitalist economics began tearing through the USSR’s republics, Pinchuk spied an opportunity to play middleman as Western countries started sizing up Ukraine’s vast riches, so founded engineering consulting firm Interpipe. Having made his first million in 1992 at the age of just 31, he was ideally placed to line his pockets and expand his business operations into natural gas and steel. Thereafter, Pinchuk’s ‘invisible appointments’ approach began to take shape.
Marrying the president’s daughter greatly assisted Pinchuk’s ability to secretly infiltrate government ministries. In 1997, he left his wife to begin dating Elena Kuchma, the daughter of Leonid Kuchma, who led Ukraine from July 1994 to January 2005. Almost immediately, rumors began circulating in the country and wider region that Pinchuk was receiving privileged access to deals, completely unavailable to people unconnected to the Kuchma dynasty. He even became an MP in 1998, a position he held for almost a decade. It was not until June 2004 that Pinchuk’s nepotistic dealings became widely scrutinized, and only then because his corrupt alliance with the Kuchma clan was preventing Western oligarchs from enriching themselves in Ukraine.
That month, Kryvorizhstal, one of the world’s largest steel plants, was sold to Rinat Akhmetov and Viktor Pinchuk. Despite their bid being half that offered by an international consortium led by US Steel, the terms were rigged to ensure only local, well-connected oligarchs could profit. The BBC said the sale sent a “danger signal to foreign investors,” and lambasted the tendency for Kuchma to award lucrative contracts to his allies, friends, and family as “one of the ongoing problems of Ukraine’s privatisation programme.” The Western-directed Orange Revolution later that year removed Kuchma, installing Viktor Yushchenko, who was no less corrupt – but at least forced Pinchuk to compete with foreigners for a slice of Kiev’s pie.
What doesn’t Pinchuk like to talk about publicly?
Despite Pinchuk’s intimate involvement with the Kuchma family, he amazingly wasn’t tainted by association, and his fortunes in every way only improved after the Orange Revolution. Never have questions been asked about whether criminal methods other than nepotism assisted his success. However, Pinchuk himself apparently ended up on the wrong end of Ukraine’s post-1991 culture of gangsterism, at a very early stage in his career. Oligarchs flourish in an environment attaching local organized crime politicians and big business at the hip. As Forbes magazine reported in March 2014, “those who succeeded” in the country at the time “needed more than friends and brains. They needed survival skills.”
Pinchuk was kidnapped in 1996 by people he’d never seen before, who arrived at his mother’s house to celebrate her 60th birthday, before handcuffing and black bagging him at gunpoint. He was held for two days, then released after negotiating to pay $2 million for his freedom. Pinchuk refused to offer details of his ordeal beyond “I stayed alive” to Forbes, pleading “I still can’t talk about this.” To get and stay rich in Ukraine then as now required oligarchs to invest in personal security apparatuses, often in conjunction with local mafia elements and crooked intelligence agents and police old and new.
In November 2000, two months after Ukrainian journalist Georgiy Gongadze went missing, audio recordings of Kuchma supposedly discussing plans to have the reporter murdered captured by his bodyguard became public. Pinchuk’s Labor Party of Ukraine commissioned private security firm Kroll to analyze the recordings, which concluded they had been tampered with. Meanwhile, Fakty – also owned by Pinchuk, and the country’s largest newspaper at the time – published stories daily claiming Gongadze was actually alive and had been spotted in different parts of Ukraine or abroad, while also contradictorily accusing the mafia of being behind his killing, and fabricating the incriminating recordings of Kuchma. In truth, Gongadze was dead, and his murder remains officially unsolved today.
Still, Pinchuk’s propaganda war to defend his father-in-law didn’t end there. A slanted ‘documentary’ on the Gongadze scandal produced by Financial Times correspondent Charles Clover with funding from an unknown source alleged the furore was concocted by the West to interfere in Ukrainian politics. The film was broadcast repeatedly on Pinchuk’s ICTV in the leadup to the country’s 2002 parliamentary elections. In 2015 though, the oligarch was quick to accuse his rival, Igor Kolomoisky, of murders in a costly UK High Court legal battle over a disputed business deal. Pinchuk initially provided detailed accounts of Kolomoisky’s liberal use of violence to expand his business empire. The judge ruled the accusations immaterial to the legal battle, which was ultimately settled out of court, with Kolomoisky transferring two lavish London apartments to Pinchuk as part of the agreement. Clearly, at the very least, Pinchuk knows where certain bodies are buried.
What is the nature of Pinchuk’s relationship with George Soros?
Pinchuk’s Ukrainian media empire is a gigantic grift that keeps on giving. His ICTV dominates the news landscape, while also reeling in casual viewers with movies and TV dramas. Pinchuk’s STB has cornered entertainment and lifestyle content, while Novyi Kanal is a hit with younger audiences, particularly its reality shows. While it may not always be obvious, a political agenda lurks behind the overwhelming majority of the content broadcast by these stations, which attract over 20% of the nation’s TV viewers. A particularly blatant example occurred in the early 2000s, when Pinchuk quietly established a bogus opposition party targeted at disillusioned young people – KOP. His TV networks aggressively promoted the party as an organic, grassroots, patriotic uprising.
This not only took the form of fake news reports, but slick ads hyping KOP’s supposed ‘cool’ factor, and an interactive reality show broadcast on both ICTV and STB. In it, average Ukrainian citizens competed to win a place running for the party in parliament. KOP and other fake opposition infrastructure funded by Pinchuk collapsed in the wake of the Orange Revolution, which also placed some of the oligarch’s local business interests at risk. No matter. Pinchuk simply moved assets abroad, headquartering his empire in the UK under the name EastOne, and increasing his ‘philanthropic’ investments alongside Western foundations. On top of a hedge against rising anger at oligarchs such as himself at home, the time had come for Pinchuk to leverage his wealth to command global geopolitical influence.
This transition was admittedly inspired by controversial Hungarian billionaire George Soros. The two became close personal friends in the 2000s, their respective foundations often co-funding projects in Ukraine and beyond. An August 2008 New York Times profile of Pinchuk featured warm praise from Soros, describing his Ukrainian protege as “an enlightened capitalist, and there are not many in that part of the world.” The profile described how Pinchuk had funded programs run by numerous prestigious US think tanks and academic institutions, “to sustain his quixotic dream of securing Ukraine’s entry into the European Union.” Pinchuk’s famous pals, including President Bill Clinton and UK Prime Minister Tony Blair, were “lured… to give speeches… to support the cause.”
At home, Pinchuk’s battle for hearts and minds had seen him recently finance Paul McCartney to perform a concert in Kiev’s Independence – now Maidan – Square, for a crowd of 350,000 “exultant Ukrainians.” Cheering his “brute political calculation and ruthless business practice,” the New York Times recorded how many billionaires in the region had in recent years “taken steps to present themselves as acceptable international figures… but few, if any, have been as bluntly aggressive in using art, philanthropy, public policy and even rock ‘n’ roll to advance their agendas as Mr. Pinchuk.” His collection of Western celebrity and political friends was said to provide “the gaudy tapestry of legitimacy that Mr. Pinchuk so badly craves.”
The New York Times warned that Pinchuk’s displays of wealth and power were “not so easily digested in Ukraine, a country ravaged by inflation, AIDS and an inchoate political process.” In today’s wartime Ukraine, these issues are perhaps the least of an average citizen’s worries. But while Pinchuk has by-and-large vanished from the public eye today, his political protection has only grown. Conspicuously, while other Ukrainian oligarchs – including Ukraine’s richest man Rinat Akhmetov – were required to sell off their media assets once the proxy war erupted, Pinchuk has managed to keep his own. Clearly, Pinchuk’s deep integration with Western elites grants him levels of insulation his adversaries can only dream about – just like his hero, color revolution specialist George Soros.
How does Pinchuk get away with it all?
Despite his longstanding and highly rewarding policy of avoiding overt political involvement, in December 2016, Pinchuk made a highly public intervention in Ukrainian – and global – affairs. He authored an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal, outlining how his country “must make painful compromises for peace with Russia,” in reference to the brutal Anti-Terrorist Operation waged by Kiev against the defenseless citizens of Donbass. Pinchuk proposed that peace could be achieved by Ukraine; “temporarily eliminating European Union membership from our stated goals”; recognizing locally-organized elections in Donbass; understanding “Ukraine will not join NATO in the near- or midterm,” pursuing “an alternative security arrangement” to NATO, and accepting neutrality “as our near-term vision for the future.” Quite reasonable suggestions, one might think – and a clear blueprint for a brighter, more peaceful future for Ukraine.
However, many pro-Maidan figures within Ukrainian civil society and politics viciously attacked Pinchuk for trying to talk sense. Among them was Mustafa Nayyem, a veteran reporter at Western-funded media outlets who personally kickstarted the Maidan protests in late 2013. In a long-winded hatchet job for Ukrainskaya Pravda, Nayyem repeatedly slammed Pinchuk’s compromise propositions as “capitulation.” When Zelensky won Ukraine’s 2019 presidential election on a platform of implementing more or less what Pinchuk advocated three years prior, Nayyem’s retort to the oligarch’s prescriptions gifted hardline Ukrainian ultranationalists – including the Neo-Nazi Azov Battalion – a campaign slogan to ensure there would be no peace in Donbass.
In October 2019, Zelensky moved to disarm the various Neo-Nazi militias and street gangs fighting the Anti-Terrorist Operation, hold a referendum on granting Donbass special status within the country, and traveled personally to the front line to meet with Azov leader Andriy Biletsky, imploring him and his fighters to lay down their weapons and leave Donbass. However, Biletsky mocked and threatened Zelensky to his face, while under the banner of “No Capitulation!” Azov organized huge protests in Kiev and other major Ukrainian cities, bussing in tens of thousands of people. Peace was comprehensively off the table. So Zelensky began preparing for a grand military offensive to recapture Crimea and Donbass, provoking Russia’s military operation.
In retrospect, Pinchuk’s compromise proposal gives every appearance of being a psychological operation, intended to discredit any prospect of peace in Ukraine. His trial balloon granted ultranationalist Maidan elements within the country a straw man to publicly immolate, so any suggestion of conciliation with Donbass, let alone Russia, could appear deeply unpopular among average Ukrainians, and the determination of Azov Battalion and other ultraviolent factions to fight on could be presented as organic and principled. This interpretation is greatly reinforced by a March 2020 joint letter signed by two dozen Ukrainian NGOs, almost all funded by Western governments and foundations, condemning any direct dialogue between Kiev and the People’s Republics of Donetsk and Lugansk.
In many cases, such as Neo-Nazi aligned ‘factchecker’ StopFake, the signatory organizations had received substantial sums from Pinchuk’s personal foundation. Never forget, the oligarch is a master of theater and misdirection. Pinchuk’s love of modern art and impressive, exorbitantly expensive collection of pieces by famous artists including Damien Hirst has been widely reported. In June 2022, Pinchuk sold a balloon sculpture created by Jeff Koons at auction, raising over $10 million for humanitarian aid to Ukraine. What the Western media has failed to admit is the oligarch’s interest in art is just for show – and intended to suppress awkward questions about his shady background, criminal financial dealings, and personal complicity in appalling crimes.
How does Pinchuk use art for image management?
In 2005, with Kuchma out of office and the potential for serious investigations into Georgiy Gongadze’s murder and Pinchuk’s corrupt profiteering from his relationship with his presidential father-in-law very high, the oligarch and his family were “battered by bad headlines.” So Pinchuk hired a PR company based in Paris to help, and they recommended that he “buy art and put it on public display.” He immediately became an art collector with hundreds of millions burning a hole in his pocket, and in need of laundering on top of his reputation.
“Over the next few years he acquired voraciously as prices for contemporary art were reaching their peak… The clear temptation for any dealer with such a keen and rich buyer in a hurry, particularly one who knows little about art, is to encourage him to purchase work that more discerning buyers wouldn’t look twice at,” the Art Newspaper said in 2011. “Rarely has so much money been spent so quickly on so much bad art.”
Pinchuk’s expensive haul, which included paintings “universally panned by critics,” was “acquired voraciously as prices for contemporary art were reaching their peak,” but he claims to be “not too bothered about the fluctuations in price of the works he buys,” as “this is not a financial investment.” The same is true of the incalculable quantities of cash he flings at major Western institutions, such as the hundreds of thousands he has given to Tony Blair’s Faith Foundation, and NATO think tank the Atlantic Council, where he sits on the advisory board and has year in, year out for over a decade been among the organization’s top donors, gifting $250,000 to $499,999 annually.
Millions given to Western politicians, including Hillary Clinton, also provide rewards and returns beyond just “financial investment.” Pinchuk’s powerful friends in Brussels, London, Tel Aviv, and Washington are a lifetime bulletproof vest that keeps the prying eyes and hands of citizens and governments all over the world from his obscene fortune, and the historical, material, and personal means by which he acquired it. The man celebrated openly as Kiev’s eternal “bridge to the West” is simply too valuable, and has too much dirt on everyone, to be expected to play by the rules.

A Latvian and a Ukrainian were detained in Slovakia on Aug. 25, while another Latvian was arrested in Hamburg.
According to the newspaper, investigators have linked both the Munich arson attack and an attempted Aug. 4 drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport to Russian’s military intelligence agency, the GRU. Germany’s intelligence services believe the operations are being directed by the GRU’s Special Activities Service, which has built a logistics network across Europe. The Leipzig group was headed by career GRU officer Denis Smolyaninov, according to the paper’s sources.
The attacks are aimed at disrupting military supplies to Ukraine and pressuring Europe to reduce its support for Kyiv. After Russian intelligence officers operating under diplomatic cover were expelled from a range of European countries over various Russian malign activities, the GRU began recruiting operatives through Telegram and paying them in cryptocurrency. Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung found that the drone used in the Leipzig attack had been hidden in an underground cache.
On Sept. 24, French President Emmanuel Macron said in an interview with TF1 and France 2 that France could face sabotage similar to the Leipzig incident. Spanish newspaper El Mundo had previously reported that U.S. intelligence recently warned European governments about a possible Russian drone attack against Spain, France, or Italy.
