The Guardian view on Trump and Xi: a show of friendship, but no real attempt to address the tensions | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:53:49 UTC
01:53:49 KST

Within days, two high-profile Chinese visitors will arrive in the US – envoys of friendship, as Xi Jinping described them when he met Donald Trump at the White House this week. The giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be hosted at Atlanta zoo. Beijing dispatched the first panda pair to the US in 1972 following President Richard Nixon’s landmark visit to China. It uses the animals to indicate satisfaction or displeasure with other nations. But it also charges heftily for their lease: reportedly, around $1m a year per pair. Americans’ views of China have warmed from a pandemic nadir, but are unlikely to be shifted much by two animals, however charming. These days they are more of a token gesture than a striking symbol.
It is telling that the announcement was one of the main takeaways of Mr Xi’s visit to Washington. Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them. The US president gave Mr Xi a lavish welcome – unusually, travelling to meet the “strong, vibrant and fit” Chinese leader off the plane. He insisted that they had “never gotten along better”.
In a sense that is not surprising. Mr Trump admires and envies authoritarians with untrammelled powers. Chinese state media were welcome at the White House, unlike CNN, MS Now and Politico. Since he rarely pays even lip service to human rights, the treatment of Uyghurs or jailed Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong – facing another lengthy sentence for his international advocacy – were never likely to figure large, whatever the hopes of protesters outside.
Mr Trump told Mr Xi that any Chinese help for Iran is unacceptable; Mr Xi said that the US should adhere to the “correct position” of opposing Taiwanese independence. Beijing wants Washington to shift from the long-held stance of “not supporting” it. That would be a grave mistake, but Mr Trump has given worryingly mixed messages on Taiwan.
It is striking how little of consequence has emerged from the summit given that this is arguably the most consequential diplomatic relationship in the world. A two-month extension of the trade war truce was announced as Mr Xi arrived in the US. China’s curb of rare earth exports has checked Mr Trump’s appetite for an economic offensive; Beijing is anxious about its struggling economy. But if they are more wary of the fallout, they are also more fearful of the other side gaining ground. AI is central to this battle. Mr Trump has resisted all calls to restrain development because “Whoever wins AI, wins.” Mr Xi said it had to be managed responsibly, but Beijing has attacked “threat narratives”, fearing that the US wants to prevent it catching up.
CNN last week highlighted the dangers: the US military reportedly prepared to intercept a Chinese ship in the Middle East after an intelligence report said it was carrying nuclear weapons components – only for officials to realise that the partially AI-generated analysis had misidentified the cargo. Controls on development are desperately needed, but neither side is willing to accept them. Even the limited AI dialogue and “notification hotline” for AI safety proposed by Scott Bessent, treasury secretary, seem to be rather less than meets the eye. This summit should be viewed with alarm not because it saw substantive developments – but because it illustrates the dangers of drift.

Colombia cuts diplomatic ties with Iran under ‘influence of US and Zionist regime’
TEHRAN — In a move that underscores a dramatic retreat from independent diplomacy toward subservience to the US regional agenda, Colombia’s newly inaugurated right-wing administration has unilaterally severed diplomatic ties with Iran.
The decision, enacted by President Abelardo de la Espriella on September 19, marks a sharp departure from the balanced, multipolar foreign policy pursued under former President Gustavo Petro. While Bogota has framed the move under the guise of “hemispheric national security,” diplomatic observers view the measure as a choreographed political concession aimed at currying favor with the United States and demonstrating alignment with its policies.
In an effort to rationalize its decision, the Colombian Foreign Ministry released a statement accusing Iran of maintaining connections with “narco-terrorist groups that threaten the security of the country.”
Yet, as with similar anti-Iran rhetoric recycled in Washington and Tel Aviv, Bogota failed to present a shred of credible evidence, intelligence briefing, or verifiable data to substantiate its sweeping accusations.
Tehran fires back: ‘Hypocritical deflection’
Reacting swiftly to Bogota’s hostile posturing, the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued an official statement on Friday, categorically rejecting Colombia’s unfounded allegations and condemning the abrupt rupture of bilateral diplomatic relations that span more than half a century.
The ministry stated in a statement that Bogota’s baseless accusations and simultaneous severance of diplomatic ties violate the foundational principle of mutual respect and run counter to the interests of both nations.
“It is evident that none of the claims put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical,” the statement emphasized, noting that the decision was adopted “solely under the direct influence of the United States and the Zionist regime.”
Turning the spotlight onto Bogota’s own deep-seated domestic crisis, the statement underscored that Colombia—which, by undeniable evidence, remains heavily influenced by illicit drug production and distribution cartels and effectively operates as part of the transnational narco-terrorism network across the Americas and beyond—is in no moral or legal position to lecture other sovereign states on terrorism and narcotics.
The ministry further stressed that such “hypocritical deflection cannot absolve the Colombian government of its international responsibility” regarding its complicity in the trafficking of massive narcotics shipments worldwide, including to Iran.
Highlighting a recent high-profile case, the ministry revealed that Iranian law enforcement seized a 55-kilogram shipment of pure Colombian cocaine in Tehran in September, which had been directly trafficked into the country by a network linked to influential Colombian figures. It described the seizure as one of the latest exposed cases of transnational organized crime attributed to Colombian networks.
The statement noted that rather than resorting to a hasty and hostile diplomatic rupture, relevant Colombian authorities were expected, under their international legal obligations, to cooperate with Iran in identifying the primary elements involved in trafficking this illicit consignment and similar shipments to Iran and the wider region.
The ministry concluded by warning that Iran reserves the right to take necessary measures in defense of its national interests in response to Bogota’s unjustified and hostile stance.
Strategic absurdity and logical fallacies
Tehran’s firm response highlights what political analysts describe as glaring logical fallacies and strategic absurdity behind Bogota’s claims.
First, there is the deeply flawed narrative regarding counter-narcotics. The insinuation that Iran—a nation that sits on the frontline of global counter-narcotics efforts and has sacrificed thousands of security personnel in combating transnational drug cartels originating from South Asia—would align itself with Latin American drug syndicates defies strategic logic. Tehran’s comprehensive counter-narcotics record is routinely acknowledged by international organizations, including the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC). Bogota’s attempt to project its own decades-long struggle with organized crime onto an external actor thousands of kilometers away is widely seen as an expedient deflection.
Second, regarding the instrumentalization of “hemispheric security,” this phrase is historically synonymous with the Monroe Doctrine—a framework long used to justify external interference in the sovereign affairs of Latin American nations. By invoking this outdated paradigm without tangible proof, the De la Espriella government is simply parroting long-debunked talking points crafted by hawkish think-tanks in Washington to justify isolating independent nations in the Global South.
Bogota further sought to legitimize its unilateral rupture by dragging extra-regional geopolitical disputes into bilateral affairs, lambasting Tehran for allegedly “blocking maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz” and “attacking countries in the Middle East.”
This claim completely reverses cause and effect, ignoring basic realities in West Asian waters.
As a guarantor of maritime security, Iran has historically served as the primary anchor of peace, stability, and navigation security in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian naval forces have consistently safeguarded commercial shipping lanes against piracy and unauthorized foreign military incursions. Accusations of “blocking traffic” deliberately ignore that any security measures enforced by Iran are fully grounded in international maritime law, innocent passage regulations, and the sovereign right to defend its territorial waters against unilateral foreign provocations.
Furthermore, regarding legitimate deterrence versus foreign hegemony, framing Iran’s defensive posture as aggression fundamentally misrepresents the regional dynamic. The root cause of regional instability in West Asia is not Iran’s defensive capabilities, but the destabilizing military footprint of the United States and Israel’s unchecked aggression. Iran’s military actions—carried out in full accordance with Article 51 of the United Nations Charter regarding the inherent right of legitimate self-defense—have been calculated, targeted responses to illegal strikes on its diplomatic premises, territorial sovereignty, and national interests. Equating Iran’s defensive deterrence with unprovoked aggression reveals Bogota’s uncritical adoption of Western talking points.
While the Colombian government noted it will maintain consular channels with Tehran, the abrupt severing of full diplomatic ties reflects an administration eager to dismantle sovereign South–South cooperation in exchange for short-term political alignment with external patrons.

US Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial voter 'verification' system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:52:32 UTC
01:52:32 KST

US Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial voter 'verification' system
The US Supreme Court on Friday ruled the Trump administration can use a controversial new federal database that would ostensibly verify voter citizenship in November’s elections. Critics argue the administration is exaggerating the threat of non-citizen voters – an extreme rarity in US elections – to implement policies that would disenfranchise likely Democratic voters.
The US Supreme Court on Friday revived an expanded immigration database that US President Donald Trump's administration says aims to combat voting by noncitizens but that critics say will disenfranchise eligible voters.
The justices granted a Justice Department request to block a judge's order that would have prevented state officials from using Social Security numbers and other information to conduct sweeping checks of the citizenship status of registered voters against federal records.
The administration's data-sharing arrangement is one of a series of actions the federal government has taken to increase its involvement in voting ahead of November's midterm elections.
The US Constitution gives individual states the primary authority to run and administer elections.
The Department of Homeland Security last year redesigned a federal database known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, used to verify a person's citizenship and immigration status. The revamp allowed users to search many records at a time and to conduct searches using Social Security numbers.
Several Republican-led states have compared their voter lists to the database, and some voters flagged as potential non-citizens have had their registrations cancelled.
Critics say such election-related actions by Republicans are driven less by concerns over election security than by an attempt to gain political advantage by narrowing the electorate, risking the disenfranchisement of eligible, often Democratic-leaning voters.
In a June ruling blocking the revamped database, US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan in Washington, DC, said the system was haphazardly assembled and contained unreliable citizenship data.
"All in all, the federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote," Sooknanan wrote.
"This court cannot stand idly by while that happens."
Read moreTrump reviving election fraud claims to contest midterm results, say Democrats
The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in a 2-1 ruling on September 4 declined to halt Sooknanan's ruling, prompting the administration's request to the Supreme Court.
In a Supreme Court filing, Justice Department lawyers called the judge's order "indefensible", arguing that it "threatens the integrity" of the midterm elections.
False claims, real fears
Trump has repeatedly made false claims of widespread voting fraud, including in his 2020 election loss to Democratic former president Joe Biden.
Even according to data from the pro-Trump Heritage Foundation, which campaigns against “voter fraud”, cases of noncitizen voting are very rare – and most involve mistakes rather than fraud.
A 2024 review of Heritage Foundation data by the American Immigration Council found the group had found "just 68 cases of proven noncitizen voting dating back to 2000, amounting to less than 0.0001% of total votes”. The Heritage Foundation’s database has grown since 2024, adding an additional 21 cases.
Advocacy groups that sued to block the revised SAVE system said the new approach has resulted in people who were wrongfully identified as noncitizens being kicked off voter rolls. They argued that SAVE information can be outdated, and immigrants who have since become naturalised US citizens and are thus eligible to vote are sometimes labelled as noncitizens.
The modified system's overall error rate is not publicly known. The Department of Homeland Security and Justice Department did not provide that information when asked.

In their Supreme Court filing, the voter advocacy groups cited a Travis County, Texas, election official who said 25 percent of the system's noncitizen matches involved people who had already proven their US citizenship, as well as news reports finding that at least 81 percent of the system's responses in St. Louis County, Missouri, were erroneous.
The voting rights group League of Women Voters and privacy rights group Electronic Privacy Information Center sued in September 2025 to block the Trump administration's modified system. They said that the revamp violated federal privacy and other US laws.
Texas, which intervened in the case in support of the administration, has disputed claims that the system is unreliable.
Due to separate litigation in Florida, the Trump administration has been able to continue using its modified SAVE system in the Republican-led states of Florida, Iowa, Indiana and Ohio.

Malaysia’s new ambassador to Türkiye, Adlan Mohd Shaffieq, has likened the country to a big open museum, praising its rich cultural heritage and the warm hospitality he has received since arriving in Ankara.
“Your country is like a big open museum. All of the cities that I go to are like free, open museums where you can go and watch the culture,” Shaffieq told Anadolu in an interview.
“It has a very deep culture. So, it's very interesting for me to discover your country,” he added.
Shaffieq, who recently began his tenure in Ankara, shared his first impressions of Türkiye, his family life and his views on relations between the two countries.
The diplomat said he was delighted to be appointed to Türkiye for his first ambassadorial posting, particularly because he believed his four children, aged between five and 11, would enjoy living in Ankara.
“Malaysia and Türkiye are like brothers and sisters,” he said, describing the warm hospitality he has experienced since his arrival.
Shared family values and historical ties
Shaffieq highlighted similarities between Malaysian and Turkish cultures, particularly their strong family ties and respect for parents.
“I think the similarities between Malaysian and Turkish families is that we are very close-knit,” he said.
Shaffieq said families in both countries enjoy gathering during religious holidays and other occasions to celebrate, cook and share meals.
The ambassador noted that Turkish television series and films have helped Malaysians become more familiar with Türkiye, while emphasising that relations between the two countries stretch back for centuries.
“Our history has the linkage not only recently, but during the Ottoman Empire,” he said, pointing to historical contacts between the Ottoman Empire and the Sultanate of Melaka.
‘Your ice cream is the best ice cream in the world’
Touching on Turkish cuisine, Shaffieq said Malaysian food differs considerably from Turkish dishes, with Malaysians generally preferring spicier meals.
However, he was particularly enthusiastic about Turkish ice cream.
“Your ice cream is the best ice cream in the world. My kids love it,” he said.
“I think food is also one of the areas that we should focus on when it comes to cultural exchanges,” he added.
The ambassador also expressed his fondness for menemen, a traditional Turkish breakfast dish made with eggs, tomatoes and peppers.
Shaffieq said he had been learning Turkish for approximately three months and intended to learn as much of the language as possible during his posting.
Unique cultural experiences
The ambassador said he had already visited several destinations in Türkiye, including Cappadocia, Kastamonu and Konya, in addition to the capital Ankara, each of which he described as having its own distinctive character.
He mentioned that he had also recently attended tomato and carrot festivals, held separately in different parts of Ankara in late September, describing both experiences as immensely unique.
Shaffieq said the opportunity to experience different local traditions and explore the country’s cultural heritage had made his time in Türkiye particularly rewarding.
Trade, defence cooperation and tourism
On bilateral relations, Shaffieq said Malaysia and Türkiye are making significant progress, pointing to growing cooperation in trade and defence.
He said bilateral trade reached approximately $5.6 billion in 2025, while the two countries have set a bilateral trade target of $10 billion.
Although ambitious, the target is achievable, he said.
The ambassador identified defence as another important area for expanding bilateral cooperation. He said Malaysia had received or commissioned three littoral mission ships this year and hoped to procure additional vessels in the future.
Malaysia has also received three ANKA unmanned aerial vehicles, which have begun operating in the South China Sea, he said, adding that further defence procurement opportunities were under consideration.
Shaffieq also highlighted tourism as an increasingly important component of bilateral relations.
Approximately 40,000 Turkish tourists visited Malaysia in 2025, he said, noting that the figure had increased compared with the year prior.

Soviet jazz-rock pioneer Alexey Kozlov dies at 90
Jazz saxophonist Alexey Kozlov has died in Moscow at 90.
His jazz club reported his death on its Telegram channel.
Kozlov was a pioneer of Soviet jazz rock. Born in Moscow on October 13, 1935, he founded Arsenal in 1973. The band became one of the Soviet Union’s best-known groups.
Arsenal released several records and CDs. One of its albums, “Svoimi Rukami” (“With Our Own Hands”), was reissued in the U.S. The band performed in France, Germany, and the U.S. over the years, including at Carnegie Hall in New York during a joint tour with Georgian singer Tamara Gverdtsiteli.
Kozlov also hosted jazz programs on Russian television and wrote a book on the history of rock music.
Kozlov’s music is mentioned in numerous books, jazz encyclopedias, and dictionaries. Vasily Aksyonov wrote about him in his novel “Ozhog” (“The Burn”), as did American journalist Hedrick Smith in “The Russians” and historian Frederick Starr in “Red and Hot,” a study of jazz in the Soviet Union.

Marking 13 years since the murder of Greek rapper Pavlos Fyssas by a member of the neo-Nazi Golden Dawn party, MEPs at the European Parliament in Brussels were invited to a performance to pay tribute to the musician's life.
A theatrical monologue about murdered Greek rapper Pavlos Fyssas at the European Parliament. Actress Dora Chrysikou portrays a young woman who was an eyewitness to a far-right crime.
The performance unfolds the story of the murder of Fyssas, while also taking us into the Golden Dawn trial. Maria Louka wrote the text, which is based on real witness statements. Korais Damatis directed the piece.
PASOK MEP Nikolas Farantouris was behind the invitation to the European Parliament in Brussels: "No to the far-right agenda. We must not subscribe to the agenda of fear. We have to provide solutions without entering into dialogue with those who want to overturn democracy. Araghchi holds a series of talks in NY on regional security, Hormuz and Iran-EU ties

Araghchi holds a series of talks in NY on regional security, Hormuz and Iran-EU ties
TEHRAN– Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held a series of meetings with foreign counterparts on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, engaging Russian, British, Portuguese, Bruneian, Kyrgyz, Polish, Spanish, Egyptian, Jordanian, Cypriot, Pakistani and Austrian officials on regional security, the Strait of Hormuz, the war in West Asia, Palestine, Iran-Europe relations and bilateral cooperation.
Hormuz and Regional Security
The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the future of maritime navigation emerged as a recurring issue in Araghchi’s meetings with European and regional officials.
In talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Araghchi briefed his counterpart on Iran-Oman discussions concerning arrangements for a safe maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz. He also outlined diplomatic efforts by mediators to establish conditions for a return to negotiations.
In separate talks with Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel and Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger, Araghchi attributed the disruption of maritime traffic and insecurity in the Strait to US and Israeli military actions. He said, from Iran’s perspective, restoring maritime security would require an end to 'destabilizing US measures and economic pressure.'
Araghchi also raised regional security with Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, criticizing the use of the territory of regional states in military operations. He said Iran was prepared to work with neighboring countries on security arrangements based on regional cooperation rather than external military involvement.
The Iranian foreign minister’s discussions with Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski also touched on the wider regional crisis. With Sikorski, Araghchi warned against linking the Ukraine conflict to developments in West Asia, urging European governments to address security challenges on their own continent while taking positions on regional developments based on international law.
Iran-Europe relations
Relations with European governments formed another major thread of Araghchi’s meetings.
During talks with British Foreign Secretary Edward Miliband, Araghchi criticized Britain’s political and military support for Israel and called on London and other European governments to reconsider policies contributing to instability in West Asia.
The two sides also discussed Iran’s nuclear program. Araghchi reiterated Tehran’s stated preference for resolving outstanding issues through diplomacy and criticized Britain, France and Germany over their positions concerning the so-called snapback mechanism and the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran’s nuclear facilities.
Similar concerns were raised in Araghchi’s meetings with the foreign ministers of Spain and Cyprus. He called on European governments to base their policies toward Iran and the region on international law and avoid 'alignment with parties responsible for aggression.'
Palestine and wider regional conflict
The Palestinian issue was central to Araghchi’s discussions with Brunei’s Foreign Minister Abdul Mateen ibni Hassanal Bolkiah, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi.
Araghchi called for greater coordination among Islamic countries and a more active role for the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in addressing the situation in Gaza, the West Bank and Al-Quds. He also emphasized the need to support Palestinian self-determination and efforts toward establishing an independent Palestinian state.
With Abdelatty, Araghchi discussed strengthening bilateral coordination alongside regional developments, while his meeting with Safadi focused on regional security and cooperation between Iran and Jordan.
Russia, Pakistan and regional diplomacy
Araghchi and Lavrov also reviewed political, economic, trade, transportation and energy cooperation between Iran and Russia, as well as coordination within international organizations. Lavrov reiterated Moscow’s opposition to 'US and Israeli military aggression against Iran' and emphasized adherence to international law and the UN Charter.
In New York, Araghchi also held talks with Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar on bilateral relations and regional developments. The meeting came as Pakistan was pursuing a mediating role between Iran and the United States.

Dr Nighat Arif on navigating health advice in the TikTok era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:47:26 UTC
01:47:26 KST

Breadcrumb
'The danger is acting on half-truths': Dr Nighat Arif on BBC's Clickbait Clinic navigating health advice in the TikTok era
As one in three Brits reportedly turn to social media for health advice, a new series aims to educate viewers about trends that have gone viral across their social media feeds.
Whether people are using TikTok to explain unexplained symptoms or scrolling through Instagram for advice on how to live longer, social media has quickly become an influential source of health information.
But when advice is marketed as 90-second clips designed to gain views, how can people tell whether it is actually evidence-based or just made to go viral?
This is the question to be tackled in the new season of BBC’s Clickbait Clinic, which sees Stacey Dooley, Dr Alex George and Dr Nighat Arif as they investigate health trends circulating online and challenge the misinformation behind them.
As a visibly Muslim woman who appears regularly on TV and works in medicine, Dr Nighat is a representation in a space that has historically lacked people who look like her.
For Dr Nighat, the word ‘clickbait’ makes her think of "bold promises that outrun the evidence headlines," headlines designed to stop your scroll, not protect your health.
"In medicine, that gap between hype and reality can cost people time, money and sometimes even safety," she tells The New Arab.
Health advice in the age of TikTok
Dr Nighat’s decision to join Clickbait Clinic originally stemmed from her firsthand experience of patients coming in with information they had found online.
"Because this is where my patients already are: scrolling, searching, and trying. I wanted to bring calm, evidence-based clarity to the noise and do it in a way that actually sticks," she says.
Almost every consultation now involves something a patient has either "read or watched online," says Dr Nighat. She explains that while some of this information can be helpful, it can also be ‘alarming or misleading’, so she chooses to unpack it during her consultation.
The appeal of social media is hard to resist.
"Access, anonymity, and algorithmic comfort" means people find answers quickly and without judgment, especially when asking questions that may feel uncomfortable.
"The danger is acting on half-truths," Dr Nighat explains, warning that viral health trends can contribute to delaying diagnosis, wasting money or people trying risky interventions.
Her advice is to look beyond the post on your screen and instead check the creator’s credentials, look for consensus, and avoid relying on a single viral post.
Ultimately, hoping that viewers will learn to pause before trying something.
"Ask ‘who benefits?’, ‘what’s the evidence?’, and ‘does it fit my situation?’" she says before encouraging people to speak to a healthcare professional as their next step.
When misinformation goes viral
Dr Nighat believes social media platforms can play an important role in sharing accurate information, particularly because they can reach a wide range of audiences, including those who may not engage with traditional health-related messaging.
"Social media can be powerful for accurate health information if creators cite sources, show uncertainty, and signpost proper care," she says.
The difficulty with social media often lies with the fact that algorithms are not designed to prioritise medical nuance.
Social media does get some things right, says Dr Nighat. "It can normalise conversations, reach underserved communities and can democratise knowledge."
But it also ‘rewards certainty over nuance’, with algorithms prioritising engagement over safety.
This can help to explain why some people might trust a stranger on TikTok more easily than a medical professional.
"Relatability can feel like expertise," she adds.
Someone who may look like you, speaks confidently and explains "what worked for them" can quite easily become emotionally persuasive.
The use of artificial intelligence could also make this problem even more complicated.
Dr Nighat says AI can be used to amplify health trends often through "slick scripts, convincing visuals, and endless variations of the same claim," creating content so quickly that it outpaces fact-checking.
She believes that platform labels, creator accountability and teaching audiences to spot AI-polished persuasion are what is needed to address this.
"If it makes someone pause and ask, ‘Is this right for me? That’s a win," she says.
Why Muslim representation matters
For Dr Nighat, the conversation doesn’t stop at misinformation. As a visibly Muslim woman and GP appearing on mainstream television, she has become a recognisable medical voice for those who may not always see themselves represented elsewhere.
"It means patients see themselves in the room before they even walk in," she says.
"Visibility builds trust, reduces stigma, and tells communities: your health matters here too."
Dr Nighat believes representation can shift who we consider "credible" and hopes it will "make it easier for women to seek help without fear of judgment or cultural misunderstanding."
But representation cannot stop at putting diverse faces on screen.
Language, cultural context, and health literacy can all become barriers to accessing reliable information, while long appointment wait times can push people towards ‘quick online fixes.’
"When the system feels distant, TikTok feels close," Dr Nighat says.
Making health content accessible
Working alongside Stacey Dooley and Dr Alex George, Dr Nighat says the programme aims to challenge health trends without shaming the people who believed them.
"Stacey asks the questions people really have, and Alex bridges clinical rigour with real empathy," she explains. "Together, we could challenge trends without shaming people who have been sold them."
Dr Nighat’s approach to sharing health information is rooted in making information engaging without sacrificing accuracy.
"Hook with empathy, not fear," she says. "State the evidence level, show uncertainty, and end with a clear ‘when to seek help’ signpost."
Her goal is not to make people think twice about what they see online, but to not to distrust everything they encounter.
Ultimately, Dr Nighat believes social media can still be part of the solution. It can reach people quickly and open up conversations that may have previously been stigmatised.
For Muslim women watching Clickbait Clinic, Dr Nighat’s presence represents more than just another doctor on TV.
Zaynah Ahmed is a freelance journalist based in London with an interest in current affairs, women's health disparities and underrepresented voices
Follow her on Instagram: @Zaynahreports

Army halts arrests of ultra-Orthodox Haredi Jews draft dodgers: Israeli newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25

Khaled Yousef,  Lina Altawell
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
The Israeli army has halted arrests of ultra-Orthodox Haredi Jews wanted for failing to comply with military draft orders amid concerns that the arrests could trigger protests, according to Israeli media.
Haaretz reported Friday that the army had decided to suspend arrests of Haredi draft dodgers over fears of unrest and protests across the country as Israeli elections approach.
The army attributed the move to “operational needs,” without providing further details, according to the newspaper.
Haaretz said arrests had been extremely limited even before the decision was taken.
According to figures cited in an Israeli Supreme Court ruling, only 16 Haredi draft dodgers were arrested during the first half of 2026, the newspaper said.
Haaretz cited unnamed police sources as saying that “there are no plans to resume them in the near future.”
The sources said arresting wanted individuals requires the deployment of large police forces and that the suspension was initiated by the military police.
According to Haaretz, the decision on whether to carry out arrests rests with the army, while the police are responsible only for implementing them.
“The suspension has coincided with a halt in ultra-Orthodox protests against the military,” the newspaper noted.
Haredi Jews continue to protest against military service following a Supreme Court ruling on June 25, 2024, requiring them to enlist and barring financial support for religious institutions whose students refuse military service.
Haredim make up around 13% of Israel’s population of 10 million and oppose military service on the grounds that they devote their lives to studying the Torah.
Senior rabbis, whose followers view their rulings as religious directives, have called on Haredi men to refuse enlistment and even to “tear up” draft orders.
They also argue that integration into secular society threatens their religious identity and the continuity of their community.
For decades, members of the Haredi community were able to avoid military service after turning 18 by repeatedly obtaining deferments on the grounds that they were studying at religious seminaries until reaching the exemption age, currently 26.
The decision came about 33 days before Israeli elections scheduled for October amid sharp domestic political debate over Netanyahu government policies.

NHS boss says staff suspected of snooping on patients’ records should be suspended immediately
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:45:48 UTC
01:45:48 KST

NHS staff suspected of snooping on patients’ medical records should be suspended immediately and barred from using health service computers, the head of NHS England has said.
Jim Mackey urged NHS England’s 205 health trusts to pursue a “zero tolerance” approach to staff who are suspected of inappropriately accessing records.
He called for a “hardline” stance towards anyone found to have accessed patients’ notes or medical histories without a clinical justification.
His intervention comes amid growing concern that staff sometimes use their position to view medical records but rarely face any meaningful penalty for doing so.
Mackey said on Friday: “Patient records contain some of the most private information people will ever share. We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust and enough is enough.”
He wrote to all trusts demanding that they routinely implement what NHS England called a “crackdown” on breaching patients’ confidential data.
The problem has gained attention after reports that NHS staff illicitly accessed medical records of victims of the attacks by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham in 2023 and stabbings by Axel Rudakubana in Southport in 2024, among other high-profile incidents.
Mackey said: “If someone is suspected of snooping we cannot leave them in post with access to patients’ records while an investigation takes days or weeks. From now on we will expect them to be suspended and have their access to NHS systems cut off immediately, while the facts are established.”
That should happen already, but rarely does so in practice.
He added: “Anyone who thinks they can satisfy their curiosity by looking at a patient’s record should know this: they will be found out, they may lose their career and could end up with a criminal record.”
Since 2020, more than 200 NHS staff in England have been dismissed and 2,000 others sanctioned for snooping on patients’ records, an investigation by Sky News and the Health Service Journal found this month.
One employee was sacked after viewing up to 179 people’s records, another had accessed their spouse’s details in a “potential domestic violence situation”, and others had shared information they had gathered in WhatsApp groups.
Responses by 140 trusts to freedom of information requests by the media outlets showed that 214 staff were dismissed, three suspended and 540 given a final written warning over the last five years.
The Liberal Democrat MP Layla Moran, who chairs the health and social care select committee, has warned that official numbers for staff accessing patients’ records illegally under the Data Protection Act were likely to be “canaries in the coal mine”.
However, Paul Arnold, the chief executive of the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), the data watchdog, said in June that “inappropriate access is rare and does not represent the behaviour of the vast majority of healthcare staff who take their duty of confidentiality extremely seriously”.
Bristol NHS foundation trust has apologised to Paula and Tom McGowan for staff snooping on the medical records of their son Oliver, who died in 2016 aged 18. At least five members of staff, including three nurses and a doctor, accessed his records without permission.
Gillian Merron, a health minister, disclosed in July that health service bodies reported 1,445 cases of inappropriate access to the ICO between 2019 and 2025.

China’s Visibility Gap Around the Trump-Xi Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:44:00 UTC
01:44:00 KST

Beijing formally confirmed Chinese President Xi Jinping’s September 23-25 visit to the United States on September 21, just two days before the trip began. The news had barely registered among many of the Chinese people I spoke with the following day. Official coverage began appearing online following the announcement, but visible discussion among ordinary users on platforms such as Weibo, WeChat, and Xiaohongshu (RedNote) remained scarce.
That changed once Xi’s visit was underway. Chinese social media filled with reports about the summit, with much of the visible content coming from official outlets and accounts, emphasizing the diplomatic significance and choreography of the visit, including Trump’s reception of Xi and calls for “constructive strategic stability.” The shift from limited information to abundant official coverage raised a different question: How much did ordinary Chinese people know about the summit before official coverage moved into full gear?
On September 22, the day after Beijing’s formal announcement and one day before Xi’s visit began, I conducted informal interviews with a dozen individuals across China and the diaspora, including overseas students and professionals, domestic public-sector workers, private-sector employees, and an older relative. Awareness varied considerably by location and occupation.
Overseas students and professionals had generally learned of the trip earlier through foreign news outlets or private messaging groups. Some public-sector employees in China learned about it only after the official announcement, noting that senior leaders’ schedules are typically kept confidential until the last minute. Meanwhile, many of the private-sector employees I spoke with in China remained unaware of the visit even after the announcement.
Yet when asked about it, many responded by searching for the news themselves. What they found was a remarkably uniform information environment. On Weibo, Douyin, and Xiaohongshu, searches related to Xi’s U.S. visit were dominated by official and state-media content. On Xiaohongshu, some targeted searches produced either zero visible results or unrelated posts concerning personal travel and visas. Under some official media posts, comment sections were restricted or turned off. The interviews suggested that curiosity could exist even when little of it was publicly visible.
It is tempting to attribute this lack of visible discussion solely to censorship, but the interviews pointed to a more complicated picture. One respondent pointed to self-censorship: “Some of what people might say in private wouldn’t feel appropriate to post publicly.” Others suggested that interest might increase only after the meetings produced concrete outcomes.
The searches themselves could not reveal whether the lack of visible discussion reflected content controls, platform ranking, self-censorship, limited public interest, or some combination of these factors.
The summit itself added another layer to this ambiguity. Once Xi arrived in the United States, information about the visit was no longer difficult to find. Official reports and accounts circulated extensive coverage of the meetings and their diplomatic symbolism. Yet the greater volume of information did not necessarily make public opinion easier to observe: Much of what was readily visible still came from official sources rather than ordinary users.
However, in specialized, interest-driven spaces, discussion was easier to find. On WeChat financial blogs like “Liu Xiaobo Talk Finance” and their commentary threads, retail investors and market watchers debated the summit’s possible implications for tariffs, stock prices, and exchange rates. According to the CGCC-USA 2026 Business Survey Report, 79 percent of surveyed Chinese companies operating in the United States reported negative impacts from tariffs, while 36 percent anticipated a slight improvement in bilateral trade relations, underscoring the concrete economic stakes surrounding the summit.
The Trump-Xi summit thus exposed a broader “visibility gap” in China’s information environment. On September 22, even after the visit had been officially announced, many of the people I interviewed had not heard about it, although they often became curious enough to search once asked. Days later, information about the summit was everywhere, but the most visible narratives remained overwhelmingly official.
For outside observers trying to gauge public sentiment in China, the difficulty is not simply that Chinese people are silent. It is that the Chinese internet makes a lack of discussion unusually difficult to interpret.

North Korea’s Ukraine POWs Are Now in South Korea. What Comes Next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:41:00 UTC
01:41:00 KST

The immediate fate of two North Korean prisoners-of-war captured by Ukrainian forces is no longer in question, but the saga is not yet over.
Ukraine has transferred custody of the pair to South Korea in what was perhaps a predictable outcome given their reported desire not to return to North Korea. However, the circumstances surrounding the disclosure have introduced new political dynamics to the situation. Now, both the South Korean government and the two former soldiers face an unprecedented resettlement process.
Kyiv first announced that it had captured the two North Korean soldiers in January 2025, immediately prompting questions of what would come of the pair. The legal provisions surrounding their eventual disposition were complicated. International rules pointed toward repatriating them with other POWs to Russia. Before the capture happened, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was his government’s position that all POWs in Ukrainian custody would receive the same treatment.
The two soldiers, however, reportedly expressed fear of repatriation and a desire to defect to South Korea. Given the Kim Jong Un regime’s publicized insistence that soldiers kill themselves rather than be captured, returning to North Korea could have exposed them to reprisals for allowing themselves to be taken into Ukrainian custody. Under the principle of non-refoulement, the potential risk of persecution, torture, or other serious human rights violations if the soldiers were ultimately repatriated to North Korea was a necessary consideration.
The South Korean government stepped in early with offers to take the POWs into their custody. With advocacy stretching back to the previous Yoon Suk-yeol administration, there was little doubt over Seoul’s desired outcome for the two individuals.
What is now evident is that the two governments came to a confidential agreement to transfer the custody of the POWs. The handover reportedly took place ahead of the U.N. General Assembly debates, and the two former soldiers are now in South Korean government care. Details of this arrangement first came to light via Zelenskyy himself.
During his speech at the U.N. General Assembly, the Ukrainian president captured international attention when he revealed that Ukraine had transferred custody of the two POWs to South Korea. In the speech, he noted that “these guys are not easy to capture alive,” adding that one of the soldiers, “when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself.” Zelenskyy’s disclosure came unilaterally and without warning to the South Korean government.
Kyiv’s decision to reveal information despite the confidential arrangement created a diplomatic problem with Seoul, but it also served a clear Ukrainian purpose. Kyiv’s intelligence has repeatedly claimed that the Kremlin is seeking an additional 30,000-50,000 North Korean troops to support a new offensive. Zelenskyy therefore used the U.N. General Assembly debates as a platform to highlight the Kim regime’s continued support for Russia’s war effort and to put North Korea’s military involvement back on the international agenda.
But Zelenskyy’s announcement caused a stir in South Korean domestic politics. Opposition lawmakers immediately chastised the Lee Jae-myung administration for not disclosing the transfer. Some argued that the government was withholding details out of fear of how North Korea may react.
Lee took to social media to push back against this criticism. He said that there was an agreement to keep the transfer confidential, expressing that it was “deeply regrettable” that the Ukraine side released details on the matter. He added that publicly disclosing the successful repatriation could have helped boost approval ratings, but it would not have been right to risk “someone’s life or the national interest” for one’s “own petty benefit.”
There are political reasons why some in the Lee administration may have sought to avoid disclosing information about the POW transfer. The government has been working to rekindle any form of inter-Korean engagement, and some policy groups within Seoul have warned that North Korea could react strongly to the decision.
However, such concerns may be unfounded. North Korean state media has not commented on the POWs since their reported capture, and there are much more significant sticking points between the two Koreas; namely, Pyongyang’s preconditions that Seoul must drop unification and denuclearization as policy objectives. Since Zelenskyy’s announcement, the only reporting from Pyongyang directed toward the South Korean government has been a statement attributed to Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui on a familiar issue: reiterating the Kim regime’s position that denying the reality of North Korea’s nuclear weapon status “is to give up the future.”
Meanwhile, from a security perspective, there are justifiable concerns related to the information disclosure. There have been North Korean assassination attempts against South Korea-based defectors in the past. The most prominent recent example occurred in a 2011 incident in which a North Korean agent attempted to kill prominent defector-turned-activist Park Sang-hak with a poison needle.
The two POWs could therefore present a different security challenge from the average North Korean defector. Their firsthand knowledge of North Korean involvement in the Russia-Ukraine War means that there is a reasonable risk that they could become targets of elimination efforts.
Given the confidential nature of the South Korea-Ukraine agreement, there are few details on what comes next for the two former soldiers. There may have been an understanding that they will remain in custody until the conclusion of the war, or Kyiv may have conceded that South Korea can treat the individuals as they would any other defector. This would affect how long the individuals remain in the government’s custody.
Whatever the length of their initial detention in South Korea, the eventual next step will be resettlement.
Resettlement can be difficult for any defector. New arrivals generally undergo a months-long program at the Hanawon resettlement facility under the Ministry of Unification’s remit, and it includes tasks such as teaching individuals about South Korean customs and courtesies, how to manage bank accounts and finances, and finding employment.
Upon completion of the resettlement process, they are then given relocation assistance to a new residence somewhere in the country. There, they are typically assigned a local officer – either a Ministry of Unification, Korean National Police, or National Intelligence Service (NIS) official – to continue supporting their transition process and to contact in the event of any issues.
The system is different for higher profile or high-risk defectors. They may be former senior North Korean officials like Thae Yong Ho, or figures such as Park Sang-hak who have used their newfound freedom to lead civic movements in protest of the Kim regime. In those cases, the individuals can remain in NIS protective custody until officials determine that it is safe for them to return to public life. Even then, there may be continued protection services.
The two former soldiers transferred from Ukraine will likely fall into that latter category, particularly with the amount of media coverage they have received.
Thus, the arrival of the two North Korean soldiers to South Korea resolves the most immediate question surrounding their fate, but the next steps remain dynamic. The situation has now entered a new phase where South Korean politics will continue to scrutinize the issue as the government works to navigate an unprecedented resettlement process.

Evan Gershkovich says his arrest in Russia was carefully planned FSB sting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:40:12 UTC
01:40:12 KST

US reporter Evan Gershkovich, in his first detailed published account of his arrest in Russia in 2023, says he was the victim of an elaborate sting operation by Russia's FSB federal security service.
In an extract from his book "This Cursed Beautiful Land," Gershkovich says that while working on a story for the Wall Street Journal about Russian military production, he held two meetings with the union boss of a factory in Yekaterinburg, a major defense-industry hub.
At their second encounter, in a steakhouse, the source produced papers with hand-copied tables of figures, telling the reporter that they related to the production of tanks.
As he jotted down notes, Gershkovich said, he heard the sound of marching feet and looked up to see a group of masked men approaching their table.
"A pang of guilt ripped through me: Had I compromised a source? But panic immediately replaced that thought. Instinct took over, my hands moving to hide the papers in the gap between the bench and the wall," he wrote in the book extract, published by the Journal on Friday.
"The men quickly descended on us. An arm was yanking my neck, pulling me off the couch... Someone shouted: 'You are under arrest by the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation.'"
Long sentence, then a prisoner swap
Gershkovich, then 31, became the first US reporter arrested on espionage charges in Russia since the Cold War. He was later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.
He writes that he and his editors had considered the risks of the reporting trip and agreed that the source should not bring any documents to the meeting; if he did so, Gershkovich should not accept anything from him.
But at the meeting, the source had "thrust the papers into my hands."
Although he had reported on the arrests of other Americans in Russia, and on the targeting and even murder of Russian journalists, Gershkovich writes that the "unspoken rule" was that foreign correspondents enjoyed a degree of immunity: they might be expelled, but not arrested.
Reeling with shock, he was handcuffed, had a black sack placed over his head, and was whisked into a van where he was placed in a chokehold and punched in the abdomen while being questioned, he writes.
FSB 'backup plan'
Gershkovich said that since his release he had learned of evidence that the FSB had a "backup plan" to arrest him on another of his planned reporting trips, to Siberia, if the Yekaterinburg operation had failed.
He said he believes the two meetings with the source in Yekaterinburg were designed to help the FSB persuade President Vladimir Putin that he was a spy and secure approval for his arrest at the second meeting.
"Putin, it seems to me, fully bought into this narrative," he said.
The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a February 2024 interview with US television host Tucker Carlson, Putin said Gershkovich had been "caught red-handed" while collecting confidential information.
The journalist, his newspaper, and the US government all strongly deny the allegation that Gershkovich was a spy.

Israel, US officials meet Abraham Accords partners in New York to expand regional cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:39:48 UTC
01:39:48 KST

Senior officials from Israel, the United States, and countries participating in the Abraham Accords reconvened in New York on Thursday for the group’s first multilateral meeting since January 2023, signaling renewed efforts to deepen regional cooperation and expand the normalization framework after years of regional upheaval.
The high-level roundtable, convened by the N7 Foundation and chaired by its chairman and founder Jeffrey M. Talpins, brought together US Under Secretary of State Allison Hooker and senior officials from Israel, Bahrain, Morocco, the United Arab Emirates and Kazakhstan. It marked the first official engagement of Abraham Accords countries to include Kazakhstan, which is preparing to join the framework.
The meeting came nearly three years after the October 7 Hamas attack and the outbreak of the Gaza war, which significantly reshaped the regional diplomatic landscape and slowed efforts to build on the momentum created by the Abraham Accords. The United States brokered the agreements during the Trump administration, which established diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE and Bahrain in 2020, followed by Morocco.
Rather than focusing solely on additional normalization agreements, Thursday’s meeting focused on the next stage of the framework: translating diplomatic ties into practical cooperation. Participants reaffirmed the principles of the Abraham Accords and discussed opportunities to strengthen collaboration between Israel, Arab and Muslim countries, the United States and other partners.
Abraham Accords countries seek broader regional network
“The Abraham Accords have demonstrated what is possible when countries come together around shared interests with a common vision for a more integrated and prosperous region,” Talpins said. “The next phase is about deepening the relationships that already exist and identifying practical opportunities for countries to work together.”
The N7 Foundation said discussions centered on shared priorities and tangible outcomes, with the goal of using regional cooperation to promote stability, security and economic development. Potential areas of collaboration include technology, trade and investment, energy, water and food security, and strategic and security cooperation.
“The Abraham Accords have created a foundation for a more connected region, and their full potential will be realized through the practical cooperation they make possible,” N7 President Oren Eisner said. “Today's discussion focused on the work ahead: strengthening existing relationships, welcoming new partners, and advancing initiatives that deliver tangible benefits to people and economies across the region.”
Kazakhstan’s participation was one of the most significant developments of the meeting. Kazakhstan has described its decision to join the Abraham Accords as consistent with its foreign policy and has said that its accession will not change its support for a two-state solution and relevant international resolutions. Its expected entry could give the Accords a new dimension by linking Israel and its Arab partners with a strategically important Muslim-majority country in Central Asia.
The meeting does not, however, represent a return to the diplomatic environment that existed before October 7. The Gaza war has complicated Israel’s relations with much of the Arab world, while the regional confrontation with Iran and broader security concerns have created new pressures on governments that established ties with Jerusalem.
Still, the decision by senior officials from Abraham Accords countries to return to a multilateral format is significant. For much of the period following October 7, regional diplomacy focused primarily on the Gaza war, humanitarian issues, and the broader Israeli-Palestinian question. The New York gathering placed regional integration back on the agenda alongside those challenges.
The meeting also reflects continued US interest in using the Abraham Accords as a platform for broader regional cooperation. The Trump administration played a central role in establishing the framework, and the latest gathering suggests Washington still views it as an important component of its regional strategy.
The N7 Foundation, which hosted the first multilateral convening of Abraham Accords countries in 2021, said it would continue working with participating states and aligned partners to develop “durable mechanisms” for strategic cooperation.
The long-term question is whether the Abraham Accords can evolve from a series of bilateral normalization agreements into a broader regional network. Thursday’s meeting in New York aimed to take that next step by bringing existing partners back together, adding Kazakhstan to the discussion, and focusing on cooperation beyond diplomatic recognition.

The UN rights office assessed companies active in sectors including energy, food, hospitality, transport and agriculture, based on confidential submissions to the UN rights office.

Examples include supplying demolition equipment to destroy Palestinian buildings, providing surveillance for settlements, and other services like transport that help maintain their existence, according to the UN website.
Other companies, including British-registered online travel company Opodo and Spanish-domiciled online travel agent eDreams, were dropped from the original list after submitting a reassessment request.
The UN found reasonable grounds to believe they were no longer involved in the activities that previously justified their inclusion.

Travel firm Expedia has previously said that the listings in what it called "disputed areas" were clearly labeled, complied with international laws and sanctions, and underwent enhanced due diligence guided by UN standards.

====================================================================================================

Sohlberg issues injunction against Satmar org. accused of bribing voters to abstain from election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:39:22 UTC
01:39:22 KST

Central Elections Committee Chairman and Supreme Court Deputy Chief Justice Noam Sohlberg issued a temporary injunction on Friday prohibiting the "Shekel HaTahor" (Pure Shekel) organization, affiliated with the Satmar haredi (ultra-Orthodox) community, from granting, offering, or promising money to voters for the purpose of influencing them not to participate in the elections.
The court issued the injunction after the Movement for Quality Government filed a petition.
According to the petition, the association began providing “support payments” of NIS 200 to haredim who declared they would not vote in the upcoming 26th Knesset elections.
Sohlberg determined that, at this stage, the evidence accompanying the petition indicated “grave concern regarding a violation of the law that strikes at the very core of election laws.” The injunction will remain in effect pending further decision, and proceedings regarding the petition are ongoing.
About 12,000 new registrants recently joined the Shekel HaTahor program and signed a pledge not to participate in the elections. The expected grant for those eligible is approximately NIS 200.
While 12,000 people have newly registered, no data indicates how many individuals may have already received the funds.
Shekel HaTahor also operates similarly outside of election season. It is a support system associated with Satmar that assists institutions and communities that do not receive funding from the state.
The increase in the number of people turning to it is attributed, among other things, to the halting of funding for some Torah institutions. The petition is not directed at this assistance in itself. It was filed following the allegation that money was being given in exchange for an eligible voter’s declaration that they would not cast a ballot.
Offering or giving bribes to voters prohibited under election laws
Section 122 of the Knesset Elections Law prohibits giving or offering a bribe to influence a voter “to vote or refrain from voting.” The prohibition also applies to a bribe intended to cause a voter not to vote, and it is not conditional on the money having already changed hands: the offer of a bribe is also prohibited under the section.
The term "bribe" is also broadly defined in the law. Under Section 123, it may consist of money, something of monetary value, a service, or any other benefit or advantage, and the benefit need not be transferred directly from the giver to the voter.
Section 122 also applies to a voter who accepts or agrees to accept a bribe in exchange for voting or refraining from voting. The offenses fall under the "Corruption and Threats" section of the law and carry a penalty of up to five years in prison.
Satmar’s move is rooted in the Hasidic sect’s long-standing anti-Zionist ideology, which opposes participation in state institutions and Knesset elections.
Satmar is a central force within the anti-Zionist Ultra-Orthodox camp. Unlike Ultra-Orthodox parties that participate in elections and operate within the Knesset, the sect views participation in the state’s political system as ideologically and religiously objectionable.
The petition currently before Justice Solberg addresses the claim that, in this instance, a financial incentive was attached to this stance: $200 for anyone declaring they would not vote.
Satmar sect previously involved in voter bribery case
This is not the first time such an issue has arisen around the Satmar sect.
Ahead of the 2013 elections, sources involved in Shekel HaTahor reported that the sect intended to pay NIS 100 to anyone who pledged not to vote and handed over their ID card and driver's license on election day.
In the Pines-Paz v. Shas case, the chairman of the Elections Committee at the time, Justice Mishael Cheshin, explained that the purpose of prohibiting election bribery is to ensure that voters make their decisions freely and rationally, rather than under the influence of extraneous considerations and benefits.
The Supreme Court later quoted these remarks in the context of Section 122, emphasizing that the section is intended to protect the voter's freedom of choice.
Solberg issued the injunction under Section 17B of the Elections Law (Methods of Propaganda). The section allows the chairman of the Elections Committee to issue an order preventing the commission or continuation of an offense under Chapter 11 of the Knesset Elections Law, which includes Section 122. In other words, the Committee Chairman may intervene during the election campaign and halt the act at the center of the petition, without waiting for criminal proceedings that might take place after Election Day.
At this stage, this is a temporary injunction. Solberg did not determine that Shekel HaTahor had violated the law, but prohibited it from continuing the activity described in the petition pending further review.
At the time the injunction was issued, Shekel HaTahor had not yet responded to the petition.
As long as the injunction remains in effect, Shekel HaTahor is prohibited from granting, offering, or promising money to influence voters to abstain from voting.
The law stipulates that for purposes of enforcing the injunction, it is considered an order of a court, and its violation could trigger proceedings under the Contempt of Court Ordinance.
The question of whether Shekel HaTahor violated the law will be decided later, after the parties’ arguments have been examined.

Security complex anew: Iran's venture into a new architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:38:54 UTC
01:38:54 KST

Security complex anew: Iran's venture into a new architecture
QOM - The war that began with the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran has done more than destroy military targets and redraw the map of immediate threats. It has exposed the fragility of the security architecture that has governed the Middle East for decades.
The old order built around American military presence, Israeli military superiority, and the political alignment of several Arab states with Washington has lost much of its previous certainty. A new regional security complex is therefore emerging which is unmistakably different from the order that existed before the war and is particularly promising for Iran.
The central question for Tehran is no longer simply whether it can resist the pressure but whether Iran can transform the strategic consequences of that resistance into a durable regional order that better serves its national interests. Thus, a new security complex is viable in light of the following dimensions:
The most important transformation concerns the distribution of power. For decades, the Persian Gulf security system operated largely within an American-centered structure. Arab governments depended heavily on American military power, American bases constituted the backbone of deterrence, and Israel functioned as Washington's principal regional military partner. Even when Arab states disagreed with Washington, they generally operated within the limits of this security architecture.
The war has challenged this assumption. Iran demonstrated that American military installations in the region are proved liabilities rather than security guarantees. The very bases intended to protect the Persian Gulf states turned them into potential targets. Iran's retaliation reached Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, Jordan, and other locations hosting U.S. military assets. This meant something consequential: the political value of American protection has radically become less certain.
The Persian Gulf states are therefore looking for greater strategic autonomy. Pakistan and Turkey become more important as alternative security partners, while Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and other Arab states increasingly calculate their security according to their own national interests rather than simply according to Washington's regional preferences. This means the emergence of a more competitive and multipolar regional structure. For Iran, this is an opportunity, but only if Tehran understands that multi-polarity requires diplomacy as much as military power.
The second transformation concerns proximity. One of the principal assumptions of the previous security order was that the United States could project overwhelming power into Iran's immediate neighborhood. The war has complicated that assumption.
In the Caucasus, the strategic environment surrounding Iran appears less threatening than it did before the conflict. Turkey has demonstrated greater caution than a straightforward alignment with the U.S.-Israeli camp would have suggested, while Azerbaijan's relationship with Israel has become considerably more sensitive in the new environment.
This matters because Iran's security dilemma has historically been multidirectional. Tehran has had to watch the Persian Gulf, Iraq, the Levant, Afghanistan, and the Caucasus simultaneously. A reduction in immediate pressure along one of these fronts creates strategic breathing space.
Iran should therefore resist the temptation to treat the Caucasus merely as another battlefield of confrontation. The opportunity is to convert this reduced threat environment into a diplomatic belt of stability around its northern frontier.
Perhaps the most profound change is not military but conceptual. Before the war, regional competition was heavily organized around political influence, ideological rivalry, Iran's regional networks, the Yemen conflict, and the struggle over leadership in the Muslim world. The war has elevated another issue above many of these concerns, i.e., economic survival. For Saudi Arabia, the security of oil infrastructure, maritime routes, investment, Vision 2030, and economic diversification has become inseparable from national security. The closure and disruption of the Strait of Hormuz demonstrated precisely how vulnerable an economic transformation strategy could be when regional military competition threatens energy infrastructure and maritime trade.
This creates an unexpected opening for Iran. Iran does not need Saudi Arabia to become its ally. It needs Saudi Arabia to recognize that permanent confrontation with Iran is incompatible with Saudi economic ambitions. This distinction is crucial. A Saudi Arabia primarily concerned with protecting its economy is a Saudi Arabia with incentives to negotiate with Tehran.
The same logic helps explain the growing divergence between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi. Their differences over Yemen, oil policy, Israel, and regional security have become increasingly visible, demonstrating that the Persian Gulf is not a single strategic actor. Iran's opportunity is therefore not to divide the Persian Gulf through confrontation, but to encourage a regional security logic in which economic interdependence becomes more valuable than permanent military alignment with Washington.
The war has also altered the region's patterns of amity and enmity. At the governmental level, Iran's attacks on Arab territories hosting U.S. military assets generated anger and divergence. Tehran does not ignore this reality because any attempt to build a new security order while disregarding Arab perceptions would be strategically wrong. Iran's diplomatic endeavor amid the conflict showed its regional concern and responsibility for neighbors. Nevertheless, another process has occurred at the societal level. Iran's direct military resistance to the United States and Israel has changed perceptions among segments of Arab and Muslim public opinion.
Whatever their governments' disagreements with Tehran, many communities interpreted Iran's resistance as evidence that American and Israeli dominance over Muslims is far from correct. This creates an important ideational opportunity for Iran. The Axis of Resistance may have suffered organizational and material setbacks, particularly in Lebanon, but the broader idea of resistance has not necessarily weakened. Indeed, the war has strengthened its symbolic appeal among populations that view the existing regional order as dominated by external powers. If Tehran wants Arab governments to accept a new regional balance, it must translate the core idea of resistance into the broader proposition of regional sovereignty, strategic autonomy, economic security, and freedom from external domination. That would be much easier for Arab states to embrace.
The military balance also presents Iran with both opportunities and challenges. The war demonstrated that Iran possesses considerable capabilities for imposing costs on U.S. regional assets and disrupting the assumptions underlying the existing security architecture. At the same time, the conflict exposed some Iranian vulnerabilities, particularly in infrastructure and air defense, for each of them Iran needs to find a feasible solution to securely project its new role in the region.
Perhaps the most important question is who will manage regional security after the war. The United States has historically acted as the external custodian of the Persian Gulf security system. However, the war has undermined the proposition that American bases necessarily make their host countries safer. In fact, several Persian Gulf governments now increasingly view the U.S. military presence through a double lens: it provides protection, but it can also make them targets. This, at least, means that America's custodianship has become contestable. Iran, however, should not assume that the decline of American credibility automatically produces Iranian dominance. The emerging system may instead be characterized by multiple centers of coercive power.
Last but not least, the most consequential transformation is occurring inside Iran's own strategic thinking. For years, Iranian military strategy was largely reactive: respond to Israeli strikes, deter American intervention, support partners, and preserve strategic depth. The new environment encourages a different logic. Iran has demonstrated a willingness to strike directly at the military infrastructure supporting an attack against it. This represents a movement from deterrence by retaliation toward deterrence through proactive risk creation. Iran's strongest strategic position would be one in which its adversaries understand that aggression against Iran will impose unacceptable costs, while its neighbors simultaneously understand that Iranian power does not necessarily threaten their economic survival. Tehran must now construct that difficult balance.
In the end, the new architecture Iran should seek is not a revised version of the old order but a regional and peaceful security complex rooted in shared economic profit. It would require an Iran that is unsanctioned and able to participate fully in the region's economic life; Arab states that are unthreatened by Israel and free to pursue their own security and development; and Arab countries that are unexploited by great powers. Only such a settlement can transform the war's strategic upheaval into a durable order in which Iranian security, Arab autonomy, and regional prosperity reinforce one another rather than remain permanently opposed.

Spacecraft returns to Earth after rescue mission for ageing Nasa telescope fails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:38:29 UTC
01:38:29 KST

A spacecraft that was launched in July on a mission to rescue a decaying Nasa space observatory plunged back to Earth on Friday, concluding a failed mission that will be followed by the telescope’s own demise in several weeks’ time.
Link, billed as “America’s first commercial space robot”, lifted off on 3 July from Kwajalein Atoll in the South Pacific islands with the objective of lifting the orbit and prolonging the life of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a satellite that has studied gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic events for the last 22 years.
It got as close as 7 to 9 miles (12km to 15km) to Swift and was able to take a series of images detailing its condition, but a series of earlier in-flight problems that hampered motion control and communications meant Link was unable to capture the observatory as planned and release it at a higher altitude.
Katalyst Space Technologies, the company based in Flagstaff, Arizona, which won a $30m Nasa contract for the salvage mission in September 2024, and put together an ambitious rescue plan inside 22 months, announced in a press release Friday morning that its three-armed spacecraft had re-entered Earth’s atmosphere after 85 days in orbit.
Without the altitude lift, Swift, a collaboration between Nasa and Penn State University that was launched in November 2004, will follow its own descent in the coming weeks, and is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere in November.
“From the beginning, this was a high-risk, high-reward mission,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of Nasa’s astrophysics division, said in a statement.
“While we’ll be sad to see Swift’s mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way – advancing US spacecraft servicing technology, challenging us to meet unprecedented mission timelines, and testing how we operate satellites to extend their time in low Earth orbit.”
Jared Isaacman, Nasa’s administrator, also praised the mission in a statement.
“Nasa should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” he said.
“This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future.”
Ironically, Swift’s expected lifespan was shortened by the very intense flare-ups from the sun, which it was sent up to observe. Nasa suspended its observations earlier this year and repositioned Swift to try to minimize the atmosphere’s downward drag while preparing the rescue mission.
Electronics issues on board Link after launch rendered inactive two of its three reaction wheels required for maneuvering, and at one point the spacecraft went into a deep spin. Communication and control were restored, but mission managers abandoned the rescue effort last month when it became clear there was insufficient fuel left.
