HBO’s Billionaire Divorce Drama War Doesn’t Know What It’s Trying to Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:00:03 UTC
23:00:03 KST

In the third episode of War, a legal drama from HBO and Britain’s Sky TV, a tech billionaire played by Dominic West makes a generous and degrading offer. He’ll give Steven (Robert Daws), one of many hirelings advising him in a nasty divorce, a wristwatch worth a million dollars if he disrobes “down to your socks, right now.” Steven’s initial response is a nervous giggle. Then he’s frantically unbuttoning his shirt. His point duly made, West’s character, Morgan Henderson, quickly stops the striptease. “For people like me, the word trust loses all meaning,” Morgan says. “There are no lengths to which people won’t go, there’s nothing they won’t do to debase themselves, to humiliate themselves, and you, if they think they can get a slice.”
This is as close as the first season of War, premiering Oct. 1 on HBO, gets to a thesis statement. Created by Lupin and Hijack hitmaker George Kay, this planned anthology series set within the high-rent hallways of London’s elite law firms takes, as its debut subject, the protracted uncoupling of Morgan and his actress wife, Carla Duval (Sienna Miller). The show is everything you’d expect from a prestige-branded drama: persuasively acted, aesthetically polished, intricately plotted, and, with a few baffling exceptions, subtly scripted. It can be quite exciting. But as the season progresses, sparse character development and minimal insight into the absurdity of possessing—let alone fighting over—sums of money that could sustain hundreds of upper-middle-class Steven types add up to a frustrating lack of perspective.
From the very beginning, the Henderson-Duval split is sordid. After accepting an award with a high-minded speech, Morgan—the entrepreneur behind a socially responsible social media platform called Zephyr—allows himself to be seduced by a beautiful young woman, Flora (Rose Williams). It’s a honeytrap, set by Carla in a desperate scheme to investigate rumors of her husband’s infidelity. On a junket promoting a dire-sounding period drama called The Milliner (her declining film career fuels some of War’s wittiest moments), she wastes no time forwarding Flora’s selfie with a sleeping Morgan to her lawyers. And so the gears of the divorce machine shudder into motion, working to formalize a gradual estrangement that had been masquerading as the unavoidable byproduct of two demanding, international careers. We don’t learn much about either spouse as people; Carla’s personality is especially tough to pin down. At times, it’s implied that she’s cold or cutthroat. Her son from a previous relationship (Aran Murphy, in his second HBO troubled-teen role this fall) is barely mentioned before he pops up in Episode 3.
The show’s failure to flesh out these characters could have worked. The anthology’s overarching concept implies that it’s the lawyers, not the clients, that we’re supposed to be getting to know. In Morgan’s corner is Cathcarts & Sons, a venerable, old-school firm whose patrician pomp is telegraphed by stuffy, dark-wood interiors. Carla hires upstarts Taylor & Byrne, whose glassy, modern office space, by contrast, underscores a mission of operating on the light side of the legal arts—avoiding dirty tactics and putting clients first. (Flora’s photo, which is proof of Carla’s entrapment as well as of Morgan’s cheating, is an early ethical test.) The adversaries have history that goes beyond the prep-school-to-white-shoe-firm pipeline, and it gives both sides further ammunition for a fight they’re incentivized to draw out for as long as possible.
There are a few compelling characters among the attorneys. Married Taylor & Byrne partners Nick Taylor (James McArdle) and Serena Byrne (Phoebe Fox) are about to have their first child, and the question of whether she—the tougher but somewhat less senior and, of course, female of the two—will step back from work to focus on family meshes well with the show’s depiction of Carla as a mostly absent mother. Pip Torrens could make your skin crawl (complimentary) as St. John Smallwood, a cruel, sardonic leader of the opposite team, a constant reminder of how much ground there is between compromised and sociopathic on the moral spectrum.
But even these standouts feel underdeveloped. And most of the dozen or so colleagues of theirs we meet are either cyphers or types. Smallwood’s underling David Schill (Miles Jupp) is flop sweat personified. Shadow and Bone star Archie Renaux is very good at conveying the quiet calculations of Johnny Warren, a working-class junior lawyer who is basically the straight Tom Ripley, Esq., but the fact that his character can be summed up so concisely speaks to its limitations. Farther down the call sheet, for every inspired casting choice (Celia Imrie as a sprightly barrister), there are a couple of name actors wasted in roles that serve expository purposes (Patrick Fabian as a Morgan minion, Nick Mohammed as a Taylor & Byrne staffer).
There are so many characters, and Kay does so little to identify a protagonist within this cynical milieu, that—as the case progresses inevitably from a pantomime of mediation to a courtroom spectacle with the potential to make careers and ruin lives—it’s hard to know where to look. Ideas surface and either stall out, like the nihilism of Gabe’s superrich teen cohort in an era whose apocalyptic mood is a direct result of their parents’ actions, or linger redundantly. Well before the midpoint of the season, viewers will be trained to see lawyers as 24/7 performers, manipulating everyone around them through false sincerity and empathy, if not full fabrication. Glib flourishes like an episode that ends with both spouses saying "I do" to escalating their conflict and the occasional insertion of misplaced crime-drama clichés ("It's done," Flora tells Carla after sleeping with Morgan) undermine otherwise solid scripts.
The point may be that money destroys families and debases everyone who seeks it. But even if Succession hadn’t already eloquently made it (Morgan’s watch stunt is a milder version of Logan Roy’s viscerally disturbing Boar on the Floor), that’s not what War’s ultimate framing of Morgan and Carla suggests. While all the scheming and jockeying and betrayal can be thrilling, the resolution feels like a shrug. Kay invokes big, timely issues—extreme wealth, gender roles, the horrors of social media—without finding much to say about them. An anthology is supposed to be a collection of complete stories. War’s slick but shallow first outing is anything but.

NAZA, off screen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:59:45 UTC
22:59:45 KST

NAZA, off screen
BUENOS AIRES — For months, we have been living with harrowing images from Gaza, amid allegations and accusations of genocide. Images, testimonies, and an incessant flow of information—and yet nothing stops. Gaza has also become this: the repetition of unbearable scenes that we see again and again, without their accumulation seeming sufficient to interrupt the machinery that produces them.
But in recent weeks, a film burst onto the scene at the 2026 Venice International Film Festival and received an ovation lasting nearly half an hour. It is NAZA, by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, two Israeli filmmakers who construct the film from a singular vantage point: testimonies emerging from within Israel’s own military and intelligence apparatus. The film brings together 24 military and intelligence sources and was made over the course of three years.
The question then shifts: what does it mean to look from the inside? Filmed at night, on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, NAZA enters what generally remains off screen: the systems, calculations, and decisions that precede the bombing of Gaza and the mass deaths of Palestinian civilians. And that calculation has a name: NAZA. But NAZA did not originate with this film. Nor did it originate with this war. To understand what it means, we have to go back in time and enter the history of a procedure developed within the Israeli military apparatus itself.
What does NAZA mean?
NAZA comes from נז״א, an acronym for nezek agavi (נזק אגבי), literally “collateral damage,” an expression incorporated into Israeli military language. In planning certain attacks, the military apparatus makes a prior estimate of the civilian casualties the operation could cause. The so-called “NAZA number” expresses that forecast: how many civilians could die as a consequence of the attack before it is authorized.
Put simply, the calculation begins with the identification of a target, intelligence about the people who are inside it or in its vicinity, and the anticipated effects of the munition. NAZA, therefore, is neither artificial intelligence nor software: it is a military concept and calculation. New technologies may play a role in identifying and assessing targets, but the term predates them. To trace its origins, we have to go back more than two decades. Ronen Bergman, an Israeli journalist specializing in intelligence, explains in Rise and Kill First: The Secret History of Israel's Targeted Assassinations that during the Second Intifada, civilian deaths caused in targeted killing operations began to be referred to as nezek agavi, “collateral damage,” an expression that over time was condensed into the acronym NAZA.
From inside the system
Retired lieutenant colonel and former Israeli Military Intelligence member Sarit Zehavi says that nearly twenty years ago she took part in developing procedures designed to warn and monitor the evacuation of civilian populations, as well as in target-approval processes. Her public intervention is particularly revealing in relation to one of the figures associated with NAZA: 500. Zehavi maintains that “NAZA 500” does not mean an automatic authorization to kill five hundred civilians, but rather a prior estimate of potential harm that should lead to measures to reduce it through evacuations, changes in munitions, or even cancellation of the attack.
But the problem posed by NAZA goes beyond the existence of the calculation itself: what happens when the number of civilians expected to die increases and the attack is nevertheless authorized? The question took on another dimension after October 7, 2023. An investigation by The New York Times said that the Israeli military loosened certain rules of engagement and, in some operations, allowed the risk of killing up to 20 civilians even when targeting lower-ranking combatants. The procedure, however, predates this period. Testimonies from Israeli soldiers collected by Breaking the Silence after the 2014 Gaza offensive describe categories of nezek agavi—collateral damage—classified into levels 0, 1, and 2. One of those testimonies makes a fundamental point: those levels did not count buildings or material damage. They counted human lives.
NAZA is not the only mechanism involved in target selection. In recent years, other tools used by Israeli intelligence have become known. Habsora (The Gospel) processes large amounts of information to help identify possible physical targets, such as buildings or infrastructure. Lavender focuses on individuals, generating assessments of their possible links to armed organizations. And Where’s Daddy? - the name attributed by intelligence sources to a tracking system - was reportedly used to locate previously identified individuals, including when they were in their homes. NAZA serves a different function: it estimates the anticipated collateral damage before an attack. It does not determine who the target is, but how many civilians could be affected by striking it. These tools do not necessarily operate together or in every operation, but they reveal different stages of the same architecture: identify, locate, calculate the damage, and decide whether to strike.
Designing death
The precedent appears in This Is How We Fought in Gaza: Soldiers’ Testimonies and Photographs from Operation “Protective Edge” (2014), a report published in 2015 by the Israeli organization Breaking the Silence (Shovrim Shtika), which brings together testimonies from more than sixty Israeli soldiers and officers who took part in Operation Protective Edge in 2014. Among them, testimony 109 is particularly revealing. At the end, the interviewer asks whether that collateral damage also included material destruction. The answer is no: the levels referred exclusively to human lives. NAZA therefore begins long before a bomb falls on Gaza. It begins in that space cinema can almost never show: a room, a screen, a set of data, a number, and someone who ultimately decides. What we will later see as an image—a destroyed building, bodies, survivors—had already existed before in another form: as a calculation. Perhaps that is where the power of the title and the film lies: bringing into the frame what had remained off screen. Behind the abstraction of “collateral damage,” behind every level and every number, lies something that technical language turns into a figure: human lives.

EU launches infringement procedures against Greece over energy, money laundering rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
The European Commission on Friday launched infringement procedures against Greece for failing to notify the EU executive of its implementation of several EU directives covering energy, money laundering and human trafficking, Greek daily Ekathimerini reported.
The Commission said Greece was among 18 EU member states that had failed to communicate the full transposition of new electricity market rules into their national legislation.
The rules concern consumers’ rights to choose and switch electricity suppliers, access competitive and innovative offers, and participate more actively in the energy system, according to the Commission.
Greece and 25 other EU member states were also cited for failing to incorporate new rules on the hydrogen and decarbonized gas markets into national legislation.
The rules are intended to facilitate the uptake of renewable and low-carbon gases, including hydrogen, while ensuring security of supply and affordable of energy, the Commission said.
The Commission also opened infringement procedures against Greece and other EU countries for failing to incorporate new rules on money laundering and human trafficking into national legislation.
The member states have two months to respond and complete the required measures, after which the Commission may proceed to the next stage by issuing a reasoned opinion.

Jeffrey Donaldson, the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party in Northern Ireland, could be sent to prison for more than 10 years over the sexual assault of two women when they were children, a court heard on Friday.
The disgraced politician, who headed the DUP between 2021 and 2024, was found guilty of 18 counts of sexual abuse including one count of rape against the women in June.
Recounting the case, Rosemary Walsh KC reminded Judge Ramsey how the distress felt by Complainant B while giving evidence was “palpable” in the court room.
Referring to a victim statement already with the judge, she told how Complainant B had described the trial as “a terrible experience” and how the abuse she suffered as a child “affected her every day” of her life.
Sometimes she struggled so much she “wishes she could die”, Walsh said, adding that as a result of the abuse she “does not know what love and trust really is”.
The other victim, Complainant A, wrote in her victim impact statement that she felt her childhood had been “stolen from her” and this had led to feelings of shame and anger.
Her sleep and sense of wellbeing were affected to this day and sometimes she felt burnt out from the emotional stress.
Walsh spoke of various tariffs for the offences, several of which carried a maximum sentence of two years, but others which carried a maximum sentence of between 10 and 14 years under historical tariffs for crimes, she told the court.
She said historical legislation did not differentiate between a child and an adult victim in all the counts, so the disparity in age between Donaldson and his victims should be considered an “aggravating” factor in sentencing.
She said Complainant B was “nine or 10” during some of the offending by Donaldson when he was 25 or 26 years old. She had described how she felt “sick” when he abused her and “wanted to scream out” but thought it was her fault.
Complainant B suffered other types of sexual assault by Donaldson when she was as young as “seven or eight”.
Donaldson, 63, who is planning to appeal, sat stony-faced throughout the 70-minute pre-sentencing hearing in Newry courthouse.
Kieran Vaughan KC urged the judge to take into account several “mitigating” factors including Donaldson’s current age and that he was a man of “previous good character”.
He also told the court “there was no offending of this type” in the past 18 years and during this time Donaldson had significant achievements which were “obliterated” by the conviction.
Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, has already lodged an appeal against the court’s finding that she had committed acts alleged in relation to five of the charges he had faced.
She was found unfit to stand trial on mental health grounds, meaning the jury was asked to find out if she did or did not commit the acts of which she was accused.
She cannot be sent to jail but is appealing to have the court conclusions overturned.
Donaldson is expected to be sentenced next month.

The U.S. Air Force has begun conducting independent flights of Anduril’s FQ-44A Fury unmanned fighter jet following the delivery of the first aircraft to the military.
This was reported by Anduril Industries on its official X account.
According to the company, the first Fury CCA was delivered to the U.S. Air Force in August. U.S. military personnel are now flying the aircraft without direct control from Anduril staff.
The Fury was transferred to an experimental unit at Krich Air Base, where military personnel are practicing its use alongside manned aircraft.
Following the transfer of the aircraft, the military began conducting several flights per day with it, while the presence of the company’s specialists at the base was significantly reduced.
In July, the FQ-44A had already undergone testing at Krich Air Base as part of the Agile Combat Employment concept. At that time, a single U.S. Air Force operator was able to launch and recover the drone independently after just a few hours of training.
During these tests, the Fury also flew alongside F-35 fighter jets. However, the F-35 did not directly control the drone—the aircraft operated under the control of its own Mission Autonomy system.
In addition, over the summer, the Fury conducted tests of the full air-to-air engagement sequence: it received an external target designation, processed it through the autonomous Lattice system, and fired an AIM-120 AMRAAM missile.
In September, the U.S. Air Force officially designated the aircraft as the FQ-44 Fury. The second CCA model in the program’s first phase—the FQ-42 from General Atomics—was named Vengeance.
Both aircraft are being developed as part of the Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program and are designed to operate alongside manned fighter jets, extending their range, situational awareness, and combat capabilities. The U.S. Air Force plans to have approximately 500 such aircraft by 2032, and eventually, about 1,000.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that Anduril had already begun serial production of the FQ-44A at its new Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio. The first production aircraft rolled off the assembly line in the summer of 2026.
The FQ-44A has already undergone testing with aerial bombs and other air-to-surface weapons, indicating plans to expand its role beyond aerial combat.

Artificial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:58:11 UTC
22:58:11 KST

Artificial
« previous post |
From Donald Trump's recent UN speech:
The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now, hereinafter officially called Super Intelligence, changing the name, and that the use of the word "artificial" makes intelligence fake. It makes it sound fake. And it is not fake. It's actually amazing, but we have to be careful. In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports.
From this point forward, all of United States documents and, hopefully the world's will be changed to use the much more accurate term "super" as opposed to "artificial". So it's Super Intelligence. In other words, welcome to the new world of Super Intelligence-SI. SI, let's see if that goes, it sounds much better. It is much better, and it's much more accurate. Let's see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don't. We're going to find out pretty soon.
This reminds me of one of my favorite examples of semantic drift.
The OED's sense I.1.a. for artificial, dating to c1425, is "Of a thing: made or constructed by human skill, esp. in imitation of, or as a substitute for, something which is made or occurs naturally; man-made."
Scrolling down through other senses over the years, we get some negatively-evaluated senses, like 1.4.a "Contrived or fabricated for a particular purpose, esp. for deception; resulting from artifice; feigned, fictitious", as well as some positively-evaluated (or at least neutral) ones, like II.6 "According to the principles of an art or science; scientific, systematic."
But then there's II.9.a "Of a thing: skilfully made or contrived; cleverly constructed", flagged as Obsolete, with citations through 1833, for example these (quotations expanded from the original sources):
1663 How to make a brazen or stone head, in the midst of a great field or garden, so artificial and natural, that though a man speak never so softly, and even whispers into the ear thereof, it will presently open its mouth, and resolve the question in French, Latin, Welsh, Irish, or English, in good terms, uttering it out of his mouth, and then shut it until the next question be asked.
1738  The artificial and elegant Structure of the Eyes, and the great fitness of their Parts, for the offices of Vision, are illustrated by the Laws of Opticks.
1833  The collocation of the words is so artificial in Shakspeare and Milton that you may as well think of pushing a brick out of that wall with your finger as of displacing a word without injury from one of their sentences.
The 1633 example is from The Century of Inventions of the Marquis of Worcester, originally (?) published in 1825. The cited passage continues:
Albertus Magnus, a celebrated philosopher of the thirteenth century, is said to have constructed an automaton which not only performed all the apparent motions of life, but absolutely answered questions. It is recorded of Thomas Aquinas, that, having accidentally seen the head, he was so terrified that he broke it in pieces, upon which Albert exclaimed: Periit opus triginta annorum! Though this appears one of the earliest instances of a speaking automaton constructed by one of the laity, there is no doubt but that the method of conveying answers to various interrogatories, by the agency of concealed pipes or a speaking trumpet, was practised at a very early period. That the impostor Alexander, however, caused his Æsculapius to speak in this manner is expressly related by Lucan. He took, says this author, instead of a pipe, the gullet of a crane, and transmitted the voice through it to the mouth of the statue. But the invention of the invisible girl, which may be considered as an improvement on the oracular responses of the darker ages, infinitely surpassed any of those hitherto recorded.
This very ingenious apparatus was publicly exhibited both at Bristol and in London for a considerable period, during which time no discovery was made of its internal mechanism; and it is probable that its construction would have remained a secret to all but the exhibitors, but for the ingenuity of Mr. (now Professor) Millington, who, in a course of Lectures delivered in the winter of 1806, explained the manner in which it was performed.
The visible part of the apparatus connected with the invisible girl was thus constructed: first a mahogany frame resembling a bedstead, having at the corners four upright posts about five feet high, was united by a cross-rail near the top, and two or more cross-rails near the bottom, to strengthen the frame, which was about four feet square. The frame thus constructed was placed upon the floor, and to the top of each of the four pillars were attached as many strong bent brass wires converging towards the top, where they were secured by a crown and other ornaments. From these wires a hollow copper ball was suspended by slight ribbons, so as to cut off all possible communication with the frame. The globe thus supported was supposed to contain the invisible being, as the voice apparently proceeded from the interior of it: and for this purpose, it was equipped with four trumpets, placed round it in a horizontal direction, and at right angles to each other; the trumpet mouths coming to within about half an inch of the respective cross-rails of the frame surrounding them.
When a question was proposed, it was asked from any side of the frame, and spoken into one of the trumpets, and an answer immediately proceeded from the whole of them, so loud as to be distinctly heard by the inquirer, and yet so distant and feeble, that it appeared as if coming from a very diminutive being. In this the whole of the artifice consisted; and the variations were so contrived that the answer might be returned in several languages, a kiss might be returned, the breath producing the voice was felt, and songs were sung, accompanied by the piano-forte, &c. To produce this illusion, the sound was conveyed by a tube, in a manner similar to the old and well known contrivance of the speaking bust; the invisible girl only differing in one circumstance; that an artificial echo was produced by means of the trumpets and hollow globe, in consequence of which the sound was completely reversed.
In the invisible girl the orifice of the tube was in one of the handrails just opposite the mouth of one of the trumpets, the opening being concealed by reeds and other mouldings; the tube itself, which was about half an inch in diameter, ran through half the handrail, then down one of the corner posts, and from thence under the floor till it reached a large deal case almost similar to an inverted funnel, along the side of which it rose till it came nearly into contact with the ear of the confederate, who with a piano-forte, &c. was concealed in this case. Any question asked by a voice directed into one of the trumpets was immediately reflected back from the concave interior surface of the globe to the orifice of the tube, along which it was conveyed so as to be distinctly heard by the person in the deal case, who returned the requisite answer, which appeared to come precisely from the interior of the globe. A small hole closed with glass was likewise left through the deal case and side wall of the apartment, by means of which the concealed person had an opportunity of observing and commenting upon any circumstance which occurred in the room.
Unquestionably very artificial and natural!

Exclusive: Majority of companies involved in Russian Molniya drone production unsanctioned, research shows

Exclusive: Majority of companies involved in Russian Molniya drone production unsanctioned, research shows
The majority of companies supplying components for Russia's Molniya series of drones are not under sanctions, while the manufacturer itself is not currently subject to U.S. or U.K. sanctions, according to research obtained by the Kyiv Independent.
The Molniya is a low-cost strike drone manufactured by Atlant Aero LLC. According to Serhii Beskrestnov, a former adviser to Ukraine's Defense Ministry, the drone costs around $1,600, has a range of up to 50 kilometers (30 miles) and can carry a warhead weighing up to 10 kilograms.
Atlant Aero's main production facility in Taganrog, Rostov Oblast, has expanded rapidly in 2025. Satellite imagery shows construction of additional production facilities next to the company's existing site.
Since its introduction, the Molniya has become one of Russia's most widely used strike UAVs, with its low cost, relatively simple production and reported effectiveness contributing to its widespread deployment.
The research, conducted by the Center for Defense Reforms, a Ukrainian security think tank, and shared with the Kyiv Independent, also shows that the majority of companies supplying components used in the production of Molniya drones are not yet subject to Western sanctions.
Significantly, while Atlant Aero LLC is subject to EU and Canadian sanctions, it is not currently sanctioned by either the United Kingdom or the United States. Prominvest JSC, the controlling shareholder of Atlant Aero LLC, is not subject to sanctions in any jurisdiction, the research found.
Another 10 Russian companies that provide critical components and services for the production of Molniya drones are also not subject to any Western sanctions.
Viktor Grigoryev, the beneficial owner of Atlant Aero LLC, is also not subject to Western sanctions, nor are the company's four other co-owners.
The report also identifies 11 Chinese companies that are not subject to sanctions and provide critical components for the Molniya supply chain. These include Shenzhen Xingkai Technology Company, which supplies mesh network equipment that enables Russian drones to fly deep into Ukrainian territory. The company's website openly describes the technology as having military applications.
"Companies involved in the production of Russian weapons must be subject to Western sanctions," Oleksandr Danylyuk, chairman of the Centre for Defense Reforms, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Equally important is the creation of a proper mechanism for enforcing sanctions, with adequate punishment for those who attempt to evade them. Otherwise, they don't work," he added.

WTO to Weigh Russia Complaint Over EU Carbon Border Levy

The World Trade Organization will appoint experts to examine a complaint from Moscow over the European Union’s carbon border tax, a Geneva-based trade official said Friday.
The decision was reached during a WTO Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) meeting, the official said on condition of anonymity.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) aims to ensure foreign producers pay a carbon cost similar to what European companies already pay under the bloc’s internal emissions trading system.
Importers of carbon-heavy goods produced abroad like steel, aluminum and fertilizer must declare the CO2 emissions embedded in their products and pay a levy if they exceed EU standards.
The EU has promoted the key environmental policy, which took effect at the start of the year, as a “virtuous” tool that encourages greener practices worldwide.
But the policy has faced strong opposition amid charges that it restricts trade and favors European manufacturers.
Arguing that the CBAM breaches the rules of global trade, Russia filed its initial complaint with the WTO over the policy in May last year.
At that point, Moscow requested consultations with the EU and its member states regarding this issue, as well as on the two-decade-old Emissions Trading System (ETS), which enables certain industries to benefit from free carbon allowances.
Brussels swiftly rejected the consultation request, insisting such discussions could not be fruitful given the circumstances created by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine since February 2022.
Russian Drones, Missiles or Troops Could Test NATO Within Months, Danish Intelligence Says
Moscow then asked the WTO this past July 10 to establish a panel of experts to examine the case, but the EU blocked the request.
The DSB granted the second request on Friday, the trade official said.
Under WTO regulations, parties in a dispute can block a first request for an arbitration panel, but if the parties make a second request, it is all but guaranteed to go through.
In a communication sent to the WTO this week, the EU said Russia’s renewed panel request had created “an extraordinary situation” in which a country “that for more than four and a half years continues to wage a war of aggression... in violation of the most fundamental rules of international law” was asking for an assessment of the “international law compatibility of a regulatory, climate-oriented, environmental measure.”
Brussels said it would agree to take part in the process due to its “firm support for the rules-based multilateral trading system,” but stressed that it would “only engage with the panel and not directly with the Russian Federation.”
As long as Russia “is waging its war of aggression against Ukraine, it cannot expect to be able to rely on WTO rules for improved access for its exports to the market of the European Union,” the bloc said.

Scientists discovered two bizarre new sea spiders that are “nightmare fuel”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:56:06 UTC
22:56:06 KST

Scientists discovered two bizarre new sea spiders that are “nightmare fuel”
- Date:
- September 25, 2026
- Source:
- University of British Columbia
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered two strange new sea spider species in the Salish Sea, including a hairy-legged, red-eyed species that can groom itself with comb-like appendages. Another is frequently covered in tiny parasites, and researchers say many more undiscovered sea spiders may still be hiding in the region.
- Share:
If you happen to be swimming in the Salish Sea at night and imagine tiny hairy legs creeping up your body, there is now at least one unsettling reason that image feels plausible. Researchers at the University of British Columbia have identified two previously unknown species of sea spider, including one with hairy legs and striking red eyes.
The discoveries mark the first new sea spider species formally described from the Salish Sea in nearly 100 years. Published in Organisms Diversity & Evolution, the study combines detailed physical observations with genetic analysis to help fill major gaps in scientists' understanding of these unusual marine animals.
"I was interested in how sea spiders are impacted by climate change and human disturbance, because marine invertebrates in the Salish Sea are particularly at-risk, and I couldn't find anything," said lead author Cormac Toler-Scott, who conducted the work as part of his master's degree in zoology at UBC. "That's largely because people don't know much about what species exist here and what their lifestyle is."
According to Toler-Scott, that lack of basic information affects many marine arthropods. "In order to understand how marine invertebrates are being impacted by things like climate change and how we can better protect these key elements of the ecosystem, we have to be able to identify them."
Ancient Animals With Bizarre Biology
Sea spiders belong to an ancient lineage that arose roughly 500 million years ago. They are related to spiders, scorpions, and horseshoe crabs, but unlike their land-dwelling relatives, they remained entirely marine.
Their appearance is strange even by arthropod standards. Some species can have as many as 12 legs, along with a sucking proboscis used for feeding. Their size varies dramatically, from less than a centimeter long to more than 70 cm in Antarctica, where some species hunt smaller animals in deep ocean environments.
"They've retained some weird traits," said Toler-Scott. "A lot of the shallow water species are quite small, and so they'll live as parasites on larger organisms, and they use this weird apparatus called a proboscis to suck the juices out of their host."
Sea spiders also have several unusual reproductive and physiological traits. They breathe directly through their skin, and males take responsibility for carrying and raising the young.
Females have ovaries that extend through their limbs, where eggs develop before 'popping out' through a dedicated pore. During mating, the male collects the eggs using specialized appendages near the base of his head called 'ovigers'. He coats the eggs with glue secreted from his legs and attaches clusters of egg sacs to his own body while they develop.
Hairy Feet, Red Eyes, and a Strange Mouth
Researchers collected the newly described species between September 2023 and August 2024 during dives reaching depths of up to 18 meters. Specimens came from a variety of marine habitats around Quadra Island, Vancouver, Bamfield, and Victoria.
One of the species was named Callipallene pilosuspedes because of the long, curved spines covering the lower portions of its legs. The name is a reference to the Latin words for 'hairy feet'.
Its appearance is especially distinctive. The animal has red eyes and a short proboscis equipped with claws that help it grab food before biting. Its mouth is triangular, divided into three lips, and surrounded by sensory tendrils, giving it an appearance reminiscent of a tiny marine Sarlacc pit.
The species also has unusually agile ovigers that serve another purpose beyond carrying eggs. Under a microscope, researchers watched the sea spider wrap these appendages around its legs and use comb-like spines to groom and clean its body.
Despite its memorable appearance, the team found only a single specimen.
A Sea Spider Covered in Parasites
The second newly described species, Tanystylum kiixin, takes its name from an ancient Indigenous village site near the location where specimens were first collected.
Pronounced 'kee-hin', the name refers to the sound of waves crashing at the base of the village site.
Unlike Callipallene pilosuspedes, this species has much smaller and less flexible egg-carrying limbs. That appears to limit its ability to groom itself effectively.
Researchers often found dirt and debris clinging to the animals, along with tiny parasites living on their bodies. The result is what Toler-Scott describes as "an ecosystem within an ecosystem within an ecosystem."
DNA Reveals Hidden Sea Spider Diversity
The study is the first comprehensive investigation of Salish Sea sea spiders to combine detailed imaging with DNA analysis.
As part of the work, researchers generated genetic sequences for several species that had never been sequenced before. The team also produced an identification guide to help scientists distinguish sea spider species found throughout the region.
Both newly discovered species have now been registered in a global database, but Toler-Scott says the Salish Sea likely contains additional species that have yet to be documented.
"I only had one field season, but there's definitely more diversity out there that we haven't documented."
In other words, the Salish Sea may still be hiding plenty of additional nightmare fuel.
This research was funded by National Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of British Columbia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Cormac Toler-Scott, Eunji Park, Heather Gordon, Brian S. Leander. Sea spiders of the Salish Sea: Comparative morphology and molecular phylogenetic analysis of seven coastal species (Arthropoda, Pycnogonida). Organisms Diversity, 2026; DOI: 10.1007/s13127-026-00707-3

"If this happens (the unblocking of the Fund in the amount of EUR 6.6 billion) in the coming days, many member states have already stated that all the funds they receive back they will provide to Ukraine, which will also mean significant new financing for air defense, capabilities that Ukraine needs," she said.

"But, of course, this is very difficult. At the same time, of course, work is also underway to create EU interceptors together with Ukraine," she added.
The final legal decision and signing of all documents are scheduled to be formalized at the regular EU Council meeting on September 28. Germany previously stated that the EUR 6.6 billion from the Peace Facility unblocked by Hungary should be fully transferred to Ukraine – but not all EU states support this.

A bottle of flammable liquid in Poland, a nuclear option on a Russian wish-list—the hunt for Starlink widens
Unknown

13:54:01 UTC
22:54:01 KST

A Russian academic and an ultranationalist media owner have drawn up a menu of ways to knock out Starlink, the satellite network keeping Ukraine's drones and troops online, the Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported. The ideas run from jamming to a nuclear blast in space, and come as Poland investigates a suspicious fire at a Starlink ground station serving Ukraine.
Satellite internet is the nervous system of the drone war. Since a terminal cutoff early this year gutted Russian frontline coordination, Moscow's search for a workaround has widened from the spectrum to orbit—and from the battlefield toward the infrastructure that keeps the network alive.
The scenarios
Sergei Glazyev of the Russian Academy of Sciences and Konstantin Malofeyev, founder of the Russian outlet Tsargrad, laid out the proposals. Glazyev's list runs from cutting communication cables on land and undersea to crippling data centers and downing reconnaissance and command aircraft, whatever their nationality. Without American and British spotters, planners, and analysts, he claims, Ukraine's army would go blind. Glazyev's core argument is that Starlink satellites are not geostationary—nothing hangs over Ukraine, so the entire constellation must be struck at once.
For electronic warfare, they push wider use of the Volna Kupol Garant, a roughly $1.5 million system that beams a signal to briefly deafen a passing Starlink satellite over what its developers claim is up to 20 km². Kinetic options follow—the A-235 Nudol and S-500 Prometheus interceptors—though they call spending one costly missile on one cheap satellite "insane extravagance." A third idea scatters metal pellets to spark what the authors call the Kessler effect—a debris cascade that would destroy everything at that altitude.
The bluntest proposal detonates a nuclear device in space, its pulse frying electronics on low-orbit satellites. The authors admit this would also wreck Russia's own Rassvet network, which orbits at a similar altitude. "We can no longer hit Musk's creation for free," they write, "but it's still the optimal option. The legal consequences are unimportant."
Russia’s answer to Starlink was written off as a failure—its satellites are still climbing
A station burns in Poland
On 23 September, fire destroyed the distribution panel of a ground Starlink station in Wola Krobowska that feeds Poland and Ukraine. Poland's Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said sabotage could not be ruled out and that the pattern matched Russian services' modus operandi. A bottle of flammable liquid was found beside the burned distribution panel, according to sources cited by RMF24. Exatel, which the minister named as the station's operator, said it only subleases the land and transmits data there, and neither operates nor owns the infrastructure.

A spokesperson said: “At this stage, our investigation has found no evidence that members of the public’s personal data has been accessed or compromised as a result of this incident.”

“We are … continuing to investigate whether any information relating to our staff may have been accessed or compromised, and are taking all appropriate steps to protect that information, and will provide appropriate advice to colleagues if required,” said a spokesperson.
The force said it was receiving support from cybersecurity specialists and its systems had been subjected to “precautionary measures” while an investigation was under way.
Online and email contacts for the force were unavailable after the attack, which was identified on the day it happened, but have since been restored.
The Information Commissioner’s Office, the UK’s data watchdog, has been notified of the incident.
A spokesperson for the force added: “We understand the potential concern this may cause and want to reassure the public that we have and will continue to take all necessary steps to protect our information and maintain the security of our systems.
“We will provide further updates when we are in a position to do so.”
The area served by Dyfed-Powys police equates to more than 500,000 people, a number that rises significantly with tourists each year.
The investigation is being managed by Tarian, the regional organised crime unit (ROCU) for southern Wales, and force systems are being monitored.
A spokesperson for the ICO said: “We can confirm we have received a breach report from Dyfed-Powys police and we are assessing the information provided.”
In July it was revealed that hackers had breached the police national legal database (PNLD), which provides legal assistance to UK police forces. The cybercriminals claimed to have taken 135,000 pieces of data.
The PNLD said the details taken related to “police officers and those working in criminal justice including their name, the force or organisation they work for and their work email address”. However, the database does not contain confidential victim, witness or offender information.

Mosques given £66m in emergency security funds after Southport disorder

A record £66m of emergency security funding was issued by the Home Office for mosques and related community sites in the UK when violent disorder spread in the aftermath of the Southport attacks in 2024.
Exclusive figures obtained by the Guardian also reveal a record of about £41m in security funding was issued for mosques and related community sites for the year from April 2025-26 as part of the protective security scheme.
The chief executive of the British Muslim Trust, the government’s partner for monitoring anti-Muslim hatred, said the figures “tell an incredibly sombre story about the rise in anti-Muslim hostility that British Muslims are living with”.
“Security needs are increasing as a direct response to the increase in attacks that mosques are under,” Akeela Ahmed said. “If we want to bring down the costs for protecting British Muslims in the UK then we need to reduce the need for protection and address the root causes of hate against Muslim communities.”
The trust published data in July showing that one mosque was attacked every five days across Britain in the past year.
The government launched a security scheme for places of worship in 2016 for England and Wales, and in 2023 it created a dedicated scheme worth £29.4m for mosques and faith schools in the UK to provide security to ensure the safety of Muslim communities.
According to figures obtained via a freedom of information request, the security funding issued for mosques, Islamic faith schools and associated sites was £73,147 in 2016-17, before increasing to about £3m in 2022-23, £29m in 2024-25 and a record of about £41m in 2025-26.
The Home Office introduced a separate emergency security scheme as a temporary measure for places of worship when violent disorder spread across cities after a knife attack in Southport in 2024 in which three girls at a dance class were murdered.
Of the almost £69m granted to places of worship in the UK as part of this scheme, about £66m was issued to mosques and associated sites, the data revealed. At the time, mosques and hotels housing asylum seekers were targeted after false news had spread online claiming that the perpetrator of the attack was a Muslim asylum seeker.
Shaista Gohir, the chief executive of Muslim Women’s Network UK, said the figures created “the impression that substantial action is being taken to tackle anti-Muslim hostility” but the government’s response remained “limited compared with the scale of the problem”.
“There is little visible action to address the safety of Muslim women, and most of the funding doesn’t even appear to reach mosques or other community sites. One mosque leader I spoke to recently had to apply several times and still only received funding for some requested measures. Many others are still waiting for decisions,” Gohir said.
The Jami community centre in Birmingham has reported at least five incidents relating to hate crime and racially aggravated criminal damage between March and July this year, according to West Midlands police. The centre has introduced its own security measures, including gates and blackout boards, while it completes its application for security funding.
Worshippers told the Guardian about the incidents – some of which had not been reported to police – including smashed windows and Islamophobic graffiti.
Khalid, a volunteer at the centre, organised an emergency meeting with MPs, councillors and police. He criticised the lack of response from West Midlands police to the several incidents that have occurred.
“We’ve had the Prevent team from the council coming here. We’ve had the imam being verbally abused. There’s people being verbally abused … What are we waiting for? Like a disaster to happen?” he said.
He added: “The centre feels that they’re not being supported enough. More needs to be done. No one should ever feel unsafe coming to pray. It’s not safe. They feel insecure in their own home and in their own place of worship.”
Islam, a 41-year-old private hire driver who attends the centre, reported one incident to the police earlier this year, when an individual shouted abuse at worshippers.
He said the attacks had forced many women and children to attend another mosque nearby because of fears for their safety. “I don’t think any Muslim hijabi lady would walk to this centre on their own,” Islam said.
Paulette Hamilton, the MP for Birmingham Erdington, said she was “deeply concerned” by the attacks on the centre. “It’s absolutely hateful. I think the people who are doing it are cowardly and there is no place for that sort of thing in the constituency.”
West Midlands police said they remained in “close contact with leaders and worshippers” at the centre. “We take all forms of hate crime seriously, and every report of it made to us is investigated as we work to bring offenders to justice,” a spokesperson said.
The Home Office said it was working to process all applications for security funding as soon as possible. “To help protect Muslim communities from the appalling levels of hate crime they face, the government has made £40m available through protective security schemes. This is part of a record £77.4m investment in security funding for faith communities in 2026-27,” a spokesperson said.

Moldova already overpaid $330 mln for gas after cutting ties with Gazprom — ex-president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:47:29 UTC
22:47:29 KST

CHISINAU, September 25. /TASS/. Moldova has overpaid roughly $330 million for gas over the last two and a half years alone after the country decided to cut ties Gazprom and chose to buy gas from the EU the EU at prices 40% higher, Igor Dodon, former Moldovan President and leader of the country's largest opposition Party of Socialists, said, posting calculation charts on his Telegram channel.
"Moldova purchased gas at a price roughly 40% higher than the formula agreed upon and signed in autumn 2021 under the agreement with Gazprom, resulting in an overpayment of about $330 million over the last 2.5 years alone. Furthermore, the cumulative benefit of the Gazprom formula for the 2022-2026 period would have reached approximately $745 million had Chisinau not terminated the contract in late 2022," Dodon stressed.
He noted that despite breaking long-standing agreements with Gazprom, the republic failed to secure favorable European pricing in its dealings with the EU.
"Throughout the period under review, the formula agreed with Gazprom would have yielded an average price approximately 15% lower than the European average. However, after abandoning Gazprom, Moldova failed to consistently purchase gas even at the European average price. In many quarters, the actual purchase price exceeded both the Gazprom formula price and the European benchmark," Dodon added. He noted that, for this reason, Moldovan state-owned enterprise Energocom admitted it could not disclose full details of contracts and individual transactions due to confidentiality clauses.
"Energy security relies on having multiple sources and options, not on rejecting an advantageous option to buy the same resources at a higher cost through opaque agreements," Dodon stressed, noting that the arrangement with Gazprom had helped avoid the price shocks the country is currently facing.
Energy crisis in Moldova
Moldova has been grappling with an energy crisis since President Maia Sandu and her Party of Action and Solidarity came to power and moved to sever ties with Russia. In 2021, gas tariffs skyrocketed sevenfold, driving annual inflation past 30% and sparking widespread protests. In response, the government claimed it had ended its dependence on Gazprom and began withholding gas purchase prices from the public.
Gazprom was forced to halt supplies to Moldova in January 2025 after Ukraine banned transit through its territory and Chisinau refused to settle its fuel debt. The debt is estimated at $709 million according to the accounting records of the Russian-Moldovan joint venture Moldovagaz, and at approximately $500 million according to Moldova's Court of Auditors.
The Moldovan opposition blames the pro-Western government for the crisis. Critics argue that the republic is currently purchasing the same Russian gas on European exchanges through numerous intermediaries, making it significantly more expensive.
Furthermore, the country's gas transmission system was transferred to the management of Romanian company Vestmoldtransgaz, a move that resulted in higher gas transportation tariffs.

‘If we can’t fly, no one can’: Iran threatens neighbors over US aviation sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:46:09 UTC
22:46:09 KST

U.S. sanctions targeting Iran’s aviation sector expanded further across Iraq on Friday, as more airports restricted Iranian carriers and an Iranian passenger plane was reportedly forced to return home empty.
An Iraqi television channel aligned with Iran’s regional axis published footage of a Meraj Air aircraft and said authorities at Najaf International Airport prevented passengers from boarding, forcing the plane to return to Mashhad without them. Najaf airport separately suspended all flights to and from Iran from early Friday until further notice.
Two sources told Reuters that airports in Erbil and Sulaymaniyah, in Iraq’s Kurdish region, also suspended flights by Iranian airlines beginning Friday. Baghdad had already stopped accepting Iranian flights earlier in the week after Washington threatened sanctions against airports servicing Iranian carriers. The United Arab Emirates has also suspended all flights operated by Iranian airlines until further notice, while Iranian flights to Oman, Georgia and Azerbaijan have also been disrupted.
The pressure stems from a major U.S. sanctions package announced on Sept. 8. The Treasury Department sanctioned 36 targets linked to Iran’s aviation sector, including 27 Iranian airlines, accusing the network of helping the regime transport weapons, personnel and illicit cargo. Washington has since made clear that the restrictions extend beyond the Iranian airlines themselves to foreign companies that continue providing them with services.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said foreign companies risk secondary sanctions if they provide Iranian carriers with fuel or landing services or sell tickets for their flights. “You cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” he told CNBC.
‘Flights are either free for everyone, or for no one’
Iranian officials have responded with increasingly explicit warnings to neighboring countries that enforce the U.S. measures.
“Aligning with the United States in implementing hostile policies will remain in the memory of the Iranian people,” senior Iranian official Mohammad Mokhber warned in a post on X. “Our strategy on this issue is clear: Flights in the region are either free for everyone, or for no one.”
“If Iran does not have the possibility of flying and receiving airport services, no country in the region will have this possibility either,” Mokhber added.
His remarks followed a similar warning from Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, who said this week that if neighboring countries cooperated with the United States to stop Iranian flights, “their airports will not be able to operate.”
Rezaei said Iran did not seek to expand the regional war and preferred peaceful solutions, but would not accept what he described as U.S. coercion. He blamed Washington for disruptions to regional transport routes and said Tehran had already warned neighboring states against cooperating with such measures.
Iraqi lawmaker Faleh al-Khazali, meanwhile, accused Baghdad of accepting economic damage by implementing the U.S. restrictions. “We hold the Iraqi government responsible for the financial losses incurred by the country as a result of implementing U.S. Treasury Department decisions against Iranian aviation,” he said.
The widening restrictions are beginning to shrink Iran’s international aviation network. Washington says its goal is to prevent Iranian commercial airlines from being used to move weapons and personnel and to pressure foreign airports and companies into severing ties with sanctioned carriers. China and Russia, however, have not joined the campaign, leaving Tehran with some international routes even as access to airports across the region contracts.

Pakistan locks down Islamabad as Imran Khan’s party vows to march on capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:44:55 UTC
22:44:55 KST

Leaders from Imran Khan’s party have vowed to go ahead with a nationwide demonstration in Pakistan to demand the former prime minister’s release, even as the government deployed tens of thousands of police to Islamabad, barricaded highways and issued arrest warrants to try to stop the march.
The state has taken extreme measures to prevent Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party from proceeding with the march. It was announced after mounting concerns of the treatment of Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges.
On Friday, PTI leaders said they would postpone the start of the march until 4 October, a week after the original 27 September date, saying they hoped the delay would put further strain on the government.
Analysts said the protest could present a major challenge to the military-backed government, which is widely regarded as weak, illegitimate and unpopular, while Khan remains a popular rallying figure. The ruling coalition is led by the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, but the army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, is widely seen as the country’s de facto leader.
This week, dozens of PTI leaders and ministers have been detained or made subject of arrest warrants, while Khan’s three sisters were arrested on Monday and remain in jail, charged with posing a grave threat to security.
Among those facing arrest is Sohail Afridi, the chief minister of Khan’s home province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, PTI’s stronghold, from where thousands of supporters are expected to join the march to the capital.
Afridi said the PTI would carry out the march unless the government made significant concessions over Khan’s treatment and conditions in jail, including a fair hearing for Khan’s cases.
“The government is panicking – that’s why they have put Islamabad under siege, that’s why they are abducting our ministers,” he said. “But Imran Khan is the most popular leader of the country and people will come out for him. I am certain they won’t be able to stop the public power of the masses when they come out on streets and take to Islamabad.”
Afridi acknowledged that the scale of the security deployment had led many to fear there could be a violent confrontation to prevent Khan’s supporters from entering the capital, as had been seen in previous demonstrations.
The government has already deployed tens of thousands of security officials to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and shut down the main highway connecting the provincial capital, Peshawar, to Islamabad.
“I know they can go to any extent to stop us by brute force, we have no doubt about it,” Afridi said. “But if we have a large number of people, they can’t open fire at us. Our plan is to bring so many people that they surrender.”
Faisal Karim Kundi, a central government appointee as governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, defended the security measures being taken against PTI as precautionary and accused the party of trying to create “instability and violence”. “The state can’t allow any violent group to march on Islamabad,” Kundi said.
Public frustration has mounted in Islamabad as the government’s measures to stop Khan’s party supporters having any way to enter the capital has led to the city resembling a high-security fortress.
More than 1,000 shipping containers, many fortified with spikes, have blockaded roads and sandbags were placed on bridges, while a key highway into the capital was closed. Public gatherings have been banned in Islamabad and 22,000 police and other security personnel have been deployed across the capital.
The government’s shutdown has fuelled anger and frustration in the capital, with many businesses unable to get supplies. Shahid, 76, a retired businessman, said: “The entire city is suffering. The government has shut down the whole city and we, as citizens, are helpless. I have never seen such a situation. Joblessness, inflation and insecurity has made our lives hell but does the government care? No.”
Despite the considerable efforts by the government and the military to crush Khan’s party and remove the former prime minister from the public consciousness – with media organisations instructed to not even refer to him by name – Khan is still viewed by many as the political alternative to the current regime.
The PTI alleges Khan is being held in solitary confinement and has been denied adequate medical treatment and any contact with his family or his lawyers for months.
Khan denies all the charges against him and alleges he is being imprisoned due to the political threat he poses to the government and the military. All but one of the court rulings against Khan have been overturned.
Analysts say the government and its military backers fear the PTI protest could escalate into a movement that could topple their administration, similar to protests seen in nearby Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.
“They have an eye on what has happened in south Asia over the last five years, where country after country has seen huge protests snowballing suddenly out of nowhere and sweeping away a government,” said Niaz Murtaza, a Pakistani political columnist.
“Given the breadth of grievances in Pakistan at the moment, the performance of the government has been so poor on the economy and security, while the repression is so high, that they are very nervous that the whole situation could combust very quickly.”

Euthanasia expert: Belgium stands alone in its approach to end-of-life care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:44:32 UTC
22:44:32 KST

Belgium is an international outlier when it comes to end-of-life care, according to euthanasia expert Wim Distelmans. His comments to VRT follow the death by euthanasia of French actor Arnaud Denis in Namur this week.
According to Distelmans, Belgium stands out not only because of its euthanasia law but its laws on palliative care and patient rights.
“We are the only country in the world to have these three laws,” he told Radio 1. As a result, he believes Belgium is an ethical leader when it comes to euthanasia, pain management and end-of-life care.
Denis’s death by euthanasia at the age of 43 clearly illustrates the difference between Belgium and France, he says. A bill on medically assisted suicide was passed in Frane this summer, but that is not the same as euthanasia.
In assisted suicide, a doctor provides a lethal substance that the patient must take themselves. In euthanasia, the doctor administers the substance. The conditions in France are also much stricter.
The fact that Belgium has a more liberal euthanasia law does not mean that patients have easy access to euthanasia. Foreign patients, too, must meet all the conditions set out in Belgian law.
For instance, a doctor-patient relationship must be established with the doctor who is prepared to carry out the euthanasia, and a second medical opinion is required in every case. Where a person is terminally ill, a second doctor must give their opinion. In the case of a patient who is not terminally ill, as in the case of Denis, opinions from two additional doctors are required.
This means patients often have to travel to Belgium several times before a decision can be made.
A total of 110 French citizens underwent euthanasia in Belgium last year. Distelmans is reluctant to describe this as genuine “euthanasia tourism”. People who request euthanasia are often seriously ill and no longer able to travel long distances. “It is gradually increasing, but not to any great extent,” he says.
The group consists of patients with serious conditions such as ALS, advanced multiple sclerosis or cancer. These cause severe suffering without the patient necessarily being in a terminal phase.
Euthanasia for foreign nationals on psychological grounds is extremely rare. The reason is mainly practical. It must first be established that all treatment options have been exhausted, and that is particularly difficult to organise for someone who does not live in Belgium.
Distelmans argues that Belgium also has a well-developed system of palliative care, which is, moreover, enshrined in law. He singles out Flanders in particular as performing exceptionally well in this regard.
Although the end of life does not always unfold as people would wish, he believes Belgium remains one of the best places in which to spend the final stage of life. “If you compare this with other countries, it really is better to be in Belgium in that respect,” he says.
Arnaud Denis had an implant placed to treat an abdominal hernia at a clinic in Paris in 2023. Following numerous side effects, including an infection, the implant was removed in 2024 in the US. His condition continued to deteriorate and he was diagnosed with severe myalgic encephalomyelitis, a neurological and immune disease.
“I am done with medical abuse,” he wrote in a final message published on Facebook on Tuesday. He explained that he saw euthanasia as “a deliverance” after “three interminable years” of “degrading” suffering.

Lebanon’s silenced voice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:43:59 UTC
22:43:59 KST

Lebanon’s silenced voice
Diplomacy in Lebanon is growing quieter in the face of relentless Israeli aggression
BEIRUT—On September 23, President Masoud Pezeshkian seized the 81st session of the UN General Assembly not as a ceremonial platform, but as a political battlefield, directly confronting the narrative presented by Washington and Israel.
Whatever one’s political position toward Iran, the significance of the scene was unmistakable: Tehran understood that international diplomacy is also a battle over narrative, visibility and political legitimacy.
Iran did not merely submit a diplomatic complaint. It placed symbols, victims and accusations before the international audience and demanded that they be seen.
That raises a far more uncomfortable question for us as Lebanese, especially the Southerners: where is Beirut’s voice?
At a time when Israeli aggression goes unabated in Lebanon, with airspace violations, bombardment, demolitions, troop movements and repeated breaches of Lebanon’s sovereignty documented by the United Nations, the most striking feature of Lebanon’s international presence is not the absence of evidence—it is the weakness of the official voice defending that evidence.
This is where the silence of the Lebanese government, and particularly the performance expected from its Foreign Ministry, becomes a political question rather than a matter of diplomatic style.
Diplomacy is not merely the production of carefully worded statements, nor is the foreign minister’s role limited to attending meetings, exchanging courtesies and repeating familiar formulations.
When a country’s sovereignty is being violated, diplomacy is supposed to turn facts into political pressure, violations into international accountability, and national grievances into an issue that the world cannot conveniently ignore.
Lebanon already possesses the language of international law. United Nations records themselves document continuing Israeli violations of Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity.
So what exactly prevents Beirut from turning this documented reality into a sustained diplomatic campaign?
The problem is not a shortage of diplomatic vocabulary. Lebanon knows how to say “condemnation,” “sovereignty,” “territorial integrity,” “international law” and “Resolution 1701.”
The problem is whether these words are being deployed as instruments of political confrontation or merely recited as diplomatic formalities.
A state under attack cannot afford to behave as though its principal concern is avoiding discomfort in international corridors.
It cannot allow the aggressor’s narrative to circulate freely while its own narrative remains buried in technical statements and procedural correspondence. It cannot surrender the visual, political and moral dimensions of its national tragedy to the language of bureaucracy.
The contrast becomes particularly sharp at the United Nations, where political symbolism matters. The international arena is not simply a place where governments read prepared texts. It is also a battlefield of narratives, legitimacy and public memory. A country that has villages under bombardment, displaced civilians, destroyed infrastructure and repeated violations of its territory possesses material with which to confront the international community directly and relentlessly.
Lebanon should therefore be asking uncomfortable questions:
— Where is the sustained diplomatic campaign documenting every violation?
— Where are the maps, images, testimonies and legal files being placed before international audiences?
— Where is the systematic effort to force governments, media organizations and international institutions to confront the consequences of violations against Lebanese territory?
— Where is the political language that names the problem clearly rather than allowing it to disappear beneath the vocabulary of “tensions” and “escalation”?
The United Nations itself has gone further than diplomatic timidity would suggest. The Secretary-General has explicitly called on Israel to withdraw its forces from Lebanese territory and urged all parties to respect Lebanon’s sovereignty and Resolution 1701.
UN reporting has likewise described the continued Israeli military activities south of the Blue Line as obstructing the extension of Lebanese state authority and the return of residents to their homes.
This raises an uncomfortable contradiction for Beirut: international institutions are documenting violations of Lebanese sovereignty, yet the Lebanese political discourse often appears trapped in the vocabulary of caution.
Caution has its place in diplomacy. Silence does not. Nor is firmness synonymous with abandoning diplomacy.
On the contrary, effective diplomacy is often most powerful when it is precise, documented and relentless.
Lebanon does not need theatrical rhetoric. It needs a coherent diplomatic strategy that treats every violation as evidence, every victim as a human story, every destroyed village as a political fact and every breach of sovereignty as an issue requiring international action.
The Foreign Ministry, above all, should be one of the institutions translating Lebanon’s suffering into international political consequences.
If the ministry merely records violations without turning them into sustained pressure, then diplomacy becomes an archive rather than an instrument of sovereignty.
Lebanon’s problem, therefore, is not that it lacks a voice. It is that its official voice is too often quieter than the evidence before it.
A country whose territory is being violated cannot afford diplomatic silence. A government that claims to defend sovereignty must demonstrate that sovereignty beyond speeches—through documentation, international mobilization, legal action and relentless political advocacy.
The question facing Lebanon is no longer whether the world has been given enough evidence. The question is whether Beirut is willing to make the world hear it!
