EXPLAINER- How panda diplomacy became part of US-China ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:23:50 UTC
22:23:50 KST

- Chinese President Xi Jinping says 2 pandas will arrive in Atlanta ‘in a few days,’ continuing a diplomatic tradition closely associated with Nixon’s 1972 China visit
- Once goodwill gifts, pandas now travel under conservation agreements that support research, breeding and habitat protection
-  Atlanta’s incoming pair will bring US giant panda population to 6, as renewed loans offer a sign of cooperation amid wider tensions
Two giant pandas heading from China to Atlanta will join a diplomatic tradition that has linked American zoos and Chinese leaders for more than eight decades.
“In a few days, two pandas – Ping Ping and Fu Shuang – will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people,” Chinese President Xi Jinping announced Thursday before talks with US President Donald Trump at the White House.
"The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans," he added, giving a familiar symbol of cooperation a place alongside much-anticipated discussions of trade, geopolitics and technology competition.
The pandas’ destination was already known. Zoo Atlanta announced the agreement in April, identifying Ping Ping as a male and Fu Shuang as a female, both born at China’s Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.
Xi’s remarks supplied the arrival timeframe.
But how did these furry, bamboo-eating bears become symbols of US-China diplomacy? 
How it started
China’s use of pandas as diplomatic gifts predates the establishment of the People’s Republic in 1949.
Some accounts trace panda diplomacy back to the seventh century, when Empress Wu Zetian reportedly sent pandas to Japan during the Tang dynasty.
The practice reemerged in the 20th century.
In 1941, two young pandas, Pan-dee and Pan-dah, arrived at New York’s Bronx Zoo as gifts from Madame Chiang Kai-shek, China’s first lady, thanking Americans for aid to China during its war with Japan, according to the Wildlife Conservation Society’s archives.
The animals were initially thought to be a breeding pair, but both turned out to be female.
In the following decades, the People’s Republic sent pandas to friendly countries, including the Soviet Union and North Korea.
The animals offered China an unusual diplomatic advantage in that wild giant pandas live only in China, making access to them a distinctive gesture of goodwill.
Their appeal also extended beyond government officials. A panda could draw crowds to a zoo and generate public interest in a country that many visitors knew little about. 
The 1972 breakthrough
The best-known episode in US-China panda diplomacy followed President Richard Nixon’s visit to China in February 1972.
The visit helped end more than two decades of estrangement between Washington and Beijing, although formal diplomatic relations were not established until 1979.
During the visit, Nixon’s wife, first lady Pat, mentioned that she liked pandas after seeing them at a Beijing zoo.
Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai responded by offering two pandas to the American people.
Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing arrived at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in Washington and were an instant sensation. More than 20,000 people came on the first day, and the following Sunday about 75,000 visitors formed a line a quarter-mile long.
The US reciprocated with a pair of musk oxen, Milton and Matilda.
The musk oxen had a rougher start. Time magazine reported they suffered "culture shock," with runny noses and hair loss, though they eventually recovered. 
From gifts to conservation loans
China moved away from giving pandas outright in the 1980s, turning instead to loans. Over time, long-term conservation and research agreements became the basis for overseas placements.
Such arrangements commonly run for about 10 years and can involve annual payments of around $1 million per pair. Under modern loan agreements, the pandas and their offspring remain Chinese property.
The shift to loans gave panda diplomacy a stronger conservation focus, with zoos contributing funding and expertise to breeding, research and habitat protection.
The US Fish and Wildlife Service listed the species as endangered in 1984 and adopted a conservation-focused panda permit policy in 1998, requiring all panda imports to directly benefit the conservation of pandas in the wild rather than serving short-term commercial exhibition.
The arrangement has been productive. US zoos have successfully raised 17 giant panda cubs – six in San Diego, four in Washington and seven in Atlanta – according to Chinese state media.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature reclassified giant pandas from endangered to vulnerable in 2016, citing a 17% population increase over the decade to 2014, when a nationwide census counted 1,864 in the wild in China, according to the World Wildlife Fund. 
What do panda movements tell us?
Panda arrivals and departures often attract attention far beyond the zoos involved.
As US-China relations deteriorated in recent years, the departure of pandas from American zoos became a particularly visible symbol of the tensions.
In November 2023, the Smithsonian’s National Zoo returned its three pandas to China as their loan agreement expired, leaving Zoo Atlanta as the only US zoo housing giant pandas.
Later that month, after meeting then-President Joe Biden in California, Xi said China was ready to continue panda conservation cooperation with the US – a gesture of goodwill amid efforts to stabilize relations.
A new pair arrived in San Diego in June 2024, before Atlanta’s four pandas departed that October. Another pair arrived in Washington later the same month.
Four giant pandas are currently in the US. Atlanta’s incoming pair would bring the total to six, compared with a historical peak of 15 reported by CNN. 
Atlanta’s next chapter
Zoo Atlanta’s original panda partnership began in 1999 and lasted 25 years. Its pandas produced seven cubs during that period.
The return of its four remaining bears in October 2024 closed that chapter, but the new agreement announced in April opened another.
For Atlanta, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will restore a major attraction and renew a research partnership. For Beijing, their arrival offers another opportunity to present cooperation with the US through animals that have long drawn American crowds.
Their arrival will not settle disputes over tariffs or AI regulation. But the two bears will offer an adorable reminder that Washington and Beijing still have room for friendship.

The women who should enter Israel’s sukkah this Sukkot - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:23:47 UTC
22:23:47 KST

Seven women will enter the sukkah, and at the end it will remain open — inviting us to build together a world of greater opportunity and possibility for all.
The following women will enter the sukkah:
Who are the women ushpizin?
On the first evening, we will welcome the woman who built the sukkah.
In 1971, Naomi Shemer wrote the song “Shlomit Builds a Sukkah,” dedicating it to the daughter of her neighbors. These were days when women could dream not only of building a sukkah of peace, but also of leading the nation — as Golda Meir was doing at the time as Israel’s prime minister.
But since then, there has been no other Golda, and decisions about our national sukkah are still made primarily by men. In fact, if current polls are borne out, the next Knesset may have only 31 women — approximately 26% of its members.
Five decades after the song was written, Shlomit knows: the time has come for everyone to truly have a place.
On the second evening, we will welcome the woman who was left one step behind.
She did not encounter a glass ceiling; she encountered a broken rung.
She is good at her job and highly regarded, but when she went on maternity leave, someone else was promoted to the first management position. Later, because he already had the experience, he was preferred for the next promotion as well.
There is a name for this phenomenon: “the broken rung.”
A 2025 Women in the Workplace study found that for every 100 men promoted into their first management position, only 93 women were promoted.
A seemingly small gap at the bottom of the ladder becomes far more significant the higher we climb.
On the third evening, we will welcome the woman who did not put herself forward.
When the position was advertised, she thought she did not meet all the requirements. When she was encouraged to apply, she said she wasn't sure it was for her. When the list was drawn up, she waited for someone to think of her — but no one did.
We like to say that the door is open to women. Sometimes, that is even true.
But an open door is not enough if, for years, boys have been taught to walk toward it with confidence, while girls are still waiting to be invited.
You are invited. Come in.
On the fourth evening, we will welcome the woman who did everything right.
She studied, worked, excelled, raised a family, picked up the children from kindergarten and answered emails at night.
And yet, there are still very few women around her.
According to the Israel Innovation Authority’s 2025 report, women make up only 17.6% of senior management positions in privately held high-tech companies and just 10.6% of start-up CEOs in Israel.
And the gap is not only in management; it exists in pay as well. Men earn approximately 44% more than women.
She does not understand why this is still happening.
On the fifth evening, we will welcome the woman who made it.
She is a manager, an entrepreneur, an elected public official, a researcher and a commander.
But she is alone.
Women make up 64% of the civil service, yet at the very highest levels, only 9% are women.
In hi-tech, too, women make up more than 30% of entry-level and middle-management positions, but only 17.6% of senior management.
She is waiting for more women to join her.
On the sixth evening, we will welcome a girl.
She does not yet know what she wants to be when she grows up.
When she enters the sukkah, she will look around and see women of different backgrounds, different ages and different walks of life. They will smile at her and introduce her to the other girls.
She will see many chairs and many opportunities, and she will know that everything is open to her.
On the seventh evening, no one will be invited — but the sukkah will be full.
Sarah and Miriam will be there, as will Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah, and Esther.
Henrietta Szold, Naomi Shemer, Golda Meir, and Ada Yonath will be chatting together.
Because this is the real story of the ushpizin.
It is not about who receives a ceremonial invitation to enter for one evening, but about what kind of sukkah we build in the first place.
The first step in correcting injustices that have persisted for years is to recognize the challenges, bring them into the public conversation, and promote clear policies to change the situation.
The second step is to create broad partnerships — between women and men, between organizations, and between different sectors of society.
Only when all women's voices are heard — and answered — can we ensure a truly equal society.
The writer is chair of Emunah — the Religious Zionist Women’s Movement.

The US Senate on Thursday narrowly rejected a Democratic-led resolution aiming to stop the Iran war until hostilities are authorized by Congress.
The Senate voted 50 to 49 to reject the resolution, which had passed the House of Representatives in July. The vote was largely along party lines, with most of US President Donald Trump's Republicans rejecting the measure and almost every Democrat voting for it.
Seven Republicans back Iran war powers resolution, widening GOP split with Trump
Earlier in September, in the House of Representatives, seven Republicans joined Democrats in backing a similar resolution directing Trump to remove American forces from hostilities against Iran unless Congress formally authorizes the war.
The resolution invokes Section 5(c) of the 1973 War Powers Resolution and directs Trump to remove US forces from hostilities with Iran unless Congress declares war or specifically authorizes the use of military force. It preserves Trump's ability to maintain the forces necessary to defend the US or an ally against an imminent attack, subject to the law's reporting requirements.
The legal force of such congressional efforts has long been disputed, and previous resolutions have not changed the course of US military operations. The Senate would also have to act for Congress to present a unified challenge to the administration.

Lithuania and Poland are jointly developing an international population evacuation plan
Kyiv • UNN
Lithuania and Poland are assessing the logistics and infrastructure for evacuating residents of the Baltic countries. Particular attention will be paid to the Suwałki Corridor.
Lithuania, together with Poland, is developing an international evacuation plan that will be used if it becomes necessary to evacuate some residents of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia across the border. Delfi reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the director of the National Crisis Management Center (NCMC), Vilmantas Vitkauskas, procedures, logistical and infrastructure capabilities are currently being assessed jointly with Polish colleagues, and the plan itself is to be prepared after coordination between the two countries.
"We also have an international aspect of evacuation: what will happen if it becomes necessary to evacuate across the border a certain number of residents of Lithuania as well as neighboring Latvia and Estonia. In such situations, when there is a threat of war that is gradually approaching in the exercise scenario, the border regime usually changes. Border control is introduced to ensure mobilization and prevent people holding certain important positions from leaving the country, so that they remain here and perform their duties," Vitkauskas said.
According to him, in such a case, a large flow of evacuees could accumulate near the border, so it is necessary to assess in advance, together with Polish colleagues, how to manage such a situation.
"We will examine all procedural shortcomings, document them, and then a plan will emerge, to be prepared jointly by agreement between the two countries," the head of the NCMC noted.
He emphasized that, while preparing the plan, it is also necessary to assess traffic flows, transport connections, and the condition of the infrastructure. As Vitkauskas noted, it is important to anticipate how the flows of people leaving and arriving will be organized, as well as to assess the need to reinforce bridges and other infrastructure requirements.
Vitkauskas pointed out that the Suwałki Corridor is of particular importance in this process, as it is important both from a military and a logistical perspective.
"Therefore, the participation of Polish colleagues is of great importance, and we are extremely grateful to them for joining us and showing great interest… Poland's participation takes us to another level," he added.

====================================================================================================

Trump-Xi Summit: Heavy of Vibes, Light on Substance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:22:00 UTC
22:22:00 KST

When Chinese President Xi Jinping held a summit with U.S. President Donald Trump on September 24, Trump made sure Xi knew how he felt. The U.S. leader expressed no fewer than three times in the first minute of their joint remarks that it was his “honor” – or even “great honor” – to host Xi.
The “honor,” apparently was all Trump’s. Xi made no similar expression of feeling “honored” to be hosted by the U.S. president, simply saying he was “glad” to be in Washington.
That set the tone for a meeting that was long on symbolism but short on substance. Trump was eager to impress; Xi was all business.
Trump was reportedly keen to match the lavish hosting he received during his visit to Beijing in May. As Xi pointed out at the state dinner in Washington, it’s “unprecedented” for the Chinese and American presidents to exchange state visits in such a short period of time.
“Today, President Trump and I had sincere and in-depth exchanges and reached common understanding on many issues,” Xi said. “This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, and provided new strategic guidance for China-U.S. relations.”
“The constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability” is Beijing’s new mantra for the relationship – and the first that China has successfully gotten Washington to buy into. The basic gist is that China and the United States will continue to compete – something Beijing has finally admitted is happening, after years of studiously denying any rivalry – but keep their competition “within bounds.”
Other than agreeing, in principle, not to let their competition spill into conflict, though, it wasn’t immediately clear what “common understandings” were reached at the summit. No major breakthroughs were expected, and that turned out to be accurate.
The biggest deliverable was an agreement – actually reached before the summit, during China-U.S. economic talks on September 20 – to extend their trade truce through January 10. The original deal, reached at the first Trump-Xi summit in Busan, South Korea in October 2025, saw the U.S. lower tariffs on Chinese goods, while Chinese agreed to pause enforcement of export controls on certain critical minerals. The deal was only good for a year initially, and was set to expire in November.
Many experts had predicted an extension was in the offing – if that hadn’t been the case, it was suggested that there wouldn’t have been much reason for Trump and Xi to meet at all. But the short length of the extension – just two extra months – was a bit of a surprise. Bessent mentioned that China needed to make good on its promises, suggesting that the deal could be extended again if Washington is satisfied with what it sees. Or it could be eventually scrapped.
China, meanwhile, hasn’t confirmed even that limited extension. The official readout from the Chinese Foreign Ministry said a “new joint arrangement” had been reached in economic and trade discussions, but did not elaborate on what that deal was.
To recap: the biggest practical impact of the Trump-Xi summit was a possible agreement to slightly extend a pause – not a cancellation – on the worst of the trade war. Oh, and two more pandas for the Atlanta Zoo. That about sums up the fruits of the fragile truce currently in place between China and the United States.
If the outcome on trade was a mixed bag, other areas were even murkier. There was much focus on artificial intelligence (AI) prior to the summit, especially as U.S. AI companies themselves have begun raising safety concerns. There had been suggestions that the U.S. and China could unveil an “AI safety mechanism” that would see both sides notify the other of concerning incidents.
Trump, however, has consistently rejected any calls for additional oversight of AI – precisely because he wants the United States to go full speed ahead in the race against China. In a Truth Social post, prior to the summit, Trump stated that AI (which he has started referring to as “super intelligence”) “will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also.”
Xi, however, was more cautious on AI, referencing the need to “jointly prevented the misuse and abuse of AI,” and emphasizing that “AI must be kept under human control.” But, like Trump, his primary concern was the AI race and preventing the U.S. from “guarding against” China’s AI development through export controls and other restrictions. As James Wang noted in a recent analysis for The Diplomat, Beijing is well aware of Washington’s tendency to frame restrictions on Chinese technology as safety measures.
As expected, Xi also brought up Taiwan. He explicitly asked “the U.S. side” to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence.’” Much reporting ahead of the summit held that Xi was hoping to get Trump to explicitly say that the U.S. “opposes Taiwan independence.” The usual phrasing is that the U.S. “does not support Taiwan independence.” For China, an outright expression of opposition would be a key win – especially because Beijing purposefully conflates Taiwan’s ruling party and president with “Taiwan independence forces.”
Beijing is also hoping to extend the current “pause” on U.S. arms sales to Taiwan to a de facto moratorium – something it’s tried to do in the past, but without success. Whenever a U.S. administration signals openness to scaling back arms sales to please China, Beijing ups the pressure.
Rupert Hammond-Chambers, president of the U.S.-Taiwan Business Council, called the current period the “fourth Taiwan arms sale freeze,” following “two under former President George W. Bush from 2005-2007 and 2007-2008, and one under former President Barack Obama from 2011-2015.” In all these cases, Hammond-Chambers argued, the “freeze” did nothing more than embolden Beijing.
“The Trump Administration has let the fox in the henhouse. Telegraphing sensitivity to the Chinese position on Taiwan this past spring, Trump has empowered China to affect his decisions [on arms sales],” Hammond-Chambers wrote in a media release.
There’s been no movement on the arms sale, which has been on hold since before the May summit.
As with the Trump-Xi summit in May, this time there was another brief reference to an exchange of views “on major international and regional issues including the situation in the Middle East, the Ukraine crisis and the Korean Peninsula.” There was, however, no suggestion of any agreement or alignment on those issues – unlike after the May summit, when Trump got Xi to say that China opposes Iran’s development of nuclear weapons and supports “the free flow of energy” through the Strait of Hormuz.
If the actual substance showed little sign of convergence, you’d never know it from the optics. Trump lauded his “truly great friendship” with Xi and showed special deference to the Chinese president, including personally meeting him on the tarmac upon Xi’s arrival in the United States. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump also arranged an opulent welcome ceremony, featuring musical performances and drills by 479 military personnel and ending with a flyover by a B-2 stealth bomber and four F-22 fighter jets.
After the summit proper came the state dinner attended by a who’s who list of top American businesspeople: OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Google’s Sundar Pichai, and Elon Musk of Tesla, X, and SpaceX.
Notably, though, Xi did not bring his own entourage of business leaders – a marked contrast with Trump’s visit to Beijing, when he included top CEOs in his delegation. Speaking to the New York Times, Emily Kilcrease of the Center for a New American Security called the absence of Chinese business leaders “a rather depressing marks of how bad the relationship has gotten.”
Overall, the summit left the impression of a stable, positive relationship, but there was little to back up that sentiment. Trump claimed that he and Xi had “made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries” – including the “unbelievably successful” Board of Trade, which hasn’t actually even launched yet – but as always, there were no specifics.
Xi’s positive comments, meanwhile, were mostly forward-looking. “[T]hrough candid, in-depth, and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” he said – an aspiration, not an accomplishment.
Xi also emphasize the parallels between the “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation” and Trump’s “make America great again” slogan, which he argued can “be mutually reinforcing.” Xi continued: “Our competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds. It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses.”
It was a somewhat odd way of trying to cast competition as “win-win.” I don’t know what races Xi has been watching, but generally those have a winner as well – and multiple losers.
Given the shallow nature of the current era of good feelings in China-U.S. relations, it’s telling that the trade truce was extended only until January 10 – just long enough to keep relations steady through the APEC summit (to be held in Shenzhen, China from November 18-19) and the G20 summit (Miami, the United States, December 14-15). Assuming Trump and Xi attend both events, that could set up two additional summits, for a total of four in 2026 alone.
After that, all bets are off.

‘Sunlight salary’: Exactly how much solar panels knock off your energy bills – even under grey skies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:20:02 UTC
22:20:02 KST

Despite the money they can save households on electricity bills, just one in 10 European roofs has solar panels.
Britain may be famous for grey skies and rainy days, but its sunshine could still help residents shave more than €1,000 a year off household electricity bills.
An analysis of more than 15 million UK homes by solar software company GreenSketch estimates that an optimised rooftop solar and battery system could save the average household around €1,100 a year – what the company calls a ‘sunlight salary’.
Even in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, the average savings topped €930.
The findings show that household savings depend on more than sunshine alone. Electricity prices, the angle of your roof, when you use power, battery storage and payments for electricity sent back to the grid are all important factors.
Grey skies aren’t a barrier to solar power
Researchers used satellite imagery to model individual homes, accounting for the slope of rooftops as well as their orientation, local electricity use and hourly solar generation.
Southwest Wales had the highest average estimated savings at around €1,160 a year, followed by southeast England at about €1,150. In Northern Ireland, the best returns were found in the east rather than the south, which GreenSketch says shows that local weather and geography can affect solar generation as much as geolocation.
Those figures challenge the idea that solar panels only make financial sense in sunnier places. Although they generate more electricity in direct sunlight, solar panels still produce power on overcast days – good news for Europe’s less sunny stretches.
Solar can also cover the cost of installment relatively quickly. The Energy Saving Trust – an independent UK energy advice organisation – estimates that a typical system can pay for itself in 10 to 12 years.
Europe has barely tapped its rooftop potential
The UK findings point to similar potential elsewhere around Europe.
If solar panels don’t need Mediterranean sunshine to cut electricity bills – especially when paired with batteries that let households store power generated during the day and use it later – they could make financial sense far beyond southern Europe.
A Joint Research Centre (JRC) study published earlier this year found that solar panels on rooftops could meet 40 per cent of the EU’s long-term electricity needs by 2050.
In Finland and Denmark, non-residential roofs alone could provide at least 95 per cent of the solar capacity targeted for 2030.
Still, just one in ten European rooftops has solar panels, according to the JRC, leaving enormous room for further expansion.

Obesity and overweight cost European economies billions of euros a year, industry says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:19:15 UTC
22:19:15 KST

Obesity and overweight are costing European economies billions of euros every year, with the burden equivalent to what some countries spend on housing or defence, according to a pharmaceutical industry’s report.
Beyond the health impact, obesity and high body mass index (BMI) pose a growing burden for European economies, costing billions of euros annually through direct and indirect costs, according to a new pharmaceutical industry report.
The total annual costs represent 0.7% to 1.4% of national GDP across Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Ireland, Greece, Romania and the United Kingdom, the countries analysed in the study conducted by the Office of Health Economics (OHE) for the pharmaceutical lobby EFPIA.
“Tackling obesity is vital for protecting citizens' health and wellbeing, safeguarding our European health systems and ensuring sustainable growth in Europe,” said Nathalie Moll, director general at the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries (EFPIA), which financed the report.
As of 2024, 26% of adults in Europe were living with obesity, defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or more, and an additional 30% were living with overweight, a situation that is expected to worsen. It is estimated that half of the world’s adult population will be living with overweight or obesity by 2035.
In Europe, the prevalence of overweight and obesity in adults has increased by 22%, while obesity alone has risen by more than 75% relative to 1990 levels.
How much money are countries spending?
Both obesity and overweight come at a high cost across Europe. Compared with other major areas of public spending, the report found that the economic burden of elevated BMI as a share of GDP is comparable to what some countries spend on housing and defence.
The estimated annual economic burden ranges from €2.5 billion in Romania to €55.2 billion in Germany. Total annual economic costs reach €43.2 billion in the UK, with Spain, Italy, and France each incurring around €20.0 billion.
As a percentage of GDP, costs attributable to elevated BMI range from 0.7% in Romania to 1.4% in Greece and the UK.
For Germany (1.3%), Spain (1.2%) and Ireland (1.1%), the share of their domestic economy attributable to elevated BMI exceeds the countries’ defence spending.
These translate into per capita costs ranging from €131 per Romanian resident to €662 per German resident.
A combination of direct and indirect costs
Obesity and overweight are linked to 278,000 deaths and the loss of 8 million years of healthy life across the eight countries analysed in the study alone.
Besides being a health problem in its own right, obesity is also a risk factor for non-communicable diseases, including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, fatty liver disease, cancers, neurological disorders, chronic respiratory diseases and digestive disorders.
Costs derived from these conditions — also known as “direct costs” — amounted to €100.4 billion, with Germany accounting for the largest share, at €30 billion.
However, the report found a substantial additional share of costs indirectly linked to these conditions, known as “indirect costs”. These include losses from absenteeism, economic inactivity, informal care and premature mortality.
What can be done?
The report's findings show that historical approaches to prevention and management "have not had the desired impact".
“An urgent shift in perception, prevention, diagnosis and treatment is required to improve outcomes, reduce the burden of costs on health services, boost economic productivity and societal resilience,” Moll said.
The report provides recommendations to address the health and economic challenges posed by obesity and elevated BMI, ranging from recognising obesity as a disease and not just a risk factor to improving access to prevention and treatment.

Erdogan: Mecca defence pact not aimed at Iran or Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:19:04 UTC
22:19:04 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has said the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia is not directed against Iran, Israel or any other country, stressing that the pact is intended to strengthen regional security, deterrence and stability.
Speaking in an interview with Newsweek magazine, Erdogan rejected suggestions that the agreement should be viewed as an alliance aimed at countering Iran or Israel independently of US security guarantees.
“It would not be accurate to view the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement as an alliance formed against Iran, Israel, or any third country. This agreement reflects our shared responsibility to build a more secure, peaceful, and prosperous future,” Erdogan said.
The Turkish president said Ankara has long advocated for regional countries to take greater responsibility for resolving issues affecting the region.
“We want to consolidate our security, bolster our deterrence, and reinforce lasting stability across our region,” he said.
Erdogan said the agreement is based on the right to self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries would be considered an attack on all parties.
He said the nature of any response would depend on the request and needs of the country targeted.
“This support may encompass intelligence, logistics, or ammunition, while more extensive military support could also come onto the agenda depending on the scale of the threat,” Erdogan said.
He added that relevant political and military mechanisms would determine how such measures would be implemented, cautioning against assuming that the agreement would automatically trigger Turkish military intervention in the event of an attack.
“Therefore, it would not be right to draft an automatic military scenario in advance for every possible incident in Iraq, Yemen, or elsewhere,” he said.
Türkiye can engage with all sides
Erdogan also highlighted Türkiye’s diplomatic role in regional and international conflicts, saying Ankara remains capable of maintaining dialogue with different sides.
“From the Russia-Ukraine war to tensions across the Middle East, Türkiye is a nation capable of engaging with all parties to conflicts and taking the initiative for peace,” he said.
Addressing relations with Israel, Erdoğan criticised what he described as an emerging narrative portraying Türkiye as a threat.
“A misguided narrative has recently been stoked in Israel that seeks to portray Türkiye as an emerging source of threat,” Erdoğan said.
“We assess this rhetoric to be tied to Israel's domestic political processes and the current election climate. We do not regard such discourse as a responsible approach that contributes to regional peace.”
Syria's stability
Erdogan also stressed the importance of stability and unity in Syria, saying developments there would have broader consequences for the region.
“Stability in Syria will contribute to the peace and development of our entire region, including Israel,” he said.
Erdogan said integrating all armed elements under a centralised state structure was essential to strengthening Syria's sovereignty, territorial integrity and social unity.
“We support this process advancing on the basis of equal citizenship, fostering an order in which all Syrian people—including the Kurds—feel safer, freer, and more prosperous,” he said.
“As Syria's unity grows stronger, so too will our region's security.”
Developments in Iran
Erdogan said Türkiye was also closely following developments in neighbouring Iran, including what he described as attempts by the PKK/PJAK terror group to exploit the situation in the country.
“We are also closely monitoring PKK/PJAK attempts to exploit conditions arising from developments in Iran. Iran's domestic issues must be resolved by the Iranian people themselves, free from external interference,” he said.
Erdogan stressed that Türkiye's approach to regional security was not based on ethnicity.
“Türkiye's benchmark is never ethnic identity; it is terrorism, violence, and threats targeting our national security,” he said.
“We believe that no community across our region should ever be permitted to serve as an instrument in the proxy wars of third countries.”

Israeli opposition party leader says state’s global standing at all-time low, warns of economic collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:18:21 UTC
22:18:21 KST

Lina Altawell
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Yisrael Beiteinu opposition party leader Avigdor Liberman said Friday that Israel’s global standing had reached an “unprecedented low,” warning of a “real economic collapse” because of European sanctions and their impact on trade.
Liberman made the remarks in a post through US social media company X, commenting on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the UN General Assembly in New York.
“Israel’s standing in the world has reached an unprecedented low,” Liberman said.
“For years, Israel benefited from the American veto at the UN Security Council. I believe that as long as (US President Donald) Trump remains president, the veto will continue to be available to us. Under the next president, whether Republican or Democrat, the reality could change,” he added.
Liberman also addressed Israel’s relations with the UK, saying Israel has been without an ambassador in London for a year, which he attributed to “intrigues in the Prime Minister’s Office.”
He warned of the economic repercussions of European sanctions, saying: “Sanctions on trade between Israel and the EU could bring about a genuine economic collapse.”
In September 2025, the European Commission proposed suspending some trade privileges granted to Israel under the EU-Israel Association Agreement, which would subject Israeli imports to tariffs instead of preferential treatment.
The commission said the proposal came over what it described as the Israeli government’s violation of provisions concerning respect for human rights. The proposal, however, still required approval from member states and did not receive the majority needed for adoption.
The EU has also imposed sanctions on extremist Israeli settlers and organizations linked to them over violations against Palestinians in the West Bank, including asset freezes and travel bans on listed individuals.
In May 2026, the EU added three individuals and four Israeli entities to its sanctions lists, while it said in September that measures taken in this context covered a total of 12 individuals and nine entities.
Commenting on Netanyahu’s UN General Assembly speech Thursday, Liberman said: “The man (Netanyahu), and along with him Israel, has become a pariah and a burden on the Western world.”
Netanyahu addressed the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday before a largely empty hall after delegations from several countries walked out in protest against Israel’s genocidal war in the Gaza Strip and continued violations in the West Bank, Lebanon, and Syria, as large demonstrations took place across the city.
Liberman called for a change in Israel’s leadership, saying it was necessary. “On Oct. 27, the leadership that is leading Israel toward a diplomatic, security, and economic catastrophe must be replaced.”
“The next government that we establish will restore Israel’s standing in the United States and around the world,” he added.
Liberman’s remarks came 33 days before Israeli elections scheduled for October amid sharp domestic political debate over Netanyahu government policies, with opposition figures criticizing his UN speech while ministers and members of the governing coalition praised it.
The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024 over accusations of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.
Since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed and around 175,000 injured, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

Supplement
The European Peace Facility (EPF) is an off-budget EU fund. The fund will be financed through contributions from EU member states.
The ultimate goal of the Facility is to enhance the EU's capacity to prevent conflicts, support peace, and strengthen international stability and security. The instrument is intended to contribute to this by enabling the EU to assist partner countries more effectively: either by supporting their peacekeeping operations or by helping strengthen the capacity of their armed forces to ensure peace and security on their own territory, as well as through broader military and defence measures in support of the objectives of the Common Foreign and Security Policy.

'Like Auschwitz': Nova families urge authorities to block Simchat Torah festivities at massacre site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:16:49 UTC
22:16:49 KST

Following objections from bereaved families, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund has asked Israel Police and the Fire and Rescue Authority to prevent Simchat Torah celebrations from being held at the site of the Nova music festival massacre in Re’im Forest.
“Celebrating and holding festivities at a place where a massacre took place is disrespectful, both to the sanctity of the site and to Judaism,” KKL-JNF Chairman Eyal Ostrovsky told ynet.
The memorial site for those murdered at the Nova festival has become a major destination for visitors, and for some bereaved families it has taken on a significance even greater than the cemetery. Last year, Simchat Torah celebrations were held there, with images of visitors dancing, setting up meals and camping at the site causing distress among relatives of those killed.
Dassi Aviad, whose son Aviad Halevi was murdered at Nova, said she wanted people to continue visiting the site for generations, but urged them to treat it with reverence.
“Every person who comes and stands in front of a photograph or a sign warms the heart. I hope this place will be full of visitors for generations,” she said. “But people need to understand that this ground is sacred, even if it has not been officially declared so, no less than a synagogue or other holy places.”
“People should walk here on tiptoe, thinking with every step about where they are walking and what may have happened right beneath their feet,” she added. “People can, should and must come on this day just as on any other, but they should walk around in respectful silence honoring those who were murdered with unimaginable cruelty, rather than turning the place into an overnight campsite with tents as though it were a campground on the Sea of Galilee.”
Omri Rahum, whose sister Nitzan Rahum was murdered at Nova while four months pregnant, said families were horrified by footage from last year’s holiday.
“We saw videos of people setting tables and holding meals. Seeing people dancing like that... so much filth was left behind that it had to be cleaned up afterward,” he said.
“Simchat Torah is the day our lives were turned upside down. Unfortunately, the police are hesitating and saying they have no solution. The bereaved families, as usual, are being abandoned. For us, this place is like a cemetery and Auschwitz.”
KKL-JNF Director General Ilan Shohat has asked Police Commissioner Dani Levy and Southern District Commander Haim Bublil to prevent organized gatherings and activities at the site.
“Any gathering at the site during this period could have exceptional public, safety and emotional consequences,” Shohat said.
He also asked police to help prevent overnight camping, the lighting of fires and barbecues, and to maintain public order.
Ostrovsky said the site’s importance lies in its national significance and that it should remain a place where Jews of every background can feel at home.
“Every Jew, secular or religious, should feel at home there,” he said. “Initiatives of this kind only damage the delicate fabric that this place represents in such an important way.”
“KKL-JNF will do everything in its power to prevent this, and I intend to speak with the heads of the security and rescue services so they can help us maintain public order and the sanctity of the site.”
Israel Police said it would operate during the holiday period “in cooperation and coordination with all relevant authorities, each according to its area of responsibility and based on the situational assessment, in order to maintain public safety, public order and the security of visitors.”
The Fire and Rescue Authority said that, aside from the annual Oct. 7 memorial ceremony, it had not received requests to approve any large-scale events at the Nova site in the near future.
Any requests that are submitted will be examined individually, the authority said, adding that patrols would be carried out in Re’im Forest and at the Nova site throughout the holiday.
The authority added that it “strongly opposes the holding of events without its approval and in violation of the law.”

Ukrainian EW System From Unwave Participated in Drone Dominance Tests in USA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:15:53 UTC
22:15:53 KST

Ukrainian electronic warfare (EW) manufacturer Unwave participated in trials as part of the Drone Dominance program at Fort Carson in Colorado, USA.
Following its participation, the company received a request from the U.S. side to continue supporting the program’s activities, Unwave told Militarnyi. Drone Dominance calls for the Pentagon to procure more than 200,000 drones by 2027.
The tests took place from August 24 to September 2, with the participation of 14 drone manufacturers and 3 electronic warfare system developers.
The main goal of the Ukrainian developers’ participation was to create conditions as close as possible to a real battlefield to test the drones’ resilience.
As part of the training, Unwave presented four of its own electronic warfare systems.
The first system presented was the Vikha tactical-operational complex, which operates in the 300 MHz–3.2 GHz band with a power output of over 100 W and provides a range of over 300 meters.
To protect personnel and positions from FPV drones and explosive payloads, Unwave demonstrated the Boombox system. This multi-channel portable electronic warfare system, weighing 11–25 kg, operates in the 0.4–1, 1.9–2.7, and 5.8 GHz bands, providing a protective coverage radius of 50 meters.
The company also presented the Shatro system, developed specifically for installation on vehicles and military equipment. It has a channel power of 50–100 watts and covers the 0.2–5.8 GHz frequency ranges.
The fourth model was Choven-2, which suppresses FPV drones within a radius of 70 meters and Mavic quadcopters from 50 meters.
It is worth noting that Unwave’s electronic warfare system was the only one capable of jamming a drone during the NATO Baltic Trust 26 exercises in Latvia.
The exercise marked the final stage of NATO’s program to test UAV countermeasure systems.
Thanks to its successful performance in countering drones, the Ukrainian system received a special commendation from the exercise organizers.

ISW connects drone crashes in Moldova and Romania, a Starlink fire in Poland, and a Berlin airport shutdown into one Russian pattern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:11:09 UTC
22:11:09 KST

Several recent incidents across Europe were conducted by Russia or are likely attributable to Russia, ISW assessed in its 24 September report, though authorities have not officially linked the Polish and German incidents to Moscow.
Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine has expanded into a parallel campaign of provocations against European defense and logistical infrastructure. The Kremlin is using drones, arson, and undersea cable sabotage to degrade Europe's will and ability to support Ukraine, while deliberately intensifying the frequency of airspace violations to erode the boundary between hybrid and kinetic war.
Drones over Moldova and Romania
Four Russian drones flew over Bukovyna and targeted an energy facility and border crossings with Moldova and Romania, Chernivtsi Oblast Military Administration head Ruslan Osypenko reported. Ukrainian forces shot down three. The fourth flew toward Suceava County in northeastern Romania.
A drone crashed in Cernița, Florești district, Moldova—preliminarily identified as a Russian Gerbera type, the first such device found in the country. It carried an onboard camera, hit a tree, and exploded, Moldovan police said. Romania's Defense Ministry reported a second aerial vehicle entered Romanian airspace for four minutes and crashed near Solca in the same border region; geolocated footage confirmed it was also a Gerbera, ISW noted. Poland evacuated the Hrubieszów and Dorohusk border crossings for 30 minutes, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said. Three countries were put on alert by a single night of Russian strikes.
"Intentional and accidental Russian drone incursions into NATO and Moldovan airspaces are likely part of the Kremlin's efforts to normalize airspace violations by intensifying their frequency," ISW assessed.
Sabotage in Poland and Germany
A fire engulfed the power system and backup generator at a Starlink ground station in Wola Krobowska, central Poland, on the evening of 23 September. Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski confirmed it was sabotage aimed at cutting internet access, including for Ukraine's military. Authorities have not identified who was responsible, but the act aligns with Russia's "new" doctrine of attacks, Gawkowski said. The station is now operating normally.
German authorities suspended operations at Berlin-Brandenburg airport for 45 minutes the same evening after staff reported a drone sighting, Die Zeit reported. Federal police could not confirm it. ISW assessed both incidents fit Russia's wider pattern of sabotage against European defense assets, though neither has been officially attributed to Russia.
Western intelligence warnings
A Lithuanian Defense Ministry source reported on 23 September that Russia could launch Gerbera drones from a shipping container in the Mediterranean against Spain, France, and Italy. Danish Defense Intelligence assessed on 24 September that Russia will intensify its hybrid war in coming months, including destructive cyber attacks and sabotage carrying a high risk of casualties, and that there is a low but growing risk of a limited Russian military attack on a NATO border state. It sees no indications of an outright invasion. The CIA reportedly warned Poland that Russia may sabotage underwater cables to disrupt its banking system, according to Newsweek Polska journalists.
NATO tracked and confronted Russian submersibles rehearsing deployment of a new cable-disabling weapon near Svalbard in spring 2026—no cables were damaged, but the operation demonstrated Moscow's intent, Reuters reported. Shadow fleet vessels likely served as drone-launch platforms for incursions into NATO airspace, ISW noted.
"The increasing frequency of such warnings suggests that Western intelligence agencies are picking up indicators that the Kremlin is looking to diversify its platforms and means for conducting attacks against NATO and European states and is considering conducting such attacks," ISW assessed.
ISW said it has not yet seen evidence that Russia has conducted the attacks the warnings describe.
Denmark's assessment—that a limited Russian military strike on a NATO border state could come in the coming months—suggests the boundary between hybrid provocations and military action is narrower than European policy has assumed. ISW's synthesis reframes what governments have treated as separate incidents into one campaign.

Iran, India have huge potential for cooperation in health and tourism: Ambassador
TEHRAN – New Delhi’s Ambassador to Tehran Vishwesh Negi has highlighted the significant potential for Iran-India cooperation in traditional and modern medicine, pharmaceuticals and tourism, as well as in strengthening cultural and people-to-people ties.
He made the remarks in a brief interview with the Tehran Times on the sidelines of a ceremony hosted by the Indian Embassy in Tehran on September 23 to mark National Ayurveda Day.
Today’s ceremony to mark Ayurveda Day, brought together a number of Iranian physicians who shared views on the ancient Indian medicine system alongside views on the ancient Iranian medicine system. It was a fruitful gesture for promoting cultural heritage and exchanging ideas. Tell us about your embassy’s collaboration and efforts to promote other aspects of Indian heritage in Iran and plans for mutual cooperation.
Well, there are a lot of things we want to do with Iran at this point in time. We really want to establish Iran as one of the major centers where we can promote and practice wellness traditions such as the concept of yoga, what comes along with yoga, Ayurveda, and a very healthy way of living, I think.
And I think these systems are very relevant. They are very relevant in today’s world because our lives have become very complex. We get exposed to a lot of elements which are alien to our body and to our culture. So I think this kind of healing, or this kind of healthy lifestyle, which involves yoga, Ayurveda and homeopathy, can help moderate our body and enable us to have, at least, a mentally healthy lifestyle.
We intend to do a lot of activities in Iran in cooperation with the government of Iran, whatever the rules and regulations allow.
And I think one of my important missions out here, first of all, at this point in time, would be to look at how we can generate greater cooperation in the health sector.
You mentioned the health sector as an important area of cooperation. What are the areas where you see the greatest potential for expanding India-Iran health cooperation?
So today I was there; I went to Iran Pharma, the largest pharmaceutical exposition in Iran. There also, a lot of Indian companies had opened up their booths. So there is a lot of cooperation in the pharmaceutical sector between the two countries.
That is also something which can be scaled up a lot, given the geopolitical situation improves. InshaAllah, when things become better, I think there is huge potential for a large amount of pharmaceutical cooperation in terms of the export of APIs to Iran, training, technical expertise exchanges between health professionals in the two countries, and also looking at new forms of medicine, research and development.

So, as I said, there is huge potential in Ayurveda, in yoga and in conventional medicine.
But given the current circumstances, we are not able to realize the full potential. But inshaAllah, in time we will be able to.
What are your views on tourism relations between the two countries and ways to promote them?
Well, tourism, as I said, is something I have already spoken to a lot of Iranian policymakers about. The honorable Prime Minister of India has identified trade, tourism and technology as the three things we need to engage with friendly countries.
Tourism is an important sector for promotion. In recent years, the number of tourists going from Iran to India has come down a bit. It might be due to the geopolitical condition; it might be due to the economic condition. But we are very keen to bring it to the same level of tourism flows to India and even beyond.
So, we intend to take a lot of measures. We are looking at possibilities for relaxing the tourist visa regime, streamlining the processes, and rationalizing tourist visa fees so that Iranians have to pay less to go to India. We are also trying to familiarize them with a lot of activities.

And I think all these things, this whole cultural connect between the two countries, will eventually promote greater tourism flows from Iran to India, and I think similarly from India to Iran.
So, I think, as I said, there is huge potential. We are trying to understand the ecosystem of the tourism infrastructure and create infrastructure so that Iranians can travel to India as easily as possible.

Shams Tabrizi mausoleum project seen as boost for cultural tourism

Zoroastrian funerary inscription from late Sasanian era discovered in southern Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:09:15 UTC
22:09:15 KST

Zoroastrian funerary inscription from late Sasanian era discovered in southern Iran
TEHRAN - A newly discovered funerary inscription dating to the late Sasanian period and associated with a Zoroastrian burial has been found in a carved frame north of the ancient city of Estakhr in Marvdasht plain of Fars province, southern Iran.
The inscription is written in Pahlavi script and is believed to be associated with one of the burials of Zoroastrian followers during the late Sasanian period, Jamaran.ir quoted archaeologist Abolhassan Atabaki as saying on Thursday.
The archaeologist explained that with the expansion of Zoroastrianism in the post-Achaemenid period and later during the Sasanian era, burial practices underwent fundamental changes. Many burials in the ground were abandoned and funerary practices were transferred to elevated and mountainous areas, a shift he attributed primarily to Zoroastrian beliefs concerning bodily resurrection and life after death.
According to Atabaki, Zoroastrians regarded the world beneath the ground as dark, stagnant and associated with evil. They therefore avoided burying the dead directly in the soil.
The corpse was also considered capable of contaminating sacred elements such as earth, vegetation and water. At the same time, Zoroastrians believed that the soul of the deceased should ascend toward the rays of the sun.
For this reason, the body was placed in elevated structures known as “sun towers” before the final funerary stage, where rituals including “khorshid-negahreshni” were performed and the bones were purified. After birds of prey and other scavenging animals removed the flesh, the cleaned bones were transferred to places among rocks and cliffs, Atabaki said.
In that regard, Najmeh Ebrahimi, a history expert, said the Sasanian period saw a variety of burial practices, depending on the social status and financial means of individuals.
These included rock-cut graves, stone cairns, grave towers, trough-shaped graves, jar burials, small “dakhmaks” and ossuaries. Such funerary structures are referred to as “dakhmak” in many Sasanian inscriptions.
Ebrahimi highlighted the archaeological importance of the Marvdasht plain, saying that the area contains the largest known concentration of Sasanian inscriptions, with more than 50 inscriptions discovered and reread to date.
The plain also ranks first in terms of Sasanian funerary inscriptions, she added.
The inscription is believed to provide further evidence for the funerary practices and religious beliefs of Zoroastrian communities in the Marvdasht region during the final centuries of the Sasanian period.

Healey appoints Labour manifesto writer, adding to election speculation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:07:46 UTC
22:07:46 KST

Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour’s 2024 manifesto, is taking on a senior role as an adviser to John Healey, in a move likely to fuel speculation about an early general election.
The chancellor is keen to strengthen his team before the critical budget on 28 October, as the economy is buffeted by high oil prices and rising government borrowing costs.
Healey has poached Athwal to be his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Andy Burnham’s chief of staff, the former Blair-era cabinet minister James Purnell.
Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, was closely associated with drawing up Labour’s manifesto, and devising Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government. He worked as a senior economic adviser in Starmer’s Downing Street team but left after a year to join Flint Global.
A source close to Healey said: “Having Rav join John’s team as an experienced heavyweight economist at the Treasury ahead of this budget will be invaluable. His political nous will add to the special adviser team, providing John with guidance and counsel to the chancellor.”
Burnham flatly denied that he planned to call an early election on Friday. Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next general election would be in 2029, he said, “well, yes, that’s when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead.”
Nevertheless, Athwal’s presence on Healey’s team could be seen as a strength if the prime minister did decide to draw up a fresh manifesto.
Athwal’s arrival is also likely to increase concerns among some in Labour that the Treasury’s instinctive caution is fuelling a “continuity Starmer” approach to economics.
The pledge at the heart of the manifesto not to increase income tax, national insurance or VAT was seen by Starmer’s team as key to Labour’s landslide victory two years ago. But it is widely agreed that it has restricted the party’s room for manoeuvre once in power.
People with knowledge of Athwal’s thinking suggest he has learned from the travails of Labour’s early months in office, however. One left-of-centre economist said: “I’d say he was at the more interesting and curious end of the Starmerite project.”
Before joining Labour, Athwal was a Treasury civil servant, rising to be head of growth strategy. One former colleague described him as “nice and clever – a good combination”.
After taking over at the Treasury in July, Healey hired Will Straw, who played a leading role in the remain campaign during the Brexit referendum, to be his chief of staff; some of Rachel Reeves’s economic advisers, including Spencer Thompson, stayed on.
Reeves’s chief economic adviser, the former Clean Bandit violinist Neil Amin-Smith, who was closely involved in her plans to devolve more tax revenue to local leaders, has moved across to Burnham’s No 10.
Athwal is expected to arrive in post next week, a month before Healey’s first budget.
With inflation and borrowing costs expected to have wiped out at least half of the headroom Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules, Healey faces a series of tough decisions.
He has promised to maintain a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly smaller than the £24bn in the spring forecast.
Depending on the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, restoring the cushion in full would be likely to require large tax rises or spending cuts. But government sources say Healey wants this to be a “focused” budget, after Reeves used her two budgets as chancellor to increase taxes by £70bn a year.
Key decisions about future tax and spending appear likely to be delayed until a Treasury spending review next year, which will come after Burnham has set out his long-term priorities in a 10-year plan, expected after the budget.
Healey has made clear he does not intend to set a timetable for when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence at the budget, for example – a target he insisted, when he resigned from Starmer’s government in June, must be met by 2030.
However, hopes of a low-key budget are under pressure from persistently high global oil and gas prices, which make it likely that the energy price cap, which determines UK consumer bills, will rise sharply in January.
Treasury sources have said officials are working “at pace” on options for consumer support, though help is expected to fall far short of the costly universal approach taken by Liz Truss in 2022.
Flint Global was approached for comment.

Small businesses in rural France bears the brunt of energy crisis triggered by Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:03:25 UTC
22:03:25 KST

In the Oise department, soaring energy prices driven by the war in Iran are hitting rural businesses hard, as they face rocketing bills for heating oil and diesel.
France's rural communities are feeling the full force of the global energy crisis sparked by the war in Iran. Almost 21 million people — nearly a third of the French population — live in the countryside, which covers around 90% of the country's landmass.
In Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, a town of around 6,000 people in the northern Oise department, rising energy prices are being felt even in the local bakery.
Kevin Luce bakes his bread in two heating oil-fired ovens — a fuel that was once cost-effective but has become increasingly expensive. "At the outset it was a good deal: an oil-fired oven was cheaper to run than an electric one, until the price went up by 50%," he said.
His last delivery, two days ago, came to 2,200 euros for 1,200 litres. Six months earlier, he had paid 2,100 euros for 2,000 litres. The difference is being absorbed directly by the business.
"All this excessive spending on energy is money we are losing. It's wages we can't take, pay rises we can't give our employees, investments we can't make," Luce said.
Small businesses forced to cut back
Food truck owner Martial Realland has taken a different approach — he has stopped refilling his oil tank altogether. "Last year I had 1,500 litres delivered. It cost me 1,600 euros. Now, at 1.80 or 1.90 euros a litre, it's almost double. So I'm not getting any delivered," he said.
Realland has also begun turning down jobs that involve long distances. "Ever since I was born there have always been crises. But this is no longer bearable," he said.
The surge in energy costs is reviving memories of the gilets jaunes movement, which erupted in autumn 2018 after a rise in fuel taxes. The protest gained its strongest momentum in rural and outer-suburban areas — the same communities now bearing the heaviest burden of the current crisis.

What are the Lib Dems for? They must champion localism to stay relevant in an age of single-issue politics | Simon Jenkins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:02:14 UTC
22:02:14 KST

September is the cruellest month for political commentators because it is when something has to be said about the Liberal Democrats. They are a play without a plot, a chorus line of seemingly endless “don’t knows”. Their leader, Ed Davey, recently warned that “we’re in the fight of our lives” to defend the values of liberty and equality. Really? How can this be when Davey is becoming about as relevant as Count Binface?
The Lib Dems’ central predicament has remained unchanged for a century, ever since the decline of David Lloyd George and the rise of the Labour party. There is simply no space in Britain for a centrist party when so little divides the big parties and they broadly stick to the prevailing ecomomic orthodoxy.
But there is now a ray of hope. One of the newer developments in British politics is the rise of single-issue parties. In Scotland and Wales, the Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru demand independence from the UK, while in England the Reform party has dedicated itself to curbing immigration.
A lack of a clarifying message could partly explain why the Lib Dems have suffered heavy defeats at recent byelections, and slipped to fourth or fifth place in many national opinion polls, regularly trailing the Greens and Reform.
In order to improve their electoral fortunes, the Lib Dems need an equally straightforward cause, one that should have broad appeal and identify an area neglected by the other parties. That cause is now glaring: the devolution of government authority.
Time and again in national league tables, England ranks as having one of the most concentrated central governments in Europe, and by some measures in the world. English citizens’ ability to participate in local democracy is extremely weak compared to other countries such as France, Germany and those in Scandinavia.
Welfare comparisons show the UK’s local services fare poorly and inequitably compared with those, for instance, in localised Scandinavia. The authority of Britain’s central executive over local government is overbearing, with ever more disappointing outcomes for citizens.
Localism is the issue and one that has featured prominently in political debate for decades. New Labour even proposed a “new localism”. The result was just 12 elected mayors in England and Wales between 2001 and 2005.
In 2010, David Cameron pledged a “radical shift in power from central government to neighbourhoods”. He then did the opposite through enforced housing targets and a fierce programme of austerity. Similarly, in 2024 Keir Starmer promised to “deepen democracy by … devolving power to communities”. Yet one of his first moves was to overrule local discretion in planning approvals, describing councils as “blockers and nimbys”.
Over the years, the phrase “shifting power locally” became an almost ritualistic election chant, clearly based on polling data. No government really meant it. Ever since Margaret Thatcher, the centre has taken ever more control of local taxation, education, housing, care services and planning. The job of a British local council today is in effect to do what the centre tells it. It has not much money nor power for anything else. It is therefore no wonder that local democracy is subject to ridicule: see, for instance, the recent “independence” vote in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington.
Unquestionably the most headline-grabbing of Westminster’s pseudo-localists is Andy Burnham. Does he mean it? His innovation of a cohort of metro mayors – introduced under the Conservatives – inserts a new level of regional bureaucracy between central and local government. Their role will primarily be to enforce national targets of housebuilding and energy investment, and presumably to override decisions of local councils beneath them.
Burnham’s announcement that mayors in England will be able to keep a share of income tax and business rates was cited as proof of his commitment to his so-called devolution agenda. But the extent to which mayors will be able to wield these powers remains to be seen.
The prime minister’s moving of parts of the No 10 operation to Manchester hardly reduces the power of the centre. It merely relocates it, temporarily. Here, surely, is a Liberal Democrat cause.
Significantly, the one area in which the Lib Dems have flourished is local government. At last May’s local elections, the party took their control of councils up to 76, establishing them as a major political force across local government. This was a major achievement. There are now more Liberal Democrat council leaders in Britain than the 71 Lib Dem MPs. As such, their impact on the actual government of the country is substantial.
This cries out for revolution and the Lib Dems have every reason to be its champions. The party should go flat out for democratic, truly local self-government. Models of appropriate tiers and functions can be found across Europe. The cause is now aided by mountainous evidence that Britain’s centrist model – the famous “Rolls-Royce” of Whitehall – is now a clapped out jalopy. Every week the headlines cry that nothing seems to work.
This is the all-consuming challenge for the Lib Dems to make their own. Propose a major constitutional reform. The party’s 76 local councils can list the powers they want restored to them. It is these council leaders who must stand on stage at their conference, not Westminster’s indolent parliamentarians. Liberal Democrats should become the party of local Britain and restore the government of the people to the people.
- 
  Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Nearly 60% of Armenians favor referendum on EAEU membership — poll

22:01:28 KST

YEREVAN, September 25. /TASS/. Nearly 60% of Armenian citizens surveyed favor holding a referendum on the country's membership in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), according to a poll presented by Gallup International.
"Some 38.9% stated that a referendum should definitely be held, while 20.3% said it likely should be. This means approximately 60% of citizens believe a referendum is necessary. Meanwhile, 9.3% of respondents felt a referendum likely should not be held, 25.1% stated it is definitely not needed, and 6.9% were undecided," Aram Navasardyan, head of Gallup International's Armenian branch, said during the presentation of the poll results.
He also noted that when choosing between Armenia's membership in the EAEU or the European Union, supporters of both paths were almost evenly split: 29.4% of citizens said the country should remain in the EAEU, while 35.1% favored moving toward EU membership. "Another 24.7% stated they would not vote, and 10.9% found it difficult to answer," Navasardyan reported.
The telephone poll of 1,001 respondents was conducted from September 22 to 24, with a margin of error of ±3%.
On March 26, 2025, the Armenian parliament passed a law initiating the process of the republic's accession to the EU. Russian President Vladimir Putin previously noted that EU integration would automatically terminate Armenia's cooperation with the EAEU and lead to the loss of all associated preferences. At the EAEU summit in Astana on May 29, the leaders of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan issued a joint statement backing a nationwide referendum in Armenia on whether to join the EU or remain in the EAEU.
On August 11, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told TASS that Armenia
needed to hold a nationwide referendum before December of this year, when potential steps regarding Yerevan will be discussed at a meeting of EAEU heads of state.
On August 24, Dmitry Medvedev, Deputy Chairman of the Russian Security Council, told TASS that Yerevan would never become an EU member but would instead severely damage its long-term relations with the EAEU and Moscow.

CERN has begun disconnecting the Large Hadron Collider
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:01:20 UTC
22:01:20 KST

CERN has begun disconnecting the Large Hadron Collider
- Date:
- September 25, 2026
- Source:
- CERN
- Summary:
- CERN has started replacing some of the Large Hadron Collider’s most important magnets as part of its High-Luminosity upgrade. The new superconducting magnets will produce fields about 40% stronger, allowing particle beams to be squeezed more tightly before they collide. That should create far more collisions for the ATLAS and CMS experiments to analyze, giving physicists a much larger window into the fundamental workings of the universe.
- Share:
The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) stretches 27 km around and relies on thousands of magnets of different types - dipoles, quadrupoles, sextupoles, octupoles, decapoles, etc. - to steer and control its particle beams. Each type performs a specialized task.
Some of the most important are known as inner triplets. These groups of three quadrupole magnets (hence the name) sit on both sides of the LHC's four main experiments. Their job is to focus the particle beams as tightly as possible just before the particles collide inside the detectors.
The tighter the beams are "compressed," the greater the chance that particles will collide. That makes the inner triplets essential for increasing the LHC's luminosity, i.e. the number of collisions that occur in a given period of time. More luminosity means more collisions, giving researchers more data to analyze.
Preparing the LHC for a New Era
A major part of the future High-Luminosity LHC (HiLumi LHC) project involves replacing the existing inner triplets with a much more powerful generation of magnets.
The work is taking place during the third long shutdown (LS3). Reently, crews cut the first magnet interconnection, formally beginning the replacement operation. CERN Director-General Mark Thomson also visited LHC Point 1 (the ATLAS experiment) to mark the milestone.
"The replacement of these magnets with the new HiLumi LHC inner triplets is crucial for the coming high-luminosity years. The first quadrupole of the new triplets should arrive in the tunnel at the start of 2029. In total, 16 cryostats and 28 cryo-assemblies will be installed - a major undertaking," explains Jean-Philippe Tock, Head of the LS3 Coordination Team.
Magnets About 40% Stronger
The new inner triplets are the product of years of research and development. They represent a major technological advance over the niobium-titanium magnets currently operating inside the LHC.
Instead of niobium-titanium, the upgraded magnets use niobium-tin superconducting coils. This allows them to generate magnetic fields reaching 11.3 tesla, about 40% stronger than the fields produced by the current magnets.
The new equipment will be installed around the ATLAS and CMS experiments, where the increased collision rate will be especially important.
ALICE and LHCb operate differently and pursue different physics programs, so they do not need the same increase in instantaneous luminosity. Their existing inner triplets can therefore remain in place. However, those magnets will still be upgraded so that both experiments can benefit from the overall increase in luminosity.
Removing 28 Superconducting Magnets
Since September 7, CERN teams have been dismantling sections of the collider on either side of ATLAS and CMS. The goal is to remove 28 superconducting magnets (including the inner triplets) that are scheduled to be replaced.
The operation marks the end of an era for hardware that has been part of the LHC since its construction.
"Today's event is a major milestone for CERN, especially for the HiLumi LHC project team. The current inner triplets date back to the LHC construction phase and were installed in the machine between 2005 and 2007. After nearly twenty years of operation, they will give way to a new generation of even more powerful magnets. It's truly remarkable to witness such a handover from one generation of innovation to the next," says Markus Zerlauth, the HiLumi LHC Project Leader.
Story Source:
