What US doesn't tell about its army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:34:55 UTC
21:34:55 KST

It is still far too early to fully grasp the scope of the costs and consequences of the US war waged against Iran. A conflict that Washington’s initial calculations envisioned as short-lived has dragged on for months, keeping a significant portion of US military capabilities tied down in the region for an extended period. What we know about this war today is largely derived from official statements, media reports, remarks by US officials, and scattered documents—a picture in which significant aspects appear to remain hidden.
The latest example is the aircraft carrier *Abraham Lincoln*. According to an ABC News report, the Acting Secretary of the US Navy confirmed in a letter to Congress that a total of eight suicide attempts have been recorded among the personnel of this strike group since the *Lincoln* began its deployment. These figures are not limited to the ship's own crew but also encompass personnel from the air wing, the strike group staff, accompanying destroyers, and the aviation squadrons deployed aboard the vessel.
Of course, US Navy officials have stated that this figure does not necessarily fall outside the typical pattern for a long deployment and that they treat every case seriously. Yet, that is precisely the crux of the matter: the *Lincoln* is not merely an aircraft carrier; it could serve as a case study of the pressures the US military has endured during this conflict.
The ship was scheduled for a routine six-month mission in the Pacific, but the war with Iran altered its course, resulting in an unusually long deployment. The *Lincoln* ultimately remained at sea for 286 days—spending more than 200 of them in the operational zone, according to published reports—and the families of some service members spoke about the strain caused by this extended deployment.
Even the Acting Secretary of the US Navy acknowledged in August that the war disrupts routine schedules and that extended missions and combat operations place immense strain on the forces. At the time, he cited figures including 266 days of deployment, 200 days spent in a combat zone, over 10,000 flight sorties, and the expenditure of approximately 1.5 million pounds of munitions.
However, alongside this official narrative, other details have gradually emerged. Reports concerning the *Lincoln* have highlighted the restriction of contact between troops and their families during critical periods, changes to meal plans when resupply was difficult, technical issues, and the strain caused by a prolonged deployment. US officials have acknowledged some of these issues, contrasting with the different account of the carrier's situation that had been presented previously.
To that, the *Lincoln* must be viewed as more than just a story about eight suicide attempts. The significance of this vessel lies in the fact that it has been one of the largest and most iconic instruments of US military power during a protracted war. If an aircraft carrier—with its thousands of military personnel—has faced such a combination of pressures and issues after nearly 300 days of deployment, the more critical question is: what has been the situation for other US forces at the bases, on the ships, and in the units involved in this war?
There is an important fact: information regarding the actual performance of the US military in a conflict is typically released with a time lag. Some information remains classified for security reasons, while other details may only come to light months later through congressional documents, audit reports, military investigations, troop testimonies, or media coverage. The US Navy itself maintains a vast volume of operational documents and ship-related reports—compiled as operational records and logs—to which public access is not immediate.
Thus, what we know about the *Lincoln* today likely resembles a single piece of a larger puzzle rather than the complete picture. Eight suicide attempts do not, in themselves, prove the collapse or failure of the US military; yet, when viewed alongside 286 days of deployment, over 200 days in a combat zone, operational strain, limited contact with family, and issues that U.S. officials have been compelled to acknowledge, a serious question arises: what aspects of the US military's actual condition in this war remain undisclosed to the public?
It may take months or even years for a more complete picture of the true cost of this war for the US military to emerge. Only then will it become clear whether what we know today about the *Lincoln* was an isolated case or a sign of broader problems about which there is not yet sufficient information.
In such circumstances, one should not look solely at statistics regarding casualties and destroyed equipment. War is not limited to what is visible on maps or in footage of attacks; the attrition of forces, the prolongation of missions, psychological strain, supply chain disruptions, diminished readiness, and the costs of maintaining a military force during a protracted conflict are also part of the reality on the ground.
The *Lincoln* holds special significance in this regard, as it served as a symbol of US military might during the conflict. Now, after a deployment spanning nearly 300 days, the vessel itself has revealed information indicating that a more complex reality lies behind the imposing imagery of aircraft carriers and the projection of American military power.
And perhaps this is the most important point: what has been published so far regarding the state of the US military in this war is not necessarily the end of the story; it may well be just the beginning of the revelation of costs—aspects of which have not yet been fully disclosed to the public.
MNA

It will predict the enemy's actions — what is known about the SPECTR AI platform being tested by Ukrainian combat units
Kyiv • UNN
SPECTR analyzes combat data, identifies patterns, and predicts the enemy's actions. The system is already undergoing testing in combat units.
The Artificial Intelligence Center "A1" under the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine is developing the SPECTR AI system for analyzing combat data and planning operations. The ministry reported that the solution is already being tested by several combat units, UNN reports.
How the SPECTR AI system will change operational planning
According to Danilo Tsvok, head of the "A1" center, Ukraine has a unique body of data on modern warfare. SPECTR will help turn it into a real advantage on the battlefield.
The system's main tasks include:
-  analyzing information; 
-  identifying patterns; 
-  developing recommendations for operational planning and organizing processes in the military; 
-  automating routine work at headquarters. 
This will enable the military to interact more quickly with information from the battlefield, while the data will remain within a secure perimeter.
In fact, we are building an operating system for waging war that will help the military choose effective courses of action and predict the enemy's possible moves.Danilo TsvokHead of the "A1" AI Center
SPECTR will operate within existing systems used by the Defense Forces, as well as on local devices designed to work with sensitive data.
How the "A1" Artificial Intelligence Center is building an AI-driven army
The Ministry of Defense established the "A1" Artificial Intelligence Center in March 2026 with the support of the government of the United Kingdom. The team was launched with a clear mission—to turn AI into Ukraine's advantage on the battlefield and build an AI-driven army, that is, a military strengthened by artificial intelligence.
Building an AI-driven army includes three main areas:
-  faster and more effective data-based decision-making; 
-  using AI in weapons systems; 
-  reducing bureaucracy in the military. 
The ministry reported that the Center is already working on three flagship projects—in the areas of combat data analysis and improving defense innovations. Some solutions are being tested by units.

‘A fighter at heart’: Two soldiers, two homes facing each other, one community in mourning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:32:10 UTC
21:32:10 KST

Master Sgt. (res.) Nadav Kali, 24, had barely finished his mandatory military service before returning to uniform as a reservist. On Thursday, he was killed alongside fellow reservist Master Sgt. (res.) Ofek Moalem in an accidental drone explosion at an IDF post in northern Gaza.
Kali, from the small community of Har Halutz in northern Israel, completed his regular military service in 2024 and went almost immediately into reserve duty amid the war.
He and Moalem, 23, were serving with the 7007th Battalion when the accident occurred. According to the military’s initial investigation, the two soldiers approached a drone that had malfunctioned and crashed inside their post. The drone then exploded, fatally wounding them.
The military is investigating the circumstances of the incident and suspended use of the same drone model for two days while the investigation is underway.
For Har Halutz, Kali’s death marked the second time since the war began that the close-knit community has lost one of its young soldiers in Gaza. Staff Sgt. Itay Saadon, Kali’s former classmate, was killed fighting in the Gaza Strip in November 2023. Saadon’s family lived directly across from Kali’s parents.
Kali is survived by his parents, Yoav and Dr. Yael Kali, his older brothers Roi and Itamar and his longtime partner, Rotem, whom he had been dating since they were teenagers.
Friends mourning Kali on Friday described a young man whose broad smile, loyalty and determination made him a central presence in their group.
“All the way back from my apartment to Har Halutz, I keep thinking about Nadav and seeing his huge smile,” his friend Yoav Sivan Ben Yosef said. “I remember that smile from when we were very young. He was simply a golden person, incredibly sociable.”
He recalled that Kali and Rotem had been together since they were 17 and attended high school with the same circle of friends.
Amit Dagan said Kali occupied a central place not only in his own life but throughout their group of friends.
“Nadav was a central person in our circle and for everyone,” Dagan said. “Besides being a fighter in the army, he was truly a fighter at heart in every sense. He was one of the strongest people I personally knew.”
Dagan said Kali remained steadfast in pursuing what mattered to him regardless of the risks or what others thought.
“He was always true to himself in everything and never strayed for a second from his path or from what he wanted, no matter the risks or what people told him,” he said. “I and everyone else will miss him terribly.”
Friend Ido Marom remembered the long conversations they shared, which could move effortlessly from everyday jokes to much larger questions.
“We would sit for hours, talk about nonsense and end up having conversations about stars and science, and everything just flowed,” Marom said. “He was always with us for all the important decisions in life.”
For Sahar Sarig, Kali’s absence was still difficult to comprehend because his presence remained embedded in the places, relationships and creative projects the friends had shared.
“It’s impossible to grasp that something like this has ended,” Sarig said. “He is still so present and still with us. The home he shared with his partner is still their home, and the things he did are still so present. You can’t separate him from all the things he was part of.”
Music formed an especially important part of their friendship.
“For me, Nadav was more than a true friend. He was such a significant part of my journey in this world, particularly when it came to music,” Sarig said.
The two had played together from elementary school, forming a musical group and later performing a jazz recital together and collaborating on other projects. Sarig said he had recently been working on a project and wanted Kali to play piano on it.
“Despite the reserve duty and all the complications, I wanted him to be part of it, and fortunately we managed to complete a large part of it,” he said. “I can’t believe I won’t create with him anymore. It’s impossible to comprehend.”
The Misgav Regional Council, which includes Har Halutz, issued a statement expressing condolences to Kali’s family.
“The Misgav Regional Council bows its head and shares in the grief of the Kali family upon learning of the death of Master Sgt. (res.) Nadav Kali, a soldier in Battalion 7007 of the 16th Brigade, in the Gaza Strip,” the council said.
Kali was scheduled to be buried Friday at 1 p.m. at the Misgav cemetery.

Turkish army to withdraw from strategic military base in northern Iraq
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:31:56 UTC
21:31:56 KST

Turkey will gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zilkan camp, where it has had troops since 2015, to the Iraqi government.
Turkey has reached an agreement with Baghdad to gradually transfer control of the strategic Bashiqa-Zilkan military base in northern Iraq to the Iraqi government.
The deal follows an understanding between the two countries over the progress Iraq has made with regard to strengthening security measures in the area as well as reasserting Iraqi state authority there.
The decision was announced in a joint statement issued after a meeting in New York between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on the margins of the United Nations (UN) General Assembly.
According to the statement, Turkey will hand over the camp in stages, in line with an agreed timetable.
However, no specific date has yet been set for the withdrawal of Turkish troops.
The United States Ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, has welcomed the agreement.
"History rarely announces its turning points; it stitches them quietly," he wrote in a post on X. "Ankara returning Zilkan to Baghdad by agreed mechanism and timeline is one such thread: Iraqi sovereignty and Turkish security, both served. What looks like chaos from afar is a region weaving its own order".
The deal
Turkey and Iraq have agreed on fully establishing the authority of the Iraqi state in Sinjar and ending the presence of "banned foreign armed elements" in the region.
In the joint statement, it was also stated that the two countries had agreed to deepen their security cooperation.
Turkey has long been calling on the Iraqi government to curb the activities of Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK)-linked groups other non-state armed actors operating in Sinjar.
Earlier this month, the Iraqi government announced that the Sinjar Resistance Units, a Yazidi armed group affiliated with PKK, had agreed to lay down their arms and that fighters who met the conditions would be integrated into the Iraqi security forces.
The group, which is reported to have played a role in the fight against ISIL, is regarded by Turkey as a security threat because of its ties to the PKK.
Why is Bashiqa-Zilkan important?
Bashiqa-Zilkan is one of several Turkish military facilities that have long been a point of contention between Turkey and Iraq.
Turkey established a military presence in the area in 2015 to support operations against ISIL and assist local security forces.
Turkey maintains other military bases in northern Iraq, where it conducts operations against the PKK. The Bashiqa-Zilkan camp is the furthest from the Turkish border.
Iraq has previously called on Turkey to withdraw its troops from the area. Ankara, however, has insisted that its military presence is necessary to carry out operations against the PKK and to protect Turkey's national security.
The Bashiqa-Zilkan agreement comes as Turkey's latest effort to end its long-running conflict with the PKK continues.
As part of this new peace process, the PKK announced last year that it was dissolving itself and would cease armed actions against Turkey.
US withdrawal from Iraq
The United States is also in the process of winding down its military presence in Iraq.
US officials say a plan is in place for the hundreds of American troops stationed in the north of the country to leave by 30 September.

Pakistan’s Punitive Gamble in Afghanistan: An Open War With No End in Sight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:28:00 UTC
21:28:00 KST

In the early hours of September 24, Pakistan carried out air and drone strikes on ten locations inside Afghanistan. Subsequently, Afghan media identified Kandahar – where the Taliban’s supreme leader (Amir-al-Mu’minin) Hibatullah Akhundzada is based – as well as Khost and Paktia as the provinces targeted. A few hours later, Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar posted on social media that the strikes were “deliberate, precise, calibrated and proportionate” and were “strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan.” “Attempted attacks” was a reference to earlier Pakistani claims that it had shot down ten rudimentary drones launched from inside Afghanistan that entered Pakistani territory with a “soft kill” approach.
Two days earlier, on September 21, Pakistani air strikes on Kunar and Paktika provinces killed three civilians – a man, a woman, and a girl – in Kunar’s Nurgal district. Islamabad claimed to have killed 28 militants in the attack. The civilian casualties, which were confirmed by UNAMA, saw Afghan protesters hitting the streets in Kabul and elsewhere.
This Pakistani strike was in response to an attack on a police compound in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kohat, killing at least 16 police officers on September 18. On that day a vehicle-borne explosive device breached the police compound during Friday prayers. This was followed by an armed assault by militants. The attack was claimed by the Ittihadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), an alliance led by the Hafiz Gul Bahadar (HGB) group, which shares close linkages with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). Pakistani authorities identified one of the attackers as an Afghan national.
Pakistan has carried out air and drone strikes inside Afghanistan on at least 15 occasions between October 2025 and September 2026. Private estimates suggest that more than 1,100 civilians have been killed or injured by cross-border violence in Afghanistan this year. An attack on a drug rehabilitation center in Kabul in May killed 269 people, leading to calls for the attack to be investigated as a war crime.
Inside Pakistan, the death toll of civilians and security forces in terrorism-related incidents in 2026 so far is close to 1,700. Of these, 545 have taken place in the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the TTP and the IMP operate.
Pakistani claims that Afghan soil is being used by the TTP and the IMP are supported by periodic reports from the U.N. monitoring committee, including one released in August 2026. The report unequivocally said that the Afghan Taliban “continued their support” to the TTP. The Afghan Taliban has responded to such assertions by repeated public denials.
Behind the scenes, however, the Afghan Taliban may have tried to restrain the TTP. The U.N. report mentioned that the Afghan Taliban authorities have “relocated approximately 2,000 TTP fighters and families from the Pakistani border to further inside Afghanistan.” Akhundzada has reportedly “warned the TTP leadership through back‑channel communications to halt attacks targeting Pakistan or risk losing the Taliban’s support,” it added. It is unclear if any attempt was made to reign in the IMP as well.
While efforts to control the TTP may not have worked completely, according to data by ACLED, “HGB and IMP’s activities have less than halved since the latest outbreak of hostilities between Afghanistan and Pakistan in late February, compared with the immediately preceding period.”
On February 27, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil-Haq (Righteous Fury) against the Taliban in Afghanistan, marking the first such attack on its former ally and protégé. On that occasion, “unprovoked firing” from across the border by the Taliban was cited as the reason. Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Asif declared, “Now it is open war between us.”
Given the levels of violence the TTP and the IMP continued to perpetrate inside Pakistan, the country is facing a classic case of strategic blowback. More importantly, the sense of impunity with which Islamabad has repeatedly carried out its attacks in Afghanistan, despite their low efficacy, indicates serious lacunae in Pakistan’s counterterrorism strategy. Most of these attacks have led to angry statements by Taliban officials, vows of retaliation, and incidents of cross-border firing by Taliban soldiers but little else.
In addition to reining in the TTP and IMP, Pakistan seems to be pursuing a larger strategic objective of finding its lost leverage in Kabul. In Islamabad’s view, its former ally has gone rogue and demonstrating coercive power, along with providing support to the anti-Taliban resistance fronts, is the only path forward. A weak and client state in Afghanistan is the end state Pakistani establishment has pursued for decades.
During the days of the previous Afghan Republic, the HGB largely spared the Pakistani state and instead focused its fight on American and NATO forces in Afghanistan. Post-August 2021, backed by al-Qaida, the HGB has grown to be a prominent face of jihadist insurgency against Islamabad. It is numerically smaller than the TTP, but that hasn’t stopped it from carrying out some of the more complex attacks on security installations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Therefore, eliminating the IMP threat, if not the far larger TTP, will potentially address the blowback Islamabad is currently receiving for its past policies. Similarly, repeated attacks including some directed at the Taliban regime itself, could possibly lead to internal ruptures within the faction-ridden Islamic Emirate and embolden the small pro-Pakistan elements within it.
That, however, is much easier said than done. Despite reports of factionalism and internal differences within the Kandahar (Rahbari shura or the leadership council) and Kabul (administrative) shuras of the Taliban, the Rahbari shura functioning under the strict Islamic edicts of the Supreme leader, still retains control and uncontested legitimacy. Moreover, each attack by Pakistan so far has further raised anti-Pakistan sentiment inside Afghanistan. It could embolden the Afghan Taliban as well, who have little incentive to accede to Islamabad’s demands. The ethno-nationalist Taliban regime with strong Pushtun identity across the contested Durand Line could raise its head of Pushtun nationalism once again.
The Taliban seem to have learnt from their former sponsor’s playbook the art of cultivating strategic assets and using them as leverage. Attempting to bomb them into submission could be a myopic and counterproductive strategy if there are any lessons learned from the last two decades of American intervention in Afghanistan.

Earth is tearing apart beneath the Pacific Northwest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:20:18 UTC
21:20:18 KST

Earth is tearing apart beneath the Pacific Northwest
- Date:
- September 25, 2026
- Source:
- Louisiana State University
- Summary:
- Scientists have captured a subduction zone off Vancouver Island in the process of tearing itself apart, revealing that these massive tectonic systems may die piece by piece rather than all at once. The discovery could help explain ancient plate fragments, volcanic activity, and how hidden breaks beneath Cascadia may influence future earthquakes.
- Share:
Scientists have captured an unusually detailed view of a major tectonic system beneath the Pacific Northwest beginning to come apart.
The discovery, reported in Science Advances, shows a subduction zone actively breaking into pieces. Subduction zones form where one tectonic plate is forced beneath another and pushed deep into Earth. They are responsible for some of the planet's largest earthquakes, powerful volcanic eruptions, and long term changes to continents and ocean basins.
Until now, however, scientists have had few opportunities to see clearly how one of these enormous systems reaches the end of its life.
How a Subduction Zone Dies
Subduction is one of the main processes that continually reshapes Earth's surface. As an oceanic plate sinks beneath another plate, material from the crust is carried downward toward the mantle, the hot layer beneath Earth's crust.
These systems can remain active for millions of years, but they cannot continue indefinitely. Otherwise, continents would eventually pile into one another, oceans would disappear, and much of Earth's geological history would be erased.
That leaves geologists with a fundamental question: what actually causes a mature subduction zone to stop?
"Getting a subduction zone started is like trying to push a train uphill -- it takes a huge effort," said Brandon Shuck, a geologist at Louisiana State University and lead author of the study. "But once it's moving, it's like the train is racing downhill, impossible to stop. Ending it requires something dramatic -- basically, a train wreck."
Scientists may now be watching that process unfold beneath Cascadia.
A Tectonic Plate Breaking Apart Beneath Cascadia
Off Vancouver Island, the Juan de Fuca and Explorer plates are slowly being forced beneath the North American plate. This area is part of the Cascadia subduction zone, a vast tectonic boundary stretching along the Pacific Northwest.
Researchers combined detailed earthquake records with seismic reflection imaging to look deep beneath the seafloor. The technique works somewhat like medical ultrasound. Scientists send sound waves into Earth and measure how those waves bounce back from different underground structures.
The seismic measurements came from the NSF funded 2021 Cascadia Seismic Imaging Experiment (CASIE21), during which researchers aboard a ship sent sound waves into the ocean floor. A 15-kilometer-long streamer carrying underwater listening instruments recorded the returning signals.
By analyzing those echoes, scientists created detailed images of structures hidden beneath the seafloor. What emerged was striking: large faults and fractures cutting through the sinking plate, including areas where the plate appears to be actively snapping apart.
"This is the first time we have a clear picture of a subduction zone caught in the act of dying," said Shuck. "Rather than shutting down all at once, the plate is ripping apart piece by piece, creating smaller microplates and new boundaries. So instead of a big train wreck, it's like watching a train slowly derail, one car at a time."
A 75 Kilometer Tear Through the Plate
The researchers identified several tears running through the oceanic plate. One especially dramatic feature involves an enormous offset where part of the slab has dropped by roughly five kilometers.
"There's a very large fault that's actively breaking the plate," Shuck explained. "It's not 100% torn off yet, but it's close."
Earthquake activity provides another clue about what is happening.
Along a tear stretching about 75 kilometers, some portions continue to produce earthquakes while others have become unusually quiet. That difference matters because earthquakes occur when connected blocks of rock build up stress and suddenly slip.
"Once a piece has completely broken off, it no longer produces earthquakes because the rocks aren't stuck together anymore," he said.
The absence of earthquakes along part of the tear therefore suggests that a section of the plate has already separated. According to the researchers, that detached area is gradually expanding.
Earth's Crust May Break Apart Piece by Piece
Rather than failing in one enormous event, the subduction zone appears to be shutting down through a series of smaller breakups.
Researchers describe the process as "episodic" or "piecewise" termination. Individual sections tear away at different times, slowly dismantling the larger tectonic system.
Transform boundaries play an important role. These are faults where sections of Earth's crust move sideways past one another. In this setting, they can act almost like geological scissors, cutting across the plate and helping isolate individual fragments.
Once a piece becomes separated, it can form a microplate. A microplate is essentially a smaller piece of Earth's rigid outer shell that moves somewhat independently from the major tectonic plates surrounding it.
Meanwhile, nearby portions of the larger plate can continue sinking.
As more pieces detach, the remaining plate loses some of the downward pull that keeps subduction going. Shuck compares the process to removing cars from a runaway train. Eventually, there is not enough of the system left to continue in the same way.
The breakup of each individual section can take several million years. Together, however, these episodes can eventually bring an entire subduction zone to an end.
Ancient Tectonic Mysteries Begin to Make Sense
The discovery may help explain geological puzzles seen in other parts of the world.
Scientists have found abandoned plate fragments and unusual sequences of volcanic rocks that appear to record the final stages of ancient subduction systems. Until now, researchers had evidence that these systems had broken apart, but much less direct information about how the process unfolded.
One important example can be found off Baja California.
There, geologists have identified fossil microplates left behind by the Farallon plate, an enormous ancient oceanic plate that once extended across a large portion of the eastern Pacific.
Those fragments have long suggested that the Farallon plate did not simply disappear in one event. The Cascadia observations now offer a possible explanation for how such remnants form.
Instead of collapsing all at once, a dying subduction zone may gradually unravel, leaving smaller plate fragments scattered behind as geological evidence.
Tearing Plates Could Trigger Volcanic Changes
The breakup can also change what happens deeper beneath Earth's surface.
When a piece of a sinking plate separates, an opening called a "slab window" can form. This gap allows hotter material from the mantle to rise toward the surface.
That rising material can alter magma production and potentially contribute to episodes of volcanic activity.
As the breakup continues, tectonic boundaries can shift, additional microplates can form, and different parts of the subduction system may shut down at different times.
"It's a progressive breakdown, one episode at a time," said Shuck. "And it matches really well with what we see in the geologic record, where volcanic rocks get younger or older in a sequence that reflects this step-by-step tearing."
That connection between modern observations and ancient rocks gives researchers a new way to interpret the remains of long vanished plate boundaries.
What This Means for Cascadia Earthquakes
The findings also raise an important question for the Pacific Northwest: could these newly identified tears affect future earthquakes?
Researchers now want to understand whether a large earthquake could continue rupturing across one of the breaks or whether the damaged sections of the plate might alter the path of a rupture.
A rupture is the rapid movement along a fault that produces an earthquake. The distance a rupture travels, and the structures it encounters along the way, can strongly influence the size and behavior of an earthquake.
For now, the researchers emphasize that the discovery does not significantly change Cascadia's earthquake hazard on a human timescale.
The region is still capable of producing extremely large earthquakes and tsunamis. The breakup observed beneath the ocean is unfolding over millions of years, not decades or centuries.
However, adding these newly discovered structures to earthquake models could eventually improve scientists' understanding of how future ruptures may behave.
For geologists, Cascadia is offering something even rarer: a chance to watch one of Earth's great tectonic systems slowly dismantle itself, one piece at a time.

Qatar mulls VAT amid budget pressures from Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:18:41 UTC
21:18:41 KST

Breadcrumb
Qatar mulls VAT as effects budget pressures hit suppliers and consumers due to Iran war
As part of the Qatari government's plans to diversify government revenues and modernise the financial system, the issue of imposing value-added tax (VAT) has returned to the forefront of the economic scene.
Qatari Finance Minister Ali bin Ahmed Al-Kuwari revealed on the sidelines of the Qatar Economic Forum, held recently in New York, that the government is considering imposing VAT as one of the options available to diversify public revenues and fill financing gaps.
The statement came as it was revealed that Qatar's general budget recorded a financial deficit of 36 billion riyals (amounting to around $9.8 billion) during the first half of this year.
The deficit is attributed to pressure from declining exports of liquefied natural gas and its derivatives due to regional geopolitical conditions and disruption to navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as QatarEnergy's declaration of force majeure since March.
With the expected implementation of the new tax approaching, questions are emerging about the nature of the tax, how it will be applied and its impact on companies and consumers, amid efforts to align its standards with those of the Gulf Cooperation Council countries.
How will VAT be applied?
Legal adviser Ahmed Salem Al-Omar told The New Arab that "value-added tax is an indirect tax imposed on the import and supply of goods and services. It is a tax system that Qatar intends to implement to align with the rest of the Gulf Cooperation Council countries."
"Unlike corporate tax, which is imposed on profits, value-added tax is a consumption tax imposed on the value added to goods and services at each stage of the supply chain, starting with manufacturing, through distribution and ending with the final sale," he explained.
He noted that "the imposition of this tax came through a decision issued by the Supreme Council of the Gulf Cooperation Council (leaders' summit) at the 36th session held in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, in December 2015 concerning the imposition of value-added tax in GCC countries."
The decision confirmed that member states should implement the agreement and impose the tax at a basic rate of 5%.
The Gulf Cooperation Council introduced VAT to diversify sources of revenue and establish a unified tax system across member states. It applies to most goods and services, with each country setting its own rates based on its financial needs.
Regarding how it will be applied, Al Omar explained that, in practice, companies will impose VAT on sales and can recover the tax paid on purchases, known as "input tax", while paying the difference to the relevant authority, the General Tax Authority.
The system is expected to be progressive, fair and unified.
Favourable tax environment
"Qatar has a favourable tax environment that makes it easier to understand the differences between systems. It does not impose personal income tax on the salaries of citizens and residents and applies a corporate tax of only 10% to the foreign ownership share, with a full exemption for companies owned by Qatari and GCC citizens," the legal adviser Omar noted.
In this context, VAT represents a qualitative addition targeting consumption rather than income, preserving the attractiveness of the labour and investment market.
"As of the beginning of 2025, Qatar implemented a unified customs tariff for GCC countries using 12-digit customs codes. This expanded the previous system, which relied on eight digits, and requires all importers to ensure they use the updated classification system when submitting customs declarations through the Al Nadeeb customs clearance system," Omar explained.
Customs duty exemptions are available for military projects, diplomatic imports, industrial projects financed by the Qatar Development Bank and goods imported into designated free zones.
Expected rates and sectors
Estimates and the GCC unified agreement indicate that the basic VAT rate will be 5%, which is the most likely rate for the initial phase.
According to Omar, tax treatment will be distributed as follows: the standard 5% rate will apply to most consumer and commercial goods and services, while a zero rate will apply to exports, international transport and some medicines and medical products, supporting the competitiveness of Qatari products.
VAT exemptions are expected to cover financial services, health care, education and residential real estate, with the aim of protecting essential services and reducing the burden on households.
A comparison of Gulf experiences in implementing the tax shows variation in rates: 15% in Saudi Arabia, 10% in Bahrain, 5% in the United Arab Emirates and Oman, while Kuwait has not yet begun applying it.
This makes a lower rate in Qatar consistent with the UAE and Oman model and would reduce the impact of implementation, he said.
New revenues and development spending
For his part, economic expert and financial markets analyst Ahmed Akl told The New Arab that "the impact of applying VAT on the economy in general will be reflected in increased state revenues and diversification of income sources, giving additional capacity for development spending in the coming periods."
"Economic activity will vary from one sector to another", pointing out that "some companies will benefit, particularly financial, tax and technology services companies that provide the necessary support for implementing this system," Akl noted.
"At the same time, there will be no significant impact on exempt services and goods. They may even see increased demand, as they are a preferred option for maintaining price stability," he added.
In terms of sectors to subjected to the tax, Akl said that "some companies may have to reprice their products to absorb the new cost, increasing the cost of obtaining certain goods and services."
"Other companies, however, may absorb the tax within their profit margins, particularly if the rates are moderate, reducing the impact on consumers," he said.
The economic expert stressed that Qatar already has "advanced infrastructure that qualifies it for smooth implementation of the tax, including tax, logistical, technical and digital infrastructure and cybersecurity, all of which the state has worked seriously on in recent years."
Regarding precise details such as the tax rate and exempt sectors, he explained that "the full picture will become clear when the law is finally issued. Exemptions are expected to include vital sectors affecting daily life, similar to what has been implemented in neighbouring countries."
The rates and launch date will depend on several factors, including regional economic and geopolitical developments, with the picture expected to become fully clear before the end of this year.
"The general equation combines increased costs for certain goods with stable or increased demand for other exempt goods. All of this serves the state's interests by providing a new financial resource to support development spending over the medium and long term," Akl concluded.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

Details

SBU officers exposed the enemy’s plan in advance and detained the agent

The investigation established that he had been recruited by the Russian special service through a Telegram channel offering "easy" earnings.

"We have already brought charges against the perpetrator, Mr. Ihor M., for committing the crime of intentional murder, attempted murder of the victims, and infliction of grievous bodily harm," the spokesperson said, adding that the charges carry a penalty of up to life imprisonment, PAP writes on Friday.

The police and prosecutor's office have interviewed about 20 people who were on the territory of the monastery complex, as well as Border Guard officers who processed Ihor M.'s entry. Ptashka Drones Equips Its FPV Drones With Microphones and Multizhdun Feature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:18:06 UTC
21:18:06 KST

Ukrainian company Ptashka Drones has equipped all of its FPV drones with microphones and integrated the Multizhdun feature.
The update allows operators to detect enemy equipment and personnel by sound, the company told Militarnyi.
The module provides high sensitivity for detecting potential targets at a considerable distance from the ambush position.
“From a distance of 200 meters, the microphone clearly picks up the sound of a vehicle traveling along the road,” a Ptashka Drones representative said.
The Multizhdun feature allows an unlimited number of UAVs in standby mode to be connected to a single ground control station.
The system is designed to ensure clear separation of communication and alert channels between connected drones.
“Operators can control and listen to what is happening through headphones on one selected drone, while the others display a light indication showing the volume level,” the company explained.
The drone’s standby time depends on its variant, battery capacity, and flight range.
For example, the Ptashka 15-O-30km model can remain in ambush mode for up to five hours after landing 25 km from the operator.
It is worth noting that in May, Postup Solutions unveiled the autonomous Scan Horizon counter-FPV drone system equipped with a net launcher from Ptashka Drones.
Scan Horizon combines several types of sensors, including acoustic, visual, and radar.
This combination has enabled the developers to significantly reduce false alarms while improving the system’s reliability and accuracy.

Poltava Polytechnic building modernized for EUR 1.75 mln
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:12:32 EEST
21:12:32 KST

Building "F" of the National University "Yuri Kondratiuk Poltava Polytechnic," used by almost 3,000 students and teachers, has reopened in Poltava following a EUR 1.75 million energy-efficiency modernization, the European Investment Bank (EIB) said.
The works lasted about 20 months, from January 2025 to September 2026. Funding was provided as a grant from the Eastern Europe Energy Efficiency and Environment Partnership (E5P) Fund.
As part of the modernization, automated heat supply controls were installed in the building and energy metering systems were upgraded, which is expected to reduce energy consumption. New ramps and tactile navigation were installed for people with disabilities.
In addition, the building has been equipped with a shelter for more than 400 people, allowing in-person classes to continue during air alerts.
The teaching facilities can accommodate 1,422 students simultaneously. The building also houses lecture rooms, specialized laboratories and computer classrooms.
"Even during the war, Ukrainian universities remain places where people learn, teach and build their future. By modernizing them, we help keep education going today while investing in the skills and knowledge Ukraine will need for recovery and in the future," EIB Vice President Karl Nehammer said.
The modernization of Building "F" is part of a broader upgrade of Poltava Polytechnic. Work is currently underway at Dormitory No. 2, while the reconstruction of Buildings "7" and "P" is planned. Overall, the EIB's Ukraine Higher Education project covers 10 university buildings and provides EUR 10.8 million in financing.
The Ukraine Higher Education project aims to improve the energy efficiency of buildings at 16 Ukrainian universities. Thermal modernization of 13 of them is financed through a EUR 120 million EIB loan, of which EUR 50 million was reallocated in 2022 for urgent support for Ukraine. Another three universities receive loan financing from the Nordic Environment Finance Corporation (NEFCO) totaling EUR 12 million.
Six of the 16 universities are also to receive EUR 10 million in grant funding from the E5P Fund. The European Commission has additionally provided EUR 3.15 million in technical assistance for implementation of the project, which is coordinated by the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine.

Speaking to NBC News and other news organizations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Thursday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said, “We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections.” He urged the US to return to a June memorandum of understanding outlining a temporary ceasefire, which later collapsed.

US seeking to revive Russia-Ukraine ceasefire talks

US seeks to revive Russia-Ukraine ceasefire talks as seven killed in Kyiv
Deadly attacks continue on the ground as Kyiv and Moscow both confirm plans to relaunch trilateral talks.
The United States is working to arrange a new round of talks in a bid to end the four-and-a-half-year Russia-Ukraine war, while deadly attacks continue on the ground.
Kyiv and Moscow both confirmed on Friday the plan to relaunch trilateral talks. The move follows negotiations that started earlier this year before the US efforts to broker an end to hostilities petered out amid Washington’s war on Iran. The United Arab Emirates has been proposed as the host of the new talks.

“The American side has proposed meeting at a technical level in a three-way format,” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters. “We are awaiting a proposal from the United States regarding the date, and the US has suggested the Emirates as a possible location.”
Zelenskyy also said he urged US President Donald Trump to press China’s Xi Jinping to use his influence in Moscow to help diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
Later on Friday, the Kremlin confirmed that a trilateral meeting could take place soon, although spokesman Dmitry Peskov said there were no details to add currently.
Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, visited Russia and Ukraine earlier this month in a bid to jump-start the bid to secure a ceasefire.
The US stance has previously been criticised for favouring Russia’s narrative, with Moscow insisting that Ukraine cede territory that Russia has illegally occupied, demilitarise and drop ambitions to join NATO.
Russia’s presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev reportedly met with Witkoff and Kushner in the US on September 24. Peskov said those talks were about potential economic cooperation.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Friday that all proposals for a deal to end the fighting remained on the table, but Moscow still needed to assess what was in its best interest, Russian news agencies reported.
Putin said that Moscow was ready to resume negotiations with Kyiv after last week’s Russian parliamentary elections, but Ukraine had launched attacks on Moscow and hit polling stations. “They should therefore be made to feel Russia’s retaliatory strikes and understand that no provocative actions, no stirring up the situation to secure a result, will work,” Putin said.
Russia and Ukraine trade attacks
As efforts to renew peace negotiations continue, Moscow and Kyiv have not ceased attacks.
Ukraine’s air force said it shot down 267 out of 295 drones launched by Russia overnight.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least seven people, including a 14-year-old boy, were killed in Russian strikes on the capital on Friday. Another 46 were injured in the attacks, including 15 people receiving treatment in hospitals in Kyiv.
In the southern Odesa region, Governor Oleh Kiper said one person was killed and another injured in a series of “massive” Russian strikes on a residential area and logistics premises of a postal operator.
Separately, steelmaker ArcelorMittal said it was shutting down production at Ukraine’s largest steel plant after four strikes in five weeks caused extensive damage and killed five workers at the southeastern plant.
On the other side of the conflict, emergency services said one person was killed and one wounded in a drone attack on a market near the Russian-controlled town of Horlivka in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
Russia said its air defence units destroyed about 50 drones over the Rostov region overnight and a drone attack damaged the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery, forcing it to suspend operations.
Dmitry Makhonin, governor of Russia’s Perm region, said in a statement on Telegram that air defences in the region shot down 39 drones during overnight strikes, which he said killed one person who succumbed to wounds inflicted during the attack.
Aleksandr Gusev, governor of the Russian border region of Voronezh, said 13 people were injured in the regional capital, and that debris from downed drones damaged several non-residential and industrial buildings.
Ukraine recently struck two other major Russian oil refineries in Moscow and Yaroslavl. Zelenskyy asserted that refineries in Bashkortostan and the Samara region had also been hit in the past 24 hours.
The Ukrainian leader also reported unspecified strikes in the Black Sea. He added that he has held talks with India, Turkiye, Egypt and other Middle East countries concerning efforts to unblock shipping in the Black Sea, where Russia has targeted cargo vessels.
Defence aid for Ukraine
Separately, Zelenskyy said that Trump told him Ukraine will be granted permission to produce advanced Patriot air defence missiles.
Kyiv desperately needs additional air defences to counter Russia’s increasing drone and missile attacks, but Trump has delayed approval.
Should a licence be issued, it would be more than a year before Kyiv could put any new Patriot systems into service, leaving Zelenskyy in the US to attend the United Nations General Assembly to continue his pleas for additional support from allies.
“In recent days, during our meetings, Ukraine has openly informed our partners: Russia will only escalate as winter approaches unless there is pressure,” Zelenskyy wrote on X on Friday.
“For diplomacy to work, US sanctions must be implemented and European sanctions must be strengthened.”
European Union member countries agreed on Friday to release $7.5bn in EU funds linked to military aid for Ukraine.
In a post on X, Kaja Kallas, EU foreign policy chief, said the money will come from the European Peace Facility and will go towards joint procurement of equipment.
“Moscow’s hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing the opposite,” she said.

US arms sales to Israel surge to $21.6 bn in 20 months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:07:35 UTC
21:07:35 KST

Breadcrumb
US arms sales to Israel worth $21.6 billion in 20 months
Notifications submitted by the US President Donald Trump administration to Congress, along with US State Department data covering the period from 20 January 2025 to 17 September 2026, show that the Trump administration has approved arms deals for Israel worth $21.6 billion in just 20 months.
The value of military aid, funded by US taxpayers, and arms deals approved by former President Joe Biden for Israel between October 2023 and early 2025 exceeded $17.9 billion, according to a study by Brown University.
These weapons were used in the genocide in Gaza and the killing of more than 50,000 civilians, children and women during this period.
September 2026: $2.8 billion in weapons
The US State Department informally notified the offices of the four top Republican and Democratic members in the House of Representatives and Senate last week of a $2.8 billion military aid deal involving new weapons for Israel that Washington is preparing to conclude.
The deal includes 40,000 2,000-pound bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrating warheads.
A 2,000-pound bomb is considered one of the most destructive munitions in the world, as its explosion sends metal fragments thousands of feet in all directions and can penetrate metal and thick concrete.
Despite opposition from Democrats, the deal is expected to pass as usual under emergency authority that allows the administration to bypass congressional objections.
Historically, Congress has failed to stop any arms deal.
The following are the main previous large deals:
January 2025: $2.04 billion
After the Biden administration had previously sent shipments of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, and as criticism mounted following their use in the genocide in Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of children and women, his administration suspended one shipment in 2024.
In the first week of the Trump administration after his return to the White House in January 2025, he announced the immediate lifting of the ban on that shipment.
The shipment was valued at $2.04 billion.
February 2025: $7.4 billion
In the first week of February 2025, the US State Department informed Congress in two separate statements that it had approved an arms deal for Israel worth $7.4 billion.
It included 20,000 bombs, guidance systems and equipment worth $6.75 billion, and 3,000 Hellfire air-to-ground missiles worth $660 million.
The administration bypassed congressional notification to obtain approval.
The Trump administration used emergency powers that allow for immediate sales, citing national security interests, to bypass the usual congressional review procedures.
It provided Israel with a $675 million deal including 5,000 1,000-pound bombs and guidance kits and a $295 million deal including Caterpillar bulldozers.
The deal was announced at a value of $3.01 billion, but it included what the administration had announced in January 2025.
June 2025: $510 million
Following the US-Israeli attack on Iran in June 2025, and to rebuild Israel's stockpile, the Trump administration approved the provision of high-precision guidance systems to the Israeli military, worth $510 million.
The deal included more than 7,000 guidance kits for offensive munitions.
January 2026: $6.67 billion
In September 2025, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing sources, that the Trump administration was seeking congressional approval for an arms deal with Israel worth more than $6 billion.
The deal would be funded through the Foreign Military Financing programme, or military aid.
In January, the deal was announced with a total value of $6.67 billion. It includes 30 Apache helicopters, doubling Israel's fleet of this type of aircraft, 3,250 assault vehicles and other equipment.
March 2026: $650 million
One week after the US-Israeli war on Iran began this year, Israel requested more than 20,000 bombs.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as stated in a statement in March 2026, determined that an emergency existed requiring the sale to Israel to be completed immediately and the deal to be exempted from congressional review.
The deal was announced at a value of $650 million and included 12,000 1,000-pound bombs, as well as 500-pound bombs.
Reuters also quoted an official as saying that Israel would purchase an additional $298 million worth of munitions through direct sales.
May 2026: $992 million
On 1 May, Rubio again used emergency powers to approve a deal for Israel to purchase 10,000 APKWS laser-guided rocket systems worth $992.4 million.
These rockets have been used as countermeasures against Iranian drones because of their lower cost compared with expensive weapons.
This means that the total value of the deals announced and approved by the administration so far is $19.2 billion.
It will rise to $21.6 billion when the administration completes procedures for the latest deal, with at least half of the amount being military aid funded by US taxpayers.

The Promises the Afghanistan War Left Behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:06:00 UTC
21:06:00 KST

“It felt almost like you were playing God with their life at that moment,” recalled Joe Laude, executive director of the Operation Allies Refuge Foundation (OAR), reflecting on the final days of the U.S. evacuation from Kabul. A Marine machine-gunner with Echo Company, 2nd Battalion, 1st Marines who served at Abbey Gate during the evacuation in August 2021, Laude witnessed firsthand the impossible choices facing Americans as approximately 123,000 people were evacuated and thousands of Afghans sought a way out.
Every decision – to let someone through the gate, to turn someone away – carried life-altering consequences. When the last U.S. aircraft departed Kabul on August 30, 2021, those decisions lingered. For people like Laude, the uncertainties remained: Who could he have helped? Who was left behind? And what did it mean to feel responsible for people he could not protect?
Psychologists describe these experiences as moral injury, the psychological and ethical harm that occurs when individuals witness, participate in, or are unable to prevent actions that violate their deeply held moral beliefs and values. In the aftermath of the United States’ 20-year war in Afghanistan, that injury can take the form of responsibility, helplessness, perceived betrayal, and the painful belief that a promise was left unfulfilled.
For two decades, Americans and Afghans worked shoulder to shoulder in pursuit of a shared mission. Afghan interpreters, journalists, civil society leaders, educators, and security personnel risked their lives alongside American soldiers, diplomats, and aid workers. These relationships were often more than professional. They were built through years of shared danger, trust, friendship, and a belief that those who had stood beside one another would be protected if the situation deteriorated. However, with the Taliban’s return in August 2021, much of that shared progress disappeared almost overnight.
Lida Kharooti Sayeed, who served as a judge on Afghanistan’s Anti-Corruption Serious Crimes Court for 13 years before the Taliban returned to power, remembers with gratitude the Americans who tried to help her and others like her.
“I do not blame the individuals who tried to help us,” she said. “Many of them showed kindness and compassion where people were frightened and uncertain about their future. Their efforts meant a great deal to Afghan people like me.”
Sayeed’s gratitude complicates an easy narrative of American failure. The people who formed these relationships fought on the same side of a war. They were people who trusted one another.
That trust also made the withdrawal so difficult for those who were unable to protect the people they had worked beside. Laude describes the guilt he felt: “I had betrayed the Afghan community, even though it was ultimately our leadership’s decision that led to what happened.”
That distinction did not necessarily ease the burden. Knowing that institutions and leaders made the ultimate decisions did not erase the responsibility he felt toward the Afghans who were calling, asking for help, and waiting for a way out.
Helping Afghan allies became a way to channel that unresolved feeling into action. Through OAR, Laude has turned his experience in Kabul into work supporting veterans struggling with moral injury through peer support, humanitarian service, research, and advocacy.
Laude acknowledged that staying busy also meant putting his own emotions aside. “Part of what I did was try to mask the emotional side of this situation through work. That’s why I started OAR. I tried to take away from my own healing and help other people.”
For some, continuing to serve Afghan partners may be a form of moral repair – not an attempt to pretend the past can be fixed, but a decision to remain accountable to the values and friendships that still matter.
For Afghan partners left behind, the story did not end with the evacuation. Families remain separated, immigration cases stretch on, and careers and lives are disrupted.
Sayeed is still rebuilding the life she lost. She’s now a visiting scholar and researcher at the William & Mary Law School.
“We survived very difficult days, but surviving was only the beginning,” she said. “We are still trying to rebuild our lives, support our families, continue our education, and find meaningful opportunities.”
Five years later, Afghanistan is still often discussed in terms of the political failures surrounding the withdrawal. Those debates are important, but they do not capture everything that remained after the last plane left Kabul. What happens to the relationships built during 20 years of war when the war itself is over? Can there be closure?
For some, the answer has been to keep showing up. “That closure isn’t necessarily going to come through the leadership that betrayed you. Instead, I think it comes through relationships at the grassroots level,” Laude said.
For Laude, those relationships offer more than a path toward closure. They shape how he answers a harder question about the war itself: whether the years of service, sacrifice, and relationships built along the way ultimately mattered.
“One of the most important long-term psychological questions is whether any of it mattered,” Laude said. “I believe it does matter.”
What endures, five years later, is not only the memory of the withdrawal, but the relationships and obligations it could not erase. The war may have ended, but for those who believed they were responsible for one another, the question of what was owed did not end with it.

Hackers steal $352 million from major crypto exchange
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:05:05 UTC
21:05:05 KST

Hackers steal $352 million from major crypto exchange
Hackers have stolen nearly $352 million from major cryptocurrency exchange Bitget, prompting the company to suspend withdrawals. The breach comes amid mounting concern that AI is making cyberattacks easier to carry out.
Bitget detected unauthorized transfers from its wallets on Thursday evening, CEO Gracy Chen said. She stressed, however, that customer funds are safe and that the loss is covered by the company’s User Protection Fund, which holds more than $464 million.
The stolen assets came from parts of Bitget’s “hot” and “warm” wallets, which are used to process transactions and hold funds readily available for transfer. Its offline “cold” wallets were not affected, according to Chen.
She added that although withdrawals have been temporarily suspended, deposits and trading remain available while the company investigates the breach.
Bitget has not identified the perpetrators, but Chen said, without elaborating, that the company suspects North Korean involvement.
Blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain has estimated that the attackers have already converted about $183 million of the stolen assets into Ether tokens.
The theft follows other major attacks on cryptocurrency infrastructure this year. Earlier this month, around $320 million in Bitcoin was drained from a wallet used by the Liquid Network, although most of it was later returned.
In August, users of Coldcard hardware wallets also lost at least $89 million after attackers exploited a flaw in how the devices generated the secret keys protecting their funds. Coldcard’s maker has warned that AI-assisted code review could uncover old software flaws faster than developers can address them.
The growing capabilities of AI have also been linked to an overall increase in cyberattacks on cryptocurrency platforms. Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said it has recorded a 440% increase in AI-assisted malicious entries since powerful open-source coding tools became widely available, from about two a day to 11.
Beyond cryptocurrency, reports of AI agents gaining unauthorized access to real systems during unrelated tasks and security tests have raised questions about whether developers can reliably keep them within their assigned limits, or prevent malicious actors from using more capable models to find vulnerabilities and carry out attacks on a larger scale.
Executives at Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind and xAI have backed calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful systems.

Three Russian defense-industrial enterprises and two oil refineries — the General Staff revealed the significance of the latest strikes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Three Russian defense-industrial enterprises and two oil refineries — the General Staff revealed the significance of the latest strikes
Kyiv • UNN
The Defense Forces struck missile-production enterprises, two oil refineries, and two Russian radar stations. Fires were recorded at plants in Perm and Novoshakhtinsk.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed that three important enemy enterprises involved in missile production, as well as two Russian oil refineries, were hit. The General Staff reported the results on September 25, UNN writes.
Details
"On the night of September 25, 2026, the NVP Iskra Plant enterprise was hit in Ulyanovsk, Ulyanovsk region, russian federation," the General Staff said in a statement.
JSC "NPP "Iskra Plant" is part of the Almaz-Antey Aerospace Defense Concern and is an enterprise of the military-industrial complex of the russian federation. It specializes in the production of semiconductor devices and component parts for military-industrial complex enterprises.
The enterprise specializes in producing component parts for manufacturers of radio-electronic equipment, measuring instruments, communications systems, and special-purpose equipment, and is part of the Almaz-Antey concern.
As part of the cooperative production system, it participates in the manufacture of Kh-59M2/M2A guided air-to-surface missiles and the 72V6 Pantsir-S anti-aircraft gun-and-missile combat vehicle (and its modifications).
"In addition, the Efremov Synthetic Rubber Plant in the city of Efremov, Tula region, and JSC Voronezhsintezkauchuk in the area of the city of Voronezh, Voronezh region, were hit," the General Staff stated.
Both enterprises are involved in the production of solid rocket fuel, in particular for Iskander tactical ballistic missile systems.
"The targeting of such facilities represents Ukraine's exercise of its inherent right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military and economic potential of the russian federation," the General Staff emphasized.
Russian army oil refineries and radar stations were also hit, the General Staff confirmed.
"On September 24 and during the night of September 25, 2026, units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine hit a number of important military, fuel-and-energy, and industrial facilities of the Russian aggressor. In Perm, Perm Krai, russian federation, the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery was hit. A fire was recorded on the facility's premises," the General Staff stated.
The enterprise's processing capacity is approximately 13 million tonnes of oil per year. The plant produces fuel and other petroleum products. The enterprise is involved in supplying the armed forces of the russian federation with fuel and lubricants.
"In Novoshakhtinsk, Rostov region, russian federation, the Novoshakhtinsky oil refinery was hit. A fire was recorded on the enterprise's premises," the General Staff added.
In addition, according to the General Staff, the 64L6 Gamma-S1 and 39N6 Kasta-2E2 radar stations were hit in the Novoshakhtinsk area.
The enterprise's processing capacity is approximately 7.5 million tonnes of oil per year. The Novoshakhtinsky plant is one of the important suppliers of petroleum products in the south of the russian federation and participates in supplying the armed forces of the russian federation.
"The targeting of oil-refining enterprises represents Ukraine's exercise of its inherent right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military and economic potential of the russian federation," the General Staff stressed.
Reminder
Earlier, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that, thanks to our long-range sanctions, two oil refineries were hit this night—in Perm and Novoshakhtinsk—as well as the Iskra Plant defense enterprise in Ulyanovsk, while in the Rostov region the occupiers had two fewer radar stations.

Two Israeli soldiers killed after their own drone explodes in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:01:23 UTC
21:01:23 KST

ALBAWABA — Two Israeli reservists were killed in northern Gaza after an explosive drone piloted by their unit fell inside a military station and detonated as they approached it, a preliminary inquiry by the Israeli military found.
The soldiers were identified as Master Sgt. (res.) Nadav Kali, 24, of Har Halutz, and Master Sgt. (res.) Ofek Moalem, 23, of Jerusalem. Both served in the 7007th Battalion of the Jerusalem Brigade.
What occurred?
The incident occurred Thursday afternoon while the soldiers were operating miniature first-person-view explosive drones, referred to by the Israeli military as “Atalef,” or “Bat,” from a tactical post in northern Gaza.
The first drone, an initial military inquiry suggests, accomplished its task successfully. But a second drone crashed in the military base during takeoff and the reasons are still being investigated.
A few minutes later, the soldiers came over the fallen drone and lifted it up. The plane then exploded, leaving both men badly injured. The victims were transported to the Barzilai Medical Center in Ashkelon, where they were declared dead.
Israeli media indicated the incident took place at a military post near Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza. Among the possible causes for the failure being considered by investigators is if a communications fault might have brought the drone down. The final cause has not yet been ascertained.
Israeli military shoots down armed drones
Following the killings, the Israeli military temporarily banned activities with small drones that may carry explosive payloads, including suicide drones and planes meant to drop explosives on targets.
Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, chief of staff of the IDF, also authorized the formation of a team of experts headed by a brigadier general of the Ground Forces to study the tragedy and to see how similar situations might be prevented.
Separately, the head of the Ground Forces ordered the drones halted for at least 48 hours while the inquiry continues, with another review due following.

Air Force, Pentagon Work to Boost Military Spouse Employment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:01:00 UTC
21:01:00 KST

New Air Force, Pentagon, and White House initiatives are taking a new swing at an issue that has long frustrated military families: barriers to spouse employment.
Unemployment and underemployment have plagued military spouses for years, with the unemployment rate among military spouses holding steady at around 20 percent—despite initiatives to promote spouse preferences for hiring on base, support for remote work, and advocacy for making professional licenses more portable across state borders.
Improving spouses employment is not a “charitable initiative,” but a major retention and readiness incentive, argued Lyndsey Akers, a consultant with AFA’s United Forces & Families program.
“When military spouses have greater access to meaningful and sustainable careers, we strengthen the economic stability of military families,” Akers said at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference last week. “We support the conditions that enable continued service, and we connect employers with an experienced, adaptable, and often overlooked talent pool.”
Top-down interest from the White House’s new Military Spouse Commission is driving renewed interest in the topic.
Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Military Community and Family Policy Stephen Simmons said at the conference that the nation “has admired” the problem for too long; but “we haven’t done enough about it, and to get an issue the attention it needs, usually, first off, you have to elevate.”
Cindy Wilsbach, wife of Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach and a senior writer for presidential correspondence at the White House employee, said the new commission President Donald Trump’s interest.
“It was marching orders from the leader of the free world to say, ‘We see the military spouse family and we recognize there are some longstanding generational problems that we need to get after,’” Cindy Wilsbach said during a panel discussion.
Both Wilsbachs are members of the commission, as are all the service chiefs, their spouses, and their senior enlisted advisors, and their spouses, including:
- Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas A. Schiess and his wife Debbie Schiess
- Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David Wolfe and his wife, Dr. Doniel Wolfe
- Chief Master Sergeant of the Space Force John F. Bentivegna and his wife Cathy Bentivegna
“With the four spouses here going to be involved with the Military Spouse Commission, we’ve got an opportunity to make some real change to laws that prevent us from hiring people fast enough and putting people into jobs and places and moving positions around,” said CMSAF David Wolfe during a panel discussion.
Cindy Wilsbach said the commission won’t try to reinvent efforts already underway but instead “will add to the work that’s being done,” while raising the profile of the issue to give advocates access to the President and other high-level decision-makers.
Global Military Spouse Connection
One program that’s newly in place and starting to grow is the Air Force’s Global Military Spouse Connection, which started in June as a pilot program for just a few installations.
Officials say the program is meant to serve as a “bridge” between Active-Duty military spouses who have PCSed to a new location and local hiring managers.
“Using career field administrators, GMSC creates a structured, active pipeline to connect the military spouse talent pool with employment opportunities,” according to an Air Force release.
“We are assisting hiring managers in finding the best-qualified individual,” said career field administrator Wyteeshia McRoberts, in a statement. “We’re not contacting them to do favors. We are looking at resumes, seeing what they qualify for and making recommendations for the right jobs.”
CMSAF Wolfe highlighted the program in his Sept. 14 keynote address to the conference, noting how the program “went from idea to first action in only 60 days,” and promising rapid expansion. On Sept. 22, the Air Force announced the program was already available for spouses moving to the following locations:
- Luke Air Force Base, Ariz.
- Goodfellow Air Force Base, Texas
- Laughlin Air Force Base, Texas
- Mountain Home Air Force Base, Idaho
- Travis Air Force Base, Calif.
- Patrick Space Force Base, Fla.
- Ramstein Air Base, Germany
- RAF Croughton, U.K.
- RAF Mildenhall, U.K.
- RAF Lakenheath, U.K.
- RAF Feltwell, U.K.
- Kadena Air Base, Japan
SpouseWorks
While the Department of the Air Force has launched the new connection program, the Office of the Secretary of Defense is focused on better publicizing the programs it already has, said Simmons.
Until recently, spouses looking for Pentagon help to land jobs, scholarships, or fellowships were on their own navigating a confusing sea of acronyms: SECO, MyCAA, MSEP.
SECO stood for Spouse Education and Career Opportunities, but wasn’t visible enough to leaders or community members, Simmons said. So his team rebranded to “SpouseWorks” and changed the organization. Before, the program “was buried in one of our directorships through no fault of their own,” Simmons said. “But in my mind, … it needed to report directly to me, so we turned it from a sub-office to a directorship.”
Other programs were folded in, so that now there are also SpouseWorks Fellowship and SpouseWorks Scholarship programs. “We’re trying to make it very simple and easy to use.”
SpouseWorks offers training, education, and professional development; career coaches; and a job board. Simmons said the goal is to be a one-stop shop for military spouses and a resource for employers seeking high-quality employees.
Early returns are promising. “We’re up well over 50 to 80 percent usage year over year,” he said. “And we’re only about halfway through the first year of the SpouseWorks rebrand.”
Challenges Remain
Headwinds continue, however. “I wish we could say that we had a lot of consistency, but what happens is with every change of leadership, somebody has a bright idea and then a great program goes away,” said Sue Luangkhot Hoppin, president of the National Military Spouse Network. “We don’t dot the Is and cross the Ts and we don’t necessarily solidify the programs before we move on to the next one.”
Lack of consistency from base to base, due to different commanders’ priorities, is also a challenge, he said. Elevating the issue to department leaders can raise the profile and relieve operational commanders of an extra burden.
One policy change that had unintended consequences for families was the widespread rollback of remote work options for federal civilians. Because of frequent PCS moves, remote work is an ideal option for many military spouses. “Remote work is a lifeline for a lot of military spouses,” Luangkhot Hoppin said. “It allows them to work even if they have childcare issues. But if they have to go back to the office, all of a sudden they need to have access to affordable child care, and that’s become an issue.”
Liz O’Brien, senior vice president at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation, argued that remote work is only a piece of the equation, noting that during the COVID-19 pandemic, when remote work options surged, spouse unemployment stayed stubbornly high. Childcare is one of the biggest barriers to better spouse employment, O’Brien, Luangkhot Hoppin, and Simmons agreed. Simmons sees an “intrinsic relationship” between the two; without ready and available childcare, many spouses can’t work. If they have to wait months for childcare openings to materialize, their window for employment can begin to close down.
Simmons said the Pentagon is working multiple fronts to reduce the wait times for childcare, both through expanded capacity at its Child Development Centers as well as through partnerships with the Armed Forces YMCA, private industry, and support for informal childcare support.
“Year over year … our childcare wait lists are down 25 percent, which is phenomenal,” Simmons said. And the tie to spouse employment is clear. “As a result, you see that wait list drop, you also see the spouse employment drop.”
