Party Invite Phishing Scams Are the New Missed Connections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

This past April, while attending his nephew’s bar mitzvah on Cape Cod, Eric Umansky woke up to an inbox full of emails from people from his past. They all wanted to know the same thing: Was he actually throwing a party Saturday night?
The New York–based journalist wasn’t sure what party they were referring to, or why random acquaintances he’d met in passing 15 years ago were emailing him. On deadline and already stressed about work, he checked his phone, where more messages inquired about a supposed Paperless Post invite he’d sent for a “Special Private Dinner Party” at 7 pm on May 2.
Except Umansky hadn't sent the invite, and he wasn’t planning to host a party anytime soon.
As it turned out, he was an early victim of an email scam that has since become more widespread. What Umansky didn’t expect was the positive effect it would have on his social life.
In May, after receiving increased reports, the Federal Trade Commission issued a consumer alert warning about scammers sending “unexpected messages that look like they’re from well-known invitation platforms like Evite or Paperless Post,” noting how some messages “make you enter your email username and password to see event details” while others “tell you to enter a phone number and share a special code to RSVP.”
Umansky wasn’t sure how it happened; he thought he'd taken the necessary precautions to safeguard his email, including using two-factor authentication. All he could think to do was post a message on Facebook, LinkedIn, and his other social networks to notify people that he was, in fact, not having a party and, more importantly, “don’t come to my house.”
Phishing scams, which have proliferated across the last two decades, remain one of the biggest security risks faced both by individuals and companies. Email scams, in particular, can now be highly sophisticated, incorporating social engineering techniques like creating urgency or fear in a target and even leveraging the personal relationships between two people to manipulate a victim, what’s known as “spear phishing.” AI has only made those deceptions harder to weed out.
But in some recent cases, like Umansky’s, the fake party invite is having an unintended outcome: It is encouraging people to check in to see whether the message was actually real and, in doing so, has reignited dormant relationships.
“It was so striking to me after it happened that I actually had a thought that I was like, ‘Oh, is this a net positive?’” says Umansky, who over the last several months has reconnected with a handful of old friends and colleagues over lunch and via text. He recently spent an hour on Zoom with a former coworker who now lives in Mexico City. They hadn’t talked to each other in over a decade. “I was like, Oh, you know, I actually want to catch up with you about something. There was an idea I wanted to bat around with him, which we talked about for maybe 10 minutes. The rest of the time we talked about our lives.”
According to a 2024 study published in the scientific journal Communications Psychology examining social withdrawal, which surveyed 2,400 adults in the US, UK, and Canada, people are sometimes unwilling to contact old friends because they believe the other person won’t want to hear from them or they fear the interaction will be awkward. The research noted that “high priority placed on work and productivity in North America has led people to cut back on social connections and social time to meet increasing demands at work,” in addition to other life transitions, such as parenthood or moving to a new city.
But a suspicious party invite is exactly the kind of low-stakes incentive that has made initiating contact easier because it represents the one thing we all crave: a sense of belonging.
According to Lara Aknin, a professor of psychology at Simon Fraser University whose research has explored the hesitancy around reconnecting with lapsed contacts, only 30 percent of people actually check in with an old friend “even when we make doing so as easy as possible by helping them identify a desirable, feasible, and low-risk contact.”
With email scams, “people are motivated and willing to reach out to an old friend because the scam provides a legitimate excuse or social cover to do so,” she says. “In fact, people may even be slightly grateful for the reconnection opportunity this context affords, even though they hope the scam is false.”
Most people will only have a small number of close relationships in their lifetime, and it is even fewer these days; nearly half of the population (44 percent) have five or fewer acquaintances. “In the course of [scammers] taking advantage of that real desire, they are actually helping fill it,” Umansky says.
He’s not the only one who has reignited old relationships after being targeted by a scam. “I heard from a friend of more than 30 years,” Larry Persily wrote in the Wrangell Sentinel, a local newspaper in Alaska, of the trend. One source confirms with WIRED that they are back in touch with an ex they haven’t spoken to in years after receiving a fake invite.
To be clear, the unintended consequence of scam attempts may be reconnecting with lost friends, but they’re not all Zoom reunions and brunch. The FBI estimates that scammers tricked Americans out of $21 billion in 2025 alone, with help from AI.
Some of us remain impervious to the lure of the phishing trap invite. In late August, I received an unexpected Paperless Post invite—“Raise a Glass! Dinner & Drinks” the subject line read—from an acquaintance I hadn’t spoken to since 2017, though I immediately deleted it because I could barely remember who he was or why we even exchanged emails. I probably should have reached out. Maybe we both would’ve enjoyed the catch-up.

Socialism is More Popular Than Ever in the U.S., According to Polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

It’s undeniable. Socialism is on the rise—or at least growing in popularity in the U.S.
Forty-three percent of Americans have a positive view of socialism, the highest share since Gallup began tracking the measure since 2010. The latest survey, conducted Aug. 3-24, found that socialism has gained ground over time as several market-oriented economic concepts have lost favor. It now ranks ahead of big business, which has fallen to a positive rating of 35% from a peak of 58% in 2012.
Capitalism and free enterprise are still more popular than socialism. Capitalism’s positive rating, however, has fallen to 55% from a peak of 61% in 2010 and 2012. Free enterprise is now favored at 77%, compared to its peak of 89% in 2012. Small business remains the most favored economic system at 95%, relatively unchanged in 2010.
Those figures, however, mask sharp partisan differences. Democrats view socialism much more favorably than Republicans do, and their views have become more positive over time.
This shift has come as progressives and democratic socialists have defeated establishment candidates in several key Democratic primary contests. Zohran Mamdani’s election as New York City Mayor last year marked a breakthrough for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). In June, all three of his endorsed candidates won against establishment Democrats in congressional primaries in New York City.
Read More: Congress Is Headed for a Massive Turnover
Progressives also won high-profile primaries elsewhere, including Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, both of whom have not adopted the socialist label, as well as DSA members and House candidates Melat Kiros in Colorado and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania. Democratic socialist Francesca Hong narrowly lost in the gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin, a battleground state.
What Brookings analysts dubbed a “DSA summer” serves to “signal that unhappiness with the Democratic establishment and, in the post-Biden world, opposition to elderly officeholders can be leveraged by young, charismatic DSA candidates—and reflect an impatience with party leadership that transcends ideology.”
Republicans have sought to portray those victories as evidence that the Democratic Party is moving too far left ahead of the November midterm elections, while Democratic leaders have tried to temper concerns about the party’s direction. In November 2025, the House voted 285-98 to approve a resolution denouncing the “horrors of socialism,” which was followed by another resolution condemning socialism that passed 220-192 earlier this month. A July analysis by the Cook Political Report found that center-left candidates dominated primaries in the competitive House seats most likely to determine control of Congress, suggesting that progressive victories may not signal a leftward shift across the country.
“If left-wing nominees manage to win in swing districts, their overall movement will be strengthened,” the August Brookings analysis said. “If they lose districts deemed winnable and cost Democrats control of the House and Senate, their mainstream presence will likely be diminished.”
Still, changing views among the American public could indicate growing openness to what was once a political red line.
Here’s what the latest polls say.
Partisan split
Socialism isn’t gaining popularity universally in the U.S.
Most of the increase in socialism’s positive rating through 2025 came from growing favorability among Democrats. In 2010, 50% of Democrats viewed socialism positively, according to Gallup. That rose to 66% last year, and remained relatively unchanged at 65% this year. Socialism now matches free enterprise in favorability among Democrats, following a sharp decline in their positive views of free enterprise since 2021.
Democrats have also viewed socialism more favorably than capitalism since 2016, when 54% of Democrats viewed capitalism positively, while 60% viewed socialism positively. That year marked a breakthrough for the DSA as longtime Senator Bernie Sanders (I, Vt.) brought the organization to national attention during his presidential run.
Capitalism’s positive rating has further fallen among Democrats, declining from 42% last year to 35%.
Other polls have found a similar pattern among Democrats. A CBS/YouGov poll, conducted Aug. 12-14, found that 58% of Democrats viewed socialism positively, compared to 32% for capitalism. College-educated Democrats were especially positive about socialism, with 71% viewing it favorably.
Meanwhile, 50% of Democrats viewed capitalism negatively, compared with 18% for socialism. That contrasts with the broader public, which overall favored capitalism to socialism.
The poll also found that half of Democrats viewed the label “democratic socialist” positively.
A Marquette Law School poll highlighted by CNN in June similarly found that the DSA had a higher net favorability among Democrats and Democrat-leaning independents than Democrats in Congress by 13 points. A national survey conducted by Data for Progress in August 2025 found that Democrats preferred democratic socialism to capitalism by a 58-percentage-point margin.
Socialism has also grown in popularity among political independents, accounting for the overall boost to socialism’s favorability in the latest Gallup poll. The share of independents rating socialism positively rose from 37% last year to 45%, surpassing big business which fell to a record low of 32%. Capitalism, free enterprise, and small business still ranked above socialism in favorability among independents.
Republicans remained overwhelmingly skeptical of socialism, with just 14% viewing it positively. Large majorities of Republicans continued to have positive views of small business, free enterprise, and capitalism, while 62% of Republicans viewed big business positively.
Still, Americans’ economic views are more complicated than the results might initially suggest, according to a Gallup analysis from August. The report, based on open-ended survey responses, found there is broad support for free-market principles like economic competition and market choice, despite concerns about capitalism spurring economic inequality and excessive corporate power.
The CBS/YouGov poll, meanwhile, found that support for government intervention crossed party lines, with 75% of Democrats, 62% of independents, and 54% of Republicans supporting government price controls.
And the Data for Progress survey showed 70% of 1,257 respondents said the U.S. economic system is “rigged in favor of corporations and the wealthy” and favored replacing it with one that “gives working people a fair shot,” including 67% of independents and 58% of Republicans. Additionally, 83% of respondents, including 81% of independents and 80% of Republicans, agreed that social work and mental health are necessary parts of a public safety budget.
Generational differences
Younger Americans are more receptive to socialism, polls show.
According to Gallup, 57% of Americans aged 18 to 34 viewed socialism positively, compared with 43% for capitalism. The pattern was reversed among older adults: 65% of those aged 55 and older viewed capitalism positively, while 34% viewed socialism positively. Of Americans aged 35 to 54, 50% rated capitalism positively, while 45% rated socialism positively.
The August CBS/YouGov poll also found that younger Americans were more likely to perceive shrinking economic opportunities. Fifty-four percent of American adults under 30 said their opportunities to succeed are worse than their parents’ generation’s, compared with 31% of those aged 65 and older. Of those under 30, 80% also said buying or owning a home is harder for their generation than previous generations, while 71% saw worse prospects for financial security and 64% for having a good job.
Among those under 30, 61% described the U.S. economic system as somewhat or very unfair. Socialism was viewed positively by 43%, compared with 38% for capitalism. By contrast, 30% of those 65 and older viewed socialism positively and 59% viewed capitalism positively.

MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. Tatneft boosted oil production by 6.7% in the first half of 2026 to 14.32 mln tons, while its gas output added 6.6% to 469 mln cubic meters, according to the company’s report.
Tatneft also produced 7.98 mln tons of petroleum products and 518,000 tons of gas products in the reporting period, which is 9.63% lower and 9% higher compared to the same period last year, respectively.
Tatneft is one of Russia’s ten largest oil companies in terms of production volume. The Republic of Tatarstan is the company’s main shareholder, holding 34% of ordinary shares. Around 3% is represented by treasury shares, while 13% is held in ADRs. Other shareholders own 50% of the company’s shares.

You can find Out There some instances of Oddesa for Odessa, consistent with the general hypothesis. Although now the data is distorted by the recent politically-motivated anti-doubling trend in favor of just "Odesa," aimed at matching the Ukrainian spelling Одеса and disowning the Russian spelling Одесса. AFAIK that's just because of different orthographic conventions and Ukrainian hostility to orthographic-doubling-in-general – it doesn't signal a relevant pronunciation difference. (The Russian spelling is closer to the ancient Greek toponym Οδησσός, which was evoked for marketing purposes when the current city was founded in the 18th century.)
Also in combinations, like "Lake Oddesa" for Lake Odessa, Mich., or "Oddesa Beulah" for the racehorse Odessa Beulah which achieved success on the track circa 1938.
Yeah, it happens all the time. It’s interesting to observe that in our ‘orthographic lexicons’ for lack of a better term – we encode the fact that there is a germinate C or V graph, and then misapply the position of gemination.
For me it's reccomend … I mean recommend. Once I see it I know it's wrong but my fingers want to type it and sometimes writing by hand I can't remember until I see it.
Ukrainian hostility to orthographic-doubling-in-general
That's why Ukrainian has spellings like Вінниця and Запоріжжя. It's simply that these are different languages, with different grammars, not some stupid "hostility to orthographic doubling".

Abbas by video, Netanyahu in person: two messages at UNGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:57:48 UTC
19:57:48 KST

Breadcrumb
Abbas by pre-recorded video, Netanyahu in person: two contrasting messages at the UN
On Thursday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly from behind a screen, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu prepared to take the same podium in person, highlighting a disparity that went beyond the two leaders' contrasting messages.
Abbas spoke by pre-recorded video after the Palestinian delegation was denied the necessary US entry visas to attend the gathering in person, according to Palestinian officials.
His address focused on the war in Gaza, Israel's occupation, settlement expansion and the displacement of Palestinians, while calling for an end to the war, an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, reconstruction and a political process leading to an independent Palestinian state.
"We will not leave our homeland, nor will we accept displacement," Abbas vowed.
The Palestinian Authority president also pointed to the growing number of countries recognising the State of Palestine, saying 160 had now done so.
He called on other countries to follow suit and reiterated the Palestinian demand for full UN membership.
Abbas also called for the implementation of international resolutions concerning the Palestinian cause and stressed that recognition should be accompanied by a political process capable of establishing an independent Palestinian state.
His speech came as the Gaza war remained the centre of international attention, with the humanitarian crisis, destruction and displacement continuing to dominate discussions surrounding the UN gathering.
Limits of international recognition
Abbas devoted part of his address to the Israel's genocide of Gaza and the humanitarian conditions facing Palestinians there, while also warning about Israel's settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank.
He argued that settlement projects threaten the possibility of establishing a geographically contiguous Palestinian state and called for international efforts to address what he described as continuing violations of Palestinian rights.
The Palestinian president also called for implementation of the 20-point plan proposed by the US administration and the UN resolution on Gaza, presenting them as elements of a broader political framework for ending the war and addressing its aftermath.
Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Ahed Ferwana told The New Arab that "Abbas's speech sought to reinforce the Palestinian position through international law, diplomatic recognition and the growing number of countries supporting Palestinian statehood."
Ferwana said the Palestinian president delivered clear messages on halting the war, rejecting displacement, ending the occupation, stopping settlement expansion and establishing a Palestinian state.
But Abbas's absence from the UN hall itself illustrated what Ferwana described as an imbalance in the political and diplomatic tools available to the two sides.
The Palestinian leadership has expanded its diplomatic presence in recent years, particularly as more countries have recognised Palestine, but Ferwana said recognition alone could not alter conditions on the ground without mechanisms capable of exerting political pressure.
"The gap between international support for Palestinian statehood and developments in the occupied Palestinian territories remains one of the central challenges facing the Palestinian leadership," he added.
He also pointed to the diplomatic significance of physical presence at the General Assembly, saying a head of state or government attending the gathering has opportunities that a recorded speech cannot fully replicate.
"A leader attending in person can interact directly with foreign delegations, international media and diplomats and respond to developments surrounding the gathering," he explained.
In Abbas's case, however, his message reached the General Assembly through a screen, while the Palestinian delegation's inability to attend became part of the wider political story surrounding his address, according to Ferwana.
"The contrast became more pronounced when Netanyahu arrived at UN headquarters to deliver his own speech from the podium," he said.
Netanyahu focuses on 'security'
When Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes and crimes against humanity, took the podium, several delegations walked out in protest against his government's policies and its conduct of the war in Gaza.
Netanyahu responded by describing those who left as "moral cowards", while continuing with an address that devoted substantial attention to Israel's security concerns, Iran, Hezbollah and Israel's military operations in the region.
He argued that Israel's military action against Iran had been necessary for the country's survival and presented the broader regional confrontation through the lens of threats facing Israel.
Palestinian political analyst Akram Atallah told TNA that Netanyahu's address represented an attempt to shift the focus of international discussion away from the destruction in Gaza and towards Israel's security concerns.
"Netanyahu entered the General Assembly knowing that the Gaza war, civilian casualties and destruction would remain central to international criticism of Israel," he said.
"The Israeli prime minister therefore sought to frame the discussion around threats facing Israel, particularly Iran and armed groups in the region," Atallah added.
Netanyahu's presentation placed the Gaza war within a broader security narrative, allowing him to address audiences concerned about Iran, Hezbollah and the possibility of a wider regional confrontation while defending Israel's military conduct.
Atallah said, "The strategy was not simply about responding to criticism but about establishing the framework through which Netanyahu's speech would be understood."
Despite the walkouts, Netanyahu was able to use the UN platform directly and speak to international media gathered around the General Assembly, he believes.
"That physical access stood in contrast to Abbas's participation by video […] The difference was particularly visible because the two leaders addressed the same international institution during the same high-level gathering but approached the conflict from fundamentally different starting points," he said.
For Abbas, the central issues were the occupation, Palestinian statehood, settlement expansion, displacement and the humanitarian consequences of the Gaza war, he added.
For Netanyahu, the emphasis was on Israel's security, Iran, regional threats and the justification of Israeli military action, he continued.
Between rhetoric, law and political power
But Gaza-based political analyst Tayseer Abdullah criticised Netanyahu's speech in a Facebook post, arguing that the Israeli prime minister sought to present himself as the victim despite the international criticism directed at his government over the war in Gaza.
Abdullah wrote that Netanyahu had "dons the guise of the oppressed, the downtrodden, and the weak", describing what he considered a reversal of the positions of victim and perpetrator.
Abdullah also referred to the International Criminal Court arrest warrant against Netanyahu and questioned how the Israeli prime minister was able to travel to New York and address the General Assembly.
At the same time, Abdullah criticised statements by some Palestinian officials, including rhetoric about repeating the events of 7 October, arguing that such language could shift international attention away from the occupation, destruction and war and allow Israel to portray itself as the threatened party.
The 81st session of the General Assembly again provided a global stage for competing narratives over the Israel's ongoing genocide of the Palestinian people.
It also spotlighted how access, diplomatic leverage and the ability to shape the international conversation surrounding a war that has continued to define the region's politics.

UN coordinator calls for joint action to protect Caspian Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:57:14 UTC
19:57:14 KST

UN coordinator calls for joint action to protect Caspian Sea
TEHRAN – Protecting the Caspian Sea is not only an environmental priority but also a priority for sustainable development, UN Resident Coordinator in Iran Christine Weigand has said, noting that the environmental challenges facing the transboundary body of water require joint and collaborative solutions.
Weigand made the remarks at the seventh meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP7) to the Tehran Convention on the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Caspian Sea in Tehran on Wednesday.
The gathering of the five littoral states around a shared ecosystem provides an important opportunity to strengthen regional cooperation and translate common commitments into practical measures to protect the Caspian Sea, she said.
Noting that 2026 marks the 20th anniversary of the entry into force of the Tehran Convention, the UN official said the Caspian Sea has sustained human life and civilizations for thousands of years and remains a source of livelihoods and well-being, an important transportation route, a valuable reservoir of natural resources and a habitat for unique marine biodiversity.
“Protecting the Caspian Sea is not only an environmental priority, but a sustainable development priority,” she said, stressing that the health of the sea is directly linked to the livelihoods and well-being of surrounding communities, economic activities, sustainable natural resource management and regional resilience.
Environmental challenges, she added, do not stop at national borders. Marine pollution, biodiversity loss and mounting pressure on shared ecosystems have transboundary consequences and therefore require cross-border and participatory solutions.
Weigand described the Tehran Convention as an important framework for joint action by the littoral states, saying it facilitates the advancement of scientific knowledge, the exchange of data and experience, the development of effective policies and the translation of shared commitments into collective action.
She also highlighted the UN’s role in supporting environmental cooperation in the region, noting that the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) hosts the Tehran Convention Secretariat, while various UN agencies operating in the region draw on their complementary expertise to support the littoral states in advancing the convention’s objectives.
In Iran, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and UNEP are working with national and local partners under the broader Caspian Sea initiative to translate regional commitments on marine litter and plastic pollution into concrete action, she said.
Strengthening waste separation and recycling in coastal communities, promoting circular approaches to plastics and providing community-based grants for local solutions are among the measures being pursued under the initiative, she added.
The UN Resident Coordinator also underscored the need to engage the private sector and local communities, including women and young people, in improving waste management systems.
 
 “Protecting our seas is a shared responsibility, and no country, institution or organization can protect this unique ecosystem alone,” she said.

autonomous robotic hand walks on its fingertips like the addams family’s thing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:55:53 UTC
19:55:53 KST

ETH ZURICH TRAINS ROBOTIC HAND TO WALK ON ITS FINGERS
A robotic hand has apparently decided it no longer needs the rest of the robot. Researchers at ETH Zurich’s Soft Robotics Lab have developed an autonomous five-fingered hand that can walk across different surfaces, steer itself, recover after falling over and interact with objects — all using the same fingers normally reserved for grasping. Rather than adding wheels or legs to the system, the team turns the hand itself into a mobile robot, allowing its fingers to alternate between supporting, moving and manipulating its body.
The prototype is based on a commercially available anthropomorphic hand equipped with five fingers and 20 actuated joints, four for each finger. Researchers Amirhossein Kazemipour, Hehui Zheng and Robert K. Katzschmann added a compact onboard system containing a battery, sensors and computing hardware, bringing the complete untethered robot to 818 grams. The resulting machine needs no external arm to carry it around and, despite looking suspiciously ready for a role in The Addams Family, is intended as a practical experiment in mobile manipulation.
the robotic hand walks using its five fingers | all images courtesy of ETH Zurich
REINFORCEMENT LEARNING PUTS FIVE FINGERS TO WORK
Teaching a hand to walk is slightly more complicated than asking it to behave like a very small quadruped. Unlike legs, its five fingers have different geometries and ranges of motion, while the palm naturally sits at an angle. When one finger leaves the ground to take a step or interact with something, the others must continue balancing the robot’s entire weight. The researchers addressed this asymmetry through reinforcement learning, training locomotion policies in simulation before transferring them to the physical hand.
The results take the robot well beyond a tabletop demonstration. ETH Zurich’s hand was able to move untethered across 14 indoor and outdoor surfaces, including carpet, tile, metal grating, asphalt, grass, gravel and weathered stone. When deliberately placed on its side, it successfully pushed itself back upright in 21 of 25 trials. Its fingers can also switch from locomotion to manipulation: in one experiment, the robot supported itself while pressing keyboard arrow keys, correctly hitting 29 out of 32 targets. It then put those keyboard skills to excellent use by completing moves in the puzzle game Sokoban.
the autonomous system weighs 818 grams
AUTONOMOUS ROBOTIC HAND BECOMES ITS OWN MOBILE MANIPULATOR
Other experiments asked the hand to approach and push a small object toward a target, demonstrating how locomotion and manipulation can operate as part of the same system. This dual role is central to the research. Conventional robotic hands generally arrive at a task attached to an arm, which itself may need a larger mobile platform to move through space. Giving the end effector its own means of locomotion removes some of that hardware and could allow a larger robot to leave its hand close to an otherwise inaccessible area.
The researchers imagine a future system in which a robot places the hand near a narrow opening or confined workspace, letting it crawl independently toward a control or object, perform the required task and return to be collected. Further development will require better onboard perception and a broader range of movement, but the experiment already reframes a familiar piece of robotic anatomy: instead of designing another mechanism to carry the hand where it needs to go, ETH Zurich simply taught the fingers to take it there.
all five fingers double as legs
20 actuated joints control the hand’s movement
the hand navigates indoor and outdoor surfaces
project info:
name: Fingers as legs, Anthropomorphic hand design: Amirhossein Kazemipour, Hehui Zheng, Robert K. Katzschmann location: Soft Robotics Lab, ETH Zurich

EU to discuss who will give up their place in queue for Patriot missiles to Ukraine – source
Defence ministers of EU member states will discuss on 28 September in Brussels the possibility of giving up their place in the "queue" to purchase Patriot interceptor missiles from American manufacturer Lockheed.
Source: European Pravda, citing an unnamed EU official
Details: According to the source, the EU will hold discussions on planning the supply of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine.
EU member states understand that Ukraine needs interceptors "as soon as possible", European Pravda source said.
They said some of the Patriot missiles will be provided directly by the United States under the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme, which supplies Ukraine with US-made weapons.
"Another portion could be provided if states agree to swap their orders with Ukraine," the senior official said. He pointed out that the Council of the EU meeting of defence ministers on 28 September "will be another opportunity to press member states on this".

According to European Pravda sources, the country in question could be Spain or Greece.

- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that during his meeting with Donald Trump in New York, the US president told him that he had decided to grant Ukraine licences to produce missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
- Zelenskyy announced earlier an agreement on a package of Patriot missiles with one state, whose name has not been disclosed.

MAHAK strengthens international cooperation in childhood cancer care
TEHRAN – MAHAK, Iran’s charity supporting children with cancer, has strengthened its international cooperation through membership in and engagement with major global cancer organizations, including the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC), Childhood Cancer International (CCI), and the International Society of Paediatric Oncology (SIOP), Arasb Ahmadian, the chief executive officer of MAHAK, has said.
He made the remarks in a ceremony held on Tuesday to mark September, the Childhood Cancer Awareness Month.
MAHAK is a full member of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC), an international organization dedicated to advancing cancer control worldwide. Through its membership, MAHAK takes part in international efforts focused on knowledge and experience sharing, capacity building, and strengthening cooperation in cancer prevention and care.
The charity is also a full member of Childhood Cancer International (CCI), a global network of organizations working to improve the lives of children and adolescents with cancer and their families. The network provides a platform for international cooperation and the exchange of experiences in childhood cancer care and support.
MAHAK also engages with the International Society of Paediatric Oncology (SIOP), a leading international organization in the field of paediatric oncology. Its participation in SIOP-related programs and networks provides opportunities for scientific and educational cooperation and professional exchange in childhood cancer treatment and care.
 
 Through these international connections, MAHAK seeks to facilitate the exchange of expertise and experience and contribute to the development of more effective approaches to childhood cancer care.
MAHAK’s activities fall into three main categories: Charity, Hospital, and Research. These efforts exclusively serve children with cancer in areas such as medical care, prevention, treatment, healthcare, and welfare services. MAHAK’s slogan, “Help us and let us help you,” reflects the essential role of civil society in supporting humanity with love and compassion.
By 2025, MAHAK had provided comprehensive support to over 45,000 children with cancer and their families across Iran.

What’s the point of the interstellar Fermi Explorer mission?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:54:39 UTC
19:54:39 KST

How many interstellar probes has humanity launched? If you’re not a die-hard space geek, the answer will probably surprise you: five. Yes, we currently have five spacecraft, all launched by NASA, heading out into the great beyond. Pioneers 10 and 11, along with the New Horizons probe that passed Pluto in 2015, are well on their way to crossing the fuzzy boundary between our solar system and the rest of the galaxy. They’ll eventually join Voyagers 1 and 2, which are already plying the black void between stars.
That makes me wonder: What’s the point of the Fermi Explorer mission?
Fermi Explorer is a private space venture dreamed up by entrepreneur Philip Johnston and a small team of like-minded people who want to send a small, relatively inexpensive spacecraft on a flyby trajectory past the sun’s nearest neighboring star system, Alpha Centauri. As you might expect, given the target distance of more than 40 trillion kilometers, it’ll be a while before the mission gets there: Fermi Explorer’s trip is projected to take just under 80,000 years.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Mark your calendars.
The mission’s specific objectives for its (as-yet-unbuilt) 100-kilogram spacecraft are to carry a payload mass of at least one kilogram, to pass by Alpha Centauri within 500,000 years at a distance of less than about 400 billion km and to launch sometime in 2029—all for a price tag below $15 million.
Mind you, none of this is infeasible. I dare say it’s not even improbable. Launch costs for such a trip used to be prohibitive, but rideshare programs—in which several small satellites are launched at the same time in a single rocket, like people sharing a cab—lower the cost significantly. Launch for such a mission could easily be less than $1 million, and by using off-the-shelf technology, the spacecraft could be designed and built relatively cheaply.
The most expensive part of Fermi Explorer would probably be operation cost, such as salaries for personnel, and that’s because of the mission’s duration, which in turn depends on the propulsion and trajectory needed to leave the solar system. While chemical rockets could be used to give the spacecraft the kick it would need to escape the sun’s gravity, that approach would violate the mission’s mass—and budget—constraints.
Instead Fermi Explorer will use solar-electric propulsion: solar panels will power a small thruster that ionizes atoms of xenon and employs a powerful electric field to shoot them at very high speed out the back of the spacecraft. The thrust from such engines is low—just a whisper of force, about the same as the weight of a sheet of paper resting in your hand. But this thrust can be maintained for days, weeks or even months, allowing the spacecraft to build up a terrific velocity. All that additional time adds to the operation cost, however.
Moreover, the trajectory out of the solar system takes years. The plan is not to simply fling Fermi Explorer out toward Alpha Centauri. Instead the idea is that the spacecraft will use a well-understood process utilizing the Oberth effect. The maneuver will start with the spacecraft thrusting backward, opposite the direction of Earth’s motion around the sun, so that Fermi Explorer will drop closer to the sun in a series of ever more elongated, elliptical paths. The spacecraft will move fastest when at its perihelion, or closest point to the sun; thrusting forward will then maximize the increase in its speed. This is very similar to pumping your legs on a playground swing to increase the height of your arc.
After a half-dozen such maneuvers, a final long burn at perihelion would give the spacecraft enough oomph to achieve escape velocity, eventually allowing it to leave the solar system at a speed of about 24 kilometers per second relative to the sun. That final perihelion thrust would occur in the year 2043, and Fermi Explorer would take roughly 15 to 20 more years to pass what is generally accepted as the boundary between the solar system and interstellar space. From there, it would be a quick 80 millennium jaunt to Alpha Centauri.
Again, to be clear, all of this is technologically doable right now.
That brings me back to my original question: Why do this?
According to Johnston and his collaborators, the point is in the name. The Fermi paradox is an apparent—but so far still unexplained—contradiction between how seemingly easy it is for intelligent life to explore the entire galaxy in cosmically short times and how there’s no compelling evidence that aliens have visited Earth. (The paradox is attributed to physicist Enrico Fermi, who allegedly stated this conundrum succinctly at a lunch with colleagues discussing aliens: “But where is everybody?”)
The team behind Fermi Explorer wants to show that the holdup is not linked to any lack of ability to send probes to other stars—one of the potential roadblocks to galactic exploration. Thus, the team’s proposal for a demonstrative mission to Alpha Centauri.
I’m scratching my head about this, however, because we’ve already blown through that roadblock by sending five probes on interstellar trajectories.
Now, to be fair, those NASA spacecraft are just heading out into space somewhat willy-nilly after flying by their planetary targets in our own solar system; none is bound for Alpha Centauri or any other nearby star. But sending something to a specific interstellar destination isn’t that much harder. Missions from NASA, the European Space Agency and others have threaded interplanetary trajectory needles with incredible precision. Targeting a star, even one that’s thousands of times farther away than anything we’ve previously visited, isn’t that big a leap.
The team also makes a point of inspiring people to think about space exploration and the Fermi paradox, as well as the possibility of “great filters,” which are potentially extinction-level barriers to a species achieving space travel. But I’m not convinced of the efficacy of its plan here. Again, we already have probes on their way to the stars, and we also know public interest in a specific mission can wane. I’d wager Fermi Explorer is especially prone to this because of its mass and cost constraints, which prohibit it from carrying equipment for maintaining long-term contact with Earth; it wouldn’t get very far before slipping permanently out of communication range. And just to state the obvious, it would beam back no science from or about Alpha Centauri itself. Out of sight, out of mind.
If inspiration is the goal, I’d argue that setting up a scholarship for young students (especially in underserved communities) to study interstellar space exploration could be more effective—and easier, too.
The timing on this announcement is a bit ironic as well: right now the New Horizons team is struggling with a NASA decision that may force it to switch off two important instruments that measure the space environment around the probe. Unlike the Voyager spacecraft, which are running out of power and need to conserve it, New Horizons’ woes are linked to budgetary shenanigans brought on, at least in part, by the Trump administration’s peculiar antipathy to many areas of scientific research. The White House has repeatedly proposed devastating cuts to NASA’s science budget, leaving the agency scrambling to essentially look for loose change between the sofa cushions. The New Horizons instruments only need about $2 million a year to operate—less than a ten thousandth of NASA’s annual budget.
And New Horizons actually returns valuable science from deep space. Fermi Explorer won’t be able to carry much in the way of scientific instrumentation and wouldn’t be able to do much actual exploration with them even if it did—again thanks to the limited range of its communications.
I am not exactly against this mission—people and private ventures are free to spend their money as they wish—but I do have serious doubts about what exactly is new here, why it’s being done and what will really be accomplished.
Is interstellar space worth exploring? Absolutely. But not all missions to get there are equal.

Egypt rolls out first homegrown robot (VIDEO)
Egypt has unveiled the first locally developed industrial robot, as the country seeks to expand domestic manufacturing and reduce reliance on imported industrial technology.
The robot was officially launched and handed over at a ceremony attended by Industry Minister Khaled Hashem on Wednesday. According to the Ministry of Trade and Industry, it was developed by Egyptian engineers using locally produced technology. Local media reported that around 80% of its components are domestically produced, with developers aiming for 90% once motor production is localized.
The robotic arm is already being used commercially. It is being integrated into packaging equipment operated by Egyptian manufacturer QB and is designed for industrial packaging and automation on production lines.
Hashem said localizing the production of machinery and manufacturing lines is a key part of Egypt’s national industrial strategy. He added that the ‘Made in Egypt’ label is intended to reflect the country’s ability to develop technology and integrate into global supply chains.
The ministry said it will monitor the robot’s performance in industrial operations to assess its effectiveness and encourage wider adoption by Egyptian factories.
Egypt is not the only African country developing local expertise in industrial robotics. Tunisia’s TIRA Robots has developed robotic arms for integration into production lines, while other local engineering companies, including XPERT-MECA, design automated machinery and integrate industrial robots produced by global manufacturers such as KUKA.
Industrial automation is also well established in South Africa and Morocco, particularly in the automotive sector. Local companies integrate foreign-made robots into production lines. Morocco-based MTS Robotics develops automated systems for welding, assembly, handling, and packaging.
Cairo has also seen locally developed robots outside the industrial sector. In September, a team from Tanta University won the national RoboDam 2026 competition with an autonomous robot designed for cleaning operations. The university said the system could be manufactured locally at a significantly lower cost than imported alternatives.

the flâneur and the birth of the modern urban spectator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:50:29 UTC
19:50:29 KST

paris becomes a city to look at
The flâneur wanders through Paris, a city that is changing quickly, with new streets and boulevards, covered passages, cafés, department stores, advertisements, and shop windows reshaping the experience of the French capital. Walking is no longer only a way of getting from one place to another; it also becomes a way of watching what is happening around you, from the people moving through the streets to the buildings, fashions, signs, and goods on display.
This change is particularly clear in the Parisian arcades, where the street moves indoors and becomes a covered passage lined with shops, cafés, and other places to stop and look. Structures such as the Passage des Panoramas and Galerie Vivienne create a space between the street and the interior, giving pedestrians somewhere to walk without necessarily having a destination. The design of these passages draws attention to what is around them, whether it is a shop window, another pedestrian, the details of the building, or the movement between the enclosed passage and the street outside.
During the transformation of Paris under Georges-Eugène Haussmann in the mid-19th century, wider streets and longer views change how people see and move through the city. The boulevard becomes a place where the city can be observed, with pedestrians, traffic, architecture, and everyday life unfolding in front of those passing through. The rise of the department store adds another layer to this experience, bringing looking and shopping closer together. The shop window, in particular, gives pedestrians a reason to pause, look, and imagine the life associated with the objects on display before they even enter the store. It is within this growing mix of streets, crowds, shops, and visual distractions that the flâneur takes shape as a particular kind of urban observer. He can move through the city without rushing toward a destination, using the freedom to wander as a way of paying attention to the changing life around him.
Boulevard de Sébastopol ca. 1853–70 | Charles Marville, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
baudelaire’s ‘passionate spectator’
In The Painter of Modern Life, written in the 1860s, Charles Baudelaire describes the flâneur as the figure of the modern observer, someone who is deeply engaged with the transient character of contemporary life. He wanders the city without looking for timeless beauty but finds significance in its changing appearances, its fashions, crowds, gestures, and fleeting encounters, treating the everyday metropolis as material for observation. Baudelaire’s understanding of modernity is important because it shifts attention toward what is temporary and unstable, suggesting that the modern city is defined precisely by its constant transformation. The flâneur walks with no purpose; his apparent idleness allows him to remain attentive to the city as it changes around him, moving between the positions of participant and observer without fully belonging to either.
This distinction also separates the flâneur from the merely curious pedestrian or the crowd gawker, since the figure described by the French poet possesses a more deliberate form of attention in which observation becomes almost a method of understanding the city. The flâneur reads the street as a collection of signs, interpreting clothing, architecture, advertisements, gestures, and crowds as evidence of a larger social world. Yet the freedom associated with this figure is also inseparable from privilege, since the ability to wander without an immediate destination requires time, mobility, and a degree of anonymity that was not equally available to everyone in the modern city. The flâneur is overwhelmingly imagined as male, while women and working-class pedestrians encountered the same streets under very different social and economic conditions, making the history of flânerie as much a history of who was permitted to observe as it is a history of urban freedom.
image © Ossip Van Duivenbode
the arcade becomes a theory of modern life
Several decades after Baudelaire, German philosopher Walter Benjamin returns to the flâneur while developing The Arcades Project, an unfinished study of 19th-century Paris in which architecture, commodities, advertising, fashion, literature, and urban experience are brought together as fragments of modern life. For Benjamin, the Parisian arcade becomes more than an architectural type, because it represents a larger transformation in the relationship between the city and its inhabitants, bringing together public movement and commercial display within an environment organized around looking. The arcade offers the flâneur an ideal setting, as it allows observation to take place alongside consumption, producing a peculiar tension between the detached pedestrian and the commodity world surrounding him. The flâneur appears to move freely through the city, yet the city he observes is increasingly organized by commercial interests, with shop windows and displays turning objects into images before they become purchases.
Benjamin’s reading complicates the romantic image of the solitary urban wanderer, revealing how spectatorship is entangled with the emerging culture of commodities. To look at the modern city is also to encounter a system designed to attract attention, desire, and consumption, meaning that the observer who believes he is simply watching may already be participating in the economic and visual structures that shape what he sees. This is one reason the flâneur remains useful beyond the specific streets of 19th-century Paris, because the figure provides an early model for understanding how urban environments can turn everyday movement into a form of spectatorship.
Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s Pont Neuf Wrapped, Paris, 1975-85. Courtesy of Christo and Jeanne-Claude Foundation | image by Wolfgang Volz
from flâneur to modern spectator
During the 20th century, this relationship between urban space and spectatorship expands far beyond the street, as cinema, photography, advertising, radio, television, illuminated signage, exhibitions, and mass-produced images introduce sophisticated ways of directing attention. The experience of the city becomes inseparable from a wider visual culture in which architecture is encountered alongside images of architecture, products are experienced through advertising, and public space becomes a surface for communication as much as a place of movement. The spectator no longer needs to physically wander through the city to encounter its images, while the city itself becomes mediated through technologies of representation. The boulevard, arcade, and department store establish early conditions for this transformation by bringing movement, commerce, and visual attention together, while later forms of media extend the same logic across increasingly large distances.
The flâneur can therefore be understood as an early prototype of the modern urban spectator rather than as a historical figure who simply disappears once the 19th century ends. His particular form of walking may belong to another era, but the underlying activity of observing, interpreting, and consuming the city through images continues to evolve as new technologies and spatial environments change the conditions of urban experience.
image by Maximilian Orlowsky
when the observer becomes part of the image
The contemporary city allows the spectator to become a producer and distributor of images at the same time, so that walking through an urban environment increasingly involves not only seeing but photographing, recording, sharing, tagging, mapping, and publishing what has been seen. This changes the position of the observer in ways that distinguish contemporary spectatorship from the classical flâneur, since the person moving through the city is no longer necessarily anonymous or detached but may instead be consciously performing the experience for an audience. A street, building, café, installation, or public square can become part of the image as much as part of the experience, with people moving through the city while also thinking about how it will appear in a photograph or on a screen. The contemporary spectator is part of a much larger network in which urban experiences are captured and recirculated, creating a city that exists simultaneously as physical space and as an enormous collection of images. What began with the flâneur as an individual practice of looking becomes, through digital media, a collective and continuously updated form of urban spectatorship.
Galerie Vivienne – interior, 1905 | Brown University Library, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
designing the gaze
The spaces of the modern city have always had a role in shaping the way we look, whether through the long views created by Haussmann’s boulevards, the shop-lined passages of the arcades, the café terraces that turn the street into something to be watched, or the department stores that bring pedestrians into carefully arranged worlds of displays and commodities. What changes over time is the ways in which that relationship is presented and mediated, from the shop window and the museum interior to the illuminated facade, the digital screen, and the camera in our pockets.
This is where the flâneur remains useful as a way of thinking about urban experience, because his wandering is less important than the attention he gives to the life around him. The city becomes something to observe while moving through it, and that habit has become so familiar that it is easy to overlook how much the spaces contribute to what we notice, where we stop, and what stays in our view. The flâneur belongs to a particular moment in the history of Paris, but the condition he represents has continued to develop as cities have become shaped by commerce, media, and technology. We still move through streets, although the experience now extends into the images we make of it, leaving the modern pedestrian somewhere between observer and participant, moving through a city that is constantly presenting itself as a spectacle.
image by Adrien Olichon
image © Ossip Van Duivenbode
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. What’s in Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:49:48 UTC
19:49:48 KST

What’s in Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz?
Tehran’s offer comes as high fuel prices put pressure on Trump ahead of the US midterm elections.
Iran says it has put forward a plan to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, as Qatar passes messages between the two countries at the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Speaking on the sidelines on Thursday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the timetable could begin as soon as Washington accepted the proposal.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Pope Leo heads to France amid assisted dying, abuse debates
- list 2 of 4Mamdani plants olive tree with Gaza families
- list 3 of 4Saudi Arabia allies line up support as Houthi attacks mount
- list 4 of 4Nepal PM says global order is broken in fighting climate crisis
Both sides have described the indirect contact facilitated by Qatar in New York positively, but neither has indicated any diplomatic breakthrough as the war approaches its seven-month mark.
Analysts have told Al Jazeera a firm peace deal remains unlikely, with Iran still wanting to follow the approach set out in an earlier agreement, which would give it and Oman a main role in managing the strait before moving on to discussing terms for a broader peace deal.
For its part, the US, which has claimed to be “in total control” of the Strait of Hormuz, wants Iran’s nuclear programme to be the subject of discussions straight away.
Iran has previously made clear that it will not engage with broader peace talks, including addressing the issue of its nuclear programme, until the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Hormuz strait is lifted, sanctions are repealed and the US provides a guarantee of an end to strikes, among other conditions.
Here’s what we know.
What has Iran proposed?
Araghchi told reporters in New York that Iran had presented its plan to the US through intermediaries. “If certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz would be open on the end of the seventh day and [peace] talks would restart,” he said.
He did not give details but said the proposal resembles the June 17 memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by Iran and the US, which briefly eased the conflict before breaking down. “The moment they accept this plan, from the next day, this timetable can start, and after seven days, the strait will be open,” he said.
Under the June agreement, Iran undertook to allow ships to pass through the strait without paying tolls for 60 days – that was the period of time given for peace talks to take place. But the MoU left open what would happen after that period.
Al Jazeera’s Gabriel Elizondo reported while the new proposal is based on the MOU, “the Iranians are condensing the timeline and changing the sequence.”
“It would look something like this: fighting would stop on all fronts, including in Lebanon, the US would lift its naval blockade and oil sanctions, and release frozen Iranian assets. After seven days, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen. After that, talks on Iran’s nuclear programme would begin.”
However, Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera that Tehran is unlikely to receive any sanction relief. “Hormuz is a clear Iranian red line,” he told Al Jazeera. “The Iranians will not get reparations for the war, so control of the strait is the only way they can recover economically. I cannot see them backing down from that.”
Why does the June agreement matter?
The MoU signed in June set out an immediate halt to military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon, where Israel has launched strikes and occupied part of the country, and triggered a 60-day period for negotiations on a lasting peace settlement. It included US waivers for Iranian oil exports and provisions to restore maritime traffic through the strait.
Similar to the Iranian proposal, it deferred other issues, including the future of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile, to broader peace talks. But the agreement unravelled the following month amid renewed confrontation over shipping routes through the strait.
Coningham told Al Jazeera that Iran’s latest proposal follows this earlier model: “Open the strait within seven days, then start talks on the nuclear file.” But “the US does not want to compartmentalise the issues, it wants them discussed as one package”, he said.
How else does this new proposal place pressure on the US?
Coningham also sees a political calculation in making the offer publicly at the UN as Americans contend with high fuel prices. “By explicitly saying this may be the only chance before the midterms, Iran is putting pressure on Trump over oil and gas prices and the strait,” he said. “It is a tactic to put more pressure on the US.”
The strait, which runs between Iran and Oman, is a vital route for oil and gas exports from the Gulf. Disruption to shipping has driven up energy prices far beyond the region, giving both governments an economic reason to reach an agreement despite their differences.
With the US midterm elections approaching, a deal to get it reopened could give Trump a chance to bring down fuel prices before voters go to the polls – potentially giving the Republican Party a much-needed electoral boost before the midterms.
Trump has presented the electoral calculation differently, however. In his address to the General Assembly on Tuesday, he accused Iran of waiting to see how his Republican Party performs in November and predicted a deal would happen after the vote. He also threatened to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if there was no agreement.
Trump claimed the election did not affect his own decision-making on Iran: “The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
That leaves an open question about whether the prospect of lower energy prices is enough to persuade his administration to accept Iran’s proposed order of talks. Coningham doubts it. “Trump is prepared for this to go on through the midterms,” he said. “The same problem remains where the proposal does not answer questions about the nuclear file.”
Where do broader US-Iran peace talks stand?
Araghchi met US envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner on Tuesday in talks mediated by Qatar. The Iranian foreign minister described the exchange as productive and said messages continued to pass between the sides.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it would be wrong to describe the meeting as a major breakthrough, however.
Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East security, told Al Jazeera that the major blockage for Washington and Tehran is that each is making different assumptions about how much pressure they can exert on the other. The Trump administration is unlikely to revive the failed MoU, she said, because it assesses its naval blockade and tighter sanctions as working.
“The US appears to believe it can wait this out until Tehran is prepared to make meaningful concessions,” Ozcelik said.
“But Iran remains defiant despite indications that it is hurting economically.”

Ukraine must finance orders for drones in October–November to ensure their availability for January–February. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated this, reports UNN.

As for the 27 billion. Certainly, this includes, in part, funding for our soldiers, but mainly it is money for our drones, missiles, and support for our soldiers. Israeli forces carry out incursion into Kfar Shuba in southern Lebanon, surrounding farm with shepherds

Wassim Seifeddine and Lina Altawell
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
An Israeli army force carried out an incursion on the outskirts of Kfar Shuba town in southern Lebanon on Friday and surrounded a farm where several shepherds were present, as Israeli strikes, artillery shelling and gunfire targeted several areas in the south.
The Israeli force raided the Sadana area on the outskirts of Kfar Shuba in Hasbaya district and surrounded a farm belonging to the family of Ghazi Nabaa, where several shepherds were present, Lebanon's National News Agency NNA reported.
Israeli soldiers opened fire around the farm, while several artillery shells landed near the Sadana area, the agency added.
In the Arqoub area of the same district, the outskirts of Hebbariyeh came under intermittent Israeli artillery shelling, accompanied by heavy machine-gun fire and movements of Israeli military vehicles in the area.
In Nabatieh district, an Israeli drone targeted an area between the towns of Kfar Tibnit and Nabatieh al-Fawqa, while intermittent artillery shelling hit the outskirts of Kfar Tibnit.
Israeli artillery also targeted Wadi al-Hujair overnight.
In Tyre district, Israeli artillery shelling targeted the town of Majdal Zoun and nearby valleys overnight.
Israel has launched attacks on Lebanon since March 2, killing at least 4,386 people, injuring 12,407 others and displacing more than 1 million, according to Lebanese authorities.
The attacks have continued despite the two countries signing a US-brokered "framework formula" agreement on June 26 providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of Hezbollah.
Israel occupies areas in southern Lebanon, some for decades and others since the 2023-2024 war, while Israeli forces have advanced more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) during the current offensive.
Israel also occupies Palestinian territories and land in Syria and refuses to withdraw from them or allow the establishment of an independent Palestinian state as stipulated in relevant UN resolutions.

‘Primetime’ Exposes the Ego-Driven Core of Vigilante Pedophile Hunting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Child predators are arguably the most reviled demographic in society.
So when someone like Chris Hansen, the former NBC Dateline journalist and host of the To Catch a Predator series, decides to take up the mantle of exposing them to the public, he is naturally praised as a hero.
But, as is revealed in Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime—a dramatized snapshot of Hansen’s life at the show’s peak—it’s not as simple as that. Exposing allegedly bad people for public entertainment brings up a lot of ethical concerns and unintended consequences. And while many of the vigilantes carrying out these sting operations claim they are doing a public service, their motivations become a lot more suspect when fame and money are involved.
To Catch a Predator launched in 2004. In the show, Hansen’s team would pair up with civilian watchdog group Perverted Justice, using adult “decoys” to pose as minors online and exchange messages with men in chatrooms and private DMs. After the conversations became sexual, the crew would set up a sting, inviting these men to a home to meet the decoy, only to have Hansen confront them, uttering his catchphrase, “Have a seat.” The men were technically free to leave instead of sitting for an on-camera interview, but often police were waiting outside to arrest them.
The show developed an intense fandom that remains active to this day in subreddits like r/tcap, which has 52,000 weekly visitors, despite the fact that NBC stopped airing the original series in 2007.
In A24's Primetime, a darkly told character study in theaters September 25, Hansen (Robert Pattinson) clearly enjoys the praise and seems desperate for more accolades. He brags to his two young sons that he’s about to be on prime-time television, despite them not understanding the importance of that, and complains that the show has “never won an Emmy or any of the significance it deserves.” When a fan recognizes Hansen on a flight and becomes bloodthirsty, asking the TV host if he ever wants to “bleed” the predators he’s outing, Hansen smiles and admits that what he does by disgracing them on national television is “a little worse.”
In real life, Hansen cofounded the streaming service Trublu in November 2022, where he continues his investigations into alleged child predators. But these days, he’s far from alone. His work has inspired copycats, who thrive on social media and streaming platforms like YouTube, Kick, and Facebook. These groups and individuals are largely disorganized, and as such, hard to track, but a 2022 Washington Post investigation identified at least 160 in the US. Arguably, the people running these operations are more reckless, in part because they’re driven by virality.
One of them, who goes by Skeet Hansen, was featured in the 2025 MTV documentary Predators, about the Dateline show. In the film, directed by David Osit, Skeet Hansen responds to the criticism of the movement by saying, “There’s never been a detective that solved a murder that didn't get paid for it. So why shouldn't I be able to monetize off of catching these guys like the original show and making this content for people’s entertainment?”
One of many issues with that argument is that these hunters aren’t professional investigators—and sometimes they get things wrong.
In April, YouTuber and Kick streamer Vitaly Zdorovetskiy apologized after publicly—and wrongly— accosting a man of Indian descent. He accused the man of wanting to “rape a 16-year-old” in a mock Indian accent and called him “Mr. Mumbai.” In March 2025, The New York Times reported that Zdorovetskiy’s tactics for ambushing suspected creeps included beating some of them up, dressing like the Joker; the Times piece found that there have been more than 170 violent vigilante attacks by predator-hunting groups since 2023.
I spent over a year investigating similar groups in Canada for Vice, starting in 2015, and found that some of the people being targeted in stings had severe intellectual and physical disabilities.
Law enforcement groups, meanwhile, have repeatedly denounced vigilantes, noting that their evidence often can’t be used within the criminal justice system and that confronting alleged pedophiles can allow the targeted person to escape before police can step in. In some cases, the so-called predator hunters have ended up being charged with child-porn offenses themselves.
Warning: The following contains spoilers for Primetime.
In Primetime, the catastrophic consequences of these rogue busts culminate in a sting taking down Louis William “Bill” Conradt Jr., a chief felony assistant district attorney in Rockwall County, Texas. Conradt doesn’t agree to come to a decoy house, so both the TV crew and police show up at his home, where he shoots and kills himself. (The real-life Hansen told the Hollywood Reporter he doesn’t regret the November 2006 sting. Neither he nor NBC responded to a request for comment for this story.)
There are no heroes in Primetime, and the movie doesn’t wrap up any of these threads neatly.
At the end, struggling actor “Decoy Dan,” played excellently by Skyler Gisondo, finally gets career validation when his appearances on the show earn him a SAG-AFTRA card, but it’s clear from his expression that he’s not comfortable with what he had to do to get it.
Meanwhile, Hansen’s character, who repeats the phrase “What would have happened if I wasn’t here?” to suspected predators throughout the film, leaves the audience to grapple with that question. The answers are far from black-and-white.

Trump and first lady Melania Trump are set to host Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan at the White House for tea, before the couples drive to the National Archives, which include records highlighting the history of the US.

Xi’s visit follows Trump’s state visit to China in May, when the two leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability.”
He is the only Chinese leader to pay two state visits to the US since the two countries established diplomatic ties in 1979.

US intervenes to stop $136 million fine imposed by EU on X social media, Elon Musk's companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:43:57 UTC
19:43:57 KST

The United States challenged the €120 million ($136.51 million) fine the European Union imposed on Elon Musk's X (formerly Twitter) over alleged breaches of online rules.
The alleged breach falls under a new series of regulations imposed by the EU, which has caused more friction with Washington, with the US arguing that the fines cannot be imposed on American companies operating outside the EU.
“The European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority to reach American companies not present or operating within its jurisdiction,” said US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division.
“We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory overreach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth,” he added.
According to the US Department of Justice, the fine also stepped over the "corporate veil" principle and targeted not only X as the company committing the breaches, but Musk himself and other companies he owns.
It also warned that the approach could "have significant implications for 'very large online platforms' and other similar entities operating in the digital services sector within the EU."
Musk-EU clash erupts after two-year-long investigation
The legal battle began in December 2025, after an almost two-year investigation found that X was not doing enough to tackle illegal and harmful content posted on the platform.
The case also represents a wider crackdown on Big Tech in the EU that aims to regulate the industry in order to allow smaller companies to compete and, in exchange, offer more choice to European consumers, something that has been widely criticized by the Trump administration.
Reuters reported that the European Commission, which acts as the EU's executive arm, issued a response saying that the case didn't target any specific nationality, making the US argument to intervene on the grounds of the Article 40 of the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU void.
The article, according to the US Department of Justice, "provides that a natural or legal person, including a State, may intervene in disputes before the Court where that person 'can establish an interest in the result of the case to the Court.'"
The European Commission also said that the case aims to "defend its digital and democratic standards, which it says serve as the benchmark for the rest of the world."

German prosecutors investigate alleged 105-year-old former-Nazi PoW camp guard over WWII crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:43:45 UTC
19:43:45 KST

A 105-year-old German citizen is being investigated over crimes committed at a Nazi prisoner of war (PoW) camp during World War II, German prosecutors announced on Thursday, the BBC reported.
The prosecutors allege that the man was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at the Stalag VI K PoW camp in Senne, northwestern Germany, the BBC explained. Futher details about the former guard have been kept private.
Prosecutors attempting to investigate Nazi-era crimes face a host of challenges as most of the remaining suspects and witnesses are already dead. Of the 5.3 million Red Army soldiers held by the Germans during WWII, only 50% are thought to have made it home.
A similar case involving a seperate former guard at Senne had been underway when the supect died, aged 99, prosecutors explained. Many cases have been abandoned in recent years after the accused died or became physically unable to stand trial.
Germany hasn't had a statute of limitations for murder or accessory to murder since 1979, allowing the prosecution of Nazi crimes from WWII.
Stalag VI Prisoner of War camp, one of Nazi Germany's largest
According to records, one in three Soviet PoWs were processed through Senne, which was one of the largest PoW camps in Nazi Germany.
Approximately 300,000 prisoners, including 180,000 to 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war were held in the camp during WWII. When American troops liberated Senne in 1945, only 9,000 living prisoners were still inside.
Many of the surviving PoWs were treated like traitors when they finally returned to their home countries.
Precedent for investigating former Nazi Guards
A 100-year-old guard from Stalag VI A (Helmer) is also currently under investigation on suspicion that he served as a Nazi camp guard and took part in executions during the final years of World War II.
The legal landscape for prosecuting former guards shifted in 2011 with the conviction of John Demjanjuk, a former Sobibor death camp guard. Prior to his conviction, the courts had required evidence of direct involvement in the atrocities committed during WWII.
Since then, several former concentration camp guards have been found guilty of being accessories to murder, on the same basis as Demjanjuk.
In 2020, a 93-year-old former concentration camp guard was found guilty of being complicit in the murders of more than 5,000 people held in the camp.
These cases set a legal precedent for charging former Nazi camp guards; however, with each passing year, the window for further prosecutions narrows.
 
More than 80 years after the end of WWII, most former guards who are still alive are at least 100 years old, and time is running out to convict them for their involvement in crimes during the war.
