Meta debuts Tamagotchi-style AI agent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:15:05 UTC
19:15:05 KST

Meta debuts Tamagotchi-style AI agent
Meta is creating a tiny, portable Muse Charm device for carrying around the company's AI agent, chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has announced.
Produced by Meta's new design team, led by former Apple design chief Alan Dye, the device resembles an Apple Watch but with a small lanyard instead of a strap.
A customisable cartoon character occupies the entire two-inch screen, prompting comparisons to an AI-powered Tamagotchi.
This avatar acts as the cutesy embodiment of the Muse AI agent the company launched earlier this month, billed as a "personal assistant" that can automate daily admin such as writing emails and booking appointments, rather than just answering questions.
The Muse Charm features a fingerprint sensor in the corner that users can tap to start talking to the AI, with a built-in 5G modem for Wi-Fi-less internet access. There also appears to be a small camera, allowing the agent to take in information about the user's surroundings.
Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg teased the product, set to go on sale ahead of the Christmas holidays, during the company's annual Meta Connect showcase, which also saw the launch of two new smart glasses.
"We've packed a lot of technology into this little guy," Zuckerberg said in his keynote. "So if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what's going on around you."
The avatar can be set to a menagerie of characters, from a Muse mascot known as "Jolly" to an anthropomorphic mango, a labradoodle and a piece of toast wearing sunglasses.
Combined with playing into Gen Z's love for bag charms and Labubu-style plushies, the device seems to be pitched at a younger demographic, who are already more likely to see AI bots as companions rather than mere helpers.
Meta's Muse AI has been downloaded more than 2.5 million times since its launch in early September, according to Sensor Tower data, and is set to be added to Meta smart glasses over the coming months.
The company does not have the best track record when it comes to handling private and sensitive information.
Meta Glasses have faced backlash for being used to film people – especially women – without their consent, and for sharing private videos captured by users with subcontractors in Kenya as part of training Muse AI.
These issues may be compounded by adding an AI agent into the mix and giving it eyes and ears. In the two weeks since its launch, Muse AI has already been accused of reading users' private messages, attempting to hack their Gmail and nudging them to share their passport information and bank account details.
Using cuteness as a way to encourage users to adopt a product they might otherwise be sceptical of is not new. Robotics companies have been following a similar playbook in recent years, with launches including fluffy robots that clip onto a handbag and emotionally intelligent AI pets.

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah has slammed the current global system, saying it allows weapons to be moved efficiently but leaves poorer countries struggling to secure food, fuel, and other essentials for their populations. 
“We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food,” Shah told the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Thursday.

Rifles and ammunition cross borders, clear every bottleneck, meet each deadline,” Shah, who was elected to Nepal’s top job earlier this year following ‘Gen Z’ protests against corruption, told the assembled world leaders. “But a peasant in Nepal cannot procure his fertilizer or fuel at market price at a time of need.”

Voronezhsynthezkauchuk Petrochemical Plant Hit in Voronezh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:09:36 UTC
19:09:36 KST

Drones attacked the Voronezhsynthezkauchuk plant in Voronezh, Russia, overnight on September 25.
The OSINT outlet Exilenova+ reported the incident.
The attack began on the evening of September 24 and continued overnight. Local residents reported a series of explosions, while an air raid alert was issued several times in the city.
Voronezhsynthezkauchuk is a major Russian petrochemical plant specializing in the production of synthetic rubber and thermoplastic elastomers. The plant is wholly owned by the Russian petrochemical company SIBUR.
The plant produces butadiene and styrene-butadiene rubbers, as well as thermoplastic elastomers used in tire manufacturing, road construction, and roofing materials. The facility has a total annual production capacity of 226,000 tonnes of rubber and 135,000 tonnes of SBS polymers. In 2023, the plant employed around 1,500 people.
Such products have dual-use applications and can be utilised, among other things, in the production of tires and rubber components for various types of equipment. In addition, at the Voronezhsynthezkauchuk site SIBUR is building a large n-Butyllithium production facility, a component required for manufacturing the products.
A combined heat and power (CHP) plant is also located near the facility. According to an OSINT analysis by ASTRA, a Pantsir SPAAGM system position is located less than two kilometers from the facility, while a position of S-300/S-400 systems may be nearby.

The Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in Russia’s Rostov region.
The region’s governor, Yury Slyusar, confirmed that the refinery was damaged in the attack. The OSINT community Exilenova+ also published video footage showing explosions at the facility.
According to Slyusar, Russian air defenses shot down 50 Ukrainian drones over the region. Despite this, the refinery was damaged and has temporarily suspended operations.
“Following the drone attack, the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery was damaged. The facility has temporarily suspended operations,” Slyusar said.
The Novoshakhtinsk refinery has a designed processing capacity of around 7.5 million tonnes of crude oil per year, equivalent to approximately 112,000–115,000 barrels per day. However, some sources cite a capacity of 5.6–7.5 million tonnes, depending on the estimate.
The refinery began operations in 2009. It was one of the first major oil refineries to be built in Russia in a long period.

Disgust predicts conservative views most strongly in people with low bodily awareness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

People who are easily disgusted tend to hold more conservative political views, but a new study indicates that this connection depends heavily on how well individuals tune into their own bodily sensations. The research suggests that the link between feeling disgust and identifying as a conservative is strongest in those who are less aware of their internal physical states. The findings were published in Politics and the Life Sciences.
To understand these findings, it helps to look at two psychological concepts: disgust sensitivity and interoceptive sensibility. Disgust sensitivity refers to how intensely and easily a person experiences disgust in response to things like germs, taboo sexual acts, or moral violations like lying. Interoceptive sensibility is a person’s conscious awareness of their internal bodily signals. For instance, it involves noticing a racing heartbeat, a tense stomach, or shallow breathing during an emotional moment.
Early studies in political psychology suggested that visceral reactions to threat and disgust drive conservative political beliefs. A 2008 study reported that people with stronger involuntary physical reactions to startling or disturbing images leaned more politically conservative. Following this line of thought, research covered by PsyPost in 2019 found a psychological association in which higher self-reported disgust sensitivity predicted higher endorsement of conservative political beliefs.
Later large-scale replications challenged the biological aspect of this narrative, failing to find a dependable link between physical reactions and political ideology. A 2019 replication study found no evidence that conservatives and liberals actually differ in their automatic physiological responses to threats. Three studies covered by PsyPost in 2020 also failed to reproduce the idea that conservatives exhibit stronger physical threat responses.
This created a puzzle in the field of political psychology. Why do self-reported feelings of disgust consistently predict political ideology, even when automatic bodily reactions do not? The study was conducted by Mariana von Mohr, now a lecturer in social and affective neuroscience at the University of Kent, and Manos Tsakiris at the Centre for the Politics of Feelings. The researchers sought to address this stalemate by testing whether a person’s conscious awareness of their internal bodily signals explains why the connection appears in some people but not others.
“There is a long-standing idea that political attitudes are linked to emotional responses such as disgust, but this relationship has been surprisingly inconsistent across studies,” von Mohr told PsyPost. “We wondered whether interoception might help explain why.”
To explore this, the researchers recruited 632 adults from the United States through an online survey platform. The sample was evenly split by design, featuring 321 participants who identified as Democrats and 311 who identified as Republicans. The participants completed a series of questionnaires designed to measure their bodily awareness, their disgust triggers, and their political leanings.
To measure interoceptive sensibility, participants answered questions about how often they notice changes in their body, whether they trust their physical sensations, and how they use bodily cues to regulate their emotions. To measure disgust sensitivity, the researchers used a scale that divides disgust into three domains. These domains included pathogen disgust (like stepping on dog waste), sexual disgust (like hearing strangers engage in sexual acts), and moral disgust (like deceiving a friend).
Finally, the participants reported their political ideology on a seven-point scale ranging from very liberal to very conservative. They also confirmed their political party affiliation. The researchers then used statistical models to see how disgust sensitivity, bodily awareness, and political ideology interacted with one another.
Overall, the results confirmed past findings: higher overall disgust sensitivity was associated with a greater likelihood of identifying as a Republican and holding a conservative ideology. However, the researchers found that interoceptive sensibility changed the strength of this relationship. The connection between disgust and conservatism was most prominent among individuals who reported low awareness of their bodily sensations.
Among people with low interoceptive sensibility, those who were highly sensitive to disgust were highly likely to identify as Republicans. Statistical estimates showed that a person with high disgust sensitivity and low bodily awareness had a 64.1% probability of identifying as a Republican. They also scored on the more conservative end of the ideology scale.
In contrast, this relationship weakened among people who were highly attuned to their bodily signals. For individuals with high interoceptive sensibility, having high disgust sensitivity resulted in only a 55.4% probability of identifying as a Republican. For this group, the link between feeling easily disgusted and holding conservative views was not statistically significant after certain data corrections were applied.
When the researchers looked at the three specific domains of disgust, they found that moral disgust was the primary driver of these results. Pathogen disgust and sexual disgust did not show the same interaction with bodily awareness. The tendency for low bodily awareness to strengthen the link between disgust and conservatism was specific to situations involving moral violations and broken social norms.
“The main takeaway is that the relationship between disgust and political orientation may be more conditional than is often assumed,” von Mohr noted. “More broadly, our findings suggest that understanding the link between emotions and political attitudes may require looking not only at what people feel, but also at how much they attend to the bodily signals accompanying those feelings.”
The authors suggest that when people are less tuned into their actual physical sensations, they might rely more on socially acquired meanings to interpret their feelings. Disgust is a complex emotion shaped by culture, and conservative political frameworks often place a heavy emphasis on moral purity.
“One possibility is that people who pay less attention to their internal bodily signals may rely more on socially learned expectations to interpret what they are feeling, including ideas about what is disgusting, inappropriate, or morally wrong,” von Mohr explained. “In other words, when bodily cues are less salient, contextual and socially learned information may play a greater role in shaping how an emotion is interpreted.”
If a person is not closely monitoring their internal physical state, they might lean on these cultural scripts to make sense of what they are feeling. On the other hand, individuals who are highly attuned to their internal signals might ground their emotional experiences more in their actual biology. Because they rely more on their direct physical sensations to figure out how they feel, social and political framing might play a smaller role in their emotional interpretations. This could explain why their feelings of disgust do not map as strongly onto their political party or ideology.
There are a few things to keep in mind about this research. The data is based entirely on self-reported surveys at a single point in time, which means the study cannot determine whether feeling disgusted causes someone to become conservative, or vice versa.
“It is important not to interpret these findings as showing that bodily processes determine someone’s political beliefs, or that people with one political orientation are simply more or less ‘in touch’ with their bodies,” von Mohr clarified. She emphasized that the idea that people with lower interoceptive sensibility may rely more on socially learned interpretations is just one possible explanation for the pattern they observed, rather than something they directly tested.
The researchers also note that the direction of this relationship might depend heavily on the specific culture being studied. In a different society where liberals moralize a different set of disgust triggers, the ideological pattern might look different. Additionally, the study did not measure actual physiological responses, such as heart rate or skin conductance. The researchers measured how aware people thought they were of their bodies, rather than their objective ability to detect physical changes.
“The next step is to test the mechanism more directly,” von Mohr said. “A particularly important direction is to incorporate physiological measures, for example by examining autonomic responses such as heart rate or skin conductance while people are exposed to disgust-evoking stimuli.”
“This would allow us to distinguish more clearly between the bodily response itself, how accurately or strongly people perceive that response, and how they subsequently interpret it,” she added. “Ultimately, the broader goal is to understand how physiological responses, awareness of those responses, and socially learned meanings interact in shaping political attitudes, rather than treating emotion, physiology, and ideology as separate influences.”
The study, “The embodied roots of ideology: Interoceptive sensibility moderates the link between disgust sensitivity and political orientation,” was authored by Mariana Von Mohr and Manos Tsakiris.

The Data Center Debate Taking Over Native American Tribes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Whether to support data center development is a defining issue in this campaign season, and it is a debate that has taken over many Native American tribes. And on this issue, many Native leaders on the ballot—including Deb Haaland running for governor of New Mexico, Sharice Davids running for the House of Representatives from Kansas, Mary Peltola running for the U.S. Senate from Alaska, and Peggy Flanagan in a race for U.S. Senate in Minnesota—are being forced to address the issue head-on.
Flanagan won the Democratic-Farmer-Labor primary for the U.S. Senate last month. Her Ojibwe name, Gizhiiwewidamookwe, means Speaks in a Loud and Clear Voice Woman. She has spoken forcefully on data centers, calling AI an “existential threat to us if it gets out of control,” in a July Minnesota Public Radio News debate.
This fits a pattern. In her primary against Rep. Angie Craig, Flanagan ran ads attacking Craig’s ties to the crypto industry: “Angie Craig voted to let Trump make billions selling crypto coins. I won’t.” Analysts see AI and data centers as a natural extension of that same anti-corporate-money lane heading into November. Her “existential threat” framing is about AI broadly, tied to job loss, safety, and runaway systems.
Davids is a former MMA fighter and lawyer by training; she knows how to throw a punch and how to build a case. On data centers, she’s done neither publicly. But she took a quieter and pragmatic approach in a July KSHB voter guide, stating that “no data center should move forward if it raises electricity costs for families, wastes our limited water resources, or shifts the burden onto Kansas communities.”
“Data center decisions are primarily made at the state and local level,” Davids said. It’s also a convenient position: she sits on Transportation, Small Business, and Agriculture committees, not those that would put data centers in her lane anyway. In February, Davids met with the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers, which proceeded to formally vote against the Section 106 rollback in July, warning it would weaken tribal consultation and expand unilateral agency power. But showing up for a meeting doesn’t carry the same weight as making a public statement.
Haaland’s campaign has proposed sun, wind, and geothermal energy generation to offset data center energy consumption alongside requiring high-energy-demand industries to build their own energy infrastructure. But on the state’s biggest data center project, Project Jupiter, she’s said comparatively little. Pressed by a voter in Los Lunas last week, she said: “I don’t have the power to stop Project Jupiter.”
Then, last week, her position seemed to have shifted. Haaland’s campaign now says she supports a moratorium on new data center development “until we have strong, reliable guardrails.” This follows Searchlight New Mexico’s report of $87,200 in campaign donations from executives at Oracle and Clayco, the firm actually building Project Jupiter. Santa Fe and Socorro Counties have already passed data center moratoriums. Four Democratic state legislators already proposed one months ago. Haaland’s is a narrower, later, and far more carefully hedged version of the same idea.
But the demand for accountability didn’t end there. Over the weekend, a New Mexico climate justice petition started circulating, calling on Haaland to return the $87,200 and commit to no AI data centers, with no carveout for Project Jupiter. Haaland responded fast that she hasn’t discussed returning the money with her team, but “cannot be bowled over” by campaign donations. Realistically, the carveout isn’t nothing: the project is 26% complete according to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure’s own vice president, up from 9% in July, despite the fact that two of its permits have been paused by the New Mexico Supreme Court.
Peltola takes a different tack. Asked about data centers at a Fairbanks Labor Day event, she said she takes her “cue from the people of that region,” deferring to local support provided it doesn’t strain the grid for existing ratepayers. It’s a notably different posture from her opponent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who has pushed to bring data centers onto Alaska’s military installations, and from a $500 million Stak Energy data center proposal already drawing scrutiny in the North Slope.
But “the people of that region” is complicated in Alaska. As I’ve reported, a lot of the state’s land—roughly 44 million acres, or 12% of all land in the state—is controlled by Alaska Native corporations, for-profit entities created by a 1971 federal law, whose boards answer to fiduciary duty, not shareholder votes. That structure has already let corporations like the Bering Straits Native Corporation go after federal contracts, ICE included, despite loud shareholder objections boards aren’t obligated to address. In other words, the “local support” Peltola invokes in her interview may not translate into actual votes.
This debate also coincides with proposed changes to Section 106, a clause in the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 that requires federal agencies to assess how development affects historic sites, which are decades in the making. If these changes are enacted, federal land, where Native Nations hold consultation rights under extant law, could theoretically become terrain AI data center developers could claim without a federal review process.
More than 700 organizations, including Native Nations, have already signed a letter opposing this change to Section 106—but this isn’t the first time it has been targeted.
Near the end of President Donald Trump’s first term, the Secretary of the Interior issued Secretarial Order 3389, exempting major energy and land-management projects from standard Section 106 review. It was a move the Biden administration noticed early on and swiftly reversed.
The current Advisory Council on Historic Preservation rewrite picks up where that order left off, and is part of energy, transmission, and mining’s long game to weaken Section 106 as a source of delay for infrastructure—one that predates the AI boom by years.
Data center developers are merely the newest, best-capitalized arrivals to a fight that oil and transmission companies have been taking punches at since Trump’s first term.
Native candidates may differ in their approach to data centers, but they should be united on this: Native Nations must not lose their voice just as another powerful industry comes for their land.

Why You Should Join a Choir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Last year, I couldn’t shake the feeling that something wasn’t right. My life was fine—wonderful, even—and yet mercurial feelings of anxiety, disconnect, and vague dread nagged me.
Aside from the occasional car ride or shower, I didn’t sing much. But on a whim, I joined a secular community choir without knowing how to read music or having any real expectation beyond wanting to try singing under the guise of anonymity.
Billed as “drinkers with a singing problem,” and more importantly, not requiring auditions, Choir League practice began with a happy hour before rolling into light-hearted rehearsals. As I softly sang the words of an old Appalachian hymn, “Am I born to die?” with over 100 other voices, standing amid a sea of people with diverse beliefs and backgrounds, I felt something unexpected and new to me—but that people have experienced for millennia.
People have been singing together since the beginning. Early humans employed coordinated rhythmic chants for hunting and socializing. Oral storytelling was often delivered through song, whether via Greek chorus, work songs, or sea shanties. But this age-old tradition of communal singing saw a steep decline over the last century as the advent of radio, television, and recordings encouraged a passive, often individual consumption of music. Aside from religious settings or concerts, many Americans only experience group singing briefly and sporadically. Maybe while singing “Happy Birthday.”
And yet, at this fraught moment when everyone is politically polarized, lonely, disillusioned, and cringe-averse, choirs are attracting a new generation of singers. Viral videos abound of one-day choirs where throngs of strangers huddle in warehouses as they gleefully sing Natasha Bedingfield or Tracy Chapman. People with dementia are finding joy singing together as their musical memory outlasts their ability to speak. Unhoused folks in San Diego have formed a chorus and created community.
Why the choir camaraderie? One reason: singing together is a low-cost, inclusive activity. Plus, recent studies show that singing with others helps bolster social cohesion, as well as providing numerous physical benefits, from lowering blood pressure and cortisol levels to bolstering lung health. Group singing is on the rise, and it couldn’t have come at a better time.
Dr. Frank Russo, a psychology Professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, who studies the science behind what happens physically, mentally, and to our sense of connection when we sing together, pointed to the recent World Cup as an example.
“Thousands of people who may never have met are synchronizing their voices, movements, and attention around a shared identity. For a few minutes, they behave almost like a single coordinated social unit,” he says, explaining that by singing together, fans bolster their connection and collective identity. “People sing because they feel united, but the act of singing may make them feel more united.”
This phenomenon also occurs outside of the stadium, at religious gatherings, vigils, and protests. Earlier this year, at the height of ICE violence in Minnesota, trending clips emerged of residents joining in songs of protest. Among them was Sarina Partridge.
One of the co-founders of the Twin Cities Resistance Singers, Partridge’s musical path began when she was an elementary school teacher and noticed that if she had her classes sing, “It transformed them from a group of nervous kids into a community.”
As a result, Partridge began studying resistance singing around the world in places like South Africa and Spain’s Basque Country and helped create a national toolkit for singing-centered public action.
When Renee Good was killed by ICE, that toolkit was put to use. “It was unclear how to organize big actions because people were really afraid,” Partridge says. “But a big group of people singing is so much safer. It helps people feel safe, and I’ve observed singing to be literally disarming.”
She remembers walking the frigid streets with crowds of singers. People fearfully hiding inside their homes came to their porches to listen, some even smiling. One person held a pet puppy to their window, creating a much-needed moment of levity and human connection.
To be sure, group singing has long been a successful resistance tool, from protests against Apartheid in Cape Town, South Africa, to the marches for Civil Rights in Selma, Alabama. For instance, in 1989, Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia helped overthrow the Soviet occupation after 2 million of their citizens joined hands to create an approximately 430-mile-long human chain spanning all three nations. They sang together for 15 minutes.
“Political turmoil can produce uncertainty, stress, isolation, and a feeling that forces around us are much larger than we are. Singing doesn’t make those forces disappear,” explains Russo. “But singing together can change how people experience themselves in relation to them.”
This is exactly why more people should consider joining a choir. The 2025 World Happiness Report ranked the United States with its lowest score ever, citing cost of living and political uncertainty. More than half of young Americans struggle with climate anxiety. A Pew Research survey found that 69% of Americans are dissatisfied with the state of their country.
I understand this dissatisfaction. The world can feel undeniably bleak, without relief in sight.
But last month, I piled into an Elks Lodge with my beloved Choir League on a sweltering Denver evening as smoke blanketed the Rocky Mountains. I clutched a cold drink and laughed with people I’d gotten to know over the last year. Accompanied by a local band, we sang four songs from the 90s, just for fun.
I still wore anxiety like a stifling scarf around my neck. I still didn’t know how to read music and often sang the wrong notes. My shirt was damp with sweat. But as I belted the bridge of “Creep” by Radiohead as loud as I could, goosebumps prickled my arms. I heard my voice, its power buoyed by the might of every other voice behind me, and felt a sense of belonging.
Singing together is an embodied, experiential way of understanding that nothing must be endured alone. And in that moment, joyfully vulnerable with folks who were no longer strangers but favorite new friends, everything was okay.
Relief was not only in sight—it was in sound.

What Peacemaking Loses When Women Are Left Out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Wars exact a heavy toll on women and yet, too often their voices and concerns are pushed to the margins of global peacemaking. Since the end of the Cold War, the United Nations has made halting but real progress in bringing women into peace negotiations and postwar reconstruction from Guatemala to Bangsamoro and beyond.
Now that progress is being reversed. As peacemaking organizations fracture and lose their ability to press warring groups toward compromise, an assortment of social conservatives and warlords is finding new ways to exclude women from discussions about war and peace. Finding space for gender diversity could do more than ensure that women are heard; it could also give peace efforts a better chance of success.
About a decade ago, Colombia’s peace process culminated in an agreement that seemed to offer a lesson in how to end a deeply rooted conflict. Negotiators brought in the belligerents but they also consulted civil society groups on rural reform, inclusive governance, and accountability for wartime atrocities, including sexual violence. Women’s groups had a voice in these discussions.
The process had its shortcomings. Civil society was unevenly represented, and many of the peace agreement’s provisions on gender have yet to be fully carried out. Still, it rested on the premise that people with local relationships, legitimacy, and knowledge should be engaged in the peace process to help shape an enduring agreement.
That conviction is fading. Women are increasingly absent from the negotiating table. Recent diplomatic efforts—from Sudan’s peace talks, trade negotiations with China, Gaza’s Board of Peace—have featured teams composed entirely of men. Women’s representation may still be a top priority for some governments in prominent contexts, such as the selection of the next United Nations secretary-general, but it has become less visible in the daily diplomatic practice of making peace.
Today’s narrow ceasefire agreements struggle to secure even minimal protections against sexual violence: none of the 13 ceasefire agreements reached in 2025 prohibited it. The loss is both practical and moral. In many conflicts, women have political networks that men do not. They can connect humanitarian actors with communities, and act as bridges and brokers who can link local leaders with national processes.
A combination of factors helps explain why diplomacy has become less inclusive. Stalemates on the battlefield have encouraged a minimalist approach to peacemaking: diplomats and envoys bring military and political leaders together to stop the fighting, with less attention to conditions that would sustain peace.
As conflicts and postwar transitions grow more complex, diplomats have less room to pursue longer term goals such as political representation. Finally, diversity has become a point of contention. The Trump Administration has challenged efforts to increase representation of historically marginalized groups.
No countries for women
Sudan’s bloody war has raged for more than three years, and the need for an armistice is urgent. In September 2025, the United States, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Egypt, who are leading mediation efforts, proposed a humanitarian truce. The effort failed. Other diplomatic initiatives have tried to bring civilians into the conversation. An April conference in Berlin included women’s groups and other organizations, but it failed to persuade the warring parties to engage with anyone, much less with civil society. For now, even progress toward a basic ceasefire seems unattainable, making a broader approach to ending the violence ever more distant.
Diplomats with involvement and knowledge of the Sudan talks describe gender as a “non-starter” with the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces. Both factions have an interest in avoiding accountability for sexual violence and other atrocities while remaining focused on retaining their power. As Sudanese communities endure the war, diplomats are pursuing a narrow but pragmatic goal: finding a path to ceasefire while preserving space for later talks on who will have a voice in Sudan’s political future.
Elsewhere too, hopes for fair representation even in a postwar future remain bleak. Diversity is slipping off the diplomatic agenda in postwar Syria. Immediate concerns over stabilization and security takes precedence over any discussions of women’s representation between influential foreign governments and President Ahmad Al-Sharaa’s administration.
It remains unclear whether President al-Sharaa intends to build a government that reflects Syria’s diversity among women and men, and across its many ethnic and religious communities. Women hold just 22 of the recently formed parliament’s 207 seats. That number falls below the 20% quota for women in the electoral bodies from which the candidates were selected, and well short of the 30% target that civil society groups and the United Nations have often urged to increase political representation of women in Syria and elsewhere.
Across Syria, women hold meaningful influence in local community life. Parliamentarians might earn some communities’ trust over time, but women’s absence from national politics leaves a gap that a more inclusive system would be better equipped to close.
The manicured avenues of Washington are now home to some of the most powerful forces opposing diversity and gender justice. Even before the Trump Administration cast itself as a global peacemaker, its overwhelmingly male leadership had made opposition to diversity a defining feature of its foreign policy, rejecting the idea that a group can be considered oppressed based primarily on characteristics such as sex, race, or religion.
In its diplomacy at the United Nations and elsewhere, the Administration has made clear its opposition to quotas and other goals for representation. Senior U.S. officials have portrayed diversity as a weakness and linked traditional markers of masculinity, such as testosterone levels, to the ability to effectively deter battlefield threats.
The result is a vision of global power that places men at its center. Given Washington’s prominent role in many ongoing peace efforts, and Trump’s apparent affinity for strongmen, that stance reinforces the other two trends of minimalist peacemaking with a narrow set of elite interlocutors and an equally narrow set of issues to discuss. Some governments hesitate to raise diversity issues with the Trump Administration for fear of retaliation. Others, once more guarded in their opposition to diversity, now feel validated.
What communities can teach diplomats
Diversity may be losing ground in elite diplomacy, but it remains vital closer to the ground. Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms offer an example. When war broke out in April 2023, women who had worked in political resistance committees began organizing around their communities’ most urgent needs: protection, health care and psychosocial support.
They established Women’s Response Rooms to carry that work forward, drawing on networks built through years of efforts to claim a voice in public decisions. Across the wider network of Emergency Response Rooms, volunteers have negotiated humanitarian access, while women have mediated local disputes and helped hold communities together through conflict and displacement.
This extraordinary work takes place largely outside formal peace talks. Those peace processes may have changed, perhaps irreversibly, but local peacemaking persists. High-level negotiators should remember a lesson they once seemed to understand: Peace must be made not only by and for the belligerents in a conflict but also with and by people who have the legitimacy and relationships necessary to sustain societies through war and into peace.
The question now is whether diplomats will stay connected to those efforts and recognize what a peace process loses when it leaves the people sustaining their communities outside the room.

Reasoning together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
22 minute listen
Jürgen Habermas died on 14 March 2026, in the German town of Starnberg, aged 96. Every fall, from the mid-1990s into the late-2000s, he would come to Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois to teach and give talks, a visit that a dedicated group of students looked forward to every fall term. The year that has stayed with me is 2004, when he taught what he’d spelled out in Between Facts and Norms (1992), his opus applying his theory to democratic politics. Law, philosophy, history, political science: students spanned many disciplines to come watch the famous German scholar every week, dressed in Wrangler jeans and a tweed jacket, expose his theory of deliberative politics in his unmistakable nasal voice, thick German accent, and impeccable English. Max Weber and the Frankfurt School, which were intimate to him, since he’d been Theodor Adorno’s research assistant in the 1950s, came to life in his speech and then in schemas and figures in chalk as he theorised about them.
I understood almost none of it at first: words I’d read were coming to life in the room, spoken by their author, and still not resolving into sense. After several lectures, the shape came into focus: this wasn’t just Between Facts and Norms being rebuilt in public, but decades of work arriving at a single place. Since The Theory of Communicative Action (1981), Habermas had been arguing that reason survives in modern life only as something people do together, that is, by giving each other reasons and staying open to being moved by them, rather than by force, money or tradition. Between Facts and Norms was that idea turned toward law and democracy directly: a state counts as legitimate only when its laws could in principle be justified to everyone bound by them, through exactly that kind of open exchange. I’d watched that argument take root in a decades-long intellectual history. Thinking is a practice, it involves owing each other explanations, questions, answers. It is not a fast process, and doing it in public, out loud, in front of a room, is what makes it worthwhile.
I attended all of Habermas’s seminars during my time at Northwestern with great interest and, to be honest, a sense of awe. One day, the topic of the weekly seminar was inclusion, and I had argued, with the timid conviction of a green graduate student, that deliberative publics ought to be designed for inclusion, and that entry into these publics required that members accept the terms of deliberation themselves. ‘Well, we can tell that Ms Prattico really is a Catholic in the strict, universalist sense,’ was not the answer I expected – and what took me by surprise wasn’t that he’d made a joke of my religion, but that he’d seen me as a person with a history and a set of unexamined beliefs, something he’d noticed only by teaching me.
After the seminars, the class would sometimes go out for drinks. It was on one of these occasions that I understood where the joke had come from. I’d asked him what it had been like arriving in the US as a visiting professor for the first time, at the New School for Social Research in the autumn of 1967, which decades earlier had served as a refuge for scholars fleeing the same Germany in which he’d grown up. It was the start of a long habit of crossing the Atlantic: Princeton four years later, for the Gauss Lectures where he first tried out the turn toward language that would eventually become his theory of communicative action; then, decades on, Northwestern, where I got to sit in the room.
Habermas answered my question by going back further than any of that. He’d been raised Lutheran. Visiting the US in the 1960s and ’70s, he’d been introduced to the Quakers, and something in their small meetings had stayed with him, specifically the way they sought unity with everyone present. When he came to describe the conditions under which people could reason together as equals, he said he heard an echo of those meetings: conditions that hold only when everyone who could be affected by a norm isn’t just included but has a voice, can object, and speaks with sincerity. In those conditions, which go far beyond mere inclusion, the only constraint left on discourse is ‘the unforced force of the better argument’, as he put it in Justification and Application (1993). It didn’t feel like something he’d have said at the podium.
The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962), his seminal work originally published in German, made an argument about something concrete: 18th-century coffeehouses, salons and journals, where private citizens began treating the affairs of state as something they had standing to publicly discuss and judge, rather than simply obey. That habit, Habermas argued, was where modern democratic legitimacy first took root. The book also identified tendencies that would weaken it, too. He thought that the public sphere had already started to decay, folded back into spectacle by advertising and mass media, the public reduced from participants to an audience. It took almost 30 years for an English translation to appear. By the time it did, in 1989, Habermas had gotten a great deal of mileage out of the book in its original language; indeed, it had already made him a name outside Germany. When Craig Calhoun finally gathered the English-language response into a single volume, Habermas and the Public Sphere (1992), bringing together historians and theorists who challenged the argument, closing with a long response from Habermas himself, he could have easily spent the occasion defending a book that had already proved itself. Instead, he very openly contended with these critiques.
He came to think he’d been too sceptical about one piece of that story. But the warning itself never went away
Two critics stand out. Nancy Fraser argued that the public sphere was never actually open to everyone since it had excluded women and other groups from the start. She proposed replacing one public with many, arguing with each other, including publics formed by the very groups shut out of the first one. Geoff Eley made a related point from history: working-class and plebeian public spheres had existed alongside the bourgeois one all along, not before or after it. Both were extending an argument that Oskar Negt and Alexander Kluge had made back in 1972, that a whole proletarian public sphere existed, which Habermas’s book never accounted for.
Habermas answered these criticisms directly, in an essay called ‘Further Reflections on the Public Sphere’, printed as the closing chapter of Calhoun’s book. Habermas conceded that the exclusion of women was not incidental but built into how the bourgeois public sphere had worked from the start. Unlike the exclusion of underprivileged men, which was a problem of class, and in principle correctable, the exclusion of women, he now wrote, ‘has been constitutive for the political public sphere not merely in that the latter has been dominated by men as a matter of contingency but also in that its structure and relation to the private sphere has been determined in a gender-specific fashion.’ Habermas conceded that other public spheres had existed alongside the one he had taken as foundational. And he softened the warning, without abandoning it. He came to think he’d been too sceptical about one piece of that story, the early stirrings of consumer society. But the warning itself never went away. Sixty years on, he was still diagnosing a public sphere being distorted by commercial and structural forces, only now the culprit was platforms and algorithms rather than advertising and mass circulation.
He did not give up everything. He still wanted to keep the public sphere as something to measure democracies against, even if the history behind it was messier than he’d first made it look. The criticism and his answer to it sit in the same book, printed one after the other. Habermas’s views were open to being challenged, and open for us all to witness his thought in process.
Early in my dissertation work, I wanted to explore the role of experts in democracies through Habermas’s theory of deliberative politics, though I didn’t yet know how – I was, by any measure, stuck. My advisor, Cristina Lafont, one of his most trusted students, arranged a meeting anyway, at the hotel where he stayed during his visits to Northwestern’s campus in Evanston. He didn’t seem to mind that I arrived without a fully formed argument. Over almost two hours at what was then the Homestead Hotel, he had me lay out the problem as it stood, half-formed, and began working through it himself, out loud, testing it against his own theory as he went. He explained the three types of discourse that characterise deliberation – moral, ethical, and pragmatic – and was clear that when it comes to the moral, there are no experts: only individuals working out, together, what’s right in a given context.
Followed to its conclusion, that seemed to leave no room for expertise anywhere in deliberative politics. But he then turned to pragmatic discourse, where expertise does real work: finding the most empirically sound way to reach a goal already agreed on. Experts have no authority over what’s right, fair or worth valuing – only over facts. This was, in miniature, an argument he’d been making since his early work on science and politics: that treating value-laden political questions as though they were merely technical ones corrodes democracy. Decades later, in Justification and Application, he’d given the same worry he’d laid out in the trichotomy that morning sharper philosophical shape.
In later meetings in his office, more routine than that first one, I pushed the distinction further: what did it mean for climate change – a problem almost always treated, in his terms, as a matter of pragmatic discourse, all graphs and targets and carbon budgets, and almost never as a moral one. Who pays? What do we owe the people who pay? How should the resources that caused the damage be used? He didn’t have a ready answer. He asked question after question, testing the case against his own framework as though it genuinely hadn’t occurred to him before.
Justification answers only to the standards we happen to hold now: those standards can be shown wrong later
I’ll never know for sure if he was being generous or if I had shown him something he had not yet thought of in applying his own distinction. What stayed with me wasn’t the answer but the manner of it: a philosopher in his 70s, decades into a settled framework, still willing to test that framework against a case he hadn’t considered, in real time, out loud, in front of a student.
By 1999, Habermas gave up a position he’d held since 1973, the year he’d argued that truth is simply whatever people would agree on if they argued it out under fair-enough conditions. By the end of the century, he’d decided this was a mistake: it confused truth with justification. A claim can meet every test we have for it, survive every objection anyone raises, be about as justified as a claim can be, and still turn out false. That’s because justification answers only to the standards we happen to hold right now, and those standards can later be shown wrong. Truth doesn’t move when our standards do. Moral claims were different, he still thought: what’s right can only ever be what a fair conversation would settle on. There’s nothing else for rightness to answer to. But facts about the world answer to the world itself, not just to our best current agreement about it.
Several people had been pushing him toward this change. The US philosopher Richard Rorty pushed from the side from which Habermas was now backing away: for Rorty, there was no need for truth to answer to anything beyond what an audience could be talked into agreeing on, and he’d been making that case to Habermas for years. Lafont, my advisor, who’d arranged the hotel meeting, pushed from the other side, drawing on the US philosopher Hilary Putnam, who had spent much of his career arguing against exactly the kind of view that made truth depend entirely on human agreement. Lafont had argued since 1994 that Habermas’s own philosophical tradition, in its turn toward language, had drifted into a position where it couldn’t say the world holds firm no matter how we talk about it. When Habermas changed his mind, he moved toward Lafont’s position, not Rorty’s.
What Habermas never spelled out is what this does to moral and political claims once people stop being able to agree at all. Truth, on his revised view, still has somewhere to go even if everyone stops talking: the world doesn’t care whether anyone’s listening. His philosophy of Rightness never had that option. So, when the people who’d need to agree on something splinter into groups that no longer talk to each other, a factual claim can still be true or false regardless. A moral claim has nothing left holding it up, once nobody’s left in the room to agree on it.
Habermas gave up a position he’d held for almost 30 years because the people around him showed him it didn’t hold. He’d spent decades arguing that claims get redeemed when someone can compel you to answer, and then was compelled himself, and answered, in print, aged 70. Those critiques were not meant to be damning objections: they were precisely what his theory called for and was built on, ultimately.
Habermas returned to the subject in ‘Reflections and Hypotheses on a Further Structural Transformation of the Political Public Sphere’ (2022). His starting point is a particular relationship between beliefs and reality. Constitutional democracy runs on citizens holding certain assumptions about their own disagreements, namely that the disagreements are real, that they’re about something, that better reasons could in principle settle them. The system holds together only as long as those assumptions stay reasonably close to how politics actually works. His argument is that a public sphere, run through social media, threatens that relationship and widens that gap.
For Habermas, there are two forces at play in this widening. Platforms drop the editorial filtering that newspapers and broadcasters used to perform, and they turn every user into someone who publishes. For Habermas the deeper problem isn’t the resulting noise; it’s that heavy platform use produces something smaller than a public: semi-public spheres, self-enclosed, silos whose members can no longer perceive the wider public sphere as inclusive at all – claims to universality beyond their own horizon become, in his words, ‘suspect of hypocrisy’. That perception is itself the damage, on his account, as much as anything actually happening out in the general public sphere. He ends by insisting that ‘maintaining a media structure that ensures the inclusive character of the public sphere and the deliberative character of the formation of public opinion and political will is not a matter of political preference but a constitutional imperative.’
A factual claim still has to get the world right, whether or not anyone’s around to check it. Moral claims never did: they answer only to discourse. And discourse is exactly what he’s just described coming apart. He doesn’t draw the conclusion for moral and political claims himself, but it follows from putting his two books next to each other: the very thing a claim about what we owe each other had to answer to is the thing he says is disappearing, in an age dominated by exchanges on social media.
People retreat into whichever group agrees with them and lose their grip on a shared standard of true and false
Around that time, I reached out to my advisor for help asking Habermas for a foreword to a collection I was editing on Habermas and democracy. He was known for guarding his time closely – very few people had his email address, and he accepted only a handful of the hundreds of such requests he received each year. A couple of months later, an email came from an address I didn’t recognise: he had accepted, and written to say so himself. Amid the logistics, he added one condition: ‘You should send me at least a substantive part of the book before I can and would sit down and settle a few ideas.’ At 92, he wanted the material in hand before he’d commit to anything.
What came back was not a review of the interviews that make up the book one by one. He says so himself in the opening lines: it isn’t his task to comment on the conversations directly. Instead, he used the occasion to answer the standing objections to his view of deliberative democracy, and to close with the digital transformation that turned out to run through nearly every interview in the book – a theme he noticed himself, and named as central to the collection. One section was on experts, common sense, and the chain of translation that carries specialised knowledge into public reasoning: the same distinction he’d first sketched over a hotel breakfast, worked out now in far more detail, at the very end of his working life.
At one point, he writes that what’s been lost, in the democracies now regressing, is ‘a conflict of opinions that remains recognisable as a dispute about which position is backed by the better reasons.’ That’s as close as he ever came, in anything he wrote for me directly, to stating my own premise in his own words. He names the same loss again later in the foreword, describing people who retreat into whichever group already agrees with them and lose their grip not just on the public sphere’s inclusiveness but on the idea of a shared standard of true and false. What he doesn’t do here, any more than he did in 1999, is follow that loss when it concerns a moral claim once the discourse behind it comes apart. And that is what I tried to explore in my philosophical work since my dissertation.
He still believed the gap between expert and layperson could always, in principle, be closed by the right chain of translation. It was the one thing he never revised: he revised his theory of the public sphere, his theory of truth, but never the conviction that under the right conditions people can still reach each other. I am not persuaded that these conditions are as anywhere close to being met today – but that’s a disagreement I never got to have with him.
