Tax the rich? California voters are divided, according to new poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Tax the rich? California voters are divided, according to new poll
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- California voters narrowly support a proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ assets, while showing stronger support for extending a tax on high-income earners that funds schools and healthcare, a poll shows.
- Proposition 40 has lost support as opponents spend heavily on advertising, leaving 45% of likely voters in favor, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.
- Voters also reject a proposed voter ID requirement, and large numbers remain uncertain on several measures as they confront a lengthy ballot.
The slate of statewide measures on the Nov. 3 ballot provides voters two opportunities to tax the rich, which in past years has proved tantalizing to California’s left-leaning electorate.
Only one of those measures has strong voter support, however, and it’s not the proposition that’s attracted nationwide attention, ignited a nearly quarter-billion-dollar political slugfest and created a rift among top leaders in the Democratic Party.
Likely voters expressed middling support for Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets intended to compensate for an impending $100 billion in federal healthcare funding cuts. They were far more likely to back Proposition 3, a ballot measure that would make permanent a tax increase on the wealthy that funds schools and healthcare, according to a poll released Friday by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that is co-sponsored by The Times.
Proposition 3 appears to be a much less controversial endeavor, which may explain why it has more voter support. The ballot measure would extend a tax enacted in 2012 on individuals who earn at least $360,000 a year that is set to expire in 2031. Proposition 40 proposes a brand-new tax on billionaires and is opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who fears that it could hurt the state’s finances in the long run.
“When you’re going about taxing the billionaires’ assets, I mean that’s something kind of new and different, and it’s risky, and the governor’s against it, and you know a lot of people are expressing caution about it,” said Mark DiCamillo, director of the poll.
Voters are deeply concerned about income disparity but also skeptical about the unusual approach of the billionaire tax.
Proposition 40 has drawn the greatest attention and campaign spending of the 14 ballot measures voters will decide on Nov. 3.
In the poll, 45% of likely voters support the proposal, while 42% oppose it and 13% are undecided. That’s a decline in support compared with six weeks ago, when 48% of likely voters supported it while 41% opposed it, and comes after nearly $100 million of spending on television ads, social media messages and mailers, largely from opponents.
The billionaire tax was crafted by a healthcare union in response to legislation passed by congressional Republicans and signed by President Trump last year that could result in millions of Californians losing Medi-Cal coverage, rural hospitals shuttering and other healthcare services being slashed unless a new funding source is found.
The proposal would retroactively apply to billionaires who lived in California as of Jan. 1, prompting some to preemptively move out of the state. Ninety percent of the revenue would fund healthcare programs, and the remaining funds would be spent on education programs and food assistance.
Here is a list of some of the billionaires who’ve made moves to leave California.
There are two counterproposals on the ballot that would nullify the wealth tax if either receives more votes than Proposition 40, and they have raised $144 million. Voters are torn about Proposition 41, which would prohibit any new state taxes from being excluded from a voter-approved cap that restricts how much tax revenue the state can spend each year. The billionaire tax would have such an exclusion. Voters also are divided on Proposition 42, which would prohibit new taxes on personal property, intellectual property, retirement accounts and other assets and would limit situations in which a ballot measure or state lawmakers can impose or raise taxes retroactively — both of which are essential parts of the billionaire tax initiative.
Proposition 42 has greater support, with 43% backing it, 34% opposing it and the remainder undecided, according to the poll. Even more voters were uncertain about Proposition 41: 3 in 10 said they were undecided, while 37% said they supported it and 33% said they planned to vote against it.
The large number of undecided voters this close to the election points to voters being overwhelmed by the sheer number of statewide ballot measures, DiCamillo said.
“It’s confusion,” he said, adding that many voters may make a decision once they receive more ballot information.
That said, the fact that none of these proposals has the support of more than 50% of likely voters doesn’t bode well for their prospects, DiCamillo said.
Ballots will begin arriving in the mailboxes of the state’s 23.2 million voters in days.
Democratic voters outnumber Republicans by nearly 2 to 1 in California, but the party’s leaders are deeply divided about the billionaire tax, given the volatile state budget’s reliance on the wealthy. Newsom, who is pondering a 2028 presidential campaign, and the two men vying to replace him — Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton — oppose it. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont), a potential 2028 White House contender, supports it, as does the California Democratic Party.
Additionally, Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West and architect of the ballot measure, has come under scrutiny. Regan has been accused of threatening and intimidating women who worked for the union’s parent organization, and of physically assaulting one, according to reporting by The Times. He was also accused of trying to extort SEIU’s state council, suggesting that it could face an investigation over “governance issues” if it did not support Proposition 40, according to an investigation commissioned by SEIU.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West President Dave Regan denied the allegations. He said he did not attempt to extort from union officials, or assault or threaten female labor leaders.
Regan has denied these claims, describing them as a “smear” campaign orchestrated by Proposition 40 opponents.
Much less attention has been paid to Proposition 3. Californians who earn more than $360,000 now are subject to a 10.3% tax, while those who earn more than $721,000 face a 12.3% levy. The vast majority of the billions raised through this tax go to K-12 schools, while the remainder is spent on community colleges and healthcare.
The other ballot measure that is receiving national attention is Proposition 39, which would require voters to present a government-issued identification document to cast a ballot or provide a PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
The proposal comes as Trump has continued to make claims that elections, notably in California, are being rigged by Democrats. Americans are increasingly alarmed about the security and sanctity of voting, and growing fears about intimidation efforts at polling places in the midterm elections.
Fifty-two percent of likely California voters oppose the voter ID proposal, while 39% support it and 9% are undecided, according to the poll.
“It doesn’t look like it’s in a strong position,” DiCamillo said, noting that while voters have opposed it in prior polls, the opposition has grown.
Nearly one-third of voters were undecided about two other propositions:
- Likely voters were evenly split about Proposition 4, which would repeal a ban on public funding of campaigns, with 35% supporting it and 35% opposing it, and the remainder undecided.
- Four out of 10 likely voters opposed Proposition 43, which would increase the threshold necessary to pass local taxes from a simple majority to two-thirds, while 31% supported measure and 29% were undecided.
Voters will also face questions about environmental policy, housing, recall elections and other matters, as well as statewide, congressional and local elections. Californians are fatigued by the length of the ballot.
In addition to high-stakes U.S. House races, California voters in November also will weigh in on a slew of ballot measures.
The Berkeley IGS/Times poll findings are based on an online survey in English and Spanish of 6,989 registered California voters, 4,512 of whom are considered likely voters, on Sept. 15-20. The results are estimated to have a margin of error of about 2 percentage points in either direction in the overall sample, and larger numbers for subgroups.

West replacing world politics with war, using dollar as tool of sanctions — de Gaulle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:58:55 UTC
18:58:55 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, September 25. /TASS/. The West is seeking to replace world politics with war, using the dollar as a tool of sanctions to that end, Pierre de Gaulle, grandson of French President General Charles de Gaulle (1959-1969) and head of the Foundation for Peace and Friendship Among Peoples, said at the 12th St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum.
"These countries want to replace world politics with war. The dollar has become an instrument of sanctions," he said.
At the same time, de Gaulle noted that such actions stem from the unwillingness of Western countries to accept the fact that the world order, "which a few years ago was considered the developing world, now dominates."
"This is a world that unites peoples and populations, one that calmly and freely chooses its partners while respecting sovereignty," he said. "This new dynamic is taking on fresh meaning, because it is the natural dynamic of free choice, free trade, free communication."
However, de Gaulle said that the West keeps trying to "prolong the bipolar confrontational world against Russia."
About forum
The 12th St. Petersburg International United Cultures Forum is being held on September 24-26. The forum features 10 thematic sections, bringing together Russian and foreign cultural figures, government officials and representatives of the professional community. In 2026, the forum is organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Russian government, Russia’s Culture Ministry and the St. Petersburg administration.
TASS is the forum’s general information partner.

Saudi, Turkish, Pakistani military chiefs to meet over Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:58:37 UTC
18:58:37 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi, Turkey, Pakistan military chiefs hold talks on Houthi attacks
The military chiefs of the three countries in the Mecca Defence Pact have held talks in Saudi Arabia, as the bloc moves to strengthen coordination amid escalating fighting in Yemen and continued Houthi attacks on the kingdom.
Turkey's defence ministry earlier said that Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu was travelling to Saudi Arabia to attend a meeting of the alliance's chiefs of staff.
Later on Friday, Ankara published photographs of the three military officials in uniform, stating that the meeting had taken place, without disclosing where.
The meeting comes as Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan continue efforts to institutionalise the Mecca Defence Pact, established under an agreement signed by the three countries more than a month and a half ago.
The first meeting of the political and strategic defence committee established under the agreement was held in Istanbul at the end of August.
The Saudi meeting is expected to focus on strengthening coordination between the three countries, with the agreement covering cooperation in areas including military training and defence industries.
It comes as Yemen's Houthi movement continues attacks on Saudi Arabia amid escalating fighting in Yemen.
Foreign ministers discuss urgent meeting
The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey discussed preparations for an urgent meeting of the three countries' military chiefs during talks in New York.
Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan reviewed progress towards establishing the alliance's secretariat, committees and working groups.
They also discussed preparations for those bodies to begin their work.
The ministers strongly condemned attacks targeting Mecca and civilian and economic facilities in Saudi Arabia, praising the Saudi armed forces' response.
They affirmed Riyadh's right to take measures it considers necessary to defend its security under Article 51 of the UN Charter.
The three ministers also discussed regional developments, stressing the importance of respecting international law, state sovereignty and non-interference in countries' internal affairs, as well as ensuring the security and freedom of maritime navigation.
They reiterated their commitment to working towards lasting peace and stability, de-escalation and peaceful solutions to ongoing regional crises.
Alliance moves towards formal structure
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Thursday described the Mecca Defence Agreement as a "strong step in the right direction".
"When embarking on such a highly important initiative in a difficult geographical region, it is not surprising to face some challenges," Erdogan said.
"If a new idea is put forward or a new will is demonstrated, it is natural that there will be those who do not accept it."
He added that he had "no doubt" the three countries would move forward more strongly as work to institutionalise the alliance was completed.
Pakistan's foreign ministry announced on Wednesday that retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood had been appointed the first secretary-general of the alliance.
Riyadh was previously selected as the headquarters of the alliance's secretariat, while Pakistan will hold the secretary-general position for its first three-year term before the role rotates between the three countries.
Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif had previously warned that the trilateral defence alliance could be activated if the fallout from the conflict in Yemen extended to Riyadh. His comments came as the Houthis launched attacks on oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.
The Mecca agreement is intended to strengthen defence cooperation between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan and bolster collective deterrence.
Under the pact, an armed attack against any one of the three countries is considered an attack against all three.

Gaza suffers world’s worst ever economic crisis: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:54:56 UTC
18:54:56 KST

Palestinians gather to receive bags of flour distributed by UNRWA, the U.N. agency helping Palestinian refugees, in Deir al Balah, central Gaza Strip, Nov. 2, 2024. (AP File Photo)
Gaza is suffering the world’s worst economic crisis ever recorded, with nine in 10 businesses destroyed and hundreds of thousands of people unemployed, a top U.N. development agency warned on Sept. 24.
Israel’s military offensive sparked by Hamas militants’ attack in October 2023 devastated the territory of 2 million people before a patchy ceasefire was announced in October 2025.
“The collapse of the economy of Gaza is the world’s most severe economic crisis on record,” said Pedro Manuel Moreno, acting secretary-general of the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD).
“It has wiped out decades of development and generated an acute economic crisis for its people,” he told reporters in Geneva as the organisation released a new report.
It said 92 percent of Gaza’s “economic establishments have been damaged or destroyed”.
The territory’s daily per capita GDP is $0.58 a day, the report said. Prices are 274 percent higher than in 2022.
Israel’s military offensive killed more than 73,000 people, according to the territory’s Health Ministry.
Before October 2023, “two out of three Gazans were poor. Today, everyone in Gaza is multidimensionally poor,” said Mutasim Elagraa, UNCTAD’s coordinator for assistance to the Palestinians.
Industrial activity and agricultural production have fallen by 94 percent, with only 1.5 percent of arable land accessible, forcing “total dependence on humanitarian food aid,” Elagraa said.

Iran pitches seven-day roadmap to end conflict with US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:54:40 UTC
18:54:40 KST

Iran pitches seven-day roadmap to end conflict with US
Tehran seeks rapid implementation collapsed ceasefire deal, offering to open Hormuz if regional conflicts halted.
Iran has proposed a seven-day roadmap aimed at ending the war with the United States.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi outlined the plan to reporters in New York on Thursday, according to US media. The proposal seeks to implement the conditions in the Memorandum of Understanding agreed by Washington and Tehran in June, including a halt to hostilities and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Rubio warns of Iraq ‘Balkanisation’: Is that a real threat?
- list 2 of 4Saudi-led coalition says shot down 6 ballistic missiles launched by Houthis
- list 3 of 4Iranian-American group sues Trump over war
- list 4 of 4Benjamin Netanyahu attacks Israel’s enemies and allies in UN speech
Reportedly passed to Washington via mediators earlier this week, Iran’s proposal asks the US to meet specific conditions within seven days to restart ceasefire talks and end the blockade choking the strategically important strait.
The restrictions on maritime traffic in Hormuz have become a key issue in the conflict due to the impact on oil and gas exports and the global economy.
The proposal, which was presented to reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, comes as the war, started by US and Israeli strikes, is almost into its seventh month.
The US-Iran MoU deal expired in August as each side accused the other of violations, and there has been little sign since that they could return to the agreement, although Tehran has suggested it could happen.
Under Iran’s proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Gaza and Lebanon, within seven days, The New York Times reported.
Washington would also release Iran’s frozen assets, estimated at no less than $12bn, waive sanctions on Iranian oil and lift its naval blockade.
The Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the final day of the period. Talks on Iran’s nuclear programme, ostensibly the root cause of the conflict according to President Donald Trump, would start immediately.
The proposal closely resembles the MoU, but sets out a hugely ambitious timetable. The Pakistani and Qatari-brokered deal signed on June 17 set a 60-day window for negotiations, but still unravelled within weeks.
Vague wording led to disputes over who controlled shipping through the strait, and the two sides traded attacks before US President Donald Trump declared the deal “over” on July 7.
“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators,” Araghchi told reporters.
‘America must choose’
Separately, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a US television interview that it is for the Trump administration to choose whether to end the war, as Tehran does not wish to continue fighting.
“When we can resolve issues through dialogue, we shouldn’t resort to killing one another. But with the instigations conducted by Israel, they have imposed this war on us,” he said on Fox News’ ‘Special Report with Bret Baier’.
“But we do not wish to continue. It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not,” he said in remarks translated by the broadcaster that aired on Thursday.
Pezeshkian took a defiant stand at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, telling the world that Iran would not “bend at the knee” to Washington – even as Trump acknowledged ongoing US-Iran talks.
In the Fox interview, he said: “If the current American government, within international legal frameworks, wishes to reach an agreement, fine. If not, before the [US midterm] elections or after the elections, what difference does it make for us?”
Earlier this month, Pezeshkian said Tehran would “immediately reciprocate” if the US returned to its commitments under the MoU.
Slow-moving diplomacy
An unnamed White House official told CNN that the administration was having “positive and constructive discussions through the mediators”. The New York Times quoted an official as saying that Washington would not rush into a deal.
An Iranian security source told Al Jazeera there could be room for further diplomatic engagement if Washington met Iran’s conditions and commitments.
However, analysts said the proposal suggests that diplomatic efforts between the US and Iran are not advancing significantly.
“Basically nothing has really changed,” Cyrus Schayegh, professor of international history and politics at the Geneva Graduate Institute, told Al Jazeera.
Iran “keeps insisting that it wants to keep the additional power it gained during the war and that the June memorandum still is basically key to the roadmap moving forward,” said the professor, while the US “keeps basically refusing to accept this roadmap debate”.
No significant movement towards ending the conflict is likely before the US mid-term elections in November, he asserted.
Araghchi told reporters that “it would be better” to reach a deal before that vote. Pezeshkian said earlier that any agreements with the US would not be tied to the timing of the midterms, according to CNN.
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said on Friday that top diplomat Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, one of the main mediators in the conflicts across the Middle East region, had spoken with Pezeshkian about de-escalation and conditions for dialogue.

A gull flies overhead as a boy stands with his bicycle on a beach overlooking commercial vessels anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, Sept. 7, 2026. (AP File Photo)

Araghchi also met for talks on Sept. 22 with U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff.
Iran has previously set out seven conditions for ending the war and reopening the strait.
According to Araghchi, as quoted by the New York Times, the latest plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon.
It also calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iran.
On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz.
Araghchi said he was waiting for a U.S. response to the plan and maintained that China supported the proposal.
During the same meeting with the media outlets, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied accusations that Iran was trying to kill the president, saying it has “never been the position [of the Iranian government], overtly or covertly, to seek to assassinate” Trump or his family members.

The Palestinian theatre play keeping Jaffa's El Manshiyyeh alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:50:27 UTC
18:50:27 KST

Breadcrumb
El Manshiyyeh: How a lost Jaffa neighbourhood lives on through Palestinian theatre
Imagine if Brooklyn disappeared from New York; what stories would we want to hear eight decades later? This is the comparison that Amer Khalil, artistic director of the Palestinian National Theatre, draws with the Jaffa neighbourhood depicted in his theatre’s play, El Manshiyyeh.
To describe the El-Manshiyyeh neighbourhood’s fate as a disappearance is sadly no exaggeration.
Over the course of the late 19th and early 20th century, it was subject to land grabs by Zionist settlers and bombardment by militias that displaced so much of its population and destroyed it beyond recognition — save for a few landmarks, like the Hasan Bek mosque.
When the Jerusalem-based Palestinian National Theatre, also known as El-Hakawati, was drawing up its programme for 2025, Khalil spoke to Palestinian academic and playwright Samer al-Saber about whether he was working on a "dream project."
"He was working on a play about the El-Manshiyyeh neighbourhood," Khalil tells The New Arab. "I had heard of the neighbourhood, but like many Palestinians, I did not know the details of its history. We were all very excited about the project after reading the script," he adds.
From erasure to survival
In El Manshiyyeh, running as part of the ongoing PalArt Festival of Palestinian arts and culture in London, the fragmented stories of some of this once bustling neighbourhood’s inhabitants are pieced back together, and their dreams for its future are brought to life on stage.
"The story of El-Manshiyyeh is heartbreaking… The neighbourhood was completely erased," Khalil says.
"Very little is left of it, but the most important thing left is Hasan Bek mosque, which remains as a symbol of the neighbourhood. When you go to Tel Aviv today, and you see the mosque, you naturally ask yourself: what is this mosque doing here?" he adds.
"El-Manshiyyeh still exists in this play and on stage, so do the stories of all its people across the world. They give us hope because they continue to survive, as do the Hasan Bek mosque and the neighbourhood's story."
“We want the audience to take away that when we experience the most despair, we must count on ourselves and our roots to show us the way forward.”
Remembering El-Manshiyyeh
The production for this play is deliberately sparing, with the actors’ gestures partially filling the gaps where props or scenery would usually be used.
This is done for two main reasons, Khalil says.
"The first is that the playwright chose a minimalist style to allow the audience to imagine the past based on their memory," he says.
"The second is that this play is about people and their history, not about the spectacle. The play's history and events are full of action. The lack of distraction and the focus on storytelling help the audience engage with the play."
As time passes, and with so little materially left of El Manshiyyeh, that engagement is vital; performances of the play and the audiences who see it are together helping to preserve this neighbourhood’s memory to moving effect.
"At one performance, school kids who were descendants of Jaffa chanted for the people of El-Manshiyyeh for five minutes after the standing ovation," Khalil says of the reception of the play.
"Audiences in Jaffa told us that we were able to capture the experience of their grandparents, and to remind them of an important history of a place that you can’t see on the ground anymore," he shares.
"In other cities, people originally from Jaffa loved the performance because it tells their story. We asked one of the oldest surviving people of Jaffa whether he would change anything, and he said: nothing, it’s perfect."
Under threat
Established in 1984, the El Hakawati Theatre in occupied East Jerusalem has served as a nucleus for stage acting in Palestine, with co-founders and other members going on to establish theatres elsewhere in the country.
Like so many Palestinian theatres and cultural institutions, El Hakawati has faced sustained threats to its survival from the Israeli occupation.
At the end of last year, Israeli police stormed and shut down the theatre while Palestinian children had gathered for a musical performance.
The theatre remains under real existential threat, Khalil says, and in need of solidarity across borders.
"We cannot discuss the details of the current difficulties openly, but I can tell you this: we are at risk of closure," Khalil says.
"We have an appeal process that was scheduled with the Supreme Court. We are working with local courts and authorities to resolve these risks sooner than that, and any support for El-Hakawati Theatre would be appreciated."
El-Manshiyyeh runs until 26 September as part of the PalArt Festival, at the Pleasance Theatre in north London.
Shahla Omar is a freelance journalist based in London

Greece's Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis speaks during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at U.N. headquarters in New York on September 24, 2026. (AFP Photo)
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has called for continued dialogue with Türkiye during his address to the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 24, describing bilateral ties as “delicate” and shaped by the weight of history.
“Greece’s relationship with Türkiye “is a delicate relationship” and “a relationship that carries the weight of history,” the premier expressed.
“After all, as I’ve said repeatedly, we cannot change our geography. We are destined to live side by side,” he told the high-level annual organization.
Mitsotakis said Athens remains committed to keeping communication channels with Ankara open and maintaining stability in bilateral ties, while seeking to rebuild trust through continued engagement.
He maintained that the sole dispute between Greece and its eastern neighbor concerns the delimitation of the continental shelf and exclusive economic zones, arguing that the issue must be resolved in accordance with international law and the Law of the Sea.
At the same time, Mitsotakis stressed that substantive dialogue cannot be sustained alongside unilateral steps that undermine the international legal order or threats of war.
His remarks came after his recent visit to Meis, the Greek island closest to the Turkish mainland, where he toured military facilities. The visit drew a strong reaction from Ankara, which has repeatedly objected to the militarization of the island, whose demilitarized status is established under international agreements.
Turning to Cyprus, Mitsotakis said Athens supports U.N. efforts to revive substantive negotiations aimed at reunifying the island, which has remained divided for decades.
“We expect these efforts to continue,” he said.
“Cyprus remains a litmus test of its credibility, of its ability to uphold its own resolutions and the principles of the charter, and Greece fully supports the recent efforts of Secretary-General Guterres to create the appropriate conditions for the resumption of substantive negotiations,” he said.

From ‘cheats’ to ‘great friendship’: How Trump’s rhetoric on China changed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:46:18 UTC
18:46:18 KST

From ‘cheats’ to ‘great friendship’: How Trump’s rhetoric on China changed
Warmth on display in Washington contrasts significantly with the language Trump has used to characterise Beijing and Xi for years.
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday evening, United States President Donald Trump rolled out a warm and unusually lavish welcome for his Chinese counterpart.
Trump went down to Joint Base Andrews near Washington to greet Xi on the tarmac – the first time a US president has greeted a foreign leader in such a way since 1962, when John F Kennedy welcomed UK Prime Minister Harold Macmillan.
Though the Xi-Trump meeting delivered little significant shift in relations beyond extending a fragile trade war truce for another two months, Washington laid on hours of pageantry, more pomp and lavish tours for Xi’s entourage, and praise for the Chinese president and his wife.
But the warmth on display in Washington this week contrasts starkly with the language Trump has used to characterise Beijing and Xi in the past. We map how the language of communication, and the larger relationship, has changed over a decade.
How has Trump talked about China in the past?
Here are some examples of how Trump addressed Xi and China.
‘Cheating’: August 2012
On Twitter, now X, Trump posted: “No surprise that China was caught cheating in the Olympics. That’s the Chinese M.O. – Lie, Cheat & Steal in all international dealings.”
‘Take them to McDonald’s’: July 2015
Trump said at a campaign event in South Carolina: “You can win against China if you’re smart. But our people don’t have a clue. We give state dinners to the heads of China. I said, why are you doing state dinners for them? They’re ripping us left and right. Just take them to McDonald’s and go back to the negotiating table.”
‘Enemy’: 2015
In his book, Crippled America: How to Make America Great Again, Trump wrote: “There are people who wish I wouldn’t refer to China as our enemy. But that’s exactly what they are. They have destroyed entire industries by utilizing low-wage workers, cost us tens of thousands of jobs, spied on our businesses, stolen our technology, and have manipulated and devalued their currency, which makes importing our goods more expensive – and sometimes, impossible.”
‘Rape our country’: May 2016
At an election campaign rally in Indiana, Trump stated: “We can’t continue to allow China to rape our country and that’s what they’re doing. It’s the greatest theft in the history of the world.”
‘Ripped us off’: September 2020
At a Labor Day news conference at the White House, President Trump stated: “ … there’s been no country anywhere, at any time, that’s ripped us off like China has. We’ve lost billions and billions and billions of dollars by dealing with China. And they take that money, and they build their military.”
‘Screw the USA’: April 2025
Speaking with reporters amid the escalating US-China trade war, President Trump said: I don’t blame China at all [for the US losing billions of dollars in trade with Beijing]. I don’t blame President Xi. I like him. He likes me. Who knows? Who the hell cares, frankly. … I don’t blame China. I don’t blame Vietnam. I don’t – I see they’re meeting today. Isn’t – that’s a lovely meeting. They’re meeting, like, trying to figure out, “How do we screw the United States of America?”
Why has Trump changed his tune now?
“Great gentleman.”
“Very good trading relationship.”
“Truly great friendship.”
Those are just a few of the phrases Trump has used this week to describe Xi and Beijing.
This week’s state visit was the first by a Chinese leader to the US in 11 years. But it is also the third time in less than a year that Trump and Xi have met face to face, as the two powers remain uneasily gridlocked in competition over the development of AI, access to rare-earth metals, the question of Taiwan, and the Iran war.
Overhanging it all is the paused, but simmering, trade war between two nations.
Early into his second term at the White House, Trump upped tariffs on Chinese goods as he accused China of facilitating the flow of fentanyl, a deadly drug, to the US. Beijing responded with its own levies and restricted exports of valuable rare-earth metals, crucial for the development and manufacture of everything high-tech, from smartphones to fighter jets.
At its peak, tariffs headed towards 150 percent by each side before being paused to allow time for talks in October last year.
But nearly a year since the two sides called that temporary truce, the US position is not as strong as China’s, analysts say.
Trading deficit
First, despite Trump’s ambition of reducing trade deficits with other countries via his campaign of tariffs, the gap between China and the US has widened – and not in favour of the US.
Washington’s overall trade deficit has remained stagnant and, in fact, risen in some quarters. Between May and July 2025, the US recorded a combined goods trade deficit of about $277bn, according to Census Bureau data. In the same period in 2026, the deficit reached $325bn, an increase of 17.4 percent.
Meanwhile, Beijing has been minting profits. China’s total goods exports rose 6.1 percent in 2025, reaching about $3.77 trillion, according to its National Bureau of Statistics. Until August this year, China had a goods trade surplus of about $820bn – already approaching the mammoth 2025 full-year surplus of roughly $1.2 trillion.
The equation is such that US-China’s bilateral trade has been in a near free-fall over the last two years, just as the US national debt hit a record $40bn this year – two years ahead of expectations.
“Washington is playing a high-stakes game of economic chicken with a $40 trillion debt load, an inflationary sword of Damocles, zero fiscal cushion to absorb a truce collapse and a dependence [on] Chinese industrial and manufacturing inputs,” Beijing-based Einar Tangen, a senior fellow at the Center for International Governance Innovation, told Al Jazeera.
US consumers and the economy in general will find it tough to survive yet another inflationary shock from renewed tariffs “at a time when the federal budget already operates like a high-wire Ponzi scheme,” he added.
Trump simply can’t afford for the trade truce to collapse now.
Rare earth minerals
Second is China’s ace card of rare earth metals. These are crucial for the development of AI and defence sectors as they are used in the manufacture of all things tech, from smartphones to fighter jets. China has 60 percent of the world’s known deposits of these minerals, and processes 90 percent of them. During the trade war last year, China restricted exports of seven of the 12 it has in April, and threatened to restrict five more before the truce delayed that.
China, therefore, has huge leverage and Trump has little choice but to play nice, observers say.
What are the main outcomes from the Xi-Trump summit?
The bottom line is that the meeting in Washington showcased the two nations’ potential for bilateral relations rather than any grand bargain in the making. While the trade truce was extended, major strategic disputes like the question of Taiwan, the war on Iran, as well as tensions over trade and technology remain unresolved.
Trade truce extended: The US and China agreed to extend their existing trade truce, which had been due to expire in November, giving negotiators more time to work towards a broader agreement. The extension now runs to January 10.
No breakthrough on Iran: Trump had wanted Beijing to use its influence with Tehran to help isolate Iran economically and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. No breakthrough was reported.
Taiwan remains unresolved: Xi urged Trump to oppose Taiwanese independence and handle the Taiwan issue “prudently”, China’s Xinhua news agency reported. The White House has not commented on it so far; however, a second, $14bn arms deal between the US and Taiwan, following an $11bn sale announced in December last year, remains on hold.
Push for stable relations: Both leaders signalled a desire to prevent further deterioration in ties. Xi called for competition to remain “within bounds” and warned against the “Thucydides Trap” of conflict between a rising and established power.
AI race: In advance of the talks, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington had proposed an AI “notification mechanism” with China – in effect, a hotline to alert each other when AI incidents threaten national security.

Report: Saudi Arabia, UAE urge US to maintain pressure on Iran
Riyadh and Abu Dhabi oppose easing sanctions or the US naval blockade as Qatar and Oman push to revive talks
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates pressed Washington to maintain economic pressure on Iran and reject concessions on sanctions or the US naval blockade, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
Their lobbying complicated efforts to revive negotiations to end the war. Mediators including Qatar sought talks in Oman as early as next week to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin winding down the conflict. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he expected talks to resume soon.
Gulf states generally opposed further military escalation against Iran, WSJ reported. But Saudi and Emirati officials hardened their positions after Iranian attacks on Saudi shipping and moves by Tehran’s Houthi allies in Yemen to disrupt an alternative export route through the Red Sea.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman recently told US officials the blockade should remain until Iran agreed to a new deal, according to the report. Saudi Arabia previously backed negotiations and was willing to consider an agreement recognizing some Iranian role in administering Hormuz.
UAE officials also questioned Tehran’s willingness to negotiate, citing renewed regional violence and attacks on ships. They said Gulf states should not accept permanent Iranian control of the strait.
Qatar and Oman continued to push for diplomacy. Proposals discussed during a visit by Iran’s foreign minister to Doha included a seven-day pause in fighting that could lead to an end to Iranian attacks on shipping in exchange for lifting the US blockade.
Washington repeatedly told Qatar that Trump had no intention of lifting the blockade, the WSJ reported.
“While President Trump is open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances, he has no need to negotiate with the Iranians,” a White House official told the outlet.
Arab mediators also described conflicting signals from Tehran. Iranian diplomats offered proposals and acknowledged the country’s worsening economic crisis, while the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps rejected new negotiating formulas and said it was prepared for a prolonged war.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.
Dansk Industri, DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main employers’ and business association, says companies need to pay attention to their security.
This applies both to physical security and cybersecurity, according to Rasmus Anderskouv, DI’s deputy director for societal security and emergency preparedness.
“Hybrid attacks against Denmark and Danish companies are unfortunately a new normal that we have to relate to,” he said in a press release.

Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.
The United States will pay for any new American military bases established in Greenland under a new security and defense agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen says.
“To the extent that the Americans are to build American bases in Greenland, that is of course something that the Americans finance,” Løkke told Ritzau.
At the same time, Løkke said the agreement contains “no financing elements”.
US President Donald Trump said Friday that an agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland was being reached without costs for the United States.
“There will be no cost to the US,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, with the words “no cost” written in capital letters.
Asked how that could be the case if the US will finance new bases, Løkke said:
“You’ll have to ask him about that.”
“But it is not as though they have to pay ground rent,” he added.
Løkke said the “further terms” for the two new US military bases in Greenland still need to be agreed upon.
The bases must also take the environment and Greenlandic lifestyle and culture into account, he said.
“These are important things that strengthen Greenland in relation to the 1951 agreement,” Løkke said.
He also emphasized that the US pays for improvements at Pituffik Space Base, the only US military base currently in Greenland.

Under the new security and defense agreement, the US has been granted permission to establish new bases in the settlement of Narsarsuaq and in Mestersvig.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed in a written response that the new agreement between the three countries “does not concern financing”.
Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

Denmark could become one of the four largest contributors to the Global Partnership for Education under a new funding plan running through 2030.
The government plans to provide up to 1 billion DKK to the global education fund, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a press release Wednesday.
The funding would begin with 250 million DKK in 2027 and reach a total of up to 1 billion DKK by 2030.
The money is intended to support education in developing countries.
“Education is one of the best investments we can make, both for the children who directly benefit from Denmark’s support, but also for Denmark itself,” Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said during the UN General Assembly in New York.
The funding is included in the government’s proposed 2027 finance bill. It is conditional on the proposal being passed and the funding being approved annually by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

Rasmussen said better access to education could also support economic development.

The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.
