Police were still working at the scene Wednesday afternoon. S-trains were running but were not stopping at Brøndbyøster Station, according to DSB’s website.
According to Ekstra Bladet, the area around the station was cordoned off and several patrol cars were at the scene. The newspaper also reported that an ambulance had been seen leaving from the northern side of the station.
The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.
Stena Line has ordered two new hybrid ferries for the route between Frederikshavn and Gothenburg, with the vessels expected to enter service in 2030.
The company announced the order in a press release Wednesday.
The ferries will be built at a shipyard in China. They will be E-Flexer vessels with room for 1,500 passengers.
The hybrid ferries will run on both electricity and conventional fuel. They are expected to continue doing so until charging options allow them to operate fully on electricity.
“It is a historic investment for Stena Line, which gives us the opportunity to take another step in the sustainable modernization of our fleet,” Niclas Mårtensson, CEO of Stena Line, said.
“They support our goal of reducing CO₂ emissions and preparing the fleet for future environmental requirements,” he said.
Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.
Queen Mary and Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization Christina Egelund will present the Teaching Prize 2026 to teachers from seven higher education institutions.
The award recognizes educators for inspiring and engaging students, the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization said in a press release.
Each recipient receives 500,000 DKK. Of that amount, 200,000 DKK is a personal award, while 300,000 DKK must be used to develop new teaching activities.
The awards will be presented at the Opera in Copenhagen.
“For this year’s seven prize recipients, good teaching is about awakening the students’ curiosity and creating engagement,” Egelund, from the Moderates, said.
She added that the recipients had also created learning environments where students felt comfortable asking questions and making mistakes.
The seven recipients come from different areas of higher education.
Assistant Professor Amalie Trangbæk teaches political science at Aarhus University. Assistant Lecturer Brian Jørgensen teaches communication design at Design School Kolding, while Associate Professor Bjarne Schmidt teaches mathematics, physics and engineering didactics at the University of Southern Denmark.
The other recipients are Associate Professor Lars Plauborg Pedersen from Syddansk Erhvervsakademi, Associate Professor René Kirk Johansen from the maritime and polytechnic education center Martec, Associate Professor Gry Segoli from Københavns Professionshøjskole and Associate Professor Lene Krogstrup Jakobsen from UC SYD in Esbjerg.
Educational institutions nominate candidates for the prize each year. Relevant groups of rectors then assess the nominations and decide which candidates are put forward to the Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization.
Several Danish newspapers said Wednesday that Denmark and Greenland welcomed the new security and defense agreement, even as they raised questions about its consequences.
Berlingske called the deal a “triumph for wise and persistent diplomacy” in an editorial.
“If the agreement turns out to be worth the paper it is written on, foreign policy history was written in New York on Tuesday,” the newspaper wrote.
Politiken described the agreement signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump as a “diplomatic masterpiece.”
Politiken said the deal protects Greenland’s territorial integrity, but also described it as a high-risk agreement whose details remain open to interpretation.
Kristeligt Dagblad called it a “historic agreement on the security of the Kingdom of Denmark’s Arctic area” and said the Danish government could be satisfied with the result.
Other newspapers focused more strongly on the risks.
Ekstra Bladet described the agreement as a costly victory. It raised concerns that the U.S. could use Greenland for activities unrelated to NATO, including establishing its “Golden Dome” missile defense system there.
“We are paying a high, but unavoidable price,” Ekstra Bladet wrote. “We can well call it a victory, as long as we remember how dearly it was bought.”
Information described the agreement as a victory for the Kingdom of Denmark but also as a “submission to a tyrannical superior power.”
Despite its positive assessment of the agreement, Berlingske also warned that uncertainty remains because Trump is president.

The leaders of Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign a security and defense agreement concerning Greenland on Tuesday.
The ceremony is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. local time, or 4:30 p.m. Danish time, at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office described it as “a joint agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic region.”
The agreement will be signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, head of Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government.
Few details about the agreement have been released since it was announced Friday.
Trump said on Truth Social that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen has said the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We are not ceding sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I never will as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcasters DR and TV 2 on Monday.
She said sovereignty could be maintained alongside closer defense cooperation with other countries.
The USA plans to reopen a former military base in Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and establish a military presence on Greenland’s east coast, Reuters reported Monday.
The eastern site is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish military unit operating in Greenland.
Reuters attributed the information to three unnamed sources familiar with a defense agreement involving Greenland, Denmark and the USA. Danish public broadcaster DR also reported that the USA plans two new bases.
The agreement’s text has not been published, and its details may change before it is signed, Reuters reported.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Greenlandic head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen are expected to sign the agreement Tuesday at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office said the agreement would strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Trump has said it gives the USA “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said the agreement recognizes the Kingdom of Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We do not surrender sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I will never do that as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told DR and Danish broadcaster TV 2.

Following the September 22 attack, the Kuibyshev Refinery likely halted operations completely.
The OSINT project Absolutely Reliable Source reported on this, publishing satellite imagery with the aftermath of Ukrainian strikes on the facility.
Three oil storage tanks were destroyed, while another one was likely damaged.
The pumping station and pipelines leading to the AVT-4 and AVT-5 primary oil refining units also suffered damage.
Damage to the transport infrastructure and storage tanks disrupted the stable supply of feedstock, forcing the refinery to halt production.
At the same time, no direct signs of damage were observed on the primary and secondary oil refining units themselves.
The Kuibyshev Refinery is one of the leading refineries in the Volga region. The facility is located in Samara and is part of Rosneft’s vertically integrated structure.
Together with the Novokuibyshev and Syzran oil refineries, it forms Rosneft’s Samara group of refineries. The facilities in this refining cluster process crude oil produced by the company, including in Western Siberia and the Samara region.
The Kuibyshev Refinery has a design capacity of about 7 million tonnes of crude oil per year. However, actual processing volumes have remained lower in recent years. In 2024, the refinery processed 4.7 million tonnes of crude oil, or about 94,400 barrels per day.
During that period, the refinery produced about 800,000 tonnes of gasoline, 1.4 million tonnes of diesel fuel, and 1.3 million tonnes of fuel oil.
The attack caused fires at both of the facility’s primary oil refining units, and restoring operations could take several weeks.

The push to reunify Libya: Why it matters to Türkiye and the region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:33:47 UTC
18:33:47 KST

Libya, an energy-rich North African country with Africa’s largest oil reserves, descended into a bloody civil war in 2014 between rival western and eastern factions, three years after the violent overthrow and killing of longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi.
Despite intermittent fighting between the rival forces, the internationally recognised government in Tripoli has largely retained its legitimacy, signing significant agreements with countries such as Türkiye.
In recent years, however, political dialogue between the rival administrations has gained momentum, with Türkiye promoting its "One Libya" policy and supporting rapprochement between the two sides to unify the fractured country under a single central government.
In April, the rival eastern and western factions agreed on a centralised national budget to share the country's substantial oil revenues, marking a step towards reunification.
In August, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan made a significant visit to Libya, holding talks not only in Tripoli, the seat of the internationally recognised government in the west, but also in Benghazi, the stronghold of the eastern administration led by Khalifa Haftar, General Commander of the Libyan National Army.
"It is essential that our Libyan brothers and sisters build their own future freely, securely, and prosperously. In line with the vision set out by our President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, we will continue to support dialogue and cooperation between Libya's west and east and to contribute to Libya's peace, stability, and prosperity," he said after his Libya consultations.
‘One Libya’ policy
Two weeks after Fidan’s meetings in Libya, the UN announced a roadmap outlining a two-year timeline for presidential and parliamentary elections, institutional unification, and the restructuring of the electoral commission, marking another step towards reunifying the country.
“That Türkiye is now able to engage with actors on both sides of Libya’s divide is very beneficial,” Salah Bakkoush, a Libyan political analyst, tells TRT World.
“Türkiye's leverage will be most consequential when engagement with both sides translates into institutional unification rather than accommodation of permanent parallel structures,” Bakkoush, also a former advisor to the High Council of the Libyan state, says.
Bakkoush observes a growing willingness among Libya’s rival political factions to reach a compromise.
However, he cautions that unifying competing centres of power under a single state authority will be difficult because “institutional authority remains unresolved” between the two sides.
Following Fidan’s visit, diplomatic contacts between Libya and Türkiye have intensified. Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Libya’s acting defence minister, Abdussalam Zubi, in Istanbul on Saturday to discuss ongoing efforts towards institutional unification.
On Tuesday, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan also met Mohamed Menfi, chairman of Libya’s Presidential Council, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, emphasising the importance of national dialogue and reconciliation.
"A fragmented Libya exports insecurity; a sovereign Libya can contain it," says Bakkoush. "The more Libya restores unified control over its institutions, borders and security forces" the better the country will prevent illegal trafficking networks and help regional stability, adds the Libyan analyst.
Ankara-Benghazi channels
Türkiye's efforts to unify Libya have taken shape particularly since the October 2020 ceasefire agreement between the UN-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) in Tripoli and Khalifa Haftar’s eastern-based Libyan National Army (LNA), which ended large-scale fighting in the country's civil war.
Before the ceasefire, Türkiye had already established important ties with Libya, signing a landmark maritime agreement with the Tripoli government in 2019 that delineated their respective maritime jurisdictions in the gas-rich Eastern Mediterranean. Following the ceasefire, Ankara increasingly turned its attention towards Libya's east.
“Since the 2020 ceasefire, Türkiye’s engagement with eastern Libya has evolved beyond humanitarian assistance and reconstruction to include greater political, economic, and defence-related cooperation,” Ferhat Polat, a senior researcher and analyst specialising in North African geopolitics and security, tells TRT World.
Saddam Haftar, the youngest son of Khalifa Haftar, who was appointed deputy general commander of eastern forces in August 2025, has been “an important figure in this rapprochement, visiting Türkiye several times and meeting with senior Turkish officials,” Polat says.
According to Polat, Haftar's visits, alongside growing institutional contacts between Ankara and eastern Libya, have opened new channels of communication between the two sides, contributing to the ongoing national dialogue between the rival western and eastern administrations.
He also points to Türkiye's growing defence capabilities and military ties with Libya as factors that could help the North African country establish a unified security structure across its vast territory.
In August 2025, the Turkish naval vessel TCG Kinaliada made a significant port call in Benghazi, where Turkish and eastern Libyan military officials discussed cooperation under the framework of a “One Libya, One Army” objective.
“Once security is firmly established across the country, the broader stabilization process can progress more smoothly. In this context, bringing Libya’s military institutions under a unified command structure is crucial,” Polat tells TRT World.
“Türkiye has provided training and other support to strengthen the professionalism and institutional capacity of the Libyan army.”

Splitting cells informs Shanghai research campus' interconnected buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:33:17 UTC
18:33:17 KST

Splitting cells informs Shanghai research campus' interconnected buildings
Architecture studio BDP has unveiled a pharmaceutical research campus in Shanghai, China, comprised of interconnected buildings that evoke the movement of cell division.
Located within Hongqiao International Central Business District in west Shanghai, the 186,000-square-metre research and development headquarters was developed for Chia Tai Tianqing Pharmaceutical Group (CTTQ), one of China's leading pharmaceutical companies.
BDP's design was informed by the structure of cells, with two pairs of interconnected buildings on the site.
Both pairs were designed to resemble cells splitting with glass covered bridges connecting them.
The cores of the two research buildings are split between either end of the buildings, allowing large and flexible floor plates for changing laboratory requirements.
One of the research buildings was connected to a smaller block containing staff accommodation, while the other one was connected to a taller administrative building.
The administrative building is the highest on the site, with the aim of creating a vocal point for the new headquarters. A conference centre is connected to this building.
"This is a place for research within a campus that doesn't turn its back on the city or the people using it," said BDP director Tianyi Gu.
"The central heart opens the site up to the public, while the buildings are planned to make research, collaboration and everyday life work together."
A raised sky bridge curves around the site to connect all the buildings on the campus as well as providing a series of indoor and outdoor spaces for people to meet and interact.
Cafes, a canteen and gym are located at the lower levels of the buildings, supporting the wellbeing of the staff and work-life balance.
According to BDP, the arrangement of the four blocks was designed to break down the scale of the campus into a series of destinations.
"We've paid close attention to the things that make a difference to people's working day – access to daylight and fresh air, places to meet, eat and exercise, and spaces to step away from the laboratory," said Gu.
"For CTTQ, this is a research campus built for change, but also a place for people, a place with a strong sense of identity and an identifiable connection to Shanghai."
Passive design strategies were applied across the campus, including natural ventilation, facade solar shading, as well as customised facade designs responding to different orientations and functions.
Low-E glass was used to improve energy performance, while a large array of photovoltaic panels were installed on the roof, creating a unique pattern that add to the identity of the campus.
Elsewhere in China, KPF designed a tech campus in Shenzhen wrapped by a one-kilometer-long "landscape ribbon", while RSHP has completed a mixed-use skyscraper in Shanghai, informed by the city's historical laneway network.
The photography is courtesy of BDP.

Nigeria seeks 2 permanent UN Security Council seats for Africa

Unknown Publisher

Nigeria seeks 2 permanent UN Security Council seats for Africa
Africa currently has no permanent representative on 15-member Security Council
Kabir Adeniyi
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
LAGOS
Nigeria has called for the creation of at least two permanent seats for Africa on the UN Security Council, including veto powers, as it renewed its push for reform of the global body.
Vice President Kashim Shettima made the demand Thursday while delivering President Bola Tinubu’s national statement at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Shettima said the current structure of the Security Council no longer reflected contemporary geopolitical realities and argued that Africa should have permanent representation in the body responsible for maintaining international peace and security.
“The world of 2026 cannot remain captive to the distribution of power in 1945,” he said, according to Nigeria’s state-run News Agency of Nigeria, on Friday.
“Nigeria demands, in accordance with the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration, at least two permanent seats for Africa, with all the rights and responsibilities of permanent membership, including the veto for as long as it exists, and five non-permanent seats in total.”
The African Union's common position calls for at least two permanent seats for the continent with full privileges, including the veto, alongside five non-permanent seats.
The African Union reaffirmed the position in May, saying Africa's exclusion from permanent representation constituted a historical imbalance and called for stronger coordination among African states to advance the reform agenda.
Africa currently has no permanent representative on the 15-member Security Council. The council has five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — while 10 other members are elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms.
Nigeria has repeatedly campaigned for a permanent African seat and has cited its population, economic weight, diplomatic role and contributions to international peacekeeping as grounds for a stronger role in global decision-making.
In his address, Shettima also pointed to Nigeria's participation in peace operations and regional efforts through the Economic Community of West African States and the African Union.
He said Nigeria had contributed to peace operations and diplomatic efforts in countries including Liberia, Sierra Leone, Darfur, Mali and The Gambia, while continuing to support initiatives on counterterrorism, democratic governance and maritime security.
Nigeria's renewed call comes amid broader international discussions on reforming the Security Council, whose permanent membership has remained unchanged since its establishment in the aftermath of World War II.
The reform process requires broad support among UN member states and agreement on changes to the UN Charter, making the expansion of permanent membership a complex diplomatic issue.
Nigeria has previously said it would continue engaging African and international partners in support of the continent's common position on Security Council reform.

Switzerland’s neutrality vote is asking the wrong question
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:32:58 UTC
18:32:58 KST

Switzerland’s neutrality vote is asking the wrong question
The referendum asks what Switzerland should do to remain neutral. The harder question is what neutrality can still do for Switzerland.
On September 27, Switzerland votes on whether to lock a stricter definition of neutrality into its constitution. The initiative would bar Switzerland from cooperating with a military alliance unless it were under military attack or such an attack were being prepared, and prevent it from imposing sanctions on a belligerent state unless those sanctions were mandated by the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). Polls suggest it will fail, with 63 percent intending to reject it. But that result says less about Swiss faith in neutrality — which remains overwhelming — than about how badly the vote and the surrounding debates miss the real issue: the vote asks whether to restrict sanctions and alliances; the real question is how neutrality can still deliver security and prosperity.
Neutrality has shaped Swiss identity since 1815, when the European powers recognised Switzerland’s permanent neutrality after the Napoleonic Wars. It survived two world wars and the Cold War on a basic premise: keeping foreign armies off Swiss territory would keep Switzerland out of other countries’ wars, while trading with all sides would keep its diverse economy connected to the markets on which its welfare depends.
The neutrality initiative grew out of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Switzerland had adopted European Union sanctions before, but sanctioning Russia specifically — a major power Switzerland had long sought not to antagonise — cut deeper. It sharpened a question earlier cases had already raised: whether economic measures against a belligerent power were compatible with neutrality at all. The Swiss People’s Party and Pro Schweiz, or Pro Suisse, launched the initiative to preserve the stricter model they believed had served Switzerland well.
A “yes” vote would bring significant changes, while a “no” would largely mean a continuation of the flexible, case-by-case neutrality Switzerland practises today. A “yes” could force Switzerland to unwind its existing sanctions against Russia and would prevent it from joining future EU- or United States-led sanctions against belligerent states unless those sanctions were mandated by the UNSC. It would also constrain the bilateral cyber, air-defence and joint-exercise cooperation with its neighbours (that happen to be members of NATO) that Switzerland has expanded since 2022 — precisely the kind of cooperation it may need more of as the European security environment deteriorates. But whichever way Switzerland votes, the harder questions will remain, because the initiative answers a 2022 question, and the world has moved on in three ways it cannot address.
What has changed
Three things have changed since 2022: the nature of the threat from Russia, the reliability of the US as a trading partner and the strategic implications of China’s economic weight.
The first is the threat itself. For two centuries, Swiss neutrality was designed primarily to protect its security in the context of a territorial war. Switzerland, a heavily armed state in the Alps, made invasion costly and denied foreign armies an easy route through Swiss territory. That model has much less to say about a new threat: a European war that indirectly yet significantly affects Switzerland.
Switzerland’s 2026 Security Policy Strategy warns of a “window of vulnerability” emerging in Europe around 2028 as Russia rebuilds military capacity while Europe rearms. In such a conflict, Switzerland could face missiles or drones crossing its airspace without knowing immediately who launched them or where they are headed. Switzerland is also deeply integrated into Europe’s financial, rail, electricity and data networks. A continental conflict would therefore reach it even if no foreign soldier crossed its border.
Russian hostility towards Switzerland has also increased since 2022. In 2024, Swiss authorities uncovered an alleged Russian effort to obtain sensitive military-related material in Switzerland. Cyberattacks also targeted Swiss government websites around the Ukraine peace summit that June. By 2025, Swiss intelligence was warning that the country faced growing risks of espionage, sabotage and operations involving critical infrastructure, specifically from Russia. Whether that hostility is payback for Switzerland’s sanctions or simply reflects Russia’s broader confrontation with Europe matters less than the practical conclusion: formal neutrality does not guarantee security, and security cannot be obtained in isolation.
The second change is US foreign and trade policy. In 2022, Switzerland could still assume a relatively stable relationship with its major trading partners. That is harder now. In 2025, Washington imposed a 39 percent tariff on many Swiss exports. The shock and disbelief remain, even after the tariff was reduced to 15 percent following negotiations and major Swiss investment commitments. The episode showed that neutral status buys no economic goodwill: Washington’s trade policy is driven by its own interests, not by Switzerland’s neutrality. And if neutrality cannot shield Switzerland from a partner’s tariffs, abstaining from sanctions will not shield it either. For Bern, the practical response should therefore be not stricter neutrality but greater economic diversification.
That makes China more important. Swiss-Chinese goods trade is worth more than 50 billion Swiss francs ($60.4bn) a year when gold is included, while trade with Russia was 4.7 billion francs in 2021, the last full year before the invasion, when Russia ranked 23rd among Switzerland’s trading partners. Bern and Beijing are also deepening their free-trade relationship, with negotiations on an upgraded agreement concluded in August 2026 that would make 99.8 percent of current Swiss exports to China tariff-free. Sanctioning China in a future crisis over Taiwan would therefore impose costs on Switzerland on an entirely different scale from sanctions against Moscow.
Ironically, both sides of the neutrality debate may eventually reach the same conclusion: supporters of stricter neutrality would oppose such sanctions on principle, their opponents on economic grounds. That convergence is the point. If Switzerland’s answer to the next great-power crisis is the same whichever way it votes on September 27, the constitution is not where the real decision is being made. The initiative regulates what Switzerland does — whom it joins and whom it sanctions. The new threats depend on what others do to Switzerland, whatever its posture.
The debate Switzerland should be having
Three questions will outlast the vote. The first is how closely Switzerland should cooperate with its neighbours, including NATO members, without undermining the credibility of neutrality. Modern air defence depends increasingly on shared radar, intelligence and coordination across borders. Switzerland’s accession to the European Sky Shield Initiative in 2024 is the live example. Switzerland argues that such cooperation can take place in peacetime without creating an alliance.
The deeper that cooperation becomes, however, the harder the distinction may be to sustain in the eyes of a potential adversary. Too little cooperation could leave Swiss airspace vulnerable; too much could make Switzerland appear functionally aligned with NATO. Neutrality depends not only on legal definitions but also on how other states interpret Swiss behaviour.
The second question is whether Switzerland can close its military capabilities gap fast enough for neutrality to remain credible. Defence spending fell from 1.4 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1990 to 0.7 percent by 2021 and is set to reach only 1 percent by 2032 — still four years after Switzerland’s own warning of a “window of vulnerability” from around 2028. That gap matters: a country unable to defend its territory and airspace becomes dependent on its neighbours in a crisis, reducing the freedom of action neutrality is meant to preserve.
Nor is this only a defence question: the 1907 Hague Conventions oblige a neutral state to prevent belligerents from using its territory, while armed neutrality requires Switzerland to be able to defend that territory, so the capability gap is a neutrality problem in its own right. Real deterrence, not constitutional wording, is what makes neutrality credible.
The third question is how much taking sides costs, and when. The current debate often conflates the legal requirements of armed neutrality with the morality of foreign policy: whether Switzerland can legally condemn or sanction a specific aggressor becomes mixed with whether it has a moral obligation to do so in every case, with too little attention paid to how the consequences differ in peace and war. In peacetime, being perceived as partial may weaken Switzerland’s credibility and value as a mediator — a meaningful but ultimately manageable cost. In wartime, the consequences could be far more serious. If an adversary regards Switzerland as effectively aligned with its enemy, the country could lose much of the practical protection neutrality is meant to provide while still lacking the guarantees of a formal alliance. That would leave it with the worst of both worlds: treated as aligned by an adversary, without allies obliged to defend it.
The referendum outcome therefore risks turning a strategic problem into a legal one. Switzerland certainly needs to decide what neutrality means in the 21st century. But the decisive questions concern deterrence, defence cooperation, economic vulnerability and credibility, not simply whether sanctions and alliances should be restricted in the constitution.
Neutrality was never really the question. What Switzerland can still achieve with it is.

China's Xi says pandas will soon arrive in Atlanta as part of 'panda diplomacy' tradition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:32:06 UTC
18:32:06 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping has news for the people of Atlanta: The pandas are coming
Two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will arrive at Zoo Atlanta "in a few days," Xi announced at the start of his state visit to the United States on Thursday.
"The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans," he said at a White House ceremony. "Here, I have a piece of good news."
 
A Zoo Atlanta representative said the facility would not share information about Ping Ping and Fu Shuang's planned arrival date and declined to comment further. The zoo, which previously housed pandas from 1999 to 2024, announced an agreement in April with the China Wildlife Conservation Association to host the two bears.
China closely controls the exhibition of pandas, one of its prized national symbols. The country claims ownership of all the world's bears and leases them to international zoos in what's been dubbed "panda diplomacy."
 
The tradition began in 1957 when Mao Zedong gifted panda Ping Ping to the Soviet Union. Beijing gifted two pandas to the United States in 1972 as the countries began dialogue toward normalizing relations.
China stopped gifting pandas in 1984 because of the bears' dwindling population and leased them instead, often in pairs for a decade-long period. If the pandas produce offspring while abroad, the cubs remain the property of China and generally return to the country while still young.
<strong>Beijing occasionally withholds pandas for diplomatic purposes</strong><br> <br>Ebbs in diplomatic relations have also led Beijing to occasionally keep pandas out of the United States.
San Diego Zoo's long tenure as a panda host was interrupted from 2019 to 2024. The Washington, DC, National Zoo, another traditional US home for pandas, had no bears for a period between 2023 and 2024 after the expiration of an agreement covering three bears there.
Two new pandas, Bao Li and Qing Bao, arrived in Washington in October 2024. Another pair, Yun Chuan and Xin Bao, arrived at the San Diego Zoo in June 2024.
 
Pandas once were considered endangered, but the International Union for Conservation of Nature improved the species' status to "vulnerable" in 2016. Roughly 1,800 pandas live in the wild, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

Emre Gurkan Abay and Emir Yildirim

The agricultural trade between Türkiye and Russia reached around $6 billion last year, highlighting how the two countries “complement” each other in economic relations, Russian agricultural minister told Anadolu.
 
Oksana Lut, speaking on the sidelines of the second International Forum on Veterinary Safety in Moscow, stated that the agricultural trade volume between Türkiye and Russia remained highly stable, while Russian exports to Türkiye are currently higher than imports.
“Türkiye and Russia complement each other in agriculture; while we primarily export grains, oilseeds, and processed oil products to Türkiye, we receive mainly fruits and vegetables,” she said.
Lut called her Turkish counterparts “reliable partners,” expressing optimism that broader geopolitical issues would not disrupt the mutually beneficial supply chain.

====================================================================================================

Israel is fighting a new war on the financial front – and it is not ready - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:31:42 UTC
18:31:42 KST

In May 2022, a few months after Russia invaded Ukraine, I wrote a column in these pages warning that Israel could one day find itself facing Russian-style sanctions.
The world was imposing the most sweeping sanctions regime in decades on Moscow, targeting thousands of individuals, companies, banks, and government entities. And while back in 2022 it seemed far-fetched that something like this could one day happen to Israel, there were already voices being heard on the fringes asking whether similar tools could one day be used against the Jewish state.
There was a politician in Colombia, someone on the far Left in Britain, a few pundits in Europe and the United States. It was not overly significant, but it was something.
My argument then was simple: Eventually, there would be another war in Gaza. Israel would do what it believed necessary to defend itself, and images of Palestinian casualties would fill television screens and social media feeds. Despite Israel’s efforts to minimize civilian casualties, public opinion would turn against it.
No one knew then that just 17 months later, Hamas would invade Israel on October 7, and that despite suffering the worst attack in its history, Israel would find itself experiencing the greatest diplomatic isolation since its establishment.
Which brings us to what happened this month.
On September 8, Britain, France, and Canada announced plans to impose restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements – an import ban on settlement goods, as well as measures targeting companies and individuals providing construction, infrastructure, financing, and other services that facilitate settlement expansion. British legislation is expected to take several months to implement.
For now, these measures are designed to distinguish between Israel within the Green Line and Israeli activity beyond it. Indeed, the British government has explicitly said that its planned import ban is supposed to avoid affecting Israel within its recognized borders.
But sanctions have a way of expanding.
Imagine that after the October 27 election, the next Israeli government decides to formally annex part of the West Bank. It does not have to be all of the territory or even all of Area C, where the settlements are located. It could just be the Jordan Valley, a strip of land that even opposition parties believe should belong to Israel.
What happens then? How difficult will it be for countries that have already imposed sanctions to move the dial another click?
Today it is a company building homes in a settlement. Tomorrow it could be a company building a highway serving that settlement. Then the bank financing the project. Then the financial institution underwriting the bank.
Earlier this week, I drove along Highway 60 toward Psagot and got stuck in traffic because work was underway to expand the West Bank highway. Now imagine that a construction company doing that work risks sanctions, or the bank that is financing it, as well as the American or European company that is supposed to supply the bulldozers and trucks.
Impossible? Sadly, no.
There are those who claim that America would never do that to Israel. The problem is that the line was crossed in 2024 when the Biden administration imposed sanctions on Israeli settlers accused of violence and destabilizing activity in the West Bank. While Donald Trump rescinded those sanctions immediately upon taking office in January 2025, the taboo has been broken, and what Biden did paves the way for a future Democratic administration.
Ben Gvir, Smotrich sanctioned abroad
There was also a time when the idea of Western governments imposing sanctions on Israeli cabinet ministers would have sounded absurd. But that has happened as well, with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who have been sanctioned by the UK and parts of Europe.
So why would anyone confidently assume that what we see today is the end of the process rather than just a taste of what can still come?
We need to remember that a comprehensive sanctions regime would not merely mean that a few politicians cannot travel to London, or that a few settlers would have their bank accounts frozen. A genuinely broad sanctions regime would strike at the foundation of Israel’s economy.
International companies would need to ask themselves whether maintaining operations in Israel is worth the legal exposure. Israeli tech companies would most likely decide to relocate abroad. Foreign investment would drop. The brain drain that Israel already worries about would accelerate.
And even if America were to remain outside such a sanctions regime, Israel cannot simply shrug and claim that Europe does not matter. The European Union is Israel’s largest trading partner. In 2025, trade in goods between Israel and the EU totaled €43.3 billion. The EU accounted for 33.1% of Israel’s imports and 29.4% of its exports.
Losing significant access to that market would not be an inconvenience – it would fundamentally change the Israeli economy.
So what can Israel do? On the one hand, it needs to diversify its trade and diplomatic ties. It should expand trade and diplomatic relationships in Asia, particularly with countries where Gaza and the Palestinian issue play a smaller role in determining economic ties. Israelis are innovative – supply chains can be rebuilt, and new trading partners can be found.
Israel would survive, but it would become a different country.
It would be more isolated, more expensive to live in, less attractive for investment, and increasingly disconnected from the Western economic and diplomatic system, of which Israel has spent decades playing an integral part.
None of the above means that Israel should allow foreign governments to dictate its decision-making. A sovereign country must make decisions even when they carry costs, and there will always be moments when Israelis decide a particular policy is essential to their security and are willing to pay that price.
But we should at least understand the price and stop the habit of dismissing every warning as meaningless.
Our politicians tell us that Europe doesn’t matter, that the United Nations is a waste of time, and that the International Criminal Court is irrelevant. The problem is that none of this is true. All of these institutions matter – just ask Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who cannot travel to Europe anymore – and their decisions actually affect lives here in Israel.
In this context, Netanyahu addressed the UN on Thursday. As I wrote this column, the prime minister was making his way to New York, where he was expected to give a powerful speech. Whatever one thinks of him, Netanyahu remains one of Israel’s most talented communicators, a gifted orator who understands the theater of the UN better than almost any Israeli leader before him.
There may be a prop, and there will almost certainly be a memorable line. But none of it will solve the problem, because a speech, no matter how good, cannot reverse three years of diplomatic deterioration.
Israel’s public diplomacy has been neglected throughout this war. For more than two years, Netanyahu failed to appoint a permanent head of the National Public Diplomacy Directorate. Ministers have repeatedly been allowed to say whatever they wanted without considering the diplomatic consequences.
Settler violence has been treated as a nuisance rather than as a strategic threat that hands Israel’s adversaries ammunition on a silver platter.
And only now, after years of accusations against Israel and the IDF, has the military finally decided to establish a multidisciplinary team to respond to false claims and distortions about its conduct, due to a film that received a standing ovation in Venice.
So, yes, Netanyahu stood at the UN and made Israelis proud. But speeches are not a strategy. Israel faces a campaign today being waged on several fronts: on the battlefield, in international institutions, in the information arena, and now through economic and financial pressure.
Does anyone seriously believe we are ready for what comes next?
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD Forum, a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His latest book (with Amir Bohbot), While Israel Slept, is a bestseller in the United States.

German city votes to end Stolpersteine Holocaust memorial stones for Nazi victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:31:41 UTC
18:31:41 KST

The city council of Heidenau, in the German state of Saxony, voted on Thursday to no longer permit new Stolpersteine memorial stones to be placed on the city's streets and sidewalks in memory of Jews and other victims of the Nazi regime.
The motion passed in a secret ballot, with 13 council members voting in favor, six opposed, and one abstaining. It was jointly submitted by representatives of the right-wing Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Alternative for Germany (AfD), together with representatives of the "Oberelbe Alliance for More Democracy."
German artist Gunter Demnig launched the Stolpersteine, or "stumbling stones," project in the 1990s, and it has become one of the world's largest decentralized memorial projects.
The small brass plaques are generally embedded in the pavement outside the former home or last workplace of a person persecuted or murdered by the Nazis. Each bears the individual's name and details of their fate.
Under the resolution, applications to install new Stolpersteine "in public streets and sidewalks" will now be rejected. Instead, supporters of the measure want memorials to Nazi victims concentrated at a commemorative site in the city's Northern Cemetery, where people would not walk over the memorial plaques.
Those behind the proposal argued that residents, relatives of victims and various memorial initiatives no longer regard Stolpersteine as an appropriate form of remembrance, in part because passersby step on the names of those who were murdered and persecuted.
City administration recommends rejection of proposal against Holocaust memorials
The city administration recommended that council members reject the proposal, arguing that commemoration should remain "visible and present in public space."
Five Stolpersteine have already been installed in Heidenau, a town near Dresden. The first was placed outside the town hall in 2021 to remember Paul Gröger, Heidenau's first mayor.
Gröger was removed from office after the Nazis came to power, arrested in June 1933, and sent to the Hohnstein concentration camp, where he was severely abused. Shortly after his release, on August 27, 1933, he took his own life.
Other stones in the city commemorate members of the Jewish Reiner family and were installed following an initiative by students. Local activists have sought in recent years to expand the project to commemorate additional victims, including Martha and Fritz Goldstein.
They submitted a request to the municipality as early as February 2025, with the organizers offering to finance both the stones and the installation costs.
International Auschwitz Committee denounces motion against Stolpersteine
The decision prompted sharp criticism. The International Auschwitz Committee described it as an attempt to once again push the victims of the Nazis out of the city center and particularly criticized the cooperation between CDU and AfD representatives on the issue.
The March of the Living organization said that the decision served as a "grave warning sign.
"These stones confront passersby with the atrocities committed by the Germans - the Nazis - at the very sites where they occurred; blocking their installation sacrifices historical truth for the sake of political interests."
They also called the decision "a grave injustice - an act of erasure that compounds the crime of extermination."
March of the Living urged Heidenau to retract the decision.
Opposition to the use of Stolpersteine, however, is not unique to Heidenau. Munich also does not permit them to be installed on public property, in part because of the position of Charlotte Knobloch, president of the city's Jewish community, who has argued that it is inappropriate for the names of those murdered by the Nazis to be placed where people walk over them.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Foreign Ministry aims at online younger generation in new digital public diplomacy efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:31:38 UTC
18:31:38 KST

Following Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's address to the UN General Assembly on Thursday, the Foreign Ministry is concluding a five-week digital campaign aimed at one of the most challenging audiences for Israeli public diplomacy: the younger generation.
Data from the UNmasked UN campaign shows that one of the most prominent age groups it reaches is people aged 25 to 35, with significant success in English-speaking countries, led by the US and UK. Some content has attracted hundreds of thousands of views, while meme-based posts have reached up to one million views across all platforms.
But the challenge is not only reaching young people who disagree with Israel. It is also reaching those who simply are not familiar with the facts, institutions, and terminology at the center of the debate. You could call it a knowledge gap, or, less politely, a wave of ignorance.
A 25-year-old who encounters a claim about UNRWA or a UN commission of inquiry does not necessarily know what the body is, what authority it has, or what lies behind the controversy surrounding it. It is impossible to start the conversation on page three when part of the audience hasn't read page one.
For that reason, UNmasked UN decided to speak to young people in their own language, deliberately simplifying subjects usually left to the language of diplomats and lawyers. Commissions of inquiry, UNRWA, votes, and complex UN mechanisms are turned into graphics, short videos, memes, or questions posed to Grok. Some of the team members behind the campaign are themselves part of the same age group.
Memes hook younger viewers into Israel campaign
In that sense, the campaign has also become a real-time content laboratory, testing which formats make young people stop scrolling, react, and keep reading. Memes, in particular, have stood out.
They are not used as a substitute for content, but as a hook. A meme can make an audience stop, smile, or become irritated, and then want to understand what lies behind it. Such posts have reached up to one million views across all platforms.
Alongside memes, the campaign uses videos, short posts, and the Ask Grok feature. Instead of telling users, "believe us," it asks the AI tool questions and allows its response to lead the conversation.
Over five weeks, the campaign moved through a range of topics, including the way UN bodies report on Israel, the responsibility of the organization and its senior officials, UNRWA, the commission of inquiry, and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. The timing was planned in advance so that the campaign would peak during the week of the General Assembly and Netanyahu's UN address.
Foreign Ministry's campaign on UN reaches hundreds of thousands
The Foreign Ministry views the figures so far as an indication that the approach is working. The campaign has reached a younger audience, generating exposure ranging from hundreds of thousands to as many as one million views for its most prominent content and, above all, reaching audiences in English-speaking countries that would not necessarily have sought out content about the UN on their own.
Since the campaign was launched, its messages and the discussion surrounding them have expanded, with organizations, international figures, and additional media outlets joining the conversation and amplifying some of the issues it raised.
For those behind the campaign, the lesson is simple: In the battle for young people's attention and opinions, it is not enough for information merely to exist. Young people have to want to engage with it. And when trying to combat ignorance, sometimes the answer is not to say more, but to speak their language.

Türkiye puts forward UN FAO leader candidate with global food security vision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:30:39 UTC
18:30:39 KST

Sevgi Ceren Gokkoyun, Dilara Zengin Okay and Emir Yildirim
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Türkiye’s nominee for director-general of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Mehdi Eker, is accelerating his diplomatic campaign to share Ankara’s vision to resolve the world’s deepening food security issues.
Eker told Anadolu that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan sought support for Türkiye’s candidacy during various meetings, securing direct talks and support pledges from around 100 of the 193 UN member states.
“Some 645 million people are going hungry worldwide, while 1.4 billion are obese, and 2.3 billion do not have enough food on their plates,” he said, noting that the world produces enough food for 11 billion people.
“There’s something wrong here — the issue of food security is one of global security, and ensuring global security will be very difficult so long as this is not resolved,” he added.
Eker stated that food shortages can lead to population displacement and migration, while Türkiye’s approach is based on safeguarding food as a fundamental human right.
“Food is weaponized against people in Gaza, against children — this brutality, this oppression, must somehow come to an end, and the right to food must not be violated,” he said.
“Türkiye’s perspective, approach, understanding of humanity, and vision of civilization will be reflected in the governance of this organization,” he added.
Eker noted that mitigating these humanitarian crises requires stabilizing vulnerable agricultural supply routes across the Black Sea Basin, the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and the Gulf of Aden.
He stated that the UN FAO has three core functions, starting with strengthening global agricultural standards via the international Food Codex and expanding the organization’s statistical network.
The second core function is providing technical assistance and advisory services to developing countries, while Eker’s agenda for the organization focuses on providing these gains through projects to reduce food waste and combat animal diseases threatening human health.
The third function is combating global hunger, where the UN FAO plays an active role. Eker said fulfilling this role is linked to the organization’s sound management.
“This is a matter of humanity, the future of humanity — it’s impossible for the world to function and move forward amid such oppression, darkness, and brutality, when food is weaponized against vulnerable populations like children, women, and the elderly, who are dying of hunger,” he noted.
“As Türkiye, we believe the UN FAO, like all other UN agencies, will be engaged in more effective, efficient, and beneficial work for humanity,” he added.
UN FAO Director-General Qu Dongyu’s second term will expire in 2027.
Angola, Italy, Spain, and Ireland put forward their candidates for this position.
The new director-general will be elected in Rome next summer to serve the organization from 2027 to 2031.

Voyage apostolique du Pape Léon XIV en France.
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25

18:30:00 KST

Le Président de la République a accueilli Sa Sainteté le Pape Léon XIV au Palais de l'Élysée ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026, dans le cadre de son voyage apostolique en France.
Cette visite fait suite à la première rencontre entre le chef de l’État et le Pape Léon XIV au Vatican en avril dernier.
Elle s'inscrit dans le cadre des relations traditionnelles entre la France et le Saint-Siège, et témoigne de la profondeur d'un dialogue fondé sur des valeurs et des engagements partagés.
Revoir l'accueil à l'aéroport :
 
            Le Président de la République et Madame Brigitte Macron ont ensuite accueilli le Saint-Père au Palais de l'Élysée.
Revoir l'accueil :
Les échanges entre le Président de la République et le Saint-Père ont permis d’aborder les aspects clés de la relation bilatérale, ainsi que les principaux défis globaux qui mobilisent conjointement la France et le Saint-Siège, au premier rang desquels le climat et l'intelligence artificielle.
À cette occasion ont également été abordés les grands enjeux internationaux, la guerre en Ukraine, la paix et la stabilité au Proche-Orient, les partenariats avec l’Afrique, sur la base d’une volonté conjointe d’œuvrer pour la paix et le dialogue.
Revoir les allocutions :
25 septembre 2026 - Seul le prononcé fait foi
Discours du Président de la République - Voyage apostolique de Sa Sainteté le Pape Léon XIV en France
Emmanuel MACRON
Très Saint-Père, Mesdames et Messieurs en vos grades et qualités,
C'est pour la République française un grand honneur et aussi une grande joie que de vous accueillir aujourd'hui sur notre sol. Un grand honneur et une grande joie en ce que, confrontés souvent au spectacle des misères du monde, beaucoup de nos compatriotes ressentent, avec votre visite en France, une espérance.
Oui, comme il est dit dans l'Ecclésiaste, il ne faut pas s'attrister comme ceux qui n'ont pas d'espérance, et c'est un sentiment, je le sais, que vous partagez. Vous voici, 18 mois après le commencement de votre pontificat. Et vous voici pour un temps long que vous nous offrez et qui nous touche. C'est ici que débute ce chemin de foi, si j'ose dire, qui va vous mener du cœur de Paris à Notre-Dame, de l'Elysée à l'UNESCO, de la place de la Concorde à Saint-Denis, du Stade de France à la Maison Bakhita, de Lourdes, ville de Bernadette Soubirous, à Metz, carrefour des mémoires chrétiennes de notre Europe. Autant d'étapes qui disent votre lien personnel avec notre pays. Très Saint-Père, nous sommes fiers de vos racines normandes. Et vous verrez que nous avons même trouvé des racines béarnaises et bigourdanes.
Autant d'étapes comme autant d'épisodes qui racontent aussi cette histoire si particulière qui lie le christianisme à notre pays. Histoire deux fois millénaire, dont témoignent ces paysages de France, parsemés de cathédrales, basiliques, églises, monuments venus du fond des âges, inestimables dons de ceux qui nous ont précédés et qui se faisaient de notre pays une certaine idée. Il fut long. Ce temps où la religion chrétienne, ambitieuse d'être l'architecte de l'universel, guidait nos ancêtres à tailler la pierre, afin de laisser inscrite dans la chaîne des temps la trace visible de leur idéal. Croire, c'est créer. Et c'est au nom de cet héritage que nous avons œuvré, après le terrible incendie de Notre-Dame de Paris, pour qu'elle puisse être rebâtie en cinq ans et rendue non seulement aux catholiques, mais à tous les Français et au-delà encore au monde entier, et tant de talents, d'artisans, d'apprentis, de bénévoles, s'y sont donnés avec cette espérance chevillée au cœur.
Car Notre-Dame est une part de nous, un emblème de cette volonté si française d'offrir au monde toutes les beautés que peut engendrer l'esprit humain dès lors qu'il est mu par un idéal de fraternité universelle. Oui, cette histoire deux fois millénaire a créé un lien singulier entre la France et l'Église catholique. Et lorsque la République décida, il y a un peu plus de 120 ans, de la séparation entre l'Église et l'État, elle donna forme à une laïcité française qui n'est nullement la négation de la religion. La République se fait un devoir de permettre à chacune et à chacun en conscience de penser et d'exprimer son point de vue dans toutes les sphères de son existence, de croire ou de ne pas croire, dans l'intimité comme dans la sphère publique, à condition d'en respecter les lois. C'est dans ce cadre, très Saint-Père, que vous solliciterez la conscience de tous les Français qui s'associent en pensée et en action à ce que vous représentez, à eux, à tous ceux qui, en France comme ailleurs, sont attentifs à ce que vous avez à dire au monde, et je m'en réjouis.
La République veille aussi. Depuis 15 ans, les actes commis à l'encontre de personnes ou de biens en raison de leur religion ont malheureusement connu une recrudescence. Et ces insupportables démonstrations d'intolérance frappent la religion chrétienne au cœur. Les communautés juives et musulmanes en sont aussi victimes. Et c'est un combat essentiel que nous menons et mènerons pour protéger les lieux de culte, continuer de former les esprits à la tolérance, en même temps que nous encourageons le dialogue interreligieux si vivant dans notre pays.
La quête de la paix sur tous les fronts est une nécessité existentielle. Et il n'est pas un catholique qui ne puisse être sensible à ce combat pour le bien commun. Et j'ajouterai, pas un juif, pas un musulman, pas un protestant, ni un orthodoxe ou un bouddhiste. Il n'est personne en France, croyant ou non, qui puisse refuser de faire sienne cette quête. La paix est aussi cet horizon pour lequel nous œuvrons ensemble. Vous avez placé les premiers mois de votre pontificat sous le signe d'une paix désarmée et désarmante. Exigence qui prend une force particulière alors que la guerre meurtrit notre continent et que partout tensions et conflits ressurgissent. Exigence qui rappelle aussi que la paix est davantage que le silence des armes et qu'elle suppose justice, sécurité, respect des droits de l'homme, souveraineté des nations, et droit des peuples à disposer d'eux-mêmes. Et plus fondamentalement la capacité à reconnaître l'autre pour ce qu'il entend être.
La France se tient du côté de la paix, du multilatéralisme d'action, du respect du droit international et de la charte des Nations Unies. Et nous nous y tenons partout, sans double standard, avec cohérence et constance, car une vie vaut une vie et tous les peuples sont à défendre.
Ce combat pour la paix est inséparable de celui pour la dignité humaine et la lutte contre les injustices. Partout, ce sont toujours les plus fragiles qui paient le prix des crises et des conflits, qui contraignent tant de femmes et d'hommes à fuir leur pays. A la maison Bakhita, vous rencontrerez celles et ceux qui accueillent les exilés, les plus pauvres, les plus isolés. Là encore, la République et l'Église croisent souvent les mêmes visages. Le visage de ceux qu'il nous faut voir en face, le visage de ceux dont la voix peine à porter, de ceux qui nous rappellent l'exigence de fraternité, celle-là même qui fait de l'autre son frère en République, cette attention que nous devons aux plus fragiles.
Et je veux saluer ici l'engagement quotidien de tant de Français, de bénévoles, d'associations et notamment chrétiennes qui servent quotidiennement leurs prochains. Leur dévouement, leur solidarité disent un formidable élan d'espoir. Comme je veux saluer l'engagement de tous ceux qui contribuent à l'éducation de nos enfants, qu'il s'agisse de l'enseignement public ou de l'enseignement privé dans notre pays. Tous sont aussi au service de la défense du bien commun que nous partageons par-delà les frontières, notre planète et le vivant.
C'est pour cela que la France a porté l'Accord de Paris il y a 11 ans et s'est battue pour obtenir l'Accord sur les océans l'année dernière. C'est pour cela aussi que nous continuons de défendre le pacte de Paris pour les peuples et la planète, afin que nul pays n'ait à retarder sa transition faute de moyens, ni à choisir entre son développement et la préservation de la planète et du vivant. Climat et biodiversité irriguent les choix de notre siècle. L'Église catholique, avec le pape François, puis avec vous-même, l'a toujours rappelé sans ambiguïté. Nous vous en rendons grâce. Ce n'est pas seulement affaire de technologie ou d'ajustement. Cela révèle notre manière d'habiter le monde, d'y produire, de consommer, de concevoir ensemble la voie du progrès humain. Telle est notre responsabilité commune. Et elle ne s'arrête pas là.
Les ruptures technologiques de notre époque risquent d'engendrer des ruptures anthropologiques inédites. L'être humain ne doit pas être lié par le numérique, mais libéré. Question vertigineuse pour notre génération, parce qu'elle touche non seulement à ce que nous faisons, mais plus encore à l'essentiel, à ce que nous sommes.
L'intelligence artificielle bouleverse déjà le travail, la création, la recherche, l'éducation, l'information, le lien social. Elle décuple nos capacités mais substitue la prédiction au jugement, la performance à la conscience et nous conduit à déléguer une part de notre liberté.
Dès les premiers mois de votre pontificat, vous lui avez consacré l’encyclique Magnifica Humanitas. Et ce message est essentiel. Face à la puissance de la machinerie numérique, l'être humain doit garder la place qui est la sienne. L'intelligence artificielle doit être un serviteur et non un maître. La révolution numérique doit entraîner et non enchaîner. La responsabilité nous revient donc de ne pas permettre que les modèles les plus performants ne se retrouvent entre quelques mains qui auraient à décider pour toute l'humanité, ni que ces avancées les plus exponentielles ne nous conduisent à perdre le contrôle.
C'est pour cela que nous devons trouver la voie d'une organisation internationale réconciliant progrès technologique, justice et humanisme. De la même manière, comme nous sommes en train de le faire pour les réseaux sociaux, il nous faut protéger nos enfants et accompagner nos adolescents. Leur développement affectif et cognitif suppose en effet de les protéger pour pouvoir transmettre et les préparer à la vie.
La lecture, l'apprentissage, les arts et la culture, le sport et le temps avec les autres sont des trésors à leur donner et à protéger des écrans, des algorithmes, comme des chat-box. Protéger nos enfants, accompagner notre jeunesse dans ses interrogations et accueillir son besoin de sens et son engagement sont nos plus beaux devoirs.
La veillée des jeunes que vous présiderez au Stade de France aura une force toute particulière. Des milliers de jeunes y seront en demande d'une parole de responsabilité et de lucide espérance. Leur soif d'engagement dit toute leur vitalité. Ils ne demandent pas qu'on leur promette un monde facile, ils demandent à pouvoir bâtir un monde meilleur.
Très Saint-Père, lors de votre visite, vous allez rencontrer la France, pays de la diversité, comme le disait l'un de nos plus grands historiens, Fernand Braudel. Et c'est précisément parce qu'elle est patrie de liberté et d'esprit que la France est diverse, Nation qui nourrit une passion particulière pour le débat permanent. Ainsi faut-il la considérer pour bien l'aimer. Les grands débats sociaux et sociétaux de ces dernières années en attestent. L'éthique est l'un de nos grands sujets français. Où est la frontière entre le bien et le mal ? Comment concilier les progrès technologiques, notre conscience, notre attachement à la dignité humaine ? Ainsi sommes-nous attentifs toujours à toutes les réponses qui peuvent être apportées à ces questions fondamentales.
Et soyez assuré, très Saint-Père, que tous les Français, moi le premier, vous écouteront avec le plus grand intérêt. Je veux vous redire mon attachement à cette écoute qui a pour vocation de nourrir un dialogue exigeant avec l'Eglise catholique, comme avec tous les autres cultes, avec les croyants, comme avec les non-croyants, avec toutes les traditions philosophiques et humanistes qui font notre pays. Parce que la République ne craint pas les consciences libres, parce que notre Nation est forte du dialogue nécessaire entre toutes les opinions, en demeurant fidèle à notre humanisme, notre attachement à la dignité humaine, en fondant nos décisions sur la science, tout en veillant aux plus fragiles.
Très Saint-Père, je forme le vœu que ces quelques jours vous permettent de rencontrer la France dans toute sa vérité, ses forces, sa diversité, ses débats. Une France empreinte de spiritualité et cherchant toujours l'universel. Une France émancipée, attachée à son projet de liberté, d'égalité et de fraternité, diverse et unie. Une France engagée, sensible à votre présence et dont vous sentirez la ferveur. Très Saint-Père, c'est cette France qui vous reçoit aujourd'hui avec beaucoup d'humilité, avec beaucoup d'honneur et une très grande joie. Soyez le bienvenu.

During the carrier's deployment, there were reports of shortages of food and other essentials, moldy showers and other hygiene issues, and unrepaired holes on the flight deck.
