====================================================================================================

Netanyahu turned the UN into campaign theater – but will Israelis buy the show?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:40:30 UTC
17:40:30 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu flew to New York on Wednesday in search of one powerful campaign image, while apparently having to do without another.
The first was guaranteed: Netanyahu standing before the green marble backdrop at the United Nations podium, speaking flawless English and defending Israel and its soldiers before a hostile international audience just 33 days before Election Day.
The second – the prime minister standing alongside US President Donald Trump – was not on the schedule and appeared virtually impossible to arrange. Trump was due to spend Thursday in Washington with Chinese President Xi Jinping, while Netanyahu needed to leave New York that afternoon to return to Israel before Shabbat and the Sukkot holiday began.
Unlike prime minister Ariel Sharon, who almost always made a point of returning from trips abroad before Shabbat, Netanyahu generally has no qualms about spending Shabbat in a foreign city and flying home afterward. Last year, for instance, he delivered his UN speech on a Friday and met Trump in Washington on Monday.
But this year, in the middle of an election campaign, remaining abroad for the onset of Sukkot is not the image he wanted to project.
That scheduling mismatch – and the inability to arrange a Trump meeting – inevitably generated talk of a snub. But after eight Netanyahu-Trump meetings since the president returned to office, including one less than two months ago, saying that Trump was “snubbing” Netanyahu is an overreach.
Tellingly, Trump – who has so far pointedly stayed out of the election campaign and even told Fox News last month that it was “most appropriate for me to stay out of Israeli elections,” though at some point “I may endorse somebody” – posted a link on Wednesday to a Newsmax story about last week’s Channel 13 poll. That poll, for the first time, showed Netanyahu’s coalition outpolling the opposition Zionist parties, 54-50.
It was as if Trump were telling Netanyahu: “Look, Bibi, you might not get a photo with me this time, but here’s something.”
Never mind that by Wednesday evening, a more recent Channel 13 survey had overtaken that poll, showing the trend had reversed. The opposition Zionist parties, excluding the party of Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, were now leading Netanyahu’s coalition – including Ofer Winter’s new party – 52-51.
Does Netanyahu need Trump to boost status before election?
The more pertinent question is whether Netanyahu needs another Trump photograph in this election at all – or, more precisely, how much such a photograph is actually worth electorally.
Previous steps by Trump to boost Netanyahu before an election – announcing US recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights 19 days before the April 2019 election, or rolling out the “deal of the century” one month and four days before the March 2020 election – did not produce a clear and decisive electoral victory.
Moreover, Trump’s standing with the Israeli public – and even with the Israeli Right – is not what it once was. A July poll by the Israel Democracy Institute found that the percentage of Israelis who believed Israel’s security was a central consideration for Trump had plummeted from 60% in March to 28%.
That does not mean a Trump endorsement would be meaningless. It does mean that the political value of another handshake may be less than it was seven years ago.
Netanyahu's UNGA speeches as a diplomatic tool
IF THE Trump photograph was missing, however, the UN photograph was guaranteed – and in this campaign, it may be the more valuable of the two.
Thursday’s speech marked the 15th time Netanyahu has addressed the UN General Assembly in person as prime minister. In 2020, amid the COVID pandemic, he spoke via prerecorded video.
Each time he has spoken there, he has addressed three distinct audiences: the diplomats in the hall and their bosses back in their countries’ capitals; the international – primarily American – public; and the Israeli public. Each time, however, the speech has been aimed chiefly at one of those audiences.
The best example of a speech directed toward the diplomatic community came in 2011, when Netanyahu took the podium shortly after Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas formally submitted a bid to the UN secretary-general for full recognition of a Palestinian state.
Netanyahu argued that peace could not be manufactured through UN resolutions, even though the organization’s “automatic majority can decide the sun rises in the west.”
This was a direct appeal to the various delegations not to recognize Palestine as a UN member state.
His message was aimed more at diplomats than at the public, and to appeal to them he reiterated his commitment to his 2009 Bar-Ilan University address, confirming on the global stage that he would accept a demilitarized Palestinian state alongside a recognized Jewish state.
That was Netanyahu using the annual UN General Assembly speech as a diplomatic tool.
The very next year, in 2012, he used the same podium to go over the diplomats’ heads and speak directly to international public opinion.
That was perhaps his most memorable UN address – the one in which he drew a thick red line across a Wile E. Coyote-style cartoon bomb to demarcate the point beyond which Iran must not be allowed to advance toward nuclear weapons.
The move was designed to bypass the world leaders in the room and appeal directly to the public. It was built for the television camera and aimed at the person flipping channels in Iowa or Florida who could glance at the screen and immediately understand Israel’s geopolitical predicament.
That speech, delivered in late September 2012, came just six weeks before the highly contested US presidential election between Barack Obama and Mitt Romney. Netanyahu was then locked in a bitter disagreement with Obama over the need to establish redlines for Iran.
Recognizing that he was making no headway with the president through traditional diplomatic channels, Netanyahu took his case visually to the American people. They were his core audience.
On Thursday night, however, the core audience was neither the diplomats in the hall – nor those watching from outside after choosing to boycott the speech – nor the broader international public.
This time, the core audience was the Israeli public, which will vote in another 33 days and determine whether this UN address may have been Netanyahu’s last as prime minister.
Of all the times Netanyahu has addressed the UN General Assembly, this was the first during an Israeli election campaign. The only previous speech that came even close was the redline address of 2012. New elections were called two weeks after Netanyahu returned home and were held in January 2013.
Interestingly, Netanyahu did not meet the US president during that trip either – though in 2012, unlike now, it genuinely was an Obama snub.
Netanyahu running off hostility of enemies, not endorsement from allies
THE OPTICS of another handshake with Trump would undoubtedly have been beneficial to Netanyahu’s campaign. In this particular campaign, however, images of him rebuking a hostile world may be just as valuable – if not more so.
During the September 2019 campaign, photographs of a smiling Netanyahu shaking hands with Trump were everywhere.
The message was that Netanyahu was diplomatically in another league and could pick up the phone and reach any world leader he wanted: Trump, Russia’s Vladimir Putin, or India’s Narendra Modi.
Netanyahu was then running on the strength of the diplomatic relationships he had built.
Now he is running on the hostility of his enemies.
And no venue in the world embodies that hostility more than the United Nations. Netanyahu standing there, standing up to a hostile world – to France’s President Emmanuel Macron, Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and many more – is potentially more valuable in this campaign than another photograph with Trump.
The Israeli public already knows that Netanyahu meets regularly with the US president. Faced with waves of international hostility washing over Israel, what may sell now is the ability to push back against that hostility.
That was the image Netanyahu set out to create on Thursday night, and the audience for it was not the world but Israel’s voters.
Netanyahu’s senior adviser, Yonatan Urich, has already run a mocking social media post contrasting the prime minister’s English with that of Gadi Eisenkot. The UN speech drove that message home in real time.
But does it matter?
Are those voting for the Democrats, for instance, going to hear Netanyahu’s UN speech and say, “Wow, that’s the defender we need on the world stage?” Obviously not.
But those wavering between Netanyahu’s Likud and Eisenkot’s Yashar, or considering one of the smaller parties in either bloc, may be influenced by a virtuoso performance on the world stage that they fear Eisenkot may be unequipped to deliver.
Netanyahu apparently believes it matters. Otherwise, why make a grueling 24-hour transatlantic trip without a guaranteed meeting with the president?
Much has been written over the years about Netanyahu’s use of props and gimmicks at the UN to make his point.
The cartoon bomb was the quintessential prop, but there have been others. In 2009, he waved the original Nazi blueprints of the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp to combat the Holocaust denial being preached by then-Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, who had addressed the world body that year.
In 2015, Netanyahu stood in complete silence for 44 seconds at the podium to protest the world’s “deafening silence” regarding Iran’s threats to destroy Israel.
And in 2023, just before October 7, he stood at the podium with a green marker and displayed a map illustrating a “new Middle East,” highlighting the potential normalization agreement with Saudi Arabia that at the time seemed very much in the air.
This year, the UN itself – green marble backdrop and all – was the prop: Netanyahu using it adroitly to portray himself as the man willing and uniquely able to enter the lion’s den and confront the world.
But will it play in Petah Tikva? Will it matter when Israelis vote? Or is this election so dominated by responsibility for October 7 and the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) draft that this kind of political theater will not make a dent?
Judging by the time and effort Netanyahu put into making this trip so close to the election, he apparently believes it might.

Taiwan's government on Friday denounced Chinese President Xi Jinping's comments on the island's future to US President Donald Trump as a "distortion of the facts," saying only the Taiwanese people can decide their future.
China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, a position President Lai Ching-te and his administration reject.
Xi told Trump in Washington on Thursday that China's position on safeguarding national "reunification" and territorial integrity is clear, and he hoped the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence.
'Taiwan's future can only be determined by the Taiwanese people'
Xi's remarks represent "the consistent Chinese approach of distorting facts and unilaterally conveying its position and claims," Taiwan's foreign ministry said in a statement.
"Taiwan's sovereignty belongs to all the people of Taiwan. The Chinese Communist Party has no right to represent the Taiwanese people, and Taiwan's future can only be determined by the Taiwanese people through democratic means," it added.
The US is Taiwan's most important international backer and arms supplier despite the lack of formal diplomatic ties.
After meeting Xi in Beijing, Trump said in May that he was pausing a planned new arms sale to Taiwan, describing it as a good bargaining chip.
Taiwan's foreign ministry said China was the "true disruptor" of regional peace and stability, pointing to its military threats around the island and in the East and South China Seas.
Taiwan will continue to work closely with the United States and other like-minded partners to jointly safeguard peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait, it added.

BioNTech co-founders name new pharmaceutical company ‘Arife’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:36:03 UTC
17:36:03 KST

BioNTech co-founders Uğur Şahin and Özlem Türeci (AA Photo)
BioNTech co-founders Uğur Şahin and Özlem Türeci have chosen the name “Arife” for their new pharmaceutical venture, which will focus on developing next-generation medicines.
Headquartered in Mainz, Germany, “Arife” — meaning knowledgeable — will conduct research and development, manufacturing and marketing activities for pharmaceutical products, according to information reported by the German business daily Handelsblatt and confirmed by a company spokesperson.
Şahin and Türeci announced in March their plan to leave BioNTech by year-end 2026 and establish a new enterprise. Their new venture is expected to focus primarily on mRNA-based medicines, building on the technology that helped make BioNTech one of the world’s best-known biotechnology companies during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The couple is also expected to remain shareholders in BioNTech after stepping away from its management.
The leadership transition at BioNTech was announced in early August. Guido Oelkers, currently chief executive of Swedish pharmaceutical company Swedish Orphan Biovitrum (Sobi), is set to succeed Şahin as the company’s chief executive. He is expected to take up the position no later than Feb. 1, 2027.
BioNTech gained global prominence during the coronavirus pandemic after partnering with U.S. pharmaceutical giant Pfizer to develop its COVID-19 vaccine. The vaccine became one of the first COVID-19 vaccines to receive market authorization and generated billions of euros in revenue for the company.
With the pandemic-era vaccine now established as a major part of its history, BioNTech has increasingly shifted its focus toward oncology, developing new cancer treatments based on technologies including mRNA.

MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. Air defenses intercepted 592 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions during the past night, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported on Friday.

TASS has compiled key details about the attacks.
Scope
- Between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time (8:00 p.m. GMT) on September 24 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (8:00 a.m. GMT) on September 25, alert air defense capabilities intercepted and destroyed 592 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
- Specifically, drones were downed over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Volgograd, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Rostov, Tver, Tula, Samara, Smolensk, Moscow, Krasnodar and Perm Regions, the republics of Udmurtia, Tatarstan and Crimea and the Black Sea, the ministry specified.
- Last night, air defenses destroyed 88 Ukrainian drones over the Voronezh Region in southwestern Russia, Governor Alexander Gusev wrote on Max channel.
- Approximately 50 UAVs were destroyed last night in southern Russia’s Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar reported on Max channel.
- Air defenses destroyed 36 Ukrainian drones over the Kaluga Region, according to Governor Vladislav Shapsha.
- Air defenses destroyed 33 Ukrainian drones over the Tula Region, Governor Dmitry Milyayev wrote on Max channel.
- Overnight, air defenses destroyed 17 Ukrainian drones over the Oryol Region, Governor Andrey Klychkov reported on Max channel.
Ulyanovsk Region affected
- Eight people, including two children, were injured in a drone attack on the Ulyanovsk Region, according to a post on Max channel from Governor Alexey Russkikh.
- Children aged 17 and 14 were injured, the region’s Health Ministry specified on Max channel. Three of those injured have been taken to hospital.
- In addition, damage to industrial and civilian infrastructure was reported as a result of a UAV attack.
- A plant in Ulyanovsk was damaged in the attack as an industrial facility was targeted, Russkikh said later.
- Damage was reported at the plant; also, residential buildings were damaged, the governor added.
- The Russian Investigative Committee (IC) has opened a criminal case on charges of terrorism following the Ukrainian attack on civilian facilities in the Ulyanovsk Region, IC Spokeswoman Svetlana Petrenko said.
- Specific units and Ukrainian servicemen implicated in the crime are currently being identified.
Other impacted regions
- A man was killed by shrapnel as a result of a drone attack on the Perm Region in eastern Russia, Governor Dmitry Makhonin reported on Max channel.
- A relief operation in the wake of a drone attack on an industrial facility is ongoing.
- Meanwhile, the number of those injured in last night’s drone attack on the Voronezh Region in southwestern Russia has climbed to 13, including a 6-year-old child, according to Governor Alexander Gusev.
- Two people, a woman born in 1963 and a man born in 2001, are in intensive care.
- The windows in residential buildings were damaged, and multiple vehicles were also damaged.
- In southern Russia’s Rostov Region, a petroleum plant in Novoshakhtinsk was damaged in an aerial attack, Governor Yury Slyusar said on Max channel.
- A man was killed as Ukrainian troops attacked a truck near the locality of Pyatniskoye in the Volokonovka Municipality of the bordering Russian region of Belgorod, the regional operational headquarters reported.
- Another man was hospitalized with multiple shrapnel wounds in Volokonovka.
- In Yefremov in central Russia’s Tula Region, windows were damaged in several residential buildings and private homes, Governor Dmitry Milyaev wrote on Max channel.
- According to preliminary information, no one has been injured.

Former heads of Turkish financial crime body to testify in infiltration probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:33:27 UTC
17:33:27 KST

(AA Photo)
Three former heads of Türkiye’s Financial Crimes Investigation Board (MASAK) are set to testify as part of a financial investigation into allegations that the organization was infiltrated by the FETÖ network between 2012 and 2018, allowing access to the financial records of politicians, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said Sept. 25.
Authorities have issued detention warrants for 22 suspects as part of an investigation into alleged “political or military espionage,” including a former MASAK deputy chairman who was serving in the post at the time, Gürlek said in a social media post.
Two software companies operating in the capital Ankara have also been seized as part of the investigation, while the three former MASAK chiefs from the period under scrutiny will be questioned by prosecutors.
An examination found that a security mechanism designed to prevent MASAK employees from searching the records of political figures had been disabled.
Investigators subsequently determined that searches had been conducted involving President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, members of his family and several government ministers.
Authorities also reported technical findings raising concerns over the integrity of some records in the system, including indications that certain data fields may have been deleted after the fact.
The investigation further found evidence suggesting that some shareholders of the companies in question had held senior-level positions within FETÖ’s military and IT structures, according to the statement.
The probe is examining whether confidential financial information obtained through MASAK systems was accessed or used as part of the organization’s alleged activities, Gürlek noted.

Saudi Arabia allies line up support as Houthi attacks mount

2026-09-25
08:32:48 UTC

Saudi Arabia allies line up support as Houthi attacks mount
France is sending its military to protect key Yanbu oil terminal; Pakistan and Turkiye to hold military talks with Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia’s allies are rallying to support the country as the Houthi rebels step up attacks.
France confirmed on Friday that it is sending troops to guard the major oil terminal at Yanbu. Meanwhile, Saudi officials are meeting with peers from Pakistan and Turkiye to discuss options under their mutual defence pact.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Yemen government forces claim control of Mount Qarfan in Taiz
- list 2 of 4Despite flurry of New York diplomacy, US-Iran deal remains elusive
- list 3 of 4How much is UK supporting Saudi Arabia in its war with Iran-backed Houthis?
- list 4 of 4As major powers act unilaterally, experts say UN faces crisis in New York
French President Emmanuel Macron told broadcasters TF1 and France 2 that Paris is to send “soldiers, radars, and defence systems” to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
“Not to involve ourselves in any conflict, but to protect the site,” he said.
Yanbu hosts major oil storage and refining facilities and is connected by the East-West Pipeline, which can carry up to seven million barrels a day.
The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), have repeatedly fired missiles and drones into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world’s largest energy exporter.
On Thursday, the rebel group said it had struck the facilities of state oil firm Aramco in Yanbu, and a “sensitive target” in Riyadh. Saudi forces said they had intercepted six ballistic missiles. Authorities have not confirmed any damage.
The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye met on Thursday to arrange an “urgent meeting” of their military chiefs of staff under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which treats an attack on one member as an attack on all, the Saudi foreign ministry said in a statement.
They also condemned Houthi attacks that they claimed targeted Mecca and other civilian sites.
However, doubt persists over what action Turkiye and Pakistan might take under the pact, which is yet to be officially triggered. Both of the Saudi allies are heavily involved as mediators seeking to bring an end to the conflicts across the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia’s grand mufti called on soldiers to be ready to lay down their lives to fight the Houthis, according to the Saudi state news agency.
The Iran-aligned Houthis have been battling the Saudi-backed government of Yemen for more than a decade. That conflict has been rekindled amid Israel’s wars against the Iran-aligned Hamas group in Gaza and the Hezbollah group in Lebanon, and the United States war on Iran.
At the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Yemen’s Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al-Alimi-Bawzer warned that the Houthis were using shipping security “as a tool for blackmail”.
“It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” he said.
The US has not renewed military involvement, but Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud said the kingdom was “continuing to work with our partners in the US”.
The Houthi targeting of Yanbu adds to the pressure on Saudi Arabia’s oil exports.
Earlier this month, the Houthis seized the Yemeni port of Mocha and several Red Sea islands, giving them significant control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, which usually carries about 12 percent of global oil trade.
Strikes have also disrupted the operation of the East-West Pipeline linking Yanbu to export routes. Riyadh had been using it to export crude bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, which is restricted amid the Iran-US war.
However, the Houthis have now forced the Saudis to switch some exports back to Hormuz.
Brent crude rose more than 3 percent on Thursday, briefly topping $108 a barrel, before easing to $105.77 on Friday morning.
June Goh, a senior oil market analyst at Sparta Commodities in Singapore, said oil would likely stay above $100 a barrel as long as the war on Iran continued.
“With no clear resolution in sight, the gap in oil inventories globally is getting wider,” Goh told Al Jazeera.

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Sydney Roosters roar into NRL grand final with 36-20 win over Dolphins
Sydney Roosters are through to their first NRL grand final in seven years after Mark Nawaqanitawase genius and a miracle Sam Walker injury comeback inspired a 36-20 demolition of the Dolphins.
The Roosters shot out to a 16-0 lead inside 27 minutes in front of a sold-out preliminary final crowd of 52,286 at Lang Park on Friday night.
Their defensive grit on the tryline, a feature of their finals campaign, limited the damage from a mini-Dolphins comeback, but two-try hero Nawaqanitawase has a box of unlimited magic tricks that he unfurled with a wow factor rarely seen on a rugby league field.
The Dolphins had won eight straight games to reach their first preliminary final, a wonderful achievement, but on this occasion it was the Roosters' big-game players who stood tallest.
Walker returned in a record-equalling 27 days from a syndesmosis injury to orchestrate the backline in a masterclass to set up a decider clash with either Penrith or Newcastle.
Roosters coach Trent Robinson will be angling for his fourth premiership win in as many attempts.
An error or a moment of magic was needed to turn an early set-for-set stalemate, and the paranormal Nawaqanitawase provided it in the 18th minute.
The rugby-bound revelation's pivotal moment was pure instinct and skill backed with supreme confidence.
Dolphins centre Herbie Farnworth hesitated with his pass for what would have been a Dolphins try had it hit the mark. The man known as "Marky Mark" swooped, raced 90m and the Roosters never looked back.
"Big players make big plays in big games," Billy Slater said on Channel Nine commentary.
Dolphins bench impact man Kurt Donoghoe dropped the ball when he came on and then missed a tackle for a rampant Victor Radley to score.
Walker's sublime lob for jumping Daniel Tupou had been well rehearsed and was perfectly executed.
The Roosters lost bench rake Connor Watson to a category one HIA, upgraded by the independent doctor, in the first half and the St George Illawarra-bound utility will miss the grand final.
Dolphins winger Jamayne Isaako scored tries either side of halftime, but Nawaqanitawase collected a kick and flicked it back for Robert Toia to crash over.
When Nawaqanitawase bulldozed over for his second and Walker sliced through, it was all over for the hosts.

Xi’s US visit more about spectacle than substance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:26:58 UTC
17:26:58 KST

China's President Xi Jinping (L) and U.S. President Donald Trump speak through interpreters during a State Dinner in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on September 24, 2026. (AFP Photo)
U.S. President Donald Trump treated Chinese leader Xi Jinping to pomp and pageantry on Sept. 24, as the leaders of the world's two superpowers met in Washington DC for talks.
Trump hailed his "great friendship" with Xi and pulled out all the stops to woo the Chinese leader, greeting him on the runway on his arrival, offering him a rare tour of the presidential helicopter, and gifting him a bald eagle statue.
The pomp, however, masked the lack of diplomatic breakthroughs.
"The pageantry was the point," according to Ryan Hass at the Brookings Institution.
"When the troop reviews and opening ceremony are taken out of the schedule, the two leaders had less than two hours of direct meetings with each other," he added.
Those meetings yielded "many new consensuses, "according to Xi, but the only concrete deals announced were a promise to invite 100,000 young Americans to China for exchanges, and lending two pandas to a zoo in Atlanta.
Instead, the meetings were meant to show that the two leaders could "effectively manage U.S.-China relations within tolerable bounds of competition", Hass said.
Xi once again urged the two sides to avoid the "Thucydides Trap" — the theory that a rising power will come into conflict with an established one — but there was little sign of progress on thorny issues like Taiwan or artificial intelligence.
Trump and Xi hinted at big differences in their approach to the regulation of Artificial Intelligence — or "super intelligence", as Trump referred to it.
While Trump has dismissed calls from tech leaders for regulations to "pace the frontier" of the technology, Xi said AI should "always be under human control."
One significant deal was the extension by two months of the countries' fragile trade truce, due to expire in November.
The detente paused a bruising trade war last year by reducing U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods and removing Beijing's export controls on rare earths vital to manufacturing.
Trump is "trying to stabilize relations for now until the U.S. can basically decrease its vulnerabilities to Beijing," according to Jared Mondschein, Director of Research at the United States Studies Centre, University of Sydney.
Trump, a self-styled dealmaker, has repeatedly called on China to purchase more U.S. goods to establish a more "balanced" economic relationship.
However, Xi's visit hasn't yet produced any commitments for Chinese purchases of, for example, Boeing planes or American farm produce.
Trump has repeatedly called on China to help extricate the U.S. from its conflict with Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz for shipping, calls Beijing has rebuffed.
China has also been accused of helping Iran target U.S. military assets in the Middle East.
Xi told the U.S. president to end the war and come to a negotiated settlement with Tehran as soon as possible, according to a Chinese readout of the talks.
"The idea that China is going to be a big power broker, appear publicly and negotiate solutions — I think that's really unlikely," said Rana Mitter, professor of U.S.-Asia relations at the Harvard Kennedy School.
"I don't think that China is going to be the magic card that gets the U.S. out of trouble in the region."
Xi also repeated his warning, given to Trump in May, that he should show "prudence" over Taiwan.
But he also went further than he had in that meeting by urging the U.S. to explicitly oppose Taiwan independence.

Trump asks Supreme Court to allow deportations to countries with troubling human rights records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:25:17 UTC
17:25:17 KST

Esra Tekin
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
US President Donald Trump’s administration asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to permit it to deport migrants to countries other than their countries of origin without first allowing them to present concerns that they could face human rights violations.
The Justice Department submitted an emergency request after the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals issued a ruling late Wednesday that effectively halted the deportations.
The removals had continued after the Supreme Court previously ruled in favor of the administration on the issue more than a year ago.
US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s chief attorney before the Supreme Court, argued that the latest ruling had caused significant practical difficulties for immigration authorities.
He said it had resulted in canceled flights, increased costs, possible diplomatic complications, and difficulties removing migrants considered dangerous criminals.
Sauer wrote that although delaying deportation could benefit some migrants, it would not serve the interests of the country.
The Supreme Court had previously considered the administration’s policy and allowed it to remain in effect despite objections from Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson.
The court later ruled in the administration’s favor again in a case involving a group of migrants who had spent several weeks detained at a US military facility in Djibouti.
The policy was introduced last year as part of the Trump administration’s broader immigration enforcement efforts.
A longstanding challenge for US administrations has been deporting migrants to countries that are unwilling to accept them, sometimes because of strained diplomatic relations with the US.
The Trump administration responded by sending some migrants to third countries, even when they had no personal or family connections there.
The policy attracted significant attention after immigrant advocacy organizations disclosed that a group of migrants who were originally supposed to be sent to South Sudan were instead being held in Djibouti.
The group included migrants from countries such as Cuba, Vietnam, and Laos, and they were reportedly detained in a converted shipping container.
Around 25,000 migrants have been deported under the policy.
The legal dispute centers on the Convention Against Torture, which the US Senate ratified in 1994.
The agreement generally prohibits deporting or extraditing people to countries where they could face torture.
However, the law does not clearly specify how the government must assess the risk of torture or what procedural protections migrants should receive before being removed.
In Thursday’s emergency filing, the administration asked the Supreme Court to immediately issue an “administrative” stay, which would allow deportation flights to resume.
The Justice Department said it had already canceled flights because of the lower court’s ruling and had removed nearly 150 migrants from flights scheduled to take them to at least four different countries.
The Supreme Court instructed the immigrant rights organizations challenging the administration’s policy to respond to the request by Monday afternoon.

The ceremony brought together foreign delegations, government officials, industry representatives and participants from around the world.
Calling for a more connected global halal economy, Zahid said policymakers and businesses should work together to translate the sector’s growth into concrete economic opportunities.
“Let us turn that shared ambition into trade, investment and jobs,” he said.
“Our work must continue beyond this gathering. Success will only be measured by the barriers we remove, the partnerships that endure, and the businesses that reach new markets,” he added.
“Together, we have built trust in halal, halalan tayyiban. Now let us build greater prosperity through halal,” Zahid said.
 
From certification to global markets
Zahid stressed that halal certification alone is not enough for companies seeking to expand internationally.
“Certification is only the beginning of that journey,” he said.
Companies also need consistent production, suitable packaging, working capital, reliable logistics and an understanding of their target markets, he added.

“Halal is not simply a matter of standards, certification or trade,” he said.
Zulkifli said Shariah principles, integrity, ethics and responsibility provide the foundation of trust upon which the halal economy can grow while contributing to economic development and the well-being of communities around the world.
He said Malaysia’s approach to developing the halal economy extends beyond certification to trade, investment, innovation, research, talent development and international market access.
Zulkifli also highlighted the Malaysian Halal Certification System, spearheaded by JAKIM, including its recognition of foreign halal certification bodies in different regions.
He said the system has helped establish a “chain of trust” that strengthens international confidence in halal products and services.
Malaysia, he added, remains committed to strengthening its role in the global halal sector through trusted standards, innovation, technology and strategic international cooperation.
GHaS 2026 is being held under the theme “Shariah and Integrity: Empowering the Global Halal Ecosystem.”
MIHAS 2026, meanwhile, is being held at MITEC from Sept. 23-26 under the theme “Shaping Trust, Driving Resilience,” bringing together companies and industry representatives across the global halal economy.

Polar explorer Otto Schmidt's 135th anniversary to be celebrated in St. Petersburg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
08:14:46 UTC
17:14:46 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, September 25. /TASS/. St. Petersburg will celebrate the 135th anniversary of legendary polar explorer Otto Schmidt. The event, dubbed Garden of Memory of the Arctic Heroes, will take place at the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute on September 25. The event's participants will plant shrubs on the institute's territory in honor of the researcher, press service of the Museum of the Arctic and Antarctic said.
"In 2026, the museum will organize planting shrubs in the area around the institute in memory of Otto Schmidt (1891 - 1956), an outstanding scientist, polar explorer, leader of many expeditions, head of the Main Directorate of the Northern Sea Route, and one of the first directors of the All-Union Arctic Institute," the press service said in a release.
Since 2022, the museum has been the initiator of a project under the Green Russia national environmental movement. The event on Friday will open the chain of events devoted to the museum's jubilee - it will turn 90 in 2027.
About Otto Schmidt
Otto Schmidt is a Soviet statesman, geophysicist, Arctic researcher and Hero of the Soviet Union. He led Arctic expeditions on icebreaking steamships the Sedov, the Sibiryakov, and the Chelyuskin in 1929-1934.
About the museum
The idea to have a museum dedicated to studies in the polar latitudes emerged in the late 1920s in the wake of the Arctic's active development. In 1930, the USSR leadership issued an order to establish the All-Union Arctic Institute, which was supposed to have a specialized museum. The museum was due to be in the building of the former St. Nicholas Church of the Same Faith on Marat Street. Leading polar researchers of that time participated actively in the work on the museum's exposition - Otto Schmidt, Rudolf Samoilovich, Yuly Shokalsky, Vladimir Wiese, and others.
The museum opened to the public on January 8, 1937, and in the same year it was awarded an Honorary Diploma from the Exposition Universelle in Paris. The museum has responded promptly to events in polar research. For example, back in 1938, they opened an exhibition about the North Pole-1 first drifting station, which presented a tent used by Papanin's team, and the expedition participants' personal belongings. In the 1950s, due to the active Soviet Antarctic expeditions, the collection received new objects. In 1958, the museum received its current name - the Museum of the Arctic and Antarctic. In 1998, it gained the status of a Russian State Museum.
Nowadays, the Russian State Museum of the Arctic and Antarctic is the world's largest polar museum with a collection of more than 100,000 objects.

U.S. Air Force moves to upgrade aging E-3 AWACS planes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
08:06:45 UTC
17:06:45 KST

- The U.S. Air Force is seeking contractors to replace the DAR-400 encryption unit on its 15 operational E-3G AWACS aircraft.
- General Dynamics Mission Systems told the U.S. Air Force the DAR-400 cannot be upgraded to meet changing NSA requirements.
The U.S. Air Force is looking for a contractor to replace an aging encryption unit on its E-3G AWACS radar planes after the manufacturer warned it can no longer keep up with changing National Security Agency security requirements, according to a sources-sought notice posted Sept. 25 on the federal contracting website.
The part, known as the DAR-400, is a data-at-rest unit that stores encrypted mission data on board the aircraft. The Air Force called it mission-critical and said it is in critical need of an obsolescence fix to avoid disrupting operations. Its maker, General Dynamics Mission Systems, told the service the DAR-400 cannot support or be upgraded to meet new NSA requirements.
Because the unit holds encrypted data for several of the plane’s mission and computing systems, the notice said, a failure would directly affect both operations and data security.
The Air Force already has a replacement. It is providing a government-owned solution based on the KG-204, which it said complies with current Department of War and NSA mandates. The contractor would install and integrate that equipment across the fleet. The notice did not give a cost estimate, schedule or number of units.
The notice is market research, not a solicitation. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and special operations directorate is asking companies of all sizes, including small businesses, to describe their capabilities by Oct. 12. The responses will help decide whether the work is set aside for small businesses.
The Air Force listed its operational E-3G fleet at 15 aircraft. The Boeing 707-based planes carry a large rotating radar dome on top of the fuselage and serve as airborne command posts, tracking aircraft and directing U.S. and allied forces. The fleet is based at Tinker Air Force Base, Oklahoma.
One E-3G was destroyed in a drone and missile attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia on March 27, 2026, during the war with Iran.
Air Force leaders have said for years that the E-3 is increasingly difficult to keep flying and that its Cold War-era radar is outdated. The radar dome takes 10 seconds to complete one rotation and refresh its picture of the sky.
Its planned replacement, Boeing’s E-7 Wedgetail, remains in dispute between the Pentagon and Congress. The Department of War tried to cancel the E-7 in its fiscal 2026 budget, but lawmakers blocked the move. The fiscal 2026 defense policy law also barred the Air Force from retiring any of its E-3s if the fleet would fall below 16. In March 2026, the Air Force signed about $2.4 billion in contracts to buy developmental E-7s.
The department then requested no money for the E-7 in its fiscal 2027 budget. Congressional committees have since written about $1.55 billion for the program into their bills, but the final amount has not been settled.
With the E-7’s future unresolved, the Air Force plans to keep the E-3G flying, and the DAR-400 replacement is one of the upgrades needed to do that.

Italy Promotes a UN Event on Cultural Heritage and People with Disabilities
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:25:29 CEST
16:25:29 KST

The Permanent Mission of Italy to the United Nations in Geneva organized the side event “Cultural Heritage and Collective Memory: Recognizing the Voices and Contributions of People with Disabilities.” The event took place during the Human Rights Council session and was promoted by Italy together with the other members of the Group of Friends on the Cultural Rights of Persons with Disabilities: Iraq, Cyprus, Mexico, Montenegro, Algeria, and Lebanon.
                                    
                                       
				    In his remarks—according to a press release from the Mission—Ambassador Luigi Maria Vignali noted that accessibility cannot be reduced to the elimination of physical barriers alone: sensory, digital, and cognitive barriers must also be addressed so that people with disabilities can fully participate in cultural life.
                                    
                                       
				   People with disabilities are not merely passive recipients or spectators of our cultural heritage: they are creators, innovators, and protagonists of our shared memory. Italy is committed to making its cultural heritage increasingly accessible to people with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities as well, through Easy-to-Read materials and sensory tours.
                                    
                                       
				   At the same time, the Gruppo di Amici is working, together with its academic partners, to develop international guidelines on the cultural rights of people with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities.
                                    
                                       
				   From culture to sports—drawing on Italy’s Paralympic experience as well—the principle remains the same: to value abilities, experiences, and contributions while overcoming stereotypes and barriers. “Nothing about us, without us.” A truly universal memory must recognize every mind, every voice, and every story, the press release concludes.

News from occupied Ukraine: Oleshky crisis continues, Europe's human rights chief calls for 'immediate local ceasefire'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26

News from occupied Ukraine: Oleshky crisis continues, Europe's human rights chief calls for 'immediate local ceasefire'
Vehicles carrying food and supplies into Oleshky marked with the word "people" attacked by drones, in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, Ukraine, in a screenshot from a video published on Sept. 2, 2026. (Kherson Oleshky / Telegram)
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.
Key news as of Sept. 26:
- Council of Europe rights commissioner warns of 'alarming' situation in Oleshky
- Russia used parliamentary elections to legitimize occupation of Ukrainian territories
- Ukraine strikes Russian radar stations, drone site in occupied territories
- Ukraine brought back 23 children from Russian-occupied territories over last week
- US allocates $27 million for the return of Ukrainian children kidnapped by Russia
Amid the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Russian-occupied front-line town of Oleshky, Michael O'Flaherty, commissioner for human rights at the Council of Europe, said on Sept. 25 that the situation in the city is "alarming."
The humanitarian situation in Oleshky has sharply deteriorated in recent months, as residents face prolonged shortages of food, drinking water, and basic utilities.
"I am alarmed by the rapidly deteriorating humanitarian crisis in Oleshky... Under international humanitarian law, Russia, as the occupying power, has the duty to provide food and medical supplies and to facilitate humanitarian relief. I call for an immediate local ceasefire, unhindered humanitarian access, and the safe evacuation of civilians," O'Flaherty said.
"The hardship and suffering of people caught along the frontlines of the war and in occupied territories demand international attention and action."
As winter approaches, residents are forced to remain in a city where basic necessities are disappearing or attempt to leave along mined roads threatened by Russian drones.
The last successful food delivery to the city was on May 26. Further attempts to supply the city on June 2 and Sept. 1 have been disrupted by Russian drone attacks that killed two and injured others.
Oleshky has also had no reliable electricity or running water, and the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka Dam in 2023 further degraded the city's water and utility infrastructure.
On Sept. 25, an Oleshky resident told the Kyiv Independent that the situation has not improved.
"It's been raining for almost a day, and the house I'm staying in has no roof. So it's leaking, and the walls are damp. It's getting colder. We're running low on firewood. There have been casualties and fatalities among civilians over the past week," they said.
While Russian troops occupy Oleshky and the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast, the Ukrainian military controls the western bank. Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Russian forces have placed guns, mortars, and mines in and around residential neighborhoods due to the city's proximity to Ukrainian-controlled territory, according to Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration.
Tolokonnikov said Russia shields its positions from Ukrainian strikes through the continued presence of civilians.
"Oleshky and its people are necessary for Russian troops so that Ukrainian troops cannot actively attack them in these settlements," he said.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help people from Oleshky leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips. Now, they said, the high risk made evacuation impossible.
In recent weeks, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces.
Ukraine had prepared a humanitarian evacuation mission for Oleshky and approved a list of civilians who needed to leave, according to Lubinets. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) had also expressed readiness to participate, while Ukrainian forces had been preparing to observe a temporary ceasefire during the mission, he said.
But Russia has not confirmed its readiness to proceed, according to Lubinets. Ukraine continues to press Russia to allow the evacuation and remains in contact with the ICRC and other international organizations, he added.

Russia used parliamentary elections to legitimize occupation of Ukrainian territories
As Russia held its parliamentary elections from Sept. 18 to 20, it also organized, for the first time, the vote in Ukrainian territories that Russia illegally claims as its own.
Ukraine and the European Union have rejected the vote as illegal.
Russia uses sham elections in Ukrainian territories under military occupation to project the image that residents accept Russian rule and are integrated into Russia's political system, according to Ukrainian officials and human rights organizations.
"Above all, for (the Russians), it was a matter of political loyalty. They want to show that the population of the occupied territories supports Russia's political course and is part of the Russian reality. They want to demonstrate this to the whole world," Dementiy Bilyi, a Ukrainian election expert, political scientist, and historian, told the Kyiv Independent.
The head of Russian occupation authorities in Donetsk Oblast, Denis Pushilin, called participation in the State Duma election the "last political step" in integrating the region into Russia.
Read more here.
read also
Ukraine strikes Russian radar stations, drone site in occupied territories
Ukraine's military struck several Russian military targets in occupied parts of Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts on Sept. 23 and overnight on Sept. 24, including radar stations, a site used to store and launch attack drones, and a fuel depot, Ukraine's General Staff said.
In the occupied part of Donetsk Oblast, a Russian site for storing, preparing, and launching attack drones was hit near the city of Donetsk.
In the occupied part of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, 35N6 Kasta and P-18 radar stations were struck near Yakymivka and Chekhograd, while a Russian fuel and lubricants depot was also hit near Velyka Bilozerka, according to the General Staff.
The strikes are part of a series of attacks on Russian military infrastructure in occupied Ukrainian territories.
On Sept. 22 and overnight on Sept. 23, Ukrainian forces struck Russian drone command posts in Donetsk Oblast, as well as a drone depot belonging to the Rubicon unit near Volnovakha.
They also hit a fuel and lubricants depot in occupied Luhansk Oblast and logistics depots in Donetsk Oblast.
The Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies is a sprawling Russian drone unit and the core of Russia's recently formed Unmanned Systems branch of the military.
The unit specializes in cutting off logistics, hunting Ukrainian drone teams on the ground, and intercepting high-value reconnaissance and strike drones, and is made up of detachments, each numbering several hundred personnel.
read also
Ukraine brought back 23 children from Russian-occupied territories over last week
Ukraine has brought back 23 children and teenagers from Russian-occupied territories to areas under its control in the past week, Save Ukraine, a Ukrainian humanitarian NGO, said in a statement on Sept. 21.
Among the children rescued was 17-year-old Illia, who was forced to attend a school under the occupation regime through blackmail and threats against his family, Save Ukraine said. He lived in constant tension due to regular armed searches, during which Russian soldiers would break into his home and inspect all devices.
Another child, 14-year-old Oleh, was threatened with being taken to an orphanage if he did not attend a Russian school. At school, the boy was pressured by daily propaganda. Russian soldiers regularly came to classes, openly urging teenagers to become combat drone operators.
Save Ukraine did not specify which regions the rescued children came from.
The children were brought back with the help of partners as part of the Ukrainian President's initiative, Bring Kids Back UA.
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, said on Sept. 25 that around 1.6 million Ukrainian children may still be living in the occupied territories.
"They are issued with Russian documents, placed with Russian families, subjected to propaganda and stripped of their Ukrainian identity. They are forcibly displaced," Lubinets said.
He added that Russia is forcibly militarizing childhood, as in schools Ukrainian children are forced to undergo military training, while thousands of young Ukrainians are being conscripted into the Russian army.
"The Russian leadership has a single aim: to continue the war against Ukraine using others' hands. To train a new generation of soldiers," Lubinets said.
read also
US allocates $27 million for the return of Ukrainian children kidnapped by Russia
The U.S. State Department has earmarked $27 million to help return and reintegrate Ukrainian children forcibly deported to Russia, State Department officials announced on Sept. 24.
Russia has abducted tens of thousands of Ukrainian children since the start of the full-scale invasion. As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation, though Ukrainian officials estimate the real total could number in the hundreds of thousands.
The U.S. State Department is in the process of granting $12 million to a program to identify, return, and reintegrate Ukrainian children held in Russia and in Russian-occupied territories, officials said on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. Another $15 million has been authorized for the same purpose and will be granted to an implementing organization later this year.
The announcement came during a session on Ukraine's forcibly deported children, according to a statement from Bring Kids Back, an initiative of the Ukrainian president.
"We are sincerely grateful to the United States for its unwavering and strong support of efforts aimed at the return, rehabilitation, and full reintegration of Ukrainian children and young people," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
The funding will "ensure full accountability of Russia for its actions," he said.
Maksym Maksymov, Head of Bring Kids Back UA, said that the organization welcomes the progress in implementing the US State Department program.
"Coordination among all actors is critical to its success. This result builds on our long-standing work with the State Department and the U.S. Congress. We thank Congress for its strong bipartisan engagement, which helped make this program possible," Maksymov said.
As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia.
In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Russia's Commissioner for Children's Rights Maria Lvova-Belova for their role in state-sanctioned child abductions.

Enemy drone crash sparks office building fire and damages warehouse in Kyiv, injuring one person
According to Ukrinform, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported this on Telegram.
“A fire broke out in an office building in the Solomyanskyi District after a UAV crashed,” the statement reads.
It was also reported that a warehouse in Kyiv’s Obolon district was damaged as a result of a Russian attack on September 26.
As Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko later noted, one person was injured in Kyiv’s Obolon district as a result of a Russian drone crash.
“In the Obolon district, one person was injured when a UAV crashed into a non-residential building. Medical personnel provided assistance on the scene,” Klitschko said.
As reported by Ukrinform, four people were injured in a residential building in the Solomyanskyi district of Kyiv, where a fire broke out after a Russian drone crashed.
